title: What incoming inspection protects: defect cost by stage

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

theory.p: Incoming inspection protects the SMT and THT line by confirming that a received lot matches the purchase order, is in the condition required for release, and carries evidence that the supplier controlled the characteristics that affect assembly yield. The inspection is not only a visual check; it is a gate that prevents latent material defects from entering placement, reflow, wave soldering, cleaning, ICT, functional test, and field service. Defects found at incoming usually cost inspection time, quarantine, and supplier communication. Defects found later can add rework, scrap, line stoppage, customer complaint, and warranty exposure. The cost of the same material defect typically rises as the defect moves downstream, so incoming inspection is a control point for cost avoidance. A good incoming plan also protects process stability. If paste, components, or bare PCBs are released without evidence, the line may run with marginal material, and operators may compensate with printer, placement, or reflow changes. Those changes can hide the material problem, shift the defect to other stages, and make root cause analysis harder. The incoming record should therefore capture what was checked, what was found, and what was released, so later yield problems can be traced to material condition.

theory.p: A component lot should arrive with a packing list, certificate of conformance, material declaration, restricted substances declaration, lot or date code, traceability label, and any test report required by the purchase order. The packing list proves quantity and shipment identity. The certificate of conformance proves the supplier declared conformity to the specified part, revision, and acceptance criteria. The material declaration proves the base material and plating or termination finish. The restricted substances declaration proves the supplier has screened the lot against applicable customer and regulatory requirements. The lot or date code proves traceability to the supplier batch. The traceability label proves the internal receiving record can be linked to the supplier batch. The test report proves electrical, mechanical, or reliability characteristics were measured or sampled before shipment. For components with moisture sensitivity, the packaging should include a moisture barrier bag, desiccant, and humidity indicator card, and the label should show the floor life or storage condition required by the applicable JEDEC moisture sensitivity standard. The receiving inspector should compare the label, the packing list, and the purchase order before opening the package. If the documents disagree, the lot should be quarantined until the supplier clarifies the discrepancy.

Solder paste should arrive with a certificate of analysis, safety data sheet, lot code, expiration date, storage temperature record in °C, alloy composition, metal content, flux chemistry, halogen content, and rheology or printability data when required by the purchase order. The certificate of analysis proves the paste was manufactured to the specified formulation. The safety data sheet proves hazard communication and handling requirements. The lot code proves traceability. The expiration date proves the paste is within the supplier stated shelf life. The storage temperature record proves the lot was kept within the supplier stated storage range. The alloy composition and metal content prove the solder alloy and powder size distribution. The flux chemistry and halogen content prove compatibility with cleaning, reliability, and customer restricted substance requirements. The rheology or printability data proves the paste is suitable for the intended stencil and printer settings, but verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Paste is a process material, so the incoming record should also note the carton condition, temperature excursion indicators, and whether the lot was shipped under the supplier stated temperature control. If the paste is outside the stated storage or shelf life condition, quarantine it and request supplier disposition before use. Do not rely on operator experience to decide whether aged paste is acceptable.

A bare PCB lot should arrive with a certificate of conformance, material declaration, copper thickness report in µm, surface finish report, impedance report when required, cleanliness or solderability report when required, lot code, and packaging evidence. The certificate of conformance proves the board matches the fabrication drawing, revision, and acceptance class required by the purchase order. The material declaration proves the laminate system and flame rating. The copper thickness report proves the conductor thickness used for current and impedance calculations. The surface finish report proves the finish type and thickness range. The impedance report proves controlled impedance features were measured. The cleanliness or solderability report proves the board is suitable for assembly. The lot code proves traceability. Packaging evidence proves the boards were protected from moisture, mechanical damage, and electrostatic discharge. For boards with moisture sensitivity or fine pitch, the receiving inspector should check the barrier bag, desiccant, humidity indicator, and edge condition before opening. If the board is warped, scratched, oxidized, delaminated, or has exposed copper beyond the drawing limit, quarantine it and record the location and extent of the finding. The supplier should receive enough detail to inspect the same area and determine whether the cause is fabrication, packaging, or transport.

Accept a lot when documents are complete, packaging is intact, environmental indicators are within the supplier stated limits, and sampled material conforms to the purchase order and the applicable IPC acceptance standard. Quarantine a lot when evidence is incomplete or uncertain, such as a missing certificate, damaged packaging, suspect humidity indicator, unclear lot code, or a measurement near the specification limit in mm or °C. Quarantine also applies when the lot can be dispositioned by supplier review, retest, or approved rework. Reject a lot when the defect cannot be dispositioned safely, such as wrong part, counterfeit suspicion, prohibited substance, expired paste, wet or delaminated PCB, severe mechanical damage, or a safety hazard. Use your sampling plan and your process qualification to decide the sample size and acceptance criteria. The decision should be based on evidence, not on schedule pressure. If a lot is accepted with a deviation, the deviation should be limited, time bound, and approved by the responsible engineering and quality owners. The deviation record should state the affected quantity, the risk to downstream processes, the additional checks required, and the date when the deviation expires. If the deviation is not closed, the lot should be quarantined or rejected.

theory.h: Writing a record the supplier can act on
theory.p: A useful incoming finding record identifies the part, supplier lot, internal lot, quantity received, quantity inspected, quantity affected, requirement, observed result, measurement method, location, date, inspector, disposition, and requested supplier action. The requirement should quote the purchase order, drawing, or applicable standard without copying standard text. The observed result should state what was seen or measured, not an opinion. Attach photographs, label images, document copies, and test data when available. State the containment already taken, such as quarantine, hold, or return. Request a corrective action that addresses the cause, not only the symptom, and ask for evidence of effectiveness. The record should be clear enough that the supplier can identify the batch, reproduce the finding, and prevent recurrence. For a supplier action to be useful, include the internal part identifier, customer part identifier, revision, package type, quantity affected, and the process stage where the defect would be detected if it escaped. If the finding is a document gap, state the missing document and the requirement that makes it mandatory. If the finding is a physical defect, state the measurement or visual criterion, the sample size, the quantity of affected units, and the disposition. The record should avoid blame and focus on facts, because the supplier needs facts to correct the process.

Incoming inspection protects against defects that are difficult to see after assembly, such as oxidized pads, wet PCB, expired paste, wrong alloy, wrong plating, damaged terminations, counterfeit parts, and moisture sensitive devices that were not packaged correctly. If these defects pass incoming, they can cause poor wetting, voids, insufficient solder, tombstoning, opens, shorts, thermal stress, ICT failures, functional failures, and field escapes. The cost drivers include inspection labor, quarantine space, rework labor, scrap, line stoppage, expedited replacement, customer complaint handling, and warranty. When you build the incoming inspection plan, use your own stage cost data and verify practice based values against your paste/equipment datasheet. The plan should focus on the characteristics that have the highest downstream cost and the lowest chance of being detected later. For example, a wrong surface finish on a bare PCB may pass visual inspection but cause poor solderability during reflow. A paste lot with the wrong metal content may print normally but create voids or insufficient solder. A moisture sensitive device with a compromised barrier bag may pass placement but crack during reflow. The incoming record should link each finding to the stage where it would have been detected, so the cost of prevention can be compared with the cost of escape.

calc.task: Use your plant cost table. Let N be lot quantity, f be incoming escape fraction, C_in be cost per defect found at incoming, C_reflow be cost per defect found after reflow, and C_field be cost per defect found in the field. Calculate expected cost for the same defect if it is caught at incoming, if it escapes to reflow, and if it escapes to the field. State the stage cost ratio that justifies incoming inspection.
calc.solution: Start by obtaining N, f, C_in, C_reflow, and C_field from your accounting, scrap, rework, warranty, and line stoppage records. Compute incoming cost as N times f times C_in. Compute reflow cost as N times f times C_reflow. Compute field cost as N times f times C_field. Compare the results by dividing reflow cost by incoming cost and field cost by incoming cost. Use the ratios to decide whether incoming inspection resources are justified for the part family. If the ratio is high, document the avoided cost in the incoming inspection plan and review the plan when part family, supplier, or process changes.

defect.symptom: Incoming moisture barrier bag is punctured, humidity indicator card shows exceedance, and bare PCB pads show discoloration.
defect.cause: Packaging damage or storage excursion allowed moisture ingress, and the lot was not quarantined before release.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, record lot code, quantity, packaging condition, indicator status, and pad appearance; notify supplier; request corrective action for packaging and storage; do not release until bake or replacement is approved by the applicable moisture sensitivity standard and your process qualification.

title: The documentation package: CoC/CoA, packing list, MSL label, declarations

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.

blocks.alt: Receiving desk with a stack of controlled documents, each marked present, and one flagged as missing
blocks.caption: The documentation package: certificate of conformance, certificate of analysis, packing list, MSL label and declarations checked at receiving

theory.p: At receiving, the lot should be treated as a document-controlled object, not only a physical object. For components, solder paste, and bare PCBs, the minimum package normally includes a packing list, a certificate of conformance or certificate of analysis, and any declarations required by the purchase order. Moisture-sensitive components should also arrive in a sealed dry pack with an MSL label and humidity indicator card. The exact set depends on the supplier agreement, the customer specification, and the risk of the lot, but the purpose is the same: the packing list proves identity and quantity, the CoC or CoA proves conformity or measured properties, the MSL label proves moisture handling history, and declarations prove regulatory or contractual claims. Receiving should not release material based only on a familiar carton or a supplier name. The document package is the first evidence that the lot is the lot the process was planned to use, and it gives the traceability needed if a later defect points back to incoming material. It also gives the incoming inspector a basis for deciding whether to open the pack, sample the lot, or quarantine it.

The packing list proves what the supplier says was shipped and how it was identified. It should link the purchase order, part number, revision, quantity, lot or batch code, date code, package type, and any special handling notes. For a lot of components, it lets receiving match the physical cartons to the expected quantity and traceability code, and it supports later traceability to the assembly. For paste, it should identify the paste type, container size, lot code, and any storage or handling notes. For bare PCBs, it should identify the board part number, revision, panel or array count, lot code, and any special packaging requirements. If the packing list disagrees with the purchase order, the carton labels, or the certificate, the lot should be quarantined until the discrepancy is resolved. A packing list does not prove that the lot passed tests; it proves the supplier's shipping record and gives the starting point for traceability. Receiving should record the packing list number and any mismatch in the incoming inspection record.

theory.h: CoC and CoA: what they prove
theory.p: A certificate of conformance states that the delivered lot conforms to the purchase order and referenced acceptance criteria. A certificate of analysis provides measured or tested values for selected characteristics. For components, a CoC may prove that the lot was inspected and packaged to the specified grade, while a CoA may prove lot-specific test results such as electrical parameters, plating thickness, or package integrity. For solder paste, a CoA commonly reports metal content, viscosity, or other paste properties against the specification, often referencing IPC J-STD-004, and may include shelf-life information. For bare PCBs, a CoC or CoA may prove laminate material, copper weight, plating type, plating thickness, and acceptance against IPC-A-600 or IPC-6012, depending on the contract. The certificate should be traceable to the received lot by lot code, date code, or serial range. If the certificate covers a different lot, it does not prove the received lot, even if the part number matches. The inspector should check that the certificate date, supplier name, and referenced specification match the purchase order.

For moisture-sensitive surface-mount components, the sealed dry pack should carry an MSL label and a humidity indicator card. The MSL label identifies the moisture sensitivity level and the floor life assigned under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. The humidity indicator card gives a visual indication of whether the dry pack environment has exceeded the supplier's specified humidity threshold. The label and card do not prove that the components are acceptable for placement by themselves; they prove the handling history and the conditions under which the lot was protected. If the pack is opened, the floor-life clock starts, and the remaining time must be tracked against the label value and your process schedule. If the pack is damaged, the seal is broken, or the indicator card shows an exceedance, the lot should be quarantined and evaluated before use. The dry pack documents are part of the incoming evidence, not a substitute for incoming inspection. The inspector should record the MSL value, floor-life value, indicator card status, and seal condition.

Solder paste requires documentation that supports both identity and process suitability. The packing list proves the paste type, container size, and lot code. The CoA or CoC proves that the paste was manufactured and tested against the agreed specification, often IPC J-STD-004, and may include shelf-life information. The container label should agree with the certificate and the packing list. Storage and handling conditions are process-specific; a common storage range is 2 °C to 10 °C, but verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and your facility controls. If the paste is returned to storage, the label should record the number of times it has been opened and the time outside storage, because those values affect printability and may require mixing or discard. For incoming lots, check that the paste type matches the stencil, printer, and reflow profile planned for the job. A certificate that proves the paste was acceptable at the supplier does not prove it is still suitable after transport, storage, or handling. The inspector should record the lot code, expiry date, storage condition, and any handling notes.

Bare PCBs should arrive with documents that prove the board was built to the purchased design and acceptance level. The packing list proves the board part number, revision, quantity, and lot code. The CoC or CoA proves the laminate material, copper weight, plating finish, and dimensional or electrical test results required by the purchase order. Acceptance may be referenced to IPC-A-600 for visual and dimensional criteria, while IPC-6012 may be used for qualification and performance requirements. For plated through holes, the certificate should identify the plating type and thickness range, and the board should carry a lot or panel traceability mark that matches the documents. For controlled-impedance boards, the certificate may include test coupon results or a statement that coupons were tested. For boards with special finishes, the certificate should state the finish type and any storage or handling limits. If the board revision, material class, or finish does not match the purchase order, the lot should be quarantined even if the boards look acceptable. The inspector should record the board revision, lot code, and certificate reference.

Declarations are separate from quality certificates and prove regulatory or contractual constraints. A restricted-substance declaration supports compliance with customer or market requirements, such as RoHS or REACH, when those requirements are part of the purchase order. A counterfeit-avoidance declaration supports the supplier's control of authorized distribution channels and may be important for high-reliability or safety-related products. A conflict-minerals declaration supports reporting obligations where applicable. These documents do not prove that the lot will process correctly on your line; they prove that the supplier has made a stated claim about the lot's origin, composition, or compliance. The declaration should be traceable to the lot or to a defined lot range, and it should be retained with the incoming inspection record. If a declaration is missing, the lot may still be physically acceptable, but the compliance claim cannot be released without evidence. The inspector should record the declaration type, revision, and traceability range.

theory.h: Disposition based on the document package
theory.p: Incoming disposition should be based on whether the documents prove the lot is what the process expects. A complete package shows matching part numbers, revisions, lot codes, quantities, and required certificates. A missing CoC, mismatched lot code, damaged dry pack, or expired shelf life is a document or handling defect, not necessarily a physical defect, but it prevents release until the evidence is corrected. Record the document numbers, certificate dates, MSL label values, humidity indicator status, and any deviations in the incoming inspection record. If the lot is quarantined, the record should state which document or condition failed and what action is required before release. If the lot is released, the record should show that the document package was complete and that any special handling limits were transferred to the process. This record supports traceability when a defect is found later in assembly, test, or field return. It also supports supplier corrective action when the same document failure repeats.

The document package should not stop at receiving. The values that affect the process, such as paste type, shelf-life status, MSL floor-life start time, and board revision, should be transferred to the work order or MES record. For components, the lot code should be linked to the feeder or magazine so that a later defect can be traced to the incoming lot. For paste, the opened time, storage time, and number of opens should be visible to the printer operator. For bare PCBs, the revision and lot code should be linked to the panel or array used in assembly. This handoff prevents a situation where a lot is released by quality but used with the wrong process parameters. It also makes the incoming documents useful during containment, because the process can identify which lots were exposed to a suspect condition. The handoff should be recorded in the same traceability system used for the incoming inspection.

calc.task: A dry pack label states a floor life of 168 h per IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. The pack is opened at the start of the shift. Placement is scheduled 170 h after opening. Determine whether the floor life is exceeded.
calc.solution: First, identify the floor-life value from the label: 168 h. Next, identify the elapsed time from opening to placement: 170 h. Then compare elapsed time with floor life: 170 h is greater than 168 h. Then calculate the exceedance: 170 h minus 168 h equals 2 h. Finally, disposition: do not place the components without a qualified re-bake or other approved action under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033; quarantine and record the exceedance.

defect.symptom: Incoming dry pack has an MSL label, but the humidity indicator card shows the supplier exceedance color and the pack seal is creased.
defect.cause: The dry pack was damaged or opened before receipt, so the humidity indicator card reflects exposure outside the controlled dry-pack environment.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, record the label and card status, inspect for oxidation or coplanarity issues, and follow IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 bake and re-bag requirements if the lot is to be used; notify the supplier with photos and lot traceability.

title: Sampling a lot: lot definition, sample size, inspection level, AQL concept

goals.text: Build a sampling plan for a stated lot and inspection level, and explain what the plan does and does not protect against.

theory.p: A lot is the smallest quantity of incoming material that can be treated as a population for inspection: same part number, revision, supplier, manufacturing lot or date code, packaging, and process route. If incoming material mixes revisions, date codes, or supplier plants, split it into separate lots unless your quality plan states that the differences do not affect the characteristics being inspected. For SMT/THT incoming, a lot may be a reel, a tray stack, a bag of through-hole components, or a shipment of bare PCBs, depending on how the supplier controls traceability.

theory.h: Choose inspection level based on risk and cost
theory.p: Inspection level controls how many units are inspected relative to lot size. ISO 2859-1 provides general inspection levels and special inspection levels for destructive or expensive tests. The standard's normal general inspection level is a common starting point for incoming inspection when no special reason exists. A lower general level may be used when lots are stable and defects are expensive to find; a higher general level may be used when the supplier is new, the part is critical, or recent data show variability. Special levels require a documented rationale and should be verified against your incoming inspection procedure.

theory.h: Use AQL as a supplier quality target, not a defect limit
theory.p: The acceptable quality level, AQL, is the quality level that a sampling plan is designed to accept with high probability when the supplier's process is running at that average quality. It is not a maximum allowable defect rate for every lot, and it does not mean that accepted lots are defect-free. ISO 2859-1 lists preferred AQL values; common incoming choices are 0.65%, 1.0%, and 2.5% defective, selected by defect class and risk. Critical defects often use a much tighter plan or full inspection, while minor cosmetic defects may use a looser plan.

A single AQL can hide risk if critical, major, and minor defects are counted together. For incoming SMT/THT material, define what counts as a defective unit for each class: for example, wrong part number or damaged pads may be critical, while a small cosmetic mark on a non-critical area may be minor. If you inspect multiple characteristics, decide whether a sample can be used for all classes or whether separate samples and AQLs are needed. Record the defect class in the inspection record so the plan can be reviewed with supplier data.

theory.h: Build the plan from lot size, level, and AQL
theory.p: The sampling plan is built by converting lot size and inspection level into a sample size code letter, then selecting the accept and reject numbers for the chosen AQL. In ISO 2859-1, a lot of 1201 to 3200 units at general inspection level II gives code letter K, which corresponds to a sample size of 125 units. For an AQL of 1.0% defective under normal single sampling, the accept number is 3 and the reject number is 4. The plan says inspect 125 units, accept the lot if 3 or fewer defective units are found, and reject if 4 or more are found. The code letter depends on the inspection level, so the same lot band gives code letter H (n = 50, Ac = 1, Re = 2 at AQL 1.0%) at level I and code letter L (n = 200, Ac = 5, Re = 6 at AQL 1.0%) at level III; always read the level and the lot band together before looking up the sample size. The 5000-unit lot used in the worked example below falls inside this 1201 to 3200 band, which is why it resolves to code letter K.

theory.h: Understand what the plan protects against
theory.p: A correctly chosen plan protects against accepting lots when the supplier's average quality is worse than the AQL by making rejection increasingly likely as quality degrades. It also provides a repeatable basis for normal, tightened, and reduced inspection switching when the standard's switching rules are applied. It does not guarantee that a particular accepted lot contains zero defects, does not detect defects outside the inspected characteristics, and does not replace supplier process control, incoming test coverage, or line containment when a defect escapes.

When a lot is rejected, the disposition should be defined before inspection: return, sort, use-as-is with concession, or rework, with clear traceability to the sample results. If a lot is accepted but defects appear on the line, investigate whether the lot definition was wrong, the sample missed a localized defect, the characteristic was not in the plan, or the supplier changed material or process. Feed the result back into the inspection level and AQL review, but change them through a documented quality plan revision rather than ad hoc adjustments.

calc.task: An incoming lot of 5000 SMT boards is defined as a lot. Use ISO 2859-1 general inspection level II and an AQL of 1.0% defective. Build a single sampling plan and state the accept/reject rule.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm lot definition: 5000 boards, same part number, revision, supplier lot, and packaging. 2. Select standard: ISO 2859-1 normal single sampling. 3. Find sample size code letter: lot size 1201 to 3200 at general inspection level II gives code letter K. 4. Find sample size: code letter K corresponds to n = 125 boards. 5. Select AQL: 1.0% defective. 6. Read accept/reject numbers for n = 125 and AQL 1.0%: Ac = 3, Re = 4. 7. Rule: inspect 125 boards; accept if defective boards <= 3; reject if defective boards >= 4. 8. If rejected, quarantine the lot and apply the documented disposition; if accepted, record the sample result and continue normal inspection unless switching rules indicate a change.

defect.symptom: Incoming SMT boards pass the AQL plan, but the first boards after reflow show tombstoned small chip resistors at a feeder position.
defect.cause: The incoming plan sampled for visible damage and part identity but did not test solderability, coplanarity in millimetres, or moisture sensitivity under the line reflow profile; the lot may have contained a localized tape/reel or storage issue that the sample missed.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, increase sample size for solderability and coplanarity checks, verify moisture sensitivity level and floor life against J-STD-033, review the feeder setup and reflow profile against your paste/equipment datasheet, and revise the incoming inspection plan if the characteristic should be included.

title: Component verification: part number, date code, package, counterfeit red flags

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Magnified reel and chip package showing markings and date code, with red callouts for resurfaced bodies, mismatched lead finish and sanded markings
blocks.caption: Component verification: part number, date code, package and the counterfeit red flags

theory.p: Incoming verification is the first engineering control that prevents wrong, damaged, expired, mixed, or suspect materials from entering the production flow. For components, solder paste, and bare printed circuit boards, the receiving engineer must prove four things before release: the item is the correct part or material, it is traceable to a manufacturer lot or supplier lot, it has been handled within its stated storage and process limits, and it meets the contractual quality and compliance requirements. The output is not just a pass or fail stamp; it is a record that can be used by purchasing, quality, engineering, and the supplier. A good incoming record states the purchase order, part number, lot or date code, quantity, documents reviewed, physical findings, disposition, and any required supplier action.

A component lot should normally arrive with a packing list, commercial invoice or delivery note, certificate of conformance, manufacturer lot traceability, and any special handling labels. The packing list proves what the supplier says was shipped and the quantity. The certificate of conformance states that the delivered item conforms to the purchase order and applicable specification, but it does not replace physical verification. Manufacturer lot traceability links the reels, trays, tubes, or waffle packs to a specific manufacturer lot, which is essential for recall, failure analysis, and counterfeit investigation. For moisture-sensitive devices, the package should include a moisture barrier bag, desiccant, humidity indicator card, and a moisture sensitivity level label consistent with IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, Handling, Packing, Shipping and Use of Moisture-, Heat-, and Electrostatic-Sensitive Surface Mount Devices. For regulated products, declarations such as RoHS or REACH may be required by contract; these prove the supplier's declared compliance status, not necessarily the physical composition of every lot.

theory.h: Documents that must accompany solder paste
theory.p: Solder paste is a process material, so the incoming record must prove chemistry, condition, and usable life. The supplier should provide a certificate of analysis or certificate of conformance that identifies the alloy, powder type, flux chemistry, metal content, lot number, manufacture date, expiration date, storage temperature, and any required mixing or warming instructions. The certificate proves that the paste is the specified formulation and that the lot is within the manufacturer's stated shelf life. A safety data sheet should accompany the shipment or be available through the supplier's controlled portal; it proves hazard classification and handling requirements, not process quality. The receiving engineer should verify the lot number on the jar or cartridge against the certificate, inspect the seal, and confirm that the paste has not been exposed to conditions outside the paste datasheet. If the certificate is missing, the lot should be quarantined until the supplier provides traceable documentation.

theory.h: Documents that must accompany bare PCBs
theory.p: Bare PCBs require documentation that proves material, construction, and acceptability. A typical package includes a packing list, certificate of conformance, and, when required by contract, qualification or performance evidence against IPC-6012, Qualification and Performance Specification for Rigid Printed Boards. The certificate should identify the board part number, revision, layer count, material, copper weight, finish, panel dimensions, lot number, and any special requirements such as controlled impedance, plating thickness, or flammability. Material declarations may reference IPC-4101, Specification for Base Materials for Rigid and Multilayer Printed Boards, and flammability may reference UL 94, Standard for Safety of Flammability of Plastic Materials. Acceptability of visual and dimensional features is commonly judged against IPC-A-600, Acceptability of Printed Boards, but the purchase order may impose tighter limits. The receiving engineer should verify that the board revision, material, finish, and panel size match the drawing and purchase order before release.

theory.h: Physical verification of part number, package, and date code
theory.p: Physical verification starts with the outer carton, then the inner packaging, then the component marking. Confirm that the supplier label, purchase order, and certificate agree on part number, manufacturer, package type, quantity, and lot or date code. For tape and reel, check that the tape width, cover tape, reel size, and orientation match the placement equipment requirements and the component datasheet. For trays, tubes, or waffle packs, check that the part is not mixed between cavities and that the carrier is not cracked or deformed. Date codes should be legible, consistent across the lot, and interpreted using the manufacturer's date-code convention; if the convention is unknown, request clarification before accepting. If the marking is altered, laser-etched, re-marked, or inconsistent with the package, treat the lot as suspect and quarantine it. Visual inspection can be supplemented by X-ray, decapsulation, electrical testing, or authorized-distributor traceability when counterfeit risk is high.

theory.h: Counterfeit red flags and risk-based response
theory.p: Counterfeit avoidance is not only a purchasing issue; it is an incoming engineering control. Red flags include an unusually low price, unusually short lead time, missing manufacturer traceability, unknown or unauthorized distributor, mixed date codes, mixed manufacturers, altered labels, bulk repackaging, old date codes, inconsistent tape or reel packaging, and markings that differ from the manufacturer's normal style. These indicators do not prove fraud by themselves, but they justify quarantine and further verification. For high-risk parts, use authorized distributors, request manufacturer traceability, and apply controls consistent with SAE AS6081, Counterfeit Avoidance. If a lot is suspected, isolate it, photograph the packaging and markings, record lot and date codes, and request supplier evidence. If the supplier cannot provide traceability or the part fails verification, reject the lot and update the approved supplier list or risk assessment.

theory.h: Accept, quarantine, reject, and supplier-facing records
theory.p: Acceptance requires complete documentation, correct identity, acceptable condition, and no unresolved red flags. Quarantine is used when the lot may be usable but evidence is incomplete or suspect, such as missing traceability, mixed date codes, damaged moisture barrier packaging, or a date-code age that requires engineering review. Reject is used when the lot is wrong, expired, damaged beyond use, fails verification, or cannot be proven authentic. The disposition should follow the quality management system, for example ISO 9001, Quality management systems, or ANSI/AS9100, Quality Management Systems—Requirements for Aviation, Space, and Defense Organizations, where nonconforming output must be controlled and documented. A supplier-actionable record should include the purchase order, part number, lot or date code, quantity received, quantity accepted, quantity quarantined, quantity rejected, objective evidence, required containment, corrective action request, and response due date. The record should avoid vague language such as bad packaging; it should state what was observed, where, and what action is required.

calc.task: A lot of 12,000 surface-mount ICs arrives under a purchase order that requires a single manufacturer lot, package type matching the purchase order, and a date-code age no greater than 12 months at receipt. The packing list shows 12,000 pieces. The certificate of conformance is present, but the manufacturer lot traceability sheet is missing. The reel labels show date code 2401, except a reel shows date code 2301. The receipt date code is 2504. The date-code format is assumed to be YYMM; verify the supplier convention. Counted quantity is 11,980 pieces. Classify the lot and write the supplier-facing finding.
calc.solution: Step A: compare purchase order, packing list, and certificate of conformance; part number and package type match, so identity is not the primary finding. Step B: note missing manufacturer lot traceability; without it, the lot cannot be proven to be a single manufacturer lot, so the finding is quarantine pending traceability. Step C: calculate date-code age for the main lot: 2401 to 2504 is 15 months, which exceeds the 12-month purchase-order limit by 3 months. Step D: calculate date-code age for the mixed reel: 2301 to 2504 is 27 months, which also exceeds the limit and shows mixed date codes. Step E: compare counted quantity 11,980 with packing list 12,000; shortage is 20 pieces. Step F: disposition is quarantine the entire lot, not accept, because missing traceability, mixed date codes, and date-code age exceedance are counterfeit and process-risk red flags; reject if the supplier cannot provide manufacturer traceability, authorized-distributor evidence, or an approved concession. Step G: supplier record should state purchase order number, part number, lot number, receipt date, quantity received, quantity counted, missing documents, date-code findings, mixed-lot finding, shortage, disposition, containment, required corrective action, and response due date.

defect.symptom: A reel of resistors is opened at the placement machine, and the tape contains parts with two different date codes and slightly different marking styles. The outer label shows a single lot number, but the inner reel label is partially covered by a second label.
defect.cause: The supplier or distributor likely repackaged mixed stock, relabeled the reel, or shipped an unauthorized substitute lot. The incoming inspection did not verify inner labels, date-code consistency, or manufacturer traceability before release.
defect.action: Stop the machine, quarantine the reel and the remaining lot, photograph the outer label, inner label, tape, and markings, and record the lot number, date codes, quantity, and purchase order. Quarantine the lot pending supplier traceability and counterfeit assessment. If traceability cannot be proven or the parts fail verification, reject the lot, issue a corrective action request to the supplier, and review the approved supplier list and incoming inspection plan.

title: Solder paste, flux and adhesive receipt: alloy, powder, expiry, cold chain

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Cold-storage cabinet with paste jars and a temperature log, a magnified label with alloy code and expiry, and a powder particle size distribution curve
blocks.caption: Solder paste, flux and adhesive receipt: alloy, powder, expiry and the cold chain

theory.h: Receipt is a records check before it is a visual check
theory.p: A received lot should be matched to the purchase order and the supplier's shipping documents before it is opened or moved to stores. The minimum set is a packing list, a certificate of conformance or test report, lot traceability, and any special handling label. The packing list proves what was shipped and how many units were shipped. The certificate of conformance proves the supplier tested or inspected the lot against the purchase order. Lot traceability lets you link the material to a specific manufacturing batch, date, and test result. Special handling labels prove that the lot was intended for moisture, electrostatic, temperature, or shelf-life control.

theory.h: Component lots: documents that prove identity and condition
theory.p: For components, request the packing list, certificate of conformance, lot or date code, manufacturer's test report when required, moisture-sensitive device label, desiccant and humidity indicator card when applicable, and electrostatic discharge packaging. The packing list proves quantity and part number. The certificate of conformance proves the supplier verified the lot against the purchase order. The date code proves the lot age and supports first-in, first-out control. The moisture-sensitive device label and humidity indicator card, when used under J-STD-033, show whether the lot was packaged for moisture control and whether the indicator has changed state. The electrostatic discharge packaging shows the lot was protected from electrostatic discharge during transport.

theory.h: Solder paste lots: documents that prove chemistry and storage history
theory.p: For solder paste, the certificate of conformance should state the lot number, manufacture date, expiry date, alloy composition, powder type, flux classification, viscosity or printability data, halogen or residue classification, and storage instructions. The lot number links the paste to the supplier's batch test. The manufacture and expiry dates prove the lot is within the supplier's stated shelf life. The alloy and powder type prove the paste matches the process requirement, using classifications such as those in IPC J-STD-005 for paste, IPC J-STD-006 for powder, and IPC J-STD-004 for flux. The viscosity or printability data proves the supplier measured a property that affects stencil printing. The safety data sheet proves the hazard information needed for safe handling.

theory.h: Bare PCB lots: documents that prove board class and finish
theory.p: For bare PCBs, request the packing list, certificate of conformance, IPC-A-600 class or purchase-order class, bare-board test report, finish type and thickness report, impedance report if controlled, material declaration, and moisture barrier packaging with humidity indicator card when required. The packing list proves quantity and panel type. The certificate of conformance proves the board was inspected and tested to the purchase order. The IPC-A-600 class statement proves the visual and dimensional acceptance level intended for the board. The bare-board test report proves electrical continuity and isolation were checked. The finish report proves the surface finish and thickness are suitable for soldering or wire bonding. The humidity indicator card shows whether the moisture barrier package was compromised.

theory.h: Accept, quarantine, or reject: make the decision evidence-based
theory.p: Accept when the purchase order, documents, packaging, lot identity, expiry, and physical condition all match the receiving specification. Quarantine when the material may be usable but evidence is incomplete or a control limit was exceeded, for example a missing certificate of conformance, an activated humidity indicator card, a temperature excursion beyond the supplier's shipping limit, or an expiry date that requires supplier retest. Reject when the material cannot be used safely or cannot be traced, for example wrong alloy, wrong powder type, wrong board finish, severe mechanical damage, contamination, counterfeit suspicion, or an expired lot without a valid supplier retest. The decision should be recorded with the evidence, not only with a verdict.

theory.h: Write a record the supplier can act on
theory.p: A useful incoming-material record includes the purchase order number, part number, supplier lot number, quantity received, quantity affected, requirement or drawing clause, observed condition, measurement or photo reference, disposition, containment action, and requested corrective action. Use objective wording: state the lot, the requirement, the observed deviation, and the impact. Ask the supplier to confirm the lot's test data, shipping temperature, packaging condition, and whether the lot can be retested or reconditioned. Avoid vague phrases such as 'bad paste' or 'damaged boards'; specify the lot, the failed attribute, and the evidence.

theory.h: Cold chain and expiry: calculate the remaining use window
theory.p: Paste and moisture-sensitive materials need a time and temperature record, not just a date. For paste, compare the manufacture date, expiry date, storage temperature, and any time above the supplier's storage limit. Many paste datasheets specify storage from 2 °C to 10 °C; verify against your paste datasheet. For moisture-sensitive components, check the packaging, humidity indicator card, and floor-life clock under J-STD-033. If a control limit is exceeded, quarantine the lot and request supplier data before release. If the lot is accepted, mark it for use-first and recheck the expiry and packaging before opening. Verify storage temperature, shelf life, and excursion limits against your paste or component datasheet because supplier limits vary.

calc.task: A solder paste lot has manufacture date 2025-01-01 and expiry 2025-07-01. It is received 2025-04-01. The shipping temperature logger shows 36 h above 10 °C. The supplier datasheet says the lot may be accepted without retest if cumulative time above 10 °C is less than 48 h. Determine the remaining shelf life and the incoming disposition.
calc.solution: First, confirm the lot number, manufacture date, expiry date, and storage instructions on the certificate of conformance. Second, calculate lot age at receipt: 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-01 is 90 days. Third, calculate remaining calendar shelf life: 2025-04-01 to 2025-07-01 is 91 days. Fourth, compare the temperature excursion to the supplier limit: 36 h is less than 48 h. Fifth, because the documents are complete, the lot is within expiry, and the excursion is below the supplier limit, accept the lot with use-first control and recheck the expiry and packaging before opening. If the excursion had been 48 h or more, or if the certificate of conformance were missing, quarantine the lot and request supplier retest data.

defect.symptom: Stencil printing shows paste balls, inconsistent deposit volume, and poor release from the stencil after a new paste lot is opened.
defect.cause: The lot was stored above the supplier's recommended temperature range for an extended period, causing flux separation or viscosity drift, and the incoming record did not capture the storage temperature or expiry status.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, retain the container and shipping record, measure viscosity and printability against the supplier datasheet, and issue a supplier corrective action request with the lot number, storage temperature record, observed print defects, and request for batch test data and retest or replacement.

title: Bare PCB receipt: surface finish, planarity and warpage, packaging, shelf life

goals.text: Specify the documents that must accompany a received lot of components, paste or bare PCB and state what each one proves.
Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: A PCB with exaggerated warp, a planarity measurement setup with a height gauge, a surface finish cross-section and a sealed barrier package with desiccant
blocks.caption: Bare PCB receipt: surface finish, planarity and warpage, packaging and shelf life

theory.p: A bare PCB lot should arrive with a packing list, purchase order reference, lot or batch identifier, and a certificate of conformance or certificate of analysis when required by the purchase order. The packing list proves what was shipped and how many units were shipped. The purchase order reference proves that the lot was ordered against the correct part number, revision, quantity, and delivery condition. The lot identifier proves traceability to the fabricated panel, date, and process records. The certificate of conformance proves that the supplier verified the lot against the purchase order and applicable acceptance criteria.

The surface finish must be identified unambiguously, for example immersion silver, immersion tin, organic solderability preservative, electroless nickel immersion gold, or hard gold on selected pads. The supplier should provide the finish type, thickness or coating class where applicable, and the relevant test report or certificate. For plated finishes, a report may cite IPC-4101 for base material and finish requirements and IPC-6012 for qualified product performance. For solderability, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-002 can be used for component solderability, while bare board solderability is commonly specified against IPC-6012 and the customer drawing. Verify the finish against the assembly process, reflow profile, and paste chemistry.

Planarity and warpage are usually specified on the board drawing or in IPC-6012, which gives acceptance limits for flatness and twist depending on board class and whether the board is rectangular or irregular. Incoming inspection should record the measurement method, such as a flat reference surface, feeler gauge, optical flatness gauge, or coordinate measuring machine. For fine-pitch components, press-fit connectors, or large area arrays, the assembly process may require tighter limits than the generic IPC-6012 limits. Verify the required flatness against the placement machine datasheet, stencil release behavior, and reflow support method.

Bare PCBs should be packaged to prevent mechanical damage, contamination, oxidation, and moisture absorption. Common packaging includes sealed moisture barrier bags with desiccant and a humidity indicator card, or rigid trays for high-value or fragile boards. The packaging should show the seal date, lot identifier, and any moisture sensitivity level assigned by the supplier. IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 is commonly used for handling, packing, shipping, and use of moisture-sensitive devices, and it can be referenced for moisture control practice even when the item is a bare board rather than a component. Verify the bag integrity, desiccant condition, and indicator card reading at receipt.

Shelf life is the time a material can remain in its original sealed packaging under specified storage conditions before requalification is required. Floor life is the time a moisture-sensitive item may remain exposed to factory ambient conditions before it must be reconditioned or soldered. For bare PCBs, shelf life is often controlled by the surface finish, packaging integrity, and storage environment. For moisture-sensitive assemblies and components, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 provides the framework for moisture sensitivity level, floor life, and reconditioning. Verify the supplier-stated shelf life and storage temperature range against your own storage conditions and assembly schedule.

Incoming findings should be classified as accept, quarantine, or reject. Accept means the lot meets the purchase order and documented acceptance criteria, and it can be released to stores or production. Quarantine means the lot has a nonconformance that may be dispositioned by engineering, quality, or the supplier, such as a missing report, questionable packaging, or a borderline measurement. Reject means the lot does not meet a critical requirement, such as wrong surface finish, damaged moisture barrier with failed humidity indicator, or warpage beyond the assembly limit. The disposition record should be written so the supplier can correct the cause, not merely describe the symptom.

A useful nonconformance record states the purchase order, lot identifier, quantity inspected, quantity affected, requirement violated, measured result, acceptance limit, standard or drawing reference, and requested action. For example, instead of writing “boards are bent,” write “Lot 4471, 12 of 250 boards measured with twist above the drawing limit of IPC-6012 Class 3; requested action: return affected boards, provide root cause, and submit corrected flatness data for the next three lots.” This format gives the supplier enough information to trace the lot, reproduce the measurement, and prevent recurrence.

calc.task: A lot of 500 bare PCBs is received with a drawing requirement that the surface finish be organic solderability preservative and that flatness meet IPC-6012 Class 3. Incoming inspection finds 18 boards with twist above the drawing limit, 1 moisture barrier bag with a failed humidity indicator, and a missing supplier certificate of conformance. Classify the lot and write the disposition.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the requirements. The purchase order requires organic solderability preservative finish, IPC-6012 Class 3 flatness, intact moisture barrier packaging, and a certificate of conformance. Step 2: Compare findings to requirements. The finish type is correct. Flatness fails on 18 boards. Packaging fails on 1 bag. Documentation fails because the certificate of conformance is missing. Step 3: Determine severity. Flatness failure affects assembly placement and reflow seating, so it is a product conformance issue. Packaging failure affects moisture control and shelf life, so it is a storage and reliability issue. Missing certificate of conformance affects traceability and acceptance evidence, so it is a documentation issue. Step 4: Classify the lot. The lot cannot be accepted as received. Quarantine the lot pending disposition. If the flatness failure is outside the drawing limit and cannot be dispositioned by engineering, reject the affected boards. If the packaging failure is isolated and the boards are otherwise within moisture limits, quarantine only the affected bag. Step 5: Write the supplier-actionable record. State purchase order, lot identifier, quantity received, quantity affected, measured result, IPC-6012 Class 3 reference, packaging failure, missing certificate of conformance, and requested actions: return or disposition the 18 boards, provide root cause for flatness, provide corrected flatness data for the next lots, replace the damaged bag or provide requalification evidence, and submit the missing certificate of conformance.

defect.symptom: A received lot of bare PCBs has a sealed moisture barrier bag, but the humidity indicator card shows a failed state and several boards show dull, discolored immersion silver pads.
defect.cause: The lot may have exceeded its sealed shelf life, the bag seal may have leaked, the desiccant may have been insufficient or saturated, or the boards may have been exposed to factory ambient conditions beyond the supplier-stated floor life. Discoloration can indicate oxidation or contamination of the immersion silver surface.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot. Record the lot identifier, seal date, humidity indicator reading, storage temperature, and number of affected boards. Verify the supplier-stated shelf life and storage conditions. If the boards are within the supplier requalification window and the surface finish is still solderable by your incoming test, request engineering disposition. If the surface finish fails solderability or the moisture exposure cannot be traced, reject the lot and ask the supplier for root cause, corrected packaging, and updated shelf-life documentation.

title: Nonconforming material at dock: quarantine, MRB, supplier notification

goals.text: Classify incoming-material findings as accept, quarantine or reject and write a record a supplier can act on.

blocks.alt: Quarantine cage with red hold tags, a material review board decision flow with four branches, and a feedback arrow to supplier notification
blocks.caption: Nonconforming material at the dock: quarantine, MRB and supplier notification

theory.p: Incoming material is classified against the purchase order, drawing, specification, and incoming inspection plan. ISO 9001:2015 requires control of externally provided processes, products, and services, so the dock record should show the evidence used to accept, quarantine, or reject the lot.

Quarantine is a controlled hold for material that is suspect, incomplete, or awaiting review. It should be physically segregated or system-held, labeled with part number, lot, quantity, date, and hold reason, and traceable to the receiving transaction. The hold prevents use while the material review board or quality function evaluates risk.

A material review board normally reviews the nonconformance report, drawings, measurement data, photos, supplier lot history, and downstream process risk. Dispositions may include accept, rework, sort, use-as-is with concession, return, or scrap. The disposition should state who approved it and what verification is required before release.

theory.h: Supplier notification that can be acted on
theory.p: Supplier notification should be objective and specific: part number, lot, purchase order, quantity received, quantity inspected, finding, specification requirement, measured result, and evidence. It should request containment, root cause, corrective action, and replacement or return authorization according to the contract. Vague statements such as 'bad parts' do not support effective corrective action.

Acceptance is appropriate when evidence shows conformance to the specified requirements. Quarantine is appropriate when documentation, packaging, moisture, ESD, shelf life, or measurement uncertainty leaves the status unclear. Reject is appropriate when a confirmed finding affects fit, form, function, safety, or regulatory requirements, or when the quarantine cannot be resolved within the planned disposition window.

A usable record links the finding to the lot and to any downstream use. It should include the inspector, date, location, measurement method, calibration status, sample size, observed defects, disposition, approvals, and closure evidence. For electronic components, moisture-sensitive device status should be recorded and verified against the device datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033; process limits should be verified against your paste/equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Closing the loop with the line
theory.p: Dock dispositions affect assembly flow. If material is released, the line should receive the approved status and any special handling notes. If material is rejected, the line should be notified so substitute material or schedule changes are managed. The supplier corrective action should be closed only after containment, root cause, and effectiveness checks are documented.

calc.task: A lot of 1,000 chip resistors arrives on 20 reels. The incoming plan samples 4 reels and 100 units. Findings: 5 units are outside the specified resistance tolerance, 2 reels have damaged tape pockets, and 1 reel has a moisture indicator above the limit. The internal acceptance limit for electrical nonconformance is 2%. Classify each finding and the lot, then write a supplier record.
calc.solution: Step 1: Verify the purchase order, part number, lot code, quantity, packaging, labels, and calibration status of measuring equipment. Step 2: Record the sample basis: 4 reels sampled from 20 reels, and 100 units inspected. Step 3: Calculate the electrical defect rate: 5 units outside tolerance divided by 100 units inspected equals 5%. Step 4: Compare the electrical defect rate with the internal acceptance limit: 5% is greater than 2%, so the electrical finding is classified as reject unless the MRB accepts it based on documented risk. Step 5: Classify the damaged tape pockets on 2 reels as quarantine pending MRB because damaged pockets can cause dropped components, feeder jams, or misalignment. Step 6: Classify the moisture indicator exceedance on 1 reel as quarantine pending MRB; verify the device datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 before any bake, reflow, or release decision. Step 7: Classify the lot as reject for the confirmed electrical nonconformance, with the full lot held under quarantine until MRB disposition. Step 8: Write the supplier record with part number, lot, purchase order, quantity received, quantity inspected, sample size, measured result, specification requirement, defect rate, photos of damaged tape and moisture indicator, affected reel numbers, requested containment, requested root cause, requested corrective action, and return or replacement authorization status.

defect.symptom: Small chip components tombstone on one side after reflow, and the feeder occasionally stalls on the same reel.
defect.cause: Incoming tape pockets are damaged and allow components to shift or fall, and the reel may have been exposed to handling damage before delivery.
defect.action: Quarantine the reel and lot, notify the supplier with photos and reel traceability, request packaging containment, and have the MRB decide whether to return, sort, or accept only after verified inspection.

title: Moisture inside a package: what happens during reflow and why

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

theory.h: Why moisture inside a package matters
theory.p: Most plastic packages contain hygroscopic materials such as mold compound, die attach, underfill, and polymer substrates. These materials absorb water vapor from the storage environment. The amount absorbed depends on package size, material composition, storage temperature, relative humidity, and exposure time. During reflow, absorbed moisture can vaporize quickly, create internal pressure, and stress weak interfaces. The result can be delamination, package cracking, die attach voiding, wire lift, or intermittent electrical failures that may not appear until later in the product life.

blocks.caption: Floor-life values per J-STD-033 — see table below

blocks.alt: IC package cross-section showing moisture ingress and cracking, a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and HIC, and a floor-life clock showing elapsed hours
blocks.caption: Moisture inside a package: ingress paths, barrier bag with desiccant and humidity indicator card, floor-life clock

theory.h: How moisture enters and moves through the package
theory.p: Moisture enters mainly through the package body and through seams, exposed die surfaces, and porous interfaces. At room temperature, diffusion is usually slow, but it accelerates as temperature rises. A device stored in a dry cabinet or sealed moisture barrier bag with desiccant can remain below a critical internal moisture level. Once the bag is opened, the device begins to absorb moisture from the factory environment. The rate is not uniform across all packages; thin, large, or highly hygroscopic packages can be more sensitive than thicker, smaller ones.

During reflow, the package body and internal interfaces heat rapidly. Moisture that has diffused into the package can vaporize and expand. If the vapor pressure exceeds the strength of an interface, the interface can separate. This is often called the popcorn effect. The damage may be visible as package cracking or lifted leads, but it can also be hidden as delamination at the die attach, mold compound, or substrate interface. Because the failure can be internal, electrical test may pass initially and later fail under thermal cycling or humidity stress.

The moisture sensitivity level, or MSL, is a package classification that indicates how quickly a device can absorb moisture under defined ambient conditions. The related floor life is the total time a device may be exposed to ambient conditions before it requires bake before reflow. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, typical floor lives are: MSL 1 unlimited; MSL 2 12 months; MSL 3 168 h; MSL 4 72 h; MSL 5 48 h; MSL 5a 24 h; MSL 6 has no floor life and is mandatory bake before use, with the post-bake reflow window taken from the label. These values are package-level limits, not a guarantee that every device will fail after the limit; they are the control limits used to prevent moisture-related reflow damage.

theory.p: The MSL rating may appear on the device label, moisture barrier bag, tape and reel label, or package datasheet. If the marking is missing or unclear, use the datasheet or treat the device as the most restrictive applicable MSL until verified. The bag data should include the MSL, humidity indicator card status, desiccant condition, and bag opening date. The humidity indicator card threshold is card-specific and should be verified against the card datasheet and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. A card that has exceeded its threshold indicates that the internal environment is no longer acceptable for direct reflow, even if the calculated floor life has not expired.

theory.h: Using reflow history to determine remaining floor life
theory.p: Floor life is cumulative ambient exposure, not simply time since the last bag opening. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, a qualifying reflow completed within the remaining floor life resets the floor life. If the floor life expired before reflow, the device must be baked before reflow. If the humidity indicator card exceeded its threshold before reflow, bake is required regardless of remaining floor life. Some programs also limit the number of reflows or require special handling after multiple reflows; verify against the package qualification, customer procedure, and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033.

Control begins with dry storage, sealed moisture barrier bags, desiccant, and humidity indicator cards. Typical dry cabinet relative humidity is often 5% to 10%; verify against your equipment datasheet. Bake conditions, cabinet setpoints, and reflow profiles should be verified against IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, the package datasheet, and your paste and equipment datasheets. Floor-life tracking should record bag opening time, humidity indicator card status, reflow time, bake time, and any reflow count limits. If the device is not going to be reflowed within the remaining floor life, bake it before reflow rather than relying on visual inspection or electrical test.

calc.task: A device label says MSL 3. The moisture barrier bag was opened 100 h ago. The humidity indicator card has not exceeded its threshold. The device was reflowed 70 h after bag opening, and 40 h have elapsed since that reflow. Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life.
calc.solution: 1. Read the MSL rating from the marking: MSL 3. 2. Use the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 floor life for MSL 3: 168 h. 3. Check the humidity indicator card: it has not exceeded its threshold, so the card does not force bake. 4. Check reflow history: the device was reflowed at 70 h after bag opening, which is within the 168 h floor life. 5. Under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, a qualifying reflow within the floor life resets the floor life. 6. Calculate remaining floor life after reflow: 168 h minus 40 h elapsed since reflow equals 128 h. 7. Result: MSL 3, remaining floor life 128 h, provided the reflow met the applicable profile and no reflow count limit applies.

defect.symptom: After reflow, some packages show package cracking, lifted leads, or popcorn-like deformation, while others pass electrical test but later fail with intermittent opens or delamination found by X-ray or acoustic microscopy.
defect.cause: MSL devices were exposed to ambient conditions beyond their floor life, or the humidity indicator card exceeded its threshold before reflow. Common line causes include bags left open too long, missing floor-life tracking, reflow scheduling delays, incorrect bake, or failure to reset floor life after a qualifying reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine affected lots. Verify MSL markings, bag opening time, humidity indicator card status, desiccant condition, reflow time, and bake records against IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Bake devices that exceeded floor life or humidity indicator card threshold before reflow. Review storage, bag opening, floor-life tracking, and reflow scheduling controls. Inspect suspect packages with X-ray or acoustic microscopy and update the process control plan to prevent recurrence.

title: Reading MSL reality: J-STD-033 / J-STD-020 markings, barrier bag, HIC

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

blocks.alt: A magnified MSL label with a caution symbol, a barrier bag shown as a translucent panel with a humidity indicator card and desiccant inside
blocks.caption: Reading moisture sensitivity markings: MSL label, barrier bag, humidity indicator card and desiccant

theory.h: MSL is a reflow-risk class, not a storage grade
theory.p: J-STD-020 classifies non-hermetic surface mount devices by moisture sensitivity level (MSL). The rating tells you how much ambient exposure is allowed before a reflow cycle is likely to cause package damage. It is not a measure of shelf life, ESD class, or solderability. Read the MSL code from the supplier label, bag, or device marking, then use the matching floor-life rule from J-STD-020 or the label.

theory.h: Where the rating is normally marked
theory.p: J-STD-033 handling practice commonly uses a moisture barrier bag with a label that identifies the MSL, floor life, date, and bake or exposure information when applicable. In practice, the MSL may appear on the outer box, reel label, bag label, or package marking. If the marking is missing or unreadable, do not guess; check the purchase record, supplier data sheet, or your internal material specification, and treat the part as unknown until verified.

IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 defines floor life at reference conditions of 30 °C and 60% RH for common MSL ratings; J-STD-020 assigns the moisture sensitivity level itself. Typical values are MSL 1 unlimited, MSL 2 1 year, MSL 2a 4 weeks, MSL 3 168 h, MSL 4 72 h, MSL 5 48 h, and MSL 5a 24 h; MSL 6 is special and normally requires bake before use. Use the value printed on the label when it is more restrictive, and verify the current revision of J-STD-020 because tables can be updated.

A moisture barrier bag slows moisture ingress, but it is not a permanent dry environment. J-STD-033 commonly uses a desiccant and a humidity indicator card (HIC) to show whether the bag interior is still within the intended humidity range. Read the HIC according to the card manufacturer's scale; if a spot indicates an exceeded threshold, if the bag is punctured, or if the seal is compromised, treat the contents as exposed and evaluate bake or quarantine before reflow.

The floor-life clock starts when the moisture barrier bag is opened, not when the device is first received. Time on the line, in a dry cabinet, or on a feeder counts as ambient exposure unless your controlled storage procedure explicitly allows it. A completed bake per J-STD-033 can restart the clock if your procedure accepts the bake record; otherwise, continue counting exposure from the original open time.

Reflow history matters because a reflow after the floor life has expired can drive moisture into package interfaces and cause damage. If a reflow was completed while floor life remained, that reflow is normally acceptable from a moisture standpoint, but the device can reabsorb moisture afterward. For a second reflow, check the exposure time since the last dry event (bag opening or accepted bake; verify whether your procedure also treats a completed reflow as a dry event) and verify the reflow profile against your paste/equipment datasheet. Use the paste/equipment datasheet ranges for peak temperature and time above liquidus; do not assume a universal value. If exposure exceeded the floor life before any reflow, bake before reflow and record the bake temperature, time, and device count.

To determine remaining floor life, combine the MSL rating, the floor-life value from J-STD-020 or the label, the bag open date and time, the HIC condition, and the reflow or bake records. If the sources conflict, use the most restrictive value and quarantine the material until the discrepancy is resolved. This keeps the decision traceable and avoids relying on a single marking or indicator.

calc.task: A bag label states MSL 3 with a floor life of 168 h per J-STD-020. The bag was opened E hours ago. One reflow was completed at R hours after opening. Determine the remaining floor life and whether a bake is required before a second reflow.
calc.solution: Confirm the floor life F from the label or J-STD-020; here F = 168 h. Calculate remaining floor life before the next reflow: remaining = F - E. Check the first reflow: if R was less than F, the reflow occurred within floor life and no bake was required for that reflow. If E has reached or passed F, the floor life expired before the second reflow; bake per J-STD-033 or your approved procedure before reflow. If the HIC shows an exceeded threshold or the bag was damaged, treat the device as exposed even if E is less than F, and bake or quarantine per your procedure. Record the bake, reflow profile, and exposure time so the next decision starts from a known dry event.

defect.symptom: After reflow, boards show intermittent opens, lifted leads, or package cracks on a few MSL devices, while nearby parts look normal.
defect.cause: The affected devices exceeded their floor life before reflow, or the barrier bag/HIC condition was not checked, so moisture remained in the package and expanded during reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, verify the MSL label, bag open time, HIC, and reflow records, bake per J-STD-033 or the manufacturer's limits, then reflow a sample and inspect. Correct the storage control by adding a bag-open timestamp and HIC check before kitting.
