title: Floor-life accounting: clock start, accumulation, reset rules

goals.text: Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life of a device from its markings, bag data and reflow history.

blocks.alt: A timeline with a teal arc accumulating exposure hours, clock icons for each exposure event, and a bake event resetting the arc to zero
blocks.caption: Floor-life accounting: clock start, accumulation across exposure events, and the bake reset

theory.h: Floor life is an open-air exposure budget, not a shelf life
theory.p: Floor life is the cumulative time a moisture-sensitive device may remain outside its moisture barrier bag while exposed to factory conditions that J-STD-033 treats as no more than 30°C and no more than 60%RH. It is not the same as shelf life, reflow count, solderability life, or a general quality rating. The purpose of the budget is to limit moisture uptake before reflow, because absorbed moisture can expand during soldering and contribute to package damage. The clock starts at initial exposure to ambient air, which usually means bag opening, but it can also start if the device is removed from a sealed bag, if the bag is punctured, or if the device is otherwise exposed to uncontrolled air. Once started, the clock accumulates through storage, kitting, feeder loading, placement, reflow, inspection, test, and any other open-air handling unless a qualifying reset action is performed.

theory.h: MSL rating comes from the device marking, bag label, and datasheet
theory.p: The moisture sensitivity level, or MSL, is normally shown on the device marking, tape-and-reel label, moisture barrier bag label, or datasheet. For working accounting, use the most restrictive valid source when sources disagree, then verify the discrepancy with the supplier or device owner. J-STD-033 assigns floor life values by MSL: MSL 1 has unlimited floor life under the standard's storage condition, MSL 2 is 12 months, MSL 2a is 4 weeks, MSL 3 is 168 h, MSL 4 is 72 h, MSL 5 is 48 h, MSL 5a is 24 h, and MSL 6 requires bake before use. These values are the starting point for remaining floor life, but they are not a substitute for tracking actual exposure time.

theory.h: Clock start is tied to exposure, not to the moment you notice the bag
theory.p: In storage, the practical clock start is the recorded bag-open time or the first verified exposure time. If the bag-open time is missing, the exposure time is uncertain and the device should be treated conservatively until the exposure can be bounded. A bag may appear intact but still have a compromised seal, a puncture, or a desiccant that has been exposed for an unknown period. The humidity indicator card and desiccant condition can support the assessment, but they do not replace a time record. If the device was already exposed before entering storage, that prior exposure must be included in the cumulative floor-life calculation. If the prior exposure cannot be bounded, use your facility's nonconforming material process rather than assuming the full MSL floor life remains.

theory.h: Accumulation includes all open-air time, including reflow handling
theory.p: Floor life accumulates whenever the device is outside a compliant moisture barrier bag under conditions covered by J-STD-033. This includes time on the floor, time in a feeder, time on the placement machine, time in the reflow oven, time on the conveyor, time in inspection, and time waiting between operations. Reflow itself is not a separate floor-life charge; the open-air time associated with reflow handling is what counts. If a device goes through multiple reflow passes, each pass adds the open-air time associated with that pass, and the cumulative exposure must be tracked. If the storage environment is hotter or more humid than the J-STD-033 reference condition, the simple floor-life table may not be sufficient; use the device datasheet, supplier guidance, and your facility's controlled storage limits.

theory.h: Reset rules require a qualifying bake and proper repacking
theory.p: A floor-life reset is not automatic when a device is put back into a bag. J-STD-033 allows reset after a qualifying bake performed according to the applicable bake table for the package and MSL, followed by appropriate repacking with desiccant and a humidity indicator card where required. The bake must be recorded with the start time, end time, temperature, and responsible person or system record. If the bake is not performed to the applicable J-STD-033 condition, or if the package has already exceeded its allowed exposure in a way that requires evaluation, the floor life should not be reset. MSL 6 devices require bake before use, so they should not be treated as having usable floor life simply because they were recently removed from a bag.

theory.h: Storage records must support traceable accounting
theory.p: For storage-stage accounting, the minimum useful records are part number, lot or date code, MSL, bag-open time, current cumulative open-air time, storage temperature and humidity, desiccant status, humidity indicator card status, bake records if any, and reflow or other open-air handling history. A simple spreadsheet can work for small operations, but a MES or WMS record is preferable because it reduces manual errors and supports traceability. If manual records are used, keep the time unit consistent and make the calculation method visible on the record. If the storage area is not controlled to the J-STD-033 reference condition, the record should show the actual conditions and the basis used for any adjustment or quarantine decision.

theory.h: Remaining floor life is calculated by subtraction, then checked against action limits
theory.p: The basic calculation is: remaining floor life equals the MSL floor life from J-STD-033 minus cumulative open-air time already accumulated. Cumulative open-air time includes storage outside the bag, assembly handling, reflow handling, inspection, and any other exposure. If the result is positive, the device may continue to be used only if the remaining time is sufficient for the planned process and the storage or handling environment remains within the applicable limits. If the result is not positive, the device requires bake before reflow or disposition according to your process. If the device has been baked and reset, the remaining floor life is recalculated from the reset point using the full MSL floor life, provided the reset was valid.

theory.h: Practical storage decisions should be conservative and documented
theory.p: In storage, the engineer's job is to prevent an unknown exposure from becoming an uncontrolled reflow risk. When records are incomplete, the safest practical approach is to bound the exposure, quarantine the material, and decide whether bake, supplier evaluation, or scrap is appropriate. Do not reset floor life based only on appearance, a new desiccant packet, or a new humidity indicator card. Do not assume that a short reflow pass has negligible effect if the device has already consumed most of its floor life. Verify the applicable J-STD-033 revision, the device datasheet, and your facility's controlled storage limits, because practice-based handling times and storage conditions vary by site and product.

calc.task: A tape-and-reel is marked MSL 3. The bag label shows the bag was opened 100 h ago. The MES shows 6 h of open-air reflow handling. Storage remained within the J-STD-033 reference condition of no more than 30°C and no more than 60%RH. Determine the MSL rating and remaining floor life.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the MSL from the marking and bag label. Both sources indicate MSL 3. Step 2: Look up the floor life for MSL 3. J-STD-033 gives 168 h for MSL 3. Step 3: Add the recorded open-air exposure. Bag-open storage exposure is 100 h. Open-air reflow handling is 6 h. Total cumulative open-air time is 100 h + 6 h = 106 h. Step 4: Subtract cumulative exposure from the MSL floor life. Remaining floor life is 168 h - 106 h = 62 h. Step 5: Interpret the result. The device has 62 h of remaining floor life under the stated conditions. If the planned process cannot be completed within that time, or if the exposure record is later found to be incomplete, the device should be evaluated for bake or quarantine before reflow.

defect.symptom: After reflow, multiple units from the same lot show package cracking, delamination, or popcorn-like damage, while units from another lot with the same part number and reflow profile pass inspection.
defect.cause: The failed lot had its floor-life clock started when the moisture barrier bag was opened, but the open-air time was not fully recorded. Storage time, feeder time, and reflow handling time were not added to the cumulative exposure, so the lot was reflowed after its J-STD-033 floor life had already been consumed.
defect.action: Quarantine the remaining lot and any related lots with incomplete exposure records. Verify the bag-open time, storage conditions, reflow handling time, and any bake records. If the cumulative exposure cannot be bounded, treat the material as requiring bake or supplier evaluation before reflow. Correct the storage record so that bag-open time, cumulative open-air time, and reset events are captured in the MES or WMS.

title: Baking and dry cabinets: when required, conditions by package, records

goals.text: Decide whether a batch must be baked, specify the bake/dry-storage condition and justify it by package type.

blocks.alt: A dry cabinet with trays and a humidity readout, a bake oven with a temperature-versus-time curve, package groups by body thickness and a log sheet
blocks.caption: Baking and dry cabinets: when required, conditions by package thickness, and the records

theory.h: Bake decision starts with package and exposure
theory.p: In storage, the bake decision is not based on part name alone. Use the moisture sensitivity level, package type, whether the moisture barrier bag was opened, dry pack integrity, humidity indicator card status, desiccant condition, and the planned time to reflow. If the batch can be consumed within the remaining floor life and the dry storage condition is qualified, baking may not be required. If exposure, cabinet performance, or bag condition cannot be proven, treat the batch as exposed and bake or quarantine it. The decision should be made by the person who controls the lot record, not by the line operator alone.

For plastic packages, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D assigns moisture sensitivity levels and floor life. Under typical ambient conditions, MSL 3 has 168 h, MSL 4 has 72 h, MSL 5 has 48 h, and MSL 5a has 24 h; higher levels require supplier-specified conditions. Floor life begins when the dry pack is opened or when the package is exposed to ambient. Verify the controlled revision and any supplier-specific limits, because some suppliers shorten floor life for large packages, high moisture content, or long reflow profiles.

theory.h: Dry storage can suspend or extend exposure
theory.p: IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D recognizes dry storage at 10% RH or less for eligible devices. A dry cabinet should be calibrated, alarmed, and logged; setpoints of 5% to 10% RH are common, but the qualified limit is the one in your procedure. If the cabinet is out of range, the time in the cabinet may count as floor life. For tape and reel, keep reels in sealed bags or dry cabinets after opening. For trays and tubes, use sealed containers with desiccant and a humidity indicator card when the cabinet is not available.

Use the bake table in IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D for the package type and the component or tape datasheet. Bake time in J-STD-033 is indexed to package body thickness, not to the moisture sensitivity level. Tape and reel must not be baked above 40°C, because carrier tape and cover tape soften and deform; the 40°C column is therefore long — about 9 days for bodies up to 1.4 mm, 11 days for 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 38 days for 2.0 to 4.5 mm — so a 48 h or 168 h bake at 40°C will not dry a reel. Loose parts in trays or tubes can use the 125°C column: 8 h up to 1.4 mm, 18 h for 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 48 h for 2.0 to 4.5 mm, only if the tray, tube and component materials are rated. Above 90°C the cumulative bake time is limited (96 h unless the supplier states otherwise) because of intermetallic growth and solderability loss. Verify against your tape, tray, tube, and equipment datasheet, because tape can soften, trays can warp, and some coatings can blister.

Bare PCBs and THT components can absorb moisture, but bake rules depend on laminate, coating, and package. For boards, use the board supplier bake condition; common practice is 105°C to 125°C for 2 h to 24 h, with longer times for thick boards or high moisture. For THT plastic packages, apply the same MSL logic as SMT. Bake before assembly if the board or component has exceeded its qualified exposure or shows moisture indicators. For plated through holes, confirm that bake temperature does not damage solder mask, silkscreen, or plated features.

theory.h: Records that make the decision auditable
theory.p: Record lot or reel ID, MSL, package type, dry pack open date and time, humidity indicator card reading, desiccant status, dry cabinet RH, bake start and end, bake temperature, bake humidity if controlled, operator, and disposition. If a batch is released without bake, record the remaining floor life and the planned reflow window. If baked, record the bake recipe and any reflow qualification result. Keep the record with the lot so the next shift can see whether the floor life is still valid.

theory.h: When to bake versus when to quarantine
theory.p: Bake when the batch has exceeded floor life, the dry pack or desiccant failed, the humidity indicator card is above the card threshold, or the dry cabinet was out of range. Quarantine when the MSL is unknown, the package is damaged, the bake recipe is not qualified for the package, or the device has already been reflowed and the supplier requires requalification. Avoid baking a package that cannot tolerate the temperature or time; use a qualified lower-temperature dry storage or return to supplier. The goal is to prevent moisture flashing during reflow, not to create an extra handling step.

calc.task: A batch of IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D MSL 4 ICs in tape and reel was opened 50 h ago. The dry cabinet is not qualified for floor-life suspension, so all storage time counts. The planned reflow window starts in 30 h. Decide whether bake is required and specify a tape-and-reel bake condition.
calc.solution: 1. Use IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D floor life for MSL 4: 72 h. 2. Counted exposure = 50 h. 3. Remaining floor life = 72 h - 50 h = 22 h. 4. Planned delay = 30 h. Since 30 h exceeds 22 h, bake is required before reflow. 5. A tape-and-reel bake cannot exceed 40°C, and at 40°C the J-STD-033 Table 4-1 time for a body up to 1.4 mm is about 9 days, which does not fit a 30 h window. Either move the reflow inside the remaining floor life, suspend the clock in a qualified dry cabinet at 10% RH or less, or de-reel, bake loose parts at 125°C for 8 h and re-reel; verify the chosen route against the J-STD-033D bake table, the tape datasheet and the reflow window. 6. Record lot ID, bake start and end, temperature, operator, and reflow qualification if required.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several QFN packages show lifted leads, voided solder joints, and one package has a visible crack; the lot had been stored in a dry cabinet with a logged RH of 18% while the setpoint was 10%.
defect.cause: The IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D MSL 4 floor life was exceeded because the dry cabinet excursion was not treated as exposure; moisture in the package flashed during reflow.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, verify MSL and open date, bake per a qualified tape-and-reel recipe, requalify reflow, repair the cabinet, and add alarm and log review.

title: The ESD control program: EPA, grounding, straps, mats, ionizers, packaging

goals.text: Audit an ESD protected area against a control checklist and rank the gaps by risk.

blocks.alt: A plan view of a workbench inside a marked EPA boundary with a grounded mat, wrist strap, ionizer, shielding bag and tote, and a signage post
blocks.caption: The ESD control program: protected area boundary, grounding, straps, mats, ionizers and packaging

theory.p: An ESD control program is a management system, not a collection of gadgets. In storage, the protected area is defined by the materials handled, the sensitivity of the parts, the packaging in use, and the people and equipment that move them. ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340-5-1 both require a documented program with written procedures, training, qualification, and periodic audit. For storage, the audit should start with the control plan and then verify that the physical area matches the plan: EPA boundaries, entry controls, grounding provisions, packaging inventory, ionizer coverage where needed, and records. If the plan is missing or stale, the first gap is programmatic, not hardware.

Grounding in an EPA is about controlling charge removal and keeping conductive items at a common potential. The common ground reference should be traceable to a building electrical ground or another qualified reference, and the bonding network should be continuous and inspectable. ANSI/ESD S6.1 addresses grounding and equipotential bonding; use it to verify that racks, carts, shelving, tables, and floor systems are bonded as required by the control plan. In storage, a common failure is a cart or rack that appears grounded at one point but is isolated by casters, plastic feet, painted contact surfaces, or a broken bonding jumper. Measure or inspect according to the program method and verify against the equipment datasheet and site electrical safety requirements.

theory.h: Personnel grounding: straps, footwear, and floor systems
theory.p: Personnel grounding can be achieved with wrist straps, footwear/floor systems, or a combination, depending on the task and the control plan. Wrist straps are governed by ANSI/ESD S1.1 and are typically used at static controlled workstations; footwear/floor systems are qualified using ANSI/ESD STM97.1 and ANSI/ESD STM97.2. In storage, wrist straps may be impractical for pallet movement, but they are still relevant at receiving inspection, kitting, or rework benches. The audit should check that the selected method is appropriate for the task, that the strap or footwear is worn correctly, that the floor is qualified for the footwear, and that the system is tested at the required interval. If the plan allows exceptions, document the risk basis and compensating controls.

Static dissipative or conductive mats are used where personnel handle ESD-sensitive items on a bench or staging surface. ANSI/ESD S4.1 covers static dissipative mats, and surface resistance or resistivity can be characterized using ANSI/ESD STM11.11. In storage, mats are often misused: they are placed on insulating shelves, connected to ground through a damaged cord, or used as general-purpose work surfaces without a defined ground path. The audit should verify that the mat is connected to the EPA ground reference through the required resistor or bonding method, that the connection is intact, and that the mat is not bypassed by insulating packaging, tape, or plastic trays. Verify resistance limits against the mat datasheet and the site control plan.

theory.h: Ionization for isolated conductors and insulators
theory.p: Ionizers neutralize charge on isolated conductors and insulators that cannot be grounded. ANSI/ESD STM3.1 covers ionization, and performance qualification and periodic verification are evaluated against the offset-voltage (balance) and discharge-time limits in that method, which is the ESDA counterpart of IEC 61340-4-7. Footwear and flooring systems, by contrast, are qualified under ANSI/ESD STM97.1 and STM97.2. In storage, ionizers are often installed at unpacking, kitting, or inspection stations where plastic bags, foam, labels, or tape create charge. The audit should check placement, airflow, balance, and maintenance because ionization is ineffective if the ion stream is blocked, the emitter points are dirty, or the unit is not balanced. Verify balance and discharge time against the ionizer datasheet and the program acceptance criteria.

Packaging is a primary control in storage because parts may spend hours or days in containers. ANSI/ESD S541 covers ESD packaging, including shielding bags, conductive containers, and closure methods. The audit should verify that the packaging class matches the part sensitivity and the storage environment, that shielding bags are closed and not damaged, and that containers are compatible with the EPA grounding scheme. A common storage gap is placing a shielding bag on an insulating shelf and assuming the bag protects the contents from all fields; shielding reduces electrostatic field exposure, but the package must be handled and stored according to its qualification. Verify package type, closure, and storage configuration against the packaging datasheet and the control plan.

An effective audit uses a checklist tied to the control plan and records evidence: photos, serial numbers, test dates, and operator observations. Rank gaps by risk using exposure, sensitivity, and detectability. High risk is a gap that affects many sensitive parts, is repeated daily, and is not detected by downstream inspection. Medium risk is a localized gap with limited exposure or partial detection. Low risk is a documentation or housekeeping gap with little direct charge-transfer path. The output should be a corrective action list with owner, due date, and verification method, not just a list of nonconformances.

calc.task: Audit a storage EPA with 12 checklist items. Each item is scored 0 to 3 for control strength, where 0 is absent, 1 is present but unverified, 2 is verified but has a minor gap, and 3 is fully compliant. Exposure is scored 1 to 5 based on daily part movement through the control. Sensitivity is scored 1 to 5 based on the most sensitive part family stored in the area. Calculate a risk score for each gap as (3 - control strength) x exposure x sensitivity, then rank the top three gaps.
calc.solution: Step 1: Record the control strength, exposure, and sensitivity for each gap. Example gap A: grounding jumper on rack missing, control strength 0, exposure 5, sensitivity 4. Risk score = (3 - 0) x 5 x 4 = 60. Example gap B: wrist strap tester not used for one shift, control strength 1, exposure 3, sensitivity 4. Risk score = (3 - 1) x 3 x 4 = 24. Example gap C: ionizer balance record missing, control strength 1, exposure 4, sensitivity 3. Risk score = (3 - 1) x 4 x 3 = 24. Example gap D: shielding bag closure not inspected at receiving, control strength 2, exposure 5, sensitivity 5. Risk score = (3 - 2) x 5 x 5 = 25. Example gap E: mat ground cord damaged at one bench, control strength 0, exposure 2, sensitivity 5. Risk score = (3 - 0) x 2 x 5 = 30. Step 2: Rank by risk score. Gap A is highest at 60. Gap E is next at 30. Gap D is next at 25. Gaps B and C tie at 24 and can be ranked by exposure or sensitivity; if exposure is prioritized, Gap C ranks above Gap B. Step 3: Convert to actions. Gap A requires immediate bonding repair and retest. Gap E requires bench isolation and mat ground repair. Gap D requires receiving inspection update and package closure check. Step 4: Verify closure by re-audit or test record, not only by visual confirmation.

defect.symptom: Incoming inspection finds intermittent ESD damage on a small number of connectors from a storage rack, while the same part family is acceptable when staged on a grounded bench.
defect.cause: The rack is bonded at one corner, but the shelf surface is painted or coated, and parts are placed in shielding bags that are not closed. The rack appears grounded, but the bags and shelf create an isolated charge path, and the open bags allow field exposure during movement.
defect.action: Isolate the rack, verify the bonding path to the EPA ground reference, clean or replace the shelf contact surfaces, require closed shielding bags for stored parts, and requalify the rack storage configuration against the control plan. Add a rack bonding check to the shift audit and verify closure with a follow-up inspection of the affected part family.

title: Case: expired floor life found mid-lot

goals.text: Decide whether a batch must be baked, specify the bake/dry-storage condition and justify it by package type.
Contain a moisture or ESD exposure breach and define the traceability range.

blocks.alt: A partially used reel with a floor-life clock past its limit and a red warning flag, beside a decision flow with bake, material review board and scrap branches
blocks.caption: Case: expired floor life found mid-lot — exposure clock past its limit, and the bake / MRB / scrap decision

theory.h: Floor life is a clock, not a label
theory.p: A moisture-sensitive device starts consuming floor life when its moisture barrier bag is opened and the device is exposed to ambient air. The clock is governed by the moisture sensitivity level assigned under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 and the handling rules in IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 defines floor life at reference conditions of 30 °C and 60% RH, so a hot, humid storage area can consume the clock faster than a controlled dry cabinet. When the clock expires, the batch is not automatically scrap; it is a process deviation that must be contained before reflow. The first question is not whether the part looks acceptable, but whether the exposure history is known, whether the remaining floor life is sufficient for the planned reflow, and whether the package type can be baked safely.

theory.h: Decide whether the batch must be baked
theory.p: Compare elapsed floor life with the floor life for the device level in IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. If elapsed time exceeds the allowed floor life and reflow is planned, bake before reflow unless the component manufacturer provides a documented exception. If dry storage is used, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 uses a dry storage target of 5% RH or less; if the cabinet runs above that, treat the devices as exposed and recalculate floor life. If the device is classified as the lowest moisture sensitivity level under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, baking is usually not required unless contamination, handling damage, or a customer requirement says otherwise. If floor life has not been exceeded and dry storage is compliant, the batch can normally proceed, but the storage record must be complete.

For moisture-sensitive devices, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 provides bake conditions that depend on the carrier and the maximum temperature allowed by the component. For loose parts in trays, tubes or waffle packs whose carriers and components are rated for it, the 125 °C column of the bake table is indexed to package body thickness: 8 h for a body up to 1.4 mm, 18 h for 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 48 h for 2.0 to 4.5 mm. The 24 h figure sometimes quoted for a 125 °C bake is the supplier dry-pack condition, not a user bake, so do not use it as a production recipe. For tape and reel, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 also provides a lower-temperature long bake at 40 °C, roughly 9 days for a body up to 1.4 mm, 11 days for 1.4 to 2.0 mm and 38 days for 2.0 to 4.5 mm, because the tape, reel, labels and cover tape cannot tolerate higher temperature. Cumulative bake time above 90 °C is limited to 96 h unless the supplier states otherwise. Justify the condition by package type: polymer tape and reels can deform, labels can lift, and cover tape can shift at high temperature. Verify the chosen condition against the component datasheet, carrier datasheet, and oven capability.

After baking, store the batch in a dry cabinet at 5% RH or less under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, or repackage it in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. The floor-life clock is reset only when the bake, dry storage, and packaging conditions are met and documented; otherwise the original exposure remains part of the batch history. Dry cabinets need calibrated humidity sensors and logged RH, not just a setpoint. If the cabinet RH rises above the target, the exposure clock may resume or the prior exposure may remain unresolved. For practice-based dry cabinet setpoints, alarm limits, and bake durations, verify against your equipment datasheet and your moisture control procedure.

If expired floor life is found mid-lot, stop feeding the affected reels, trays, or tubes and quarantine all devices from the same lot, date code, vacuum bag, dry cabinet, and handling window. Do not reflow the affected batch until the bake decision is made and documented. Record the MSL, lot code, date code, serial or reel identifiers, open time, elapsed floor life, dry cabinet RH, temperature, storage location, and planned reflow time. If some devices were already reflowed, isolate the boards and assess them with electrical test, X-ray, cross-section, or failure analysis as needed. The containment should be conservative enough to cover commingled lots and incomplete records.

If an ESD control failure is found in storage or staging, quarantine devices and boards in the EPA during the breach window. ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340-5-1 require an EPA with controls such as grounded personnel, ESD protective packaging, verified work surfaces, and controlled handling. Check wrist strap logs, floor and surface resistance records, ionizer status, packaging type, and operator training. ESD damage can be latent, so visual inspection alone may not reveal the problem. If the breach is discovered after assembly, trace the boards handled in the EPA from the last verified control check to the discovery time, then widen the range if records are incomplete.

The traceability range should include all units with the same lot or date code, same storage location, same dry cabinet, same vacuum bag, same shift, same feeder, same work order, same reflow oven, and same reflow profile. For ESD breaches, include all boards handled in the EPA during the breach window, plus feeders, magazines, conveyors, bins, packaging, and any adjacent lots that may have been commingled. If the storage system uses bins without full serial control, widen the range to the full bin, full lot, or full shift. The goal is to bound the exposure with evidence, not to guess the smallest possible population.

The line decision is usually one of three outcomes: bake and repackage if the package type allows it, scrap if baking is not allowed or the package is damaged, or release only after the bake record, dry storage record, and traceability disposition are complete. Document the deviation, containment, bake condition, dry storage RH, reflow qualification, and final disposition. For practice-based values such as cabinet alarm limits, bake loading density, and reflow scheduling windows, verify against your equipment datasheet and your process control plan. The decision should be defensible from the exposure record, the package type, and the reflow plan.

calc.task: A lot of MSL3 QFN devices in tape and reel is found mid-lot with expired floor life. The lot has 12 reels, each with 500 units. The vacuum bag was opened 200 h before the planned reflow. The dry cabinet RH was 7% RH at 28 °C. Two reels were placed on feeders and 180 boards were populated. An ESD wrist strap alarm was also found disabled for 4 h in the same storage area. Decide whether the batch must be baked, specify the bake and dry-storage condition by package type, and define the traceability range.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify the moisture sensitivity level. The devices are MSL3 under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, and the floor-life rules come from IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Step 2: Compare elapsed floor life with IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. MSL3 floor life is 168 h at 30 °C and 60% RH. Elapsed time is 200 h, so the floor life is exceeded by 32 h. Step 3: Check dry storage. IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 uses a dry storage target of 5% RH or less. The cabinet was at 7% RH, so the storage condition is not compliant and the exposure cannot be treated as controlled dry storage. Step 4: Decide whether to bake. Because floor life is exceeded and reflow is planned, bake before reflow unless the component manufacturer provides a documented exception. Step 5: Select bake condition by package type. The package is tape and reel, which contains polymer tape, reel, cover tape, and labels. If the carrier cannot withstand 125 °C, use the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 lower-temperature long bake at 40 °C, which is roughly 9 days for a body up to 1.4 mm and therefore does not fit a short reflow window. If the component and carrier datasheets allow 125 °C, the IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 125 °C column applies only to loose parts in trays or tubes and is indexed to body thickness: 8 h up to 1.4 mm, 18 h for 1.4 to 2.0 mm, 48 h for 2.0 to 4.5 mm. For this case, choose the 40 °C long bake as the conservative tape-and-reel condition, or de-reel, bake the loose parts at 125 °C for the thickness-indexed time and re-reel; verify the chosen route against the J-STD-033 bake table, the tape datasheet and the reflow window. Step 6: Define post-bake storage. Store at 5% RH or less under IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, or repackage in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. Step 7: Calculate affected device count. 12 reels x 500 units per reel = 6000 units. Step 8: Define moisture traceability range. Include all 12 reels, the same lot and date code, the same vacuum bag, the same dry cabinet, the same storage location, the same shift, the two reels on feeders, the 180 populated boards, the feeders, the placement program, the reflow oven, the reflow profile, the work order, the incoming lot, the operator, and the storage RH records. Step 9: Define ESD traceability range. Because the wrist strap alarm was disabled for 4 h, include all devices and boards handled in the EPA during those 4 h, plus the same lot, storage location, feeders, magazines, conveyors, bins, packaging, and work orders. If records are incomplete, widen to the full shift or full lot. Step 10: Disposition. Quarantine the 6000 units, bake the unreflowed units under the selected condition, repackage or store under compliant dry storage, and disposition the 180 boards through electrical test and failure analysis as needed.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several boards show intermittent opens and lifted leads, and X-ray shows voiding or cracking near the QFN package body on boards that used the expired-floor-life reels.
defect.cause: MSL3 tape and reel devices exceeded IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 floor life, the dry cabinet ran above the 5% RH target, and the batch was fed to placement without a bake decision or traceability containment.
defect.action: Stop the line, quarantine all reels from the same lot, date code, vacuum bag, and dry cabinet, and isolate the affected boards. Do not reflow the remaining batch. Bake the unreflowed devices using an IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033 condition allowed by the tape and reel carrier, then store at 5% RH or less or repackage with desiccant and a humidity indicator card. Trace all boards from the affected reels, feeders, work order, reflow oven, and shift, and disposition them through electrical test, X-ray, and failure analysis.

title: The paste volume budget: what the joint needs before the aperture is drawn

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.

theory.h: Paste volume is a joint requirement, not an aperture afterthought
theory.p: Before drawing an aperture, define the joint: pad geometry, component termination, target standoff, acceptable fillet, and the paste volume needed to wet the termination and form a reliable joint. The aperture must deliver enough paste to meet that requirement while staying within the pad so reflow does not create bridges. Stencil thickness, paste rheology, print speed, squeegee pressure, separation speed, and cleaning cycle all affect how much paste actually transfers. Treat the aperture as a volume source and the print process as a transfer mechanism.

blocks.caption: Geometry of paste release from a stencil aperture

blocks.alt: Stencil aperture cross-section with the aperture opening and the four sidewall faces distinguished, the area ratio and aspect ratio formulas with their minima, and a fine-pitch example
blocks.caption: Stencil aperture geometry: area ratio = aperture area / sidewall area, aspect ratio = aperture width / foil thickness, and what fine pitch does to both

theory.h: Area ratio compares paste contact area to wall adhesion
theory.p: Area ratio is the aperture area divided by the sidewall area of the stencil wall. For a rectangular aperture, sidewall area is the perimeter multiplied by stencil thickness, so area ratio equals length times width divided by perimeter times thickness. A higher area ratio gives the paste a larger bottom contact area relative to the wall area that can hold it in the aperture. IPC-7525 stencil design guidelines are commonly referenced for release indicators; a common working target is an area ratio above about 0.66, but verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Aspect ratio describes how deep and narrow the aperture is
theory.p: Aspect ratio is aperture width divided by stencil thickness. For rectangular apertures, use the smaller dimension because that dimension controls the narrowest release path. A low aspect ratio means a deep, narrow hole where paste can adhere to the sidewalls and fail to release cleanly. IPC-7525 stencil design guidelines are commonly referenced for release indicators; a common working target is an aspect ratio above about 1.5, but verify against your paste and equipment datasheet. Fine-pitch designs may fall below this target and require process or paste changes.

theory.h: Deposit volume is nominal aperture volume times transfer efficiency
theory.p: The nominal deposit volume is the aperture area multiplied by stencil thickness. The expected deposit volume is that nominal volume multiplied by transfer efficiency, which accounts for paste left in the aperture, paste smeared during separation, and paste not fully released. Transfer efficiency is process dependent and should be measured or taken from paste and equipment data. Use a measured value when possible; if a single value is needed for planning, use a conservative value from your paste datasheet or a recent print trial.

theory.h: The joint needs a volume target before the aperture is drawn
theory.p: Estimate the required paste volume from the pad area, desired deposit height, component termination geometry, and paste manufacturer guidance. For chip components, the deposit should be enough to wet the termination and form a fillet, but not so large that adjacent pads bridge during reflow. For larger pads, volume can be adjusted by aperture area, stencil thickness, or step stencil design. The calculated expected deposit volume should be compared with the required volume before committing to the aperture.

theory.h: Geometry changes can improve release without changing the pad
theory.p: If area ratio or aspect ratio is low, consider reducing stencil thickness, enlarging the aperture within the pad, using a paste with better release characteristics, or changing print parameters. Electropolished walls, laser-cut shape, wall taper, and step stencils can also help. These changes trade off volume, release, and bridging risk, so evaluate them with print trials and inspection data rather than relying on a single ratio.

Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, nominal volume, and expected deposit volume. If the ratios meet the release indicators from your applicable design guideline and the expected volume meets the joint requirement, the aperture is likely to release adequately. If either ratio is low, the aperture may release poorly even if the nominal volume looks sufficient. If the volume is low, the joint may be underfilled even if release is good. Document the assumptions and verify with paste deposit measurement.

calc.task: A small chip resistor has a 0.50 mm by 0.40 mm pad. Stencil thickness is 0.12 mm. Use a transfer efficiency of 0.90. Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, nominal deposit volume, and expected deposit volume. State whether release is adequate using the IPC-7525 release indicators.
calc.solution: Aperture area = 0.50 mm x 0.40 mm = 0.20 mm^2. Perimeter = 0.50 mm + 0.40 mm + 0.50 mm + 0.40 mm = 1.80 mm. Sidewall area = 1.80 mm x 0.12 mm = 0.216 mm^2. Area ratio = 0.20 mm^2 / 0.216 mm^2 = 0.926. Aspect ratio = smaller aperture dimension / stencil thickness = 0.40 mm / 0.12 mm = 3.33. Nominal deposit volume = 0.20 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.024 mm^3. Expected deposit volume = 0.024 mm^3 x 0.90 = 0.0216 mm^3. Release adequacy: area ratio 0.926 is above about 0.66 and aspect ratio 3.33 is above about 1.5, so release is likely adequate. Compare 0.0216 mm^3 with the required joint volume from paste and component data; if it is lower, increase aperture area, reduce stencil thickness, or improve transfer efficiency.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several small chip components show insufficient solder fillet or opens on one side, while adjacent larger pads look normal.
defect.cause: The small aperture had low area ratio or aspect ratio, or transfer efficiency was lower than assumed, so the expected deposit volume was not delivered.
defect.action: Measure paste deposit volume, compare with required joint volume, reduce stencil thickness or enlarge aperture within pad, adjust paste and print parameters, and re-run a print trial with inspection.

title: Area ratio and aspect ratio: definitions, calculation, fine-pitch consequences

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.

blocks.alt: Aperture cross-section with the area ratio and aspect ratio formulas, the sidewall area shown as perimeter times thickness, and a fine-pitch example with a low area ratio
blocks.caption: Area ratio and aspect ratio: area ratio = aperture area / sidewall area, aspect ratio = aperture width / foil thickness, and what fine pitch does to both

theory.p: Area ratio is the ratio of the aperture opening area to the sidewall area of the stencil aperture. For a simple rectangular aperture, the opening area is width times length, and the sidewall area is the perimeter multiplied by foil thickness. IPC-7525D treats area ratio as a key indicator of paste release because the paste must separate from the sidewalls and transfer to the pad.

A higher area ratio generally means the paste has a larger opening area relative to the wall area it must release from, which tends to improve transfer. A low area ratio means the sidewall contact area is large compared with the opening, so paste can stick in the aperture and leave insufficient deposit on the pad. IPC-7525D provides area-ratio guidance for stencil design, but the practical release limit depends on paste rheology, stencil wall finish, print speed, snap-off distance, and squeegee pressure; verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Aspect ratio is the aperture dimension divided by foil thickness. For a rectangular aperture, the smallest aperture dimension is usually used because it controls the narrowest paste channel. IPC-7525D discusses aspect ratio as a stencil geometry parameter related to paste release and aperture wall effects.

As pitch decreases, aperture dimensions shrink while foil thickness may remain relatively large, increasing aspect ratio and reducing area ratio. High aspect ratio apertures can make paste release more sensitive to print parameters and wall condition. For fine-pitch designs, aspect ratio should be reviewed together with area ratio, paste type, and SPI results rather than treated as a single pass/fail number.

The theoretical maximum paste deposit volume is aperture area multiplied by foil thickness. The expected deposited volume is lower because paste does not transfer perfectly; it is commonly estimated by multiplying theoretical volume by a transfer efficiency factor. Transfer efficiency should come from your paste, stencil, printer, and SPI data, not from a generic assumption.

Fine-pitch apertures can produce low area ratio, high aspect ratio, and small deposit volume at the same time. This can lead to insufficient paste for the joint, voids, opens, or inconsistent transfer. It can also increase sensitivity to paste slump, stencil wear, wall roughness, and print parameter drift.

A paste release decision should combine area ratio, aspect ratio, expected deposit volume, and process data. If area ratio is near or below the IPC-7525D guidance range, or if expected volume is close to the minimum needed for the component and pad, the design should be reviewed for foil thickness, aperture size within the pad, wall finish, paste selection, and print parameters.

calc.task: A rectangular stencil aperture is 0.25 mm by 0.25 mm, and the foil thickness is 0.10 mm. Calculate the area ratio, aspect ratio, theoretical deposit volume, and expected deposit volume using an assumed transfer efficiency of 0.85. State whether the aperture is expected to release paste adequately according to common IPC-7525D area-ratio guidance.
calc.solution: 1. Aperture area = width × length = 0.25 mm × 0.25 mm = 0.0625 mm². 2. Aperture perimeter = 2 × (width + length) = 2 × (0.25 mm + 0.25 mm) = 1.00 mm. 3. Sidewall area = perimeter × foil thickness = 1.00 mm × 0.10 mm = 0.10 mm². 4. Area ratio = aperture area / sidewall area = 0.0625 mm² / 0.10 mm² = 0.625. 5. Aspect ratio = smallest aperture dimension / foil thickness = 0.25 mm / 0.10 mm = 2.5. 6. Theoretical deposit volume = aperture area × foil thickness = 0.0625 mm² × 0.10 mm = 0.00625 mm³. 7. Expected deposit volume = theoretical volume × transfer efficiency = 0.00625 mm³ × 0.85 = 0.0053125 mm³. 8. In nanoliters, 0.0053125 mm³ × 1000 nL/mm³ = 5.3125 nL. 9. The area ratio is 0.625, which is below the commonly cited IPC-7525D area-ratio guidance value of 0.66. Therefore, paste release is expected to be marginal to inadequate for robust production unless supported by SPI data, paste datasheet, and print parameter validation. 10. Possible actions include reducing foil thickness, increasing aperture dimensions within the pad boundary, improving stencil wall finish, selecting a paste with better release characteristics, or optimizing print speed, pressure, and snap-off distance.

defect.symptom: After reflow, fine-pitch components show intermittent opens, voids, or insufficient solder joints, and stencil apertures retain paste residue after printing.
defect.cause: The aperture area ratio is too low for reliable paste release, often because the aperture is small relative to foil thickness and sidewall area. Rough or worn stencil walls, inappropriate paste rheology, or print parameters that do not support release can worsen the problem.
defect.action: Review the aperture area ratio and aspect ratio against IPC-7525D guidance and your paste/equipment datasheet. Reduce foil thickness or increase aperture size within the pad if allowed, improve stencil wall finish, verify paste selection, and optimize print parameters. Confirm the result with SPI and reflow inspection.

title: Foil, thickness, step stencils, laser cut and wall finish

goals.text: Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for a given pad stack and pitch, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.

blocks.alt: Cross-sections of a plain foil, a step stencil with two thicknesses, a rough laser-cut wall and a smooth electropolished wall
blocks.caption: Foil, thickness, step stencils, laser cut and wall finish — how the foil and its walls set the deposit

theory.h: Foil thickness sets paste volume and release risk
theory.p: Foil thickness is the primary control on deposited paste volume: for a given aperture, volume is approximately aperture area times foil thickness. Thicker foil can help large pads, thermal relief, and high-volume joints, but it increases the chance of paste slumping, bridging, and poor release on fine-pitch apertures. Choose foil from the supplier's available range, commonly 0.075 mm to 0.200 mm, and verify against your paste rheology, printer, and SPI capability.

theory.h: Aperture geometry must support paste release
theory.p: Useful release checks include area ratio and aspect ratio. Area ratio is aperture area divided by the product of aperture perimeter and foil thickness; IPC-7525 commonly uses a minimum area ratio of 0.66 for reliable paste release. Aspect ratio is aperture width divided by foil thickness; IPC-7525 commonly uses a minimum aspect ratio of 1.5. These are design guidelines, not guarantees, because paste type, wall finish, and print speed also matter.

theory.h: Pad stack and pitch drive the thickness choice
theory.p: For a given pad stack, start with the tightest pitch on the board. Fine-pitch QFP, QFN, and BGA pads usually need a thinner foil or a local thin step to keep aperture walls close enough to control paste shape. Larger pads and thermal pads may need more paste volume, so a thicker local step can be used where pitch is generous. If the board has mixed features, decide whether a single foil thickness can satisfy the requirements or whether a step stencil is required.

theory.h: Aperture size is usually reduced from the pad
theory.p: A full-pad aperture can produce excess paste and bridging on closely spaced pads, while an aperture that is too small can leave insufficient solder and cause opens. Many processes use a modest aperture reduction, often a few percent to tens of percent of the pad dimension, depending on paste slump, reflow profile, and pad finish; verify against your paste and equipment datasheet. For rectangular pads, keep the reduction balanced so the paste deposit remains centered and does not favor a lead.

theory.h: Step stencils separate conflicting paste-volume needs
theory.p: A step stencil changes foil thickness locally, allowing a thin area for fine-pitch apertures and a thicker area for large pads or thermal pads. The step should be placed where it does not disturb the support of nearby fine-pitch apertures, and the transition should be far enough from sensitive features to avoid paste leakage or uneven squeegee support. Confirm the stencil maker's minimum step size, transition method, and maximum step height; these are process limits, not universal values.

theory.h: Laser cut and wall finish affect release and bridging
theory.p: Laser cut apertures can be produced with controlled wall taper and finish. Rough or irregular walls can hold paste, increase residue, and make release less repeatable, while an overly aggressive taper can change the effective aperture at the top and bottom of the foil. Ask for the wall finish and taper specification your stencil maker can control, such as electropolished or coated walls, and verify with SPI and print inspection rather than assuming a finish will solve a geometry problem.

A practical sequence is: identify the tightest pitch and paste-volume requirements; choose a base foil thickness; size apertures to meet IPC-7525 area-ratio and aspect-ratio guidelines while controlling paste volume; add a step only when a single thickness cannot meet fine-pitch and large-pad needs; then run a print trial with SPI. Adjust aperture size before changing foil thickness when possible, because aperture changes are usually cheaper and faster to iterate.

calc.task: A board has 0.40 mm x 0.40 mm QFP pads on 0.50 mm pitch and a 1.00 mm x 1.00 mm thermal pad. Select a base foil thickness and aperture size for the fine-pitch pads, select a local step thickness for the thermal pad, and check the IPC-7525 area-ratio and aspect-ratio guidelines.
calc.solution: Start with the tightest pitch: 0.50 mm pitch QFP pads. Choose a base foil thickness of 0.100 mm to limit paste volume and reduce bridging risk; verify that the paste datasheet supports this thickness for the chosen aperture. Reduce the 0.40 mm pad to a 0.38 mm x 0.38 mm aperture to lower bridging risk while retaining paste volume. Calculate area ratio for the fine-pitch aperture: area = 0.38 mm x 0.38 mm = 0.1444 mm^2; perimeter = 1.52 mm; area ratio = 0.1444 mm^2 / (1.52 mm x 0.100 mm) = 0.95. This is above the IPC-7525 guideline of 0.66. Calculate aspect ratio: 0.38 mm / 0.100 mm = 3.8. This is above the IPC-7525 guideline of 1.5. For the 1.00 mm x 1.00 mm thermal pad, choose a local step thickness of 0.150 mm to increase paste volume without thickening the entire stencil. Use a 0.95 mm x 0.95 mm aperture. Check the thermal pad area ratio: area = 0.95 mm x 0.95 mm = 0.9025 mm^2; perimeter = 3.80 mm; area ratio = 0.9025 mm^2 / (3.80 mm x 0.150 mm) = 1.58, above the IPC-7525 guideline of 0.66. Aspect ratio = 0.95 mm / 0.150 mm = 6.33, above the IPC-7525 guideline of 1.5. Place the step transition away from the 0.50 mm pitch QFP apertures and confirm the stencil maker can hold the step and wall finish. Run SPI to verify paste volume, bridging, and release before production.

defect.symptom: Bridging appears between adjacent fine-pitch QFP leads after reflow, with excess paste visible between leads on SPI.
defect.cause: The foil thickness or aperture size was selected for larger pads and is too aggressive for the fine-pitch area; rough or poorly controlled laser-cut walls can also reduce paste release and leave paste residue between apertures.
defect.action: Reduce the fine-pitch aperture size, then reduce local foil thickness or add a thin step if volume is still too high. Recheck area ratio and aspect ratio against IPC-7525, request a smoother wall finish or verified taper from the stencil maker, and rerun SPI to confirm the change.

title: Aperture geometry by component: chip, QFP fine pitch, QFN/LGA, BGA

goals.text: Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for a given pad stack and pitch, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.

blocks.alt: Four aperture shapes side by side with a label for each component family and the deposit each produces
blocks.caption: Aperture geometry by component: chip, fine-pitch QFP, QFN/LGA and BGA

theory.h: Pad stack and stencil thickness trade-off
theory.p: Stencil foil thickness sets paste volume per aperture. For a given pad stack, choose thickness so released paste volume supports fillet and standoff without excess that causes bridging or insufficient paste that causes opens. Foil thickness is usually selected from the smallest pitch and smallest aperture in the assembly, then checked against larger components. Common foil thicknesses are 0.10 mm to 0.15 mm for fine-pitch work and 0.12 mm to 0.18 mm for mixed boards; verify against stencil supplier capability and paste datasheet. IPC-7525 provides stencil design guidance for thickness, aperture area, and sidewall finish.

theory.h: Chip components: aperture area and paste balance
theory.p: For chip resistors and capacitors, aperture geometry should match pad size but allow paste to form a wettable fillet. A common starting point is aperture area equal to 80% to 100% of pad area for many chip sizes, with reduced area for the smallest components to prevent tombstoning and bridging. For the smallest chip components, aperture width may be 0.10 mm to 0.15 mm and length 0.20 mm to 0.30 mm, but final values should be verified against IPC-7525, land pattern data from IPC-7351, and paste release behavior. If the pad stack has a large copper area, reduce aperture area to avoid excessive paste volume and solder balling.

theory.h: QFP fine pitch: area ratio and sidewall control
theory.p: For QFP and other gull-wing fine-pitch packages, the aperture must release enough paste to wet the lead foot while leaving solder mask clearance between adjacent pads. Area ratio, defined as aperture opening area divided by aperture wall area, is a useful control; IPC-7525 discusses area-ratio effects on paste release. A practical target is an area ratio of 0.66 or higher for small apertures, with sidewall polish and paste viscosity adjusted when the ratio is lower. For pitches below 0.5 mm, reduce aperture width relative to pad width, use trapezoidal or rounded apertures, and verify against IPC-7525 and paste datasheet to prevent bridging.

theory.h: QFN and LGA: peripheral pads and thermal pad escape
theory.p: QFN and LGA packages often have peripheral pads plus a central thermal pad. The peripheral apertures should be sized to prevent coplanarity defects and bridging, while the center pad aperture should be segmented or reduced to control paste volume and allow gas escape. A common approach is to divide the thermal pad into multiple small apertures with 0.10 mm to 0.20 mm spacing between segments, or to use a reduced-area pattern, and verify against IPC-7525 and the package land pattern guidance in IPC-7351. If the center pad is too large, trapped paste can cause voiding, non-wetting, or package lift; if too small, thermal performance and solder joint reliability may suffer.

theory.h: BGA: pitch, aperture area, and paste collapse
theory.p: For BGA, aperture geometry is governed by ball pitch, ball diameter, and paste collapse during reflow. IPC-7095 provides BGA design and assembly guidance, including paste deposition and land pattern considerations. Apertures are often smaller than the ball diameter to control paste volume and prevent bridging, especially at pitches of 0.5 mm and below. For larger pitches, aperture area may approach the land area, but paste rheology and reflow profile must be verified. Step stencils or local thickness changes can help when BGA pads share the board with fine-pitch components.

theory.h: Foil thickness selection for mixed component sets
theory.p: Select foil thickness by first identifying the smallest pitch and smallest aperture that must release paste reliably. A thinner foil reduces paste volume and helps prevent bridging on fine-pitch QFP, QFN, and BGA pads, but it can reduce paste volume for larger components and increase opens if the paste does not wet the pad. A thicker foil helps larger components and coplanarity, but increases bridging risk on fine pitch. When the board contains both fine-pitch and large components, consider a step stencil or local thickness change, and verify the transition location against IPC-7525 and stencil fabrication capability.

Aperture shape, sidewall finish, and aperture reduction are process controls, not just drawing choices. Rounded corners, trapezoidal apertures, and reduced-area patterns can improve release and reduce bridging, but they must be tested with the actual paste, squeegee pressure, and print speed. Use IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for solder joint inspection, and use paste volume measurement or two-dimensional or three-dimensional inspection to confirm that the printed deposit matches the intended aperture volume. For practice-based values such as area ratio targets, aperture reduction percentages, and foil thickness ranges, verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and first-article results.

theory.h: Mapping geometry choices to defect prevention
theory.p: Map each geometry choice to the defect it prevents: adequate area ratio and clean sidewalls prevent insufficient paste and opens; reduced aperture area and thinner foil prevent bridging on fine pitch; segmented center pads prevent voiding and lift on QFN/LGA; controlled BGA aperture area prevents paste collapse and bridging. The selection is a balance: the same foil thickness that prevents opens on a large pad may cause bridges on a 0.4 mm pitch QFP, so the final choice should be justified by the dominant defect risk and confirmed by inspection.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch QFP has land width 0.25 mm and land length 0.60 mm. The board also has 0.5 mm pitch BGA pads. Select foil thickness and aperture geometry for the QFP, and justify each choice by the defect it prevents.
calc.solution: 1. Identify the smallest pitch: 0.4 mm. Use IPC-7525 area-ratio guidance and choose a thin foil, 0.10 mm, to reduce paste volume and bridging risk. 2. Reduce aperture width to 0.22 mm and length to 0.55 mm to leave solder mask clearance and control volume. 3. Calculate area ratio: aperture area = 0.22 mm x 0.55 mm = 0.121 mm^2. Sidewall area = 2 x (0.22 mm + 0.55 mm) x 0.10 mm = 0.154 mm^2. Area ratio = 0.121 / 0.154 = 0.79. This is above the practical target of 0.66 associated with IPC-7525 area-ratio guidance, so release should be acceptable if sidewall finish and paste viscosity are verified. 4. Check paste volume: aperture area 0.121 mm^2 multiplied by foil thickness 0.10 mm gives 0.0121 mm^3 per aperture. For the 0.5 mm pitch BGA, verify that the same foil does not create insufficient paste; if needed, use a step stencil or local thickness change, and verify against IPC-7095 and paste datasheet. 5. Justify: thinner foil and reduced aperture prevent bridging between 0.4 mm pitch leads; adequate area ratio prevents opens from poor release; rounded corners reduce paste trapping and solder balls. 6. Inspect first article per IPC-A-610 and measure printed volume; adjust if bridges or opens appear.

defect.symptom: Solder bridges between adjacent QFP leads at 0.4 mm pitch after reflow; X-ray shows excess paste between leads.
defect.cause: Foil thickness 0.15 mm and aperture width equal to pad width produced high paste volume and poor release control; area ratio may be adequate but volume excessive.
defect.action: Reduce foil to 0.10 mm, reduce aperture width to 0.22 mm, use rounded or trapezoidal apertures, verify area ratio of at least 0.66 against IPC-7525, adjust paste viscosity and squeegee pressure, re-run first article and inspect per IPC-A-610.

title: Aperture calculator and drawing review

goals.text: Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio and expected deposit volume for an aperture and state whether it will release paste adequately.
Accept or reject a delivered stencil from its measurement report against the issued specification.

blocks.alt: A calculator panel taking pad geometry, foil thickness and wall condition and outputting area ratio, aspect ratio and volume, beside a stencil drawing review checklist
blocks.caption: Aperture calculator and drawing review — inputs, release metrics and the review checklist

theory.p: An aperture calculator converts the pad geometry, stencil foil thickness, and aperture wall condition into release metrics that can be reviewed before fabrication. The main metrics are area ratio, aspect ratio, and expected deposit volume. These values help the process engineer decide whether the stencil is likely to release paste adequately and whether the drawing needs revision before purchase.

Area ratio is the aperture opening area divided by the wall area that paste must release from. IPC-7525D recommends an area ratio above 0.66 for reliable paste release. Values below this may still work with some paste types, print speeds, squeegee pressures, and foil finishes, but they require qualification against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Aspect ratio is the aperture width divided by the foil thickness. For rectangular apertures, use the smaller dimension because it controls the release path. IPC-7525D recommends an aspect ratio above 1.5. Thick foil and small apertures reduce aspect ratio, which can increase paste sticking and incomplete transfer.

Wall taper affects how easily paste leaves the aperture. IPC-7525D recommends a wall taper in the range of 85 to 90 degrees, measured from the horizontal plane, because a slight taper reduces the effective wall area. Electropolishing, laser-drill condition, burrs, and clogging also affect release and should be reviewed on the drawing and measurement report.

Expected deposit volume starts with aperture area multiplied by foil thickness. A taper correction can be added when the bottom opening is smaller than the top opening. The paste volume actually transferred depends on transfer efficiency, which varies with paste rheology, print speed, squeegee pressure, and foil finish, so verify the value against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Drawing review should confirm aperture dimensions, tolerances, foil thickness, wall taper, fiducials, aperture-to-pad alignment, step or stair-step features, and paste type assumptions. The reviewer should also confirm that the measurement method and sample size in the supplier specification are sufficient to verify the delivered stencil.

theory.h: Accept or reject from the measurement report
theory.p: Acceptance is based on comparing measured values to the issued specification, not only to general guidelines. If a measured value is outside the issued tolerance, the stencil should be rejected or dispositioned through engineering unless a qualified deviation exists. Area ratio and aspect ratio below the qualified release limits should trigger review even if the aperture dimensions are within tolerance.

calc.task: A drawing specifies a square aperture 0.30 mm by 0.30 mm in a 0.120 mm thick foil. The issued specification requires area ratio at least 0.66, aspect ratio at least 1.5, foil thickness 0.120 mm plus or minus 0.010 mm, aperture size 0.30 mm plus or minus 0.02 mm, wall taper 85 to 90 degrees, and flatness no greater than 0.10 mm. A delivered stencil report gives measured aperture 0.295 mm by 0.298 mm, thickness 0.118 mm, area ratio 0.63, aspect ratio 2.5, wall taper 86 degrees, and flatness 0.08 mm. Calculate area ratio, aspect ratio, expected deposit volume, and accept or reject.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate nominal aperture area. Area = 0.30 mm x 0.30 mm = 0.090 mm2. Step 2: Calculate nominal perimeter. Perimeter = 4 x 0.30 mm = 1.20 mm. Step 3: Calculate nominal area ratio. Area ratio = aperture area / (perimeter x foil thickness) = 0.090 / (1.20 x 0.120) = 0.625. Step 4: Calculate nominal aspect ratio. Aspect ratio = aperture width / foil thickness = 0.30 / 0.120 = 2.5. Step 5: Calculate nominal deposit volume. Nominal volume = aperture area x foil thickness = 0.090 x 0.120 = 0.0108 mm3. Step 6: Apply a taper correction. For an 85 degree wall taper from horizontal, the wall angle from vertical is 5 degrees. Bottom side = 0.30 - 2 x 0.120 x tan(5 degrees) = 0.279 mm. Bottom area = 0.279 x 0.279 = 0.0778 mm2. Average area = (0.090 + 0.0778) / 2 = 0.0839 mm2. Tapered volume = 0.0839 x 0.120 = 0.0101 mm3. Step 7: Estimate expected paste deposit. Using an example transfer efficiency of 80 percent, expected deposit = 0.0101 x 0.80 = 0.0081 mm3. Verify transfer efficiency against your paste and equipment datasheet. Step 8: State release adequacy. The nominal area ratio 0.625 is below the IPC-7525D recommended value of 0.66, so paste release may be inadequate unless qualified by paste and equipment testing. Step 9: Review the delivered report. Thickness 0.118 mm is within 0.120 mm plus or minus 0.010 mm. Aperture 0.295 mm by 0.298 mm is within 0.30 mm plus or minus 0.02 mm. Aspect ratio 2.5 is above 1.5. Wall taper 86 degrees is within 85 to 90 degrees. Flatness 0.08 mm is within 0.10 mm. Step 10: Accept or reject. Reject the stencil against the issued specification because the measured area ratio 0.63 is below the required 0.66. Quarantine the stencil and disposition it through engineering, rework, or replacement.

defect.symptom: Fine-pitch QFN pads show low paste height, opens, or insufficient solder joints after a new stencil is introduced.
defect.cause: The aperture area ratio is below the qualified release limit because the aperture is small relative to the foil thickness, and the wall taper or wall finish is not adequate for the paste being used.
defect.action: Stop printing with the stencil, quarantine it, and verify aperture dimensions, foil thickness, wall taper, area ratio, and cleanliness. Reject or rework the stencil if it is outside the issued specification, then qualify the corrected design with SPI and cross-section before release.

title: Stencil acceptance, cleaning regime and lifetime tracking

goals.text: Accept or reject a delivered stencil from its measurement report against the issued specification.

blocks.alt: A stencil under measurement with a traceable report, a cleaning station, and a lifetime counter showing print cycles used
blocks.caption: Stencil acceptance, cleaning regime and lifetime tracking

theory.p: Treat the delivered stencil as a controlled part. Acceptance starts with a traceable measurement report that names the drawing revision, measurement method, operator, date, and serial number. Compare each reported value to the issued specification, not to a generic guideline. If the report omits a required characteristic, has no tolerance band, or shows an unapproved deviation, reject or hold until the supplier provides corrected data.

Review foil thickness, aperture width and length, wall taper, area ratio, step or stair-step depth, registration, tension, and flatness. For each item, confirm the reported value and the tolerance band. Where the specification is silent, use the design reference such as IPC-7525B and the paste or equipment datasheet, then document the accepted limit before release.

Area ratio and wall taper control paste release from the aperture. A low area ratio, poor wall taper, or damaged wall can leave paste in the aperture or cause smearing. For small apertures, verify the supplier's measured values against the paste datasheet and the printer's capability; do not accept a nominal design value if the measured geometry is marginal.

Foil thickness sets paste volume, while step or stair-step features allow different volumes on the same stencil. Check that thickness is within the issued tolerance and that step depth, location, and transition angle match the drawing. A thickness or step error can create insufficient or excessive paste even when apertures look correct.

Tension affects registration stability and contact with the board. Measure tension after fabrication and periodically during service. Flatness affects contact across the print area. Use the supplier's measurement method and the issued limit; if the specification does not define a limit, set a range from printer capability and paste process data, then verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

Define the cleaning method, chemistry, temperature, cycle time, rinse, and drying sequence in a controlled document. Ultrasonic, spray, immersion, and wipe methods differ in aggressiveness and residue removal. Verify the regime against your paste/equipment datasheet, and inspect apertures after cleaning before returning the stencil to service.

Track each stencil by serial number and log print cycles, paste exposure, cleaning cycles, cleaning method, inspection findings, tension, thickness, aperture wear, and step condition. Retirement should be based on measured drift, repeat defects, or failed inspection, not only on a fixed cycle count. Use trend data to set warning and reject limits for your process.

calc.task: Issued specification: foil thickness 0.120 mm +/-0.010 mm; aperture width 0.400 mm +/-0.025 mm; area ratio minimum 0.66 (issued spec, based on IPC-7525B guidance); wall taper minimum 85 deg; tension 25-35 N/cm; step depth 0.050 mm +/-0.010 mm. Measurement report: thickness 0.128 mm; aperture width 0.418 mm; area ratio 0.64; wall taper 87 deg; tension 28 N/cm; step depth 0.055 mm. Accept or reject and state reason.
calc.solution: Calculate foil thickness limits: 0.120 mm - 0.010 mm = 0.110 mm and 0.120 mm + 0.010 mm = 0.130 mm. Reported 0.128 mm is within 0.110-0.130 mm, so pass. Calculate aperture width limits: 0.400 mm - 0.025 mm = 0.375 mm and 0.400 mm + 0.025 mm = 0.425 mm. Reported 0.418 mm is within 0.375-0.425 mm, so pass. Compare area ratio: reported 0.64 is below the minimum 0.66, so fail. Compare wall taper: reported 87 deg is above the minimum 85 deg, so pass. Compare tension: reported 28 N/cm is within 25-35 N/cm, so pass. Calculate step depth limits: 0.050 mm - 0.010 mm = 0.040 mm and 0.050 mm + 0.010 mm = 0.060 mm. Reported 0.055 mm is within 0.040-0.060 mm, so pass. Overall result: reject or hold because area ratio fails. Request rework, replacement, or an engineering deviation only if process validation shows acceptable paste release.

defect.symptom: After a cleaning cycle, small apertures print thin or missing paste, and adjacent pads show smearing.
defect.cause: Cleaning regime left paste residue or damaged aperture walls; ultrasonic power, time, chemistry, or cleaning frequency was not qualified for the stencil and paste.
defect.action: Quarantine the stencil, inspect apertures under magnification, clean with a qualified method, re-measure area ratio and wall condition, and requalify cleaning frequency and dryness before release; if wall damage is found, retire or rework.

title: From aperture to deposit: how stencil geometry becomes paste volume

goals.text: Calculate the paste deposit volume from aperture geometry and evaluate SPI volume results against the joint requirement.

theory.p: Stencil aperture design controls how much solder paste is transferred to each pad and how cleanly the paste releases from the foil. The aperture must be large enough to deliver paste volume for the joint, but small enough to avoid bridging between adjacent pads. The design is a balance among pad geometry, paste rheology, foil thickness, print speed, squeegee pressure, and reflow behavior. For process engineers, the practical objective is to choose an aperture that produces repeatable paste deposits and predictable solder joints.
