title: Placement defect atlas: tombstone, skew, tilt, missing, wrong part, polarity

goals.text: Diagnose offset, skew, rotation, missing, wrong-part and polarity defects from measured data and name the mechanism.
Attribute a defect to placement rather than to printing or reflow using the evidence sequence.

blocks.alt: Six small board views labelled with each placement defect, shown beside a correctly placed component
blocks.caption: Placement defect atlas: tombstone, skew, tilt, missing, wrong part and polarity

theory.h: Evidence sequence before naming a mechanism
theory.p: Start with measured data, not with a visual guess. For each defect, record SPI paste volume and pad location, pre-reflow AOI component position and orientation, placement head logs, feeder slot and nozzle ID, reflow profile, and post-reflow AOI or X-ray. If the component is mispositioned before reflow while paste is centered and in volume, the mechanism is usually placement. If SPI shows paste offset, volume, or bridge before placement, printing is the primary suspect. If pre-reflow placement is correct but the component shifts, lifts, or rotates only after reflow, reflow wetting or thermal profile is the primary suspect. Tombstone can be a reflow wetting imbalance, but pre-reflow tilt or paste imbalance can make placement or printing contributory. Use pattern by feeder, nozzle, board location, and time to separate systematic placement faults from random handling faults.

Offset is the vector displacement of the component center from the land center. Measure X and Y from AOI, then calculate magnitude and direction. Common mechanisms are feeder pickup offset, tape pocket deformation, nozzle wear, vision calibration drift, board support sag, and tape peel force. If the offset vector is consistent in direction and magnitude for one feeder slot, suspect feeder pickup or tape pocket. If it is consistent by board location, suspect fiducial recognition, vision calibration, or support. If it is random across feeders and nozzles, suspect nozzle vacuum, component drop, or tape pocket release. Use your AOI limits and land geometry to set action limits; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet because acceptable offset depends on pad size, component tolerance, and reflow wetting.

Skew is angular misalignment of the component body relative to the land edges. Measure the angle from AOI and correlate it with nozzle ID, feeder slot, and component orientation. Mechanisms include rotation during pick, nozzle spin, component sitting crooked in a feeder pocket, tape pocket geometry, vision angle error, and placement head rotation error. Skew with offset often points to pick or feeder pocket; skew without offset can point to nozzle rotation or vision angle. If skew is present in pre-reflow AOI, attribute it to placement. If pre-reflow angle is acceptable and the component rotates during reflow, attribute it to reflow wetting imbalance or profile. Verify angle limits against your AOI program and equipment datasheet.

Tilt is a non-coplanar component body; tombstone is a severe tilt where one end lifts and the other remains wetted. Measure Z height, shadow, focus, and X-ray where needed. Mechanisms include nozzle height, component thickness variation, feeder pocket, board warp, paste height, and reflow surface tension. Pre-reflow tilt points to placement, nozzle, feeder, or board support. Pre-reflow paste imbalance points to printing. Correct pre-reflow placement and paste followed by lift after reflow points to reflow wetting imbalance, profile, or board warp. Tombstone is often called a reflow defect, but placement can contribute when the component is tilted, skewed, or placed on uneven paste. Verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and reflow profile.

Missing means the component is absent from the board. Mechanisms include empty feeder, pick failure, nozzle vacuum loss, component drop, vision reject, program skip, and tape pocket failure. Diagnostic sequence: check pick/place logs, feeder count, pre-reflow AOI, and post-reflow AOI. If the log shows no pick, suspect feeder empty, tape pocket, or feeder count. If the log shows pick but no place, suspect nozzle vacuum, component drop, or nozzle height. If the log shows place and pre-reflow AOI confirms the component, but it is missing after reflow, suspect reflow, transport, or handling. Verify feeder count and program against your BOM and equipment datasheet.

Wrong part means the placed component does not match the BOM, program, or expected electrical value. Mechanisms include feeder misload, wrong reel, wrong program, manual substitution, tape splice, and feeder slot mismatch. Diagnostic sequence: compare BOM to feeder map, scan reel barcode, review AOI component recognition, and use X-ray or electrical test when marking is not visible. If the wrong part is present in pre-reflow AOI, attribute it to placement feeder loading or program. If the correct part is present but the value is wrong, suspect feeder misload or wrong reel. For THT, wrong part can come from tray or tube loading and insertion program. Verify against your BOM and feeder verification system.

Polarity defects occur when a diode, IC, tantalum, electrolytic, or other polarized component is reversed. Mechanisms include feeder orientation, tape pocket orientation, manual load, disabled vision polarity check, nozzle rotation, and program angle. Diagnostic sequence: inspect polarity mark or pin 1, review pre-reflow AOI polarity check, and correlate with feeder slot. If the reversed part is present in pre-reflow AOI, attribute it to placement feeder orientation or program. If pre-reflow polarity is correct but the part reverses after reflow, suspect reflow rotation, handling, or a later manual step. For THT, polarity errors often come from insertion direction or tray orientation. Verify against your AOI polarity check and equipment datasheet.

Attribution uses the evidence sequence rather than a single image. Collect SPI, pre-reflow AOI, reflow profile, post-reflow AOI or X-ray, feeder logs, and nozzle logs. Systematic defects by feeder slot point to feeder loading, pickup, or tape pocket. Systematic defects by board location point to vision, fiducials, or support. Random defects across feeders and nozzles point to nozzle vacuum, component drop, or tape pocket release. Defects that appear only after reflow point to reflow wetting or profile. Paste defects before placement point to printing. Use your acceptance standard for disposition, but set action limits from your process capability, land geometry, and equipment datasheet. Document containment, root cause, corrective action, and verification data.

calc.task: During a 5000-board run, pre-reflow AOI reports 12 components with center offset greater than 0.15 mm, 8 components with skew greater than 1.5 deg, 3 missing components, 2 wrong-part components, and 1 reversed polarity component. Offset data: 10 of 12 offsets are +X 0.18 mm and Y 0.02 mm, all from feeder slot 14. Skew data: 7 of 8 skews are 2.0 deg clockwise, all from nozzle 3. Missing: 3 all from feeder slot 22. Wrong part: 2 boards have a capacitor from feeder slot 31 measured 100 nF instead of 10 nF. Polarity: 1 board has a diode reversed from feeder slot 41. SPI shows paste centered and in volume. Calculate defect rates, ppm, offset vector, and attribute each defect to placement, printing, or reflow using the evidence sequence.
calc.solution: Rate calculation: offset = 12/5000 = 2400 ppm; skew = 8/5000 = 1600 ppm; missing = 3/5000 = 600 ppm; wrong part = 2/5000 = 400 ppm; polarity = 1/5000 = 200 ppm; total = 26/5000 = 5200 ppm. Offset vector: magnitude = sqrt(0.18^2 + 0.02^2) = 0.181 mm; direction = atan2(0.02, 0.18) = 6.3 deg from +X. Offset attribution: 10 of 12 offsets are from feeder slot 14, SPI paste is centered, and the defect is present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement feeder pickup or tape pocket, not printing or reflow. Skew attribution: 7 of 8 skews are from nozzle 3 and are present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement nozzle rotation or pick rotation, not printing or reflow. Missing attribution: 3 missing components are all from feeder slot 22. Check pick/place logs; if no pick, feeder or tape pocket; if pick but no place, nozzle vacuum. Attribute to placement. Wrong part attribution: measured capacitance is 100 nF instead of 10 nF from feeder slot 31. Attribute to placement feeder misload or wrong reel, not printing or reflow. Polarity attribution: reversed diode from feeder slot 41 is present in pre-reflow AOI. Attribute to placement feeder orientation or program, not printing or reflow. Evidence rule: because SPI is normal and defects are present before reflow, printing and reflow are not primary causes; if a defect appears only after reflow, reflow would be primary.

defect.symptom: Pre-reflow AOI shows a systematic +X offset on one feeder slot, while SPI shows centered paste and post-reflow AOI shows the same offset without additional rotation or lift.
defect.cause: Feeder pickup position or tape pocket geometry is shifting the component before placement, producing a repeatable offset vector from that feeder slot.
defect.action: Contain the affected feeder slot, re-teach feeder pickup position, inspect tape peel and pocket, verify nozzle vacuum, then run a verification lot and confirm offset distribution against your AOI limits and equipment datasheet.

title: Component library setup, program verification and first-article check

goals.text: Verify a placement program and setup before production and identify a missing or expired calibration.

blocks.alt: A component library entry with package, nozzle and vision settings, beside a program verification screen and a first-article board under inspection
blocks.caption: Component library setup, program verification and first-article check

theory.p: Before production, verify that the placement program, component library, feeder setup, nozzle selection, and machine calibration represent the approved design and process. The verification should prove that the machine can place the correct components, in the correct orientation, at the correct coordinates, with acceptable accuracy. Use a dry run or offline simulation, then a pre-production sample under controlled conditions.

The component library defines package geometry, body size, pin or pad pitch, polarity, rotation, pick point, nozzle, feeder type, vision settings, and placement tolerance. Verify each field against the component datasheet and a physical sample. For polarized components, confirm the library polarity matches the silkscreen and the feeder orientation. For fine-pitch packages, confirm the pick point and vision reference are not obscured by tape, reel, or feeder geometry.

Check the coordinate origin, fiducial pattern, panel offsets, mirror settings, units, component side, and layer assignment. Confirm that the feeder map matches the physical feeders, that nozzles are compatible with component size and clearance, and that the program does not command collisions with panel edges, connectors, or tall components. Review the placement sequence for pick-up order, nozzle changes, and vision cycles.

Placement accuracy depends on machine calibration, vision calibration, feeder calibration, nozzle condition, and conveyance alignment. Before release, check that required calibration certificates are present, traceable, within the interval set by the equipment manufacturer or your calibration plan, and supported by verification results. If a certificate is missing, expired, or outside the required environmental or usage conditions, treat the setup as unverified until calibration is completed and recorded.

Run a pre-production sample and inspect for missing components, wrong components, polarity errors, rotation errors, tombstoning, and poor seating. Use AOI, X-ray, or manual inspection as appropriate. Measure placement coordinates against the program and compare the deviation with the tolerance from the equipment datasheet or process capability study. Record the measured values, the method, the operator, and the disposition.

Define pass/fail criteria before the sample run. Criteria may include placement coordinate tolerance, polarity, rotation, missing or wrong components, and calibration status. Use ranges from your paste, feeder, nozzle, and placement equipment datasheet, and verify them against your own process capability. Release production only when the program, setup, calibration, and sample inspection all meet the defined criteria.

If the program, component library, feeder, nozzle, panel, fiducial, or calibration status changes, repeat the relevant verification steps. Store the program version, library version, calibration records, sample results, and approval in the production record. This makes the setup traceable and supports containment if a defect is found later.

calc.task: A placement program specifies a tolerance of 0.05 mm for a component center. The pre-production sample shows a measured deviation of 0.03 mm. The machine calibration certificate is missing. Determine whether the setup can be released.
calc.solution: Compare the measured deviation with the tolerance. The deviation is within tolerance. Check the calibration certificate. The certificate is missing, so the setup is not verified. Reject release, complete calibration, then repeat the pre-production sample.

defect.symptom: AOI reports repeated polarity errors on polarized components after a feeder change.
defect.cause: The component library polarity or feeder orientation did not match the physical part, and the program was not reverified after the change.
defect.action: Stop the line, quarantine affected boards, correct the library and feeder orientation, run a pre-production sample, inspect polarity and rotation, update the change record, and release only after verification.

title: Case: shift and skew on a fine-pitch QFP

goals.text: Diagnose offset, skew, rotation, missing, wrong-part and polarity defects from measured data and name the mechanism.
Attribute a defect to placement rather than to printing or reflow using the evidence sequence.

blocks.alt: A fine-pitch QFP with measured shift and skew against a crosshair overlay, and the lead pitch tolerance band marked
blocks.caption: Case: shift and skew on a fine-pitch QFP

theory.h: Why fine-pitch QFP placement is a data problem, not just a machine problem
theory.p: A fine-pitch QFP exposes placement errors more clearly than larger components because the allowable positional margin is small relative to lead pitch. For a 0.5 mm pitch QFP, a lateral shift of 0.10 mm already consumes 20% of the pitch, and a rotation of 0.5 degrees can move an outer lead by tens of micrometres depending on body size. The practical goal is to separate true placement error from measurement noise, paste print variation, and reflow-induced movement. Use measured data from placement verification, AOI, SPI, and reflow inspection in sequence rather than judging from a single end-of-line image.

theory.h: Offset, skew, and rotation: what the measured values mean
theory.p: Offset is a translation of the component centre from the intended centre, usually reported as X and Y error. Skew is a positional mismatch between opposite sides of the component, often seen as one side closer to the pads than the other. Rotation is angular error about the component centre. On a QFP, a small rotation can look like skew if measured only at one corner, so measure at least two opposite corners or use fiducial-based centre and angle data. For fine-pitch QFPs, typical placement tolerance targets are often in the range of ±0.05 mm to ±0.10 mm for centre position and ±0.5° to ±1.0° for angle, but verify against your placement machine datasheet, component datasheet, and IPC-A-610 class requirements.

theory.h: Missing, wrong-part, and polarity defects are different failure families
theory.p: A missing QFP is usually a feeder, vision, or placement-cycle failure rather than a subtle process drift. Wrong-part defects are often caused by feeder misload, incorrect program selection, or barcode/serialisation gaps. Polarity defects on QFPs are commonly identified by pin 1 marking, chamfer, dot, or bevel orientation, and they may be missed if the placement program uses the wrong part orientation or if the feeder tape is loaded backwards. These defects are usually binary: the part is present or absent, correct or incorrect, oriented or reversed. They should be separated from dimensional placement defects such as offset, skew, and rotation.

theory.h: Using the evidence sequence to attribute defects to placement
theory.p: The strongest attribution sequence is SPI before placement, placement verification during placement, AOI after placement, and final inspection after reflow. If SPI shows acceptable paste print and placement verification shows the component was placed outside tolerance, the defect is most likely placement. If SPI shows paste offset, bridging, or volume variation and the component lands on shifted paste, the root cause may be printing. If the component is acceptable after placement but moves during reflow, the defect is reflow-related, often due to wetting imbalance, paste collapse, or thermal profile effects. Do not attribute a defect to placement if the pre-placement evidence already shows the same pattern.

theory.h: Common placement mechanisms on fine-pitch QFPs
theory.p: Common placement mechanisms include poor fiducial recognition, camera calibration drift, nozzle wear, vacuum loss, feeder repeatability, tape peel variation, and program coordinate errors. For QFPs, nozzle selection matters because a nozzle that contacts the body too hard can tilt the part, while insufficient vacuum can allow the part to shift during transfer. Feeder issues often produce repeatable skew or rotation on one side of the board because the part is presented at a slightly inconsistent angle. Program errors often produce a consistent offset across many boards, while mechanical wear often produces gradual drift or intermittent outliers.

theory.h: Distinguishing placement from printing and reflow with measured patterns
theory.p: Printing defects usually show up as paste print offset, paste volume variation, or paste shape distortion at the pad level. If the component follows the paste, the defect is likely printing. Placement defects usually show up as component position or angle error while the paste print remains acceptable. Reflow defects often show up as component movement after the paste has melted, with evidence such as acceptable post-placement AOI but shifted post-reflow AOI, tombstoning, or coplanarity issues. For fine-pitch QFPs, reflow movement may also be suspected if the component self-centres on some sides but not others, because surface tension can correct small errors only when paste volume and pad geometry are balanced.

theory.h: Practical diagnosis workflow for a fine-pitch QFP
theory.p: Start by confirming the defect type: missing, wrong part, polarity, offset, skew, or rotation. Then check whether the defect is random, board-position dependent, or repeatable across boards. Random missing parts point to feeder or vacuum issues. Repeatable offset or rotation points to program, fiducial, or calibration issues. Board-position dependent skew points to placement table flatness, support, or nozzle transfer issues. If the defect appears only after reflow, compare pre-reflow and post-reflow measurements. If the defect appears at SPI, investigate printing before blaming placement.

theory.h: Using standards and internal limits together
theory.p: IPC-A-610 provides acceptability criteria for component placement and soldering, but it does not replace machine capability targets or design-specific limits. IPC-7351 provides land pattern and package data that can be used to calculate pad-to-lead relationships. IPC-7525 and related stencil guidance can be used to evaluate paste print capability, but exact stencil aperture and paste volume targets should be verified against your paste, stencil, and printer datasheets. For process control, use internal limits tighter than the final acceptability limit so that placement can be corrected before solder defects occur.

calc.task: A 0.50 mm pitch QFP has a body diagonal of 14.0 mm. Placement verification reports centre offset X = +0.08 mm, Y = -0.06 mm, and rotation = +0.8°. The placement machine specification for this part is ±0.10 mm centre and ±0.5° angle. Calculate the resultant centre offset, the outer-lead displacement caused by rotation, and the approximate worst-case lead displacement if centre offset and rotation act in the same direction. State whether the defect is placement-related if SPI shows acceptable paste print and post-placement AOI shows the same offset pattern.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate resultant centre offset: sqrt(0.08^2 + 0.06^2) = sqrt(0.0064 + 0.0036) = sqrt(0.0100) = 0.10 mm. 2. Compare centre offset to machine limit: 0.10 mm is at the ±0.10 mm limit, so it is borderline and should be investigated. 3. Calculate rotation displacement at the outer lead. The distance from centre to corner is half the body diagonal: 14.0 mm / 2 = 7.0 mm. 4. Convert rotation to radians: 0.8° × π / 180 = 0.01396 rad. 5. Calculate arc displacement: 7.0 mm × 0.01396 = 0.098 mm. 6. Compare rotation displacement to angle limit: 0.8° exceeds the ±0.5° machine limit, so rotation is out of specification. 7. Estimate worst-case combined lead displacement if centre offset and rotation act in the same direction: 0.10 mm + 0.098 mm = 0.198 mm, approximately 0.20 mm. 8. Compare to pitch: 0.20 mm is 40% of the 0.50 mm pitch, which is a significant risk for lead misalignment, bridging, or insufficient solder joint formation. 9. Attribution: because SPI shows acceptable paste print and the same offset pattern is present at post-placement AOI, the defect is most likely placement-related rather than printing-related. If the part were acceptable after placement but shifted after reflow, reflow would be the more likely cause.

defect.symptom: A fine-pitch QFP is consistently shifted toward one side of the board, with one row of leads closer to the paste than the opposite row. Post-placement AOI reports centre offset of about 0.12 mm and rotation of about 0.7°. SPI shows acceptable paste print. The defect repeats at the same board location and is worse on the side of the board nearest the feeder.
defect.cause: The repeatable pattern points to a placement presentation or transfer issue rather than random reflow movement. Likely mechanisms include feeder tape peel variation, nozzle wear, vacuum inconsistency, or a slightly misaligned feeder causing the part to be picked up at an angle. Because the defect is board-location dependent and appears before reflow, printing and reflow are less likely primary causes.
defect.action: Stop the line if the defect exceeds the internal placement limit. Verify the feeder for the QFP, inspect the tape peel force and cover tape alignment, and check the nozzle for wear, vacuum, and centring. Re-run a placement verification test with a known-good feeder and nozzle. If the defect moves with the feeder, replace or recalibrate the feeder. If the defect remains, check placement camera calibration, fiducial recognition, and nozzle transfer settings. After correction, confirm with SPI, placement verification, and post-placement AOI before releasing production.

title: Heat transfer in the oven: convection, conduction, radiation, zone structure

goals.text: Run a thermal survey and read the profile at the coolest and hottest locations, not at the oven setpoints.

theory.p: A reflow profile is the temperature history seen by the board and components, not the oven setpoints. It is usually described by ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak temperature, and cooling. The profile controls paste activation, flux removal, wetting, intermetallic formation, voiding, and thermal stress. For a given alloy and board thermal mass, the same oven recipe can produce different results, so the profile should be measured on the assembly. A good profile is not simply the hottest or fastest one; it is the thermal exposure that produces reliable joints while keeping the board and components within qualified limits.

Typical SAC305 profile envelope — paste TDS always wins — TBD-REVIEW
head: Zone
Typical target
What it controls

theory.p: The ramp brings the assembly to a temperature where flux can activate and solvents can leave without causing violent boiling. Typical soak ranges are 140-180 °C for 90-120 s, but verify against your paste and equipment datasheet. A heavy board with large copper planes may need a longer soak to reduce temperature differences between small components and large connectors. Too short a soak can leave flux active too late, increasing solder balls and voiding; too long can dry the paste and reduce wetting. The soak should be judged from measured board temperature, not from oven air temperature.

Time above liquidus is the interval during which the solder alloy is molten. It needs to be long enough for wetting and flux removal, but short enough to limit intermetallic growth and component exposure. The time-above-liquidus window is process guidance rather than a J-STD-020 parameter: IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet typically call for 60-150 s for many assemblies. J-STD-020 has its own time figure, tp, which is the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature and is limited to 30-40 s; it is a package qualification parameter, not the paste window used to run a board. Production profiles may use a different window if qualified. The liquidus temperature should be taken from the paste or alloy datasheet, because it depends on alloy and paste formulation. In practice, the measured time above liquidus should be checked at the worst-case thermocouple location, not only at a convenient point.

Peak temperature is the highest temperature measured at the solder joint or component body, depending on the measurement point. For SAC305, J-STD-020 does not give one peak temperature: it gives classification temperatures by package size, 260 °C for small packages, 250 °C for large packages and 245 °C for very large packages, each with tp, the time within 5 °C of that temperature, limited to 30-40 s. Production peaks are often set below the classification temperature with margin, and should be verified with thermocouples on the actual board. Exceeding the classification temperature can damage components, delaminate packages, or create excessive intermetallic growth. The peak should be evaluated together with time above liquidus, because a short peak and a long peak are not equivalent thermal exposures.

Cooling solidifies the joint and influences grain size, residual stress, and warpage. Typical cooling rates are 1-4 °C/s, but verify against your paste and equipment datasheet. Very fast cooling can increase thermal shock and warpage, especially on thin boards or large BGAs. Very slow cooling can produce coarse solder structure and may allow component movement while the joint is still soft. Cooling rate should be checked with the same board thermocouples used for peak and time above liquidus, because the cooling curve can reveal lag or gradients that the oven profile does not show.

theory.h: Why thermocouples go on the board
theory.p: Thermocouples are placed on the actual board because oven air temperature is not the temperature of the solder joint. Board thickness, copper area, component mass, shielding, and mounting method create lag and gradients. A thermocouple should be attached with high-temperature adhesive or tape, with minimal added mass, and should be calibrated. Representative points include the center of a large BGA, a small passive near a heavy connector, and a location near the board edge or panel rail. If the thermocouple is attached to a bare board instead of a populated board, the measured profile may not represent production conditions.

To judge a measured profile, compare the measured peak against the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, and the measured time above liquidus against the paste-datasheet window, typically 60-150 s under IPC-7530 guidance. The comparison should use the worst-case measured point, not the oven profile or a single thermocouple. If the measured peak exceeds the classification temperature, or the time above liquidus falls outside the datasheet window, the assembly is not compliant unless a separate qualification supports the exposure. Moisture sensitivity level, floor life, and bake requirements from J-STD-020 also affect whether the component can tolerate the reflow exposure.

Start with the paste supplier recommended profile and the component qualification limits. Run a dummy board with thermocouples at the expected worst-case locations. Adjust oven zones to move the measured soak, peak, and cooling toward the target while keeping the measured curve smooth. Repeat measurements after changes to the board stackup, panelization, component placement, or oven loading. Record the profile with the board type, oven model, conveyor speed, zone setpoints, and thermocouple locations so the result can be reproduced.

calc.task: A SAC305 paste datasheet gives a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C. A 1.6 mm board with 70 µm copper and a 12 mm BGA is reflowed. The target is to stay within the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size and a time above liquidus of 60-150 s from the paste datasheet. A measured profile shows ramp 1.5 °C/s, soak 165 °C for 90 s, peak 242 °C, time above liquidus 75 s, and cooling 2.5 °C/s. Build and judge the profile.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm alloy liquidus from the paste datasheet: SAC305 has a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C, so time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. 2. Set soak target from the paste datasheet, e.g. 140-180 °C for 90-120 s; choose 165 °C for 90 s for this board. 3. Ramp to liquidus; measured ramp 1.5 °C/s is within typical practice, verify against the paste and oven datasheet. 4. Calculate time above liquidus from measured data: time when temperature exceeds 219 °C until it falls below 219 °C = 75 s. 5. Compare peak 242 °C with the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size: 242 °C passes for a small package (260 °C) or a large package (250 °C) and would fail for a very large package (245 °C), so confirm the package size before disposition. 6. Compare time above liquidus 75 s with the paste-datasheet window of 60-150 s: pass. This window is IPC-7530 and datasheet guidance, not a J-STD-020 parameter. 7. Check cooling 2.5 °C/s against the paste and equipment datasheet; if warpage or cracking is observed, slow cooling. The J-STD-020 classification ramp-down limit is 6 °C/s or less. 8. Conclusion: the measured profile passes the peak ceiling and the paste time-above-liquidus window for this board, but the package size must be confirmed for the peak ceiling, and production limits should be qualified and monitored.

defect.symptom: Solder balls on paste deposit edges after reflow
defect.cause: Soak too short or ramp too fast, causing flux and solvent boiling and paste spatter; thermocouple on board showed actual soak below paste target
defect.action: Measure with board thermocouples, increase soak time or lower ramp rate to reach paste soak range, verify paste datasheet, check stencil and paste viscosity

title: Profile anatomy: ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak, cooling — what each controls

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: A thermal profile curve with the five zones labelled and a callout under each naming what it controls
blocks.caption: Profile anatomy: what ramp, soak, time above liquidus, peak and cooling each control

theory.h: The profile as a thermal budget
theory.p: A reflow profile is a record of temperature versus time at a defined measurement point, usually a thermocouple on the package body or near a joint. It is not a single number. The shape of the curve determines how flux activates, how solder melts, how intermetallics form, and how the board and components experience thermal stress. For a working engineer, the practical question is: which segment of the curve controls which risk?

theory.h: Preheat and ramp: solvent evaporation and flux activation
theory.p: The ramp from room temperature to the liquidus region is where solvents leave the paste and the flux begins to reduce oxides. If the ramp is too steep, trapped solvent can boil violently, causing solder balling or tombstoning, and large boards can develop temperature gradients that warp. If it is too slow, flux can dry out before reflow, leaving poor wetting. Typical practice uses a ramp rate in the range of 1 to 3 °C/s up to about 150 °C, but the exact limit depends on paste chemistry and board mass; verify against your paste and oven datasheet. IPC J-STD-020 gives moisture sensitivity level (MSL) related preheat guidance for components, not a universal ramp rate for the whole profile.

The soak region, often roughly 150 to 190 °C, lets the whole assembly approach thermal equilibrium. Its purpose is to reduce temperature differences between heavy ground planes and small pads, and to let the flux chemistry work before the solder melts. A soak that is too short can leave cold spots that refuse to wet; one that is too long can over-cure the flux binder or exhaust active agents. Many paste datasheets specify a soak window, for example 60 to 120 seconds in a defined temperature band. Treat those numbers as starting points and confirm with wetting tests on your own boards.

theory.h: Reflow and time above liquidus: joint formation
theory.p: Time above liquidus (TAL) is the interval during which the solder is molten and capable of flowing and forming intermetallic compounds. For SAC305, solidus is 217 °C and liquidus is 219 °C; for SnPb eutectic, liquidus is 183 °C. TAL that is too short produces insufficient intermetallic formation and weak joints; too long promotes excessive intermetallic growth, grain coarsening, and can damage component finishes. The TAL window is process guidance from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet, typically 60-120 s or 60-150 s. J-STD-020 does not set a board-assembly TAL limit: its own time parameter is tp, the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature, limited to 30-40 s for large and very large packages and 40 s for small ones, and its peak figures are classification temperatures by package size, 260 °C small, 250 °C large and 245 °C very large. Check the classification temperature for your component's body size and MSL before comparing a measured peak.

theory.h: Peak temperature: wetting and component survival
theory.p: The peak is the highest temperature reached. It must be high enough to ensure complete melting and wetting, but low enough to protect the board and components. Peak temperature is usually set 10 to 25 °C above liquidus for common alloys, but the governing limit is the component's rated peak temperature from its datasheet or IPC J-STD-020. Exceeding the rated peak can delaminate packages, crack ceramic capacitors, or damage heat-sensitive parts. Under-reflow, where the peak is too low, leaves a dull, grainy joint and incomplete wetting.

After the peak, the cooling rate affects the solder microstructure and the residual stress in the joint. Very slow cooling can produce coarse grains and weak joints; very fast cooling can induce thermal shock, especially in large ceramic components or thick boards. Typical cooling rates are in the range of 1 to 4 °C/s, but the safe limit depends on component type and board construction. Verify against your equipment's cooling capability and component specifications. The cooling segment also determines how long the assembly stays in a temperature range where flux residues can char.

theory.h: Reading the profile against your hardware
theory.p: A profile is only valid for the specific board, paste, oven, and measurement point it was built for. A heavy board with large copper planes needs more energy and often a longer soak than a thin signal board. The same oven recipe can produce different profiles with different conveyor speeds or loading densities. Always measure with thermocouples on the actual product, not just a test coupon, and compare the measured ramp, soak, TAL, peak, and cooling against the TAL window from your paste datasheet and the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, which is the peak ceiling.

Ramp problems show up as solder balls, tombstoning, or board warpage. Soak problems appear as non-wetting, dewetting, or cold solder joints in heavy copper areas. TAL problems produce either insufficient intermetallic (too short) or brittle joints and damaged finishes (too long). Peak problems cause under-reflow or component damage. Cooling problems can lead to thermal cracking or excessive residual stress. When a defect appears, first identify which segment of the profile is most likely responsible, then adjust that segment and re-measure.

calc.task: Build and check a profile for a 1.6 mm FR-4 board with heavy ground planes using SAC305 paste. The measured profile gives: ramp from 25 to 150 °C in 60 s; soak 150 to 190 °C for 90 s; TAL above 219 °C = 45 s; peak = 248 °C; cooling from 248 to 100 °C in 40 s. Check against the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size and typical paste guidance.
calc.solution: 1. Ramp rate: (150-25)/60 = 2.08 °C/s. Typical paste guidance is 1 to 3 °C/s; this is within range but verify against paste datasheet. 2. Soak: 90 s in 150 to 190 °C. Many paste datasheets specify 60 to 120 s; this is within range. 3. Peak temperature: measured 248 °C. J-STD-020 sets classification temperatures by package size — 260 °C small, 250 °C large, 245 °C very large. For a large package 248 °C is inside the limit; for a very large package it exceeds 245 °C by 3 °C, so the package size must be confirmed before disposition. 4. TAL above 219 °C: measured 45 s. J-STD-020 does not set a board-assembly time-above-liquidus limit; its 30 s figure is tp, the time within 5 °C of the classification temperature. The applicable limit is the paste window of 60-120 s from the paste datasheet and IPC-7530 guidance, and 45 s is 15 s below the lower bound, so the profile is too short for reliable wetting rather than too long. 5. Cooling rate: (248-100)/40 = 3.7 °C/s. Typical practice is 1 to 4 °C/s; this is within range, and the J-STD-020 classification ramp-down limit is 6 °C/s or less. 6. Conclusion: the binding failure is the too-short time above liquidus, not an excessive one. Lengthen time above liquidus into the 60-120 s paste window by adding reflow dwell or slightly raising peak within the package classification temperature, confirm the package size for the peak ceiling, then re-measure.

defect.symptom: Solder joints on large ground-plane pads show dewetting and non-wetting, while joints on small signal pads look normal.
defect.cause: The soak segment is too short or the temperature gradient is too high, so the heavy copper pads never reach the flux activation temperature before the solder melts. The flux cannot reduce oxides on the large pads, and the solder does not wet.
defect.action: Increase soak time or raise the soak temperature band slightly to allow the heavy pads to reach thermal equilibrium. Verify with thermocouples on the actual board that the pad temperature enters the soak window before the liquidus is reached. Re-measure the profile and run wetting tests.

title: Running a thermal survey: thermocouple attachment, test coupon, worst-case site

goals.text: Run a thermal survey and read the profile at the coolest and hottest locations, not at the oven setpoints.

blocks.alt: A test coupon with several thermocouples attached by different methods, and a board map marking the worst-case thermal sites
blocks.caption: Running a thermal survey: thermocouple attachment, test coupon and the worst-case site

theory.h: What a thermal survey actually measures
theory.p: A thermal survey records the temperature experienced by the board, components, and solder joints as they move through the reflow oven. The oven setpoints are control targets for each zone, not proof that every joint reached the required temperature. For this lesson, the measurable outcome is the temperature at the coolest and hottest locations on a representative test coupon or production panel. Those readings are compared with the paste liquidus and solidus, the time above liquidus, and the component peak-temperature limit. The survey should be run with the same panel orientation, conveyor speed, and loading pattern used in production. If the survey is run on a bare coupon or with a different panel layout, the result may not represent the real process. The purpose is to see whether the actual joint temperatures are inside the acceptable window, not whether the oven display matches the recipe.

Use a fine-gauge type K thermocouple with a calibrated data logger. The junction should be attached to the pad, trace, or component body that represents the joint being evaluated. High-temperature tape can be used, but the tape must be rated for the peak temperature and must not lift during handling or conveyor movement. A small solder blob can improve thermal contact, but it changes the local thermal mass and may alter the reading, so the method must be consistent from survey to survey. The wire should be secured so the junction does not peel away when the board moves. A lifted junction can read low because it sees air instead of the joint. A junction attached to a large copper area can read high or lag the actual joint temperature. Verify the tape, adhesive, and logger temperature ratings against your equipment datasheet.

A test coupon should reproduce the materials and thermal mass of the production board. It should use the same laminate, copper distribution, component type, paste deposit, and panel position as the real product. If the product contains a large ground plane, dense BGA, heavy connector, or mixed SMT and THT assembly, include those features on the coupon or run the survey on a sacrificial production panel. A simple test strip with small pads may show a clean profile but miss the coolest joint under a ground plane. The coupon should be placed in the same orientation and location as production boards, because oven airflow and radiant heating can vary across the width and length of the oven. If the coupon is too light, it may heat faster than the real board and give a false pass.

theory.h: Finding the coolest and hottest sites
theory.p: The coolest site is often under a large ground plane, near a cold edge, under a heavy component, or at a panel location with poor airflow. The hottest site may be near a heater, on a small component with low thermal mass, or at a board edge exposed to radiant heat. Run several thermocouples at once and compare the curves. If the spread between sites is large, the oven setpoints are not enough to describe the process. The coolest site controls whether the paste reaches liquidus and forms a proper joint. The hottest site controls whether the component, board, or nearby parts are exposed to excessive temperature. A single thermocouple placed on a fast-heating pad can hide a cold joint elsewhere. The survey should identify both extremes, not just a convenient location.

Read the actual board temperature in each zone: preheat, soak, reflow, and cooling. The preheat zone should bring the board up without thermal shock. The soak zone should reduce temperature differences across the board and activate the flux. The reflow zone should bring the joint above the paste liquidus for enough time to form good wetting. The cooling zone should solidify the joint without excessive thermal stress. For lead-free paste, the liquidus is near the value given on the paste datasheet, and the time above liquidus should be checked against the paste and component datasheets. For component qualification, peak-temperature limits are often referenced to IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020, but the component datasheet and the applicable moisture sensitivity level control the final limit. Verify all practice-based values against your paste and equipment datasheet.

The measured temperature includes thermocouple error, logger error, attachment thermal lag, and placement error. Use a logger with a calibration certificate and record the sampling interval. Keep the attachment method consistent between surveys so changes in the profile are due to the oven, not the measurement. If the junction is lifted by tape, the reading may be low. If the junction is soldered to a large plane, the reading may be high or delayed. If the wire is loose, vibration can cause intermittent contact. If the logger is placed on a hot conveyor rail, the reference junction may be affected. Document the thermocouple type, logger model, calibration status, attachment method, and exact location of each junction. Without that information, two surveys may look different even when the oven has not changed.

Accept the survey when the coolest joint reaches the paste liquidus with enough time above liquidus, and the hottest joint stays below the component and board limits. If the coolest site is marginal, adjust the profile or investigate heat transfer, panel loading, or oven airflow. If the hottest site is close to a limit, reduce peak temperature or improve cooling. If the spread between sites is too large, the process may need better uniformity rather than a higher setpoint. Document the coupon, thermocouple locations, oven settings, measured minimum and maximum temperatures, and any deviations. The result should be a clear statement of whether the actual joint temperatures are acceptable, not just whether the oven recipe was followed.

calc.task: A 6-thermocouple survey on a lead-free SAC305 test coupon records a hottest peak of 246 °C and a coolest peak of 238 °C. The paste datasheet gives solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C. The component datasheet allows a peak of 260 °C. Calculate the margin above liquidus at the coolest site and the margin below the component limit at the hottest site.
calc.solution: First, identify the coolest peak: 238 °C. Next, identify the paste liquidus: 219 °C, because SAC305 has a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C and time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. Then subtract the liquidus from the coolest peak: 238 - 219 = 19 °C. This is the margin above liquidus at the coolest site. Next, identify the hottest peak: 246 °C. Then identify the component peak limit: 260 °C. Subtract the hottest peak from the component limit: 260 - 246 = 14 °C. This is the margin below the component limit at the hottest site. Interpretation: the coolest site is above liquidus by 21 °C, and the hottest site is 14 °C below the stated component limit. Verify time above liquidus and cooling rate against the paste and component datasheets.

defect.symptom: Cold or non-wetted solder joints appear on large ground-plane pads after the oven setpoints and a single thermocouple survey look acceptable.
defect.cause: The thermocouple was attached to a small pad or lifted by tape, so it measured a faster-heating location instead of the coolest joint under the ground plane. The test coupon did not reproduce the copper area and component thermal mass.
defect.action: Rerun the survey with a calibrated logger and a test coupon that includes the ground plane and component. Attach the thermocouple junction to the pad or component body at the worst-case site, secure the wire, and compare the coolest and hottest curves. Adjust the soak or peak only after confirming the measurement location.

title: Board thermal mass and layout: heavy planes, thermal relief, mixed population, dense vs sparse

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: Two board layouts side by side, one dense with heavy copper planes and one sparse, with a thermal mass indicator on each
blocks.caption: Board thermal mass and layout: heavy planes, thermal relief, mixed population, dense versus sparse

theory.h: Thermal mass controls how the board responds to oven heat
theory.p: Board thermal mass is the combined heat capacity and heat-transfer resistance of the laminate, copper planes, plated holes, components, and fixtures. A thick board with heavy copper reaches the oven setpoint more slowly than a thin board with sparse copper, so the same oven recipe can produce different solder-joint temperatures. For process work, measure the profile at the pad or component body, not only at the oven air, and verify the result against the paste and component datasheets.

theory.h: Heavy planes act as heat sinks at the joint
theory.p: Large power and ground planes draw heat away from small pads and can keep a joint below the paste liquidus even when nearby joints look normal. The effect is strongest when a pad is directly connected to a plane with little thermal relief, when the plane is on an inner layer with short vias, or when the component has high thermal mass. The practical fix is to balance heat flow by adjusting pad geometry, paste volume, preheat, and airflow rather than simply raising peak temperature.

theory.h: Thermal relief is a heat-balance tool, not just a solderability aid
theory.p: Thermal relief spokes reduce the copper area feeding heat away from a pad, making the pad easier to bring above liquidus. The relief must still provide electrical and mechanical integrity, so spoke count, width, and clearance should follow the board design rules and the paste stencil design. For heavy planes, verify that the pad reaches liquidus with the selected paste and component; if it does not, adjust the profile or layout before increasing peak temperature.

theory.h: Mixed population boards require a compromise profile
theory.p: A board with large connectors, QFNs, BGAs, and small chip components may contain joints that need different heat input. Large components and heavy planes need enough soak and time above liquidus, while small components can be damaged by excessive peak temperature or long soak. Build the profile around the most thermally demanding joint and the lowest component temperature limit, then confirm that all parts remain within their specified limits.

theory.h: Dense and sparse layouts heat differently
theory.p: Dense boards with many components and copper areas tend to heat more uniformly and often need more total energy to reach liquidus. Sparse boards can heat quickly and may develop local hot spots near small components or exposed copper. When the same oven recipe is used across different panel designs, compare pad-level profiles because oven air temperature can hide large differences between dense and sparse areas.

theory.h: Use alloy liquidus and standard limits to set the profile
theory.p: For lead-free paste, define the liquidus from the paste datasheet, then set time above liquidus and peak temperature using the applicable standard and component limits. The average ramp-up of 1-3 °C/s and the 60-150 s time-above-liquidus window come from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet, not from J-STD-020. J-STD-020 supplies the classification temperatures that bound the peak: 260 °C for small packages, 250 °C for large packages and 245 °C for very large packages, each with tp, the time within 5 °C of that temperature, limited to 30-40 s. Verify the applicable package size, the component datasheet and your paste supplier recommendation.

theory.h: Adjust the profile by moving heat, not just temperature
theory.p: If heavy planes cause low pad temperature, increase soak time or reduce conveyor speed to raise the board temperature before liquidus, then check that peak and time above liquidus remain within limits. If sparse areas overheat, reduce peak temperature or airflow in the reflow zone and use preheat to bring the whole board up together. Document the thermocouple location, board thickness, copper weight, alloy, and measured ramp, time above liquidus, and peak so the result can be repeated.

calc.task: A 1.8 mm board with 2 oz copper power planes uses SAC305 paste with solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C. The component limit is the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size. A pad-level profile shows ramp from 150 °C to 219 °C in 37 s, time above 219 °C of 85 s, and peak 238 °C. Build and check the profile.
calc.solution: 1. Confirm alloy liquidus: SAC305 solidus 217 °C and liquidus 219 °C from the paste datasheet; time above liquidus is measured from the 219 °C crossing. 2. Apply limits: ramp 1-3 °C/s and time above liquidus 60-150 s from IPC-7530 and the paste datasheet; the peak ceiling is the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size, 250 °C for a large package. 3. Calculate ramp: (219 - 150) / 37 = 1.86 °C/s. 4. Check ramp: 1.86 °C/s is within 1-3 °C/s. 5. Check time above liquidus: 85 s is within 60-150 s. 6. Check peak: 238 °C is below the 250 °C classification temperature and above liquidus by 19 °C. 7. Decision: the profile passes the cited limits, but heavy planes require pad-level confirmation; if pad temperature is low, increase soak or reduce conveyor speed and recheck peak and time above liquidus.

defect.symptom: After reflow, QFN pads on a 2 oz copper plane show incomplete wetting or lifted leads, while small chip components in sparse areas show discoloration or overheating.
defect.cause: The oven profile was tuned to air temperature, and the heavy plane heat sink kept the QFN pad below liquidus; sparse areas heated faster and exceeded the component limit.
defect.action: Profile at the pad, increase soak or reduce conveyor speed to raise pad temperature before liquidus, adjust airflow or zone setpoints, and verify against paste and component limits; if needed, add thermal relief or paste volume and requalify.

title: Alloy systems and profile families: SnAgCu vs SnPb, liquidus basis, nitrogen vs air

goals.text: Build a profile for a given board thermal mass and alloy and check ramp, time above liquidus and peak against limits taken from the cited source.

blocks.alt: Two thermal profile curves overlaid, one for a SAC-type alloy and one for a tin-lead eutectic, with each liquidus marked
blocks.caption: Alloy systems and profile families: SAC305 versus SnPb on a liquidus basis, and nitrogen versus air

theory.p: SnPb eutectic paste is commonly associated with a liquidus of 183 C, while SAC305 is a near-eutectic alloy with a solidus of 217 C and a liquidus of 219 C. These values come from the alloy and paste datasheet, not from J-STD-020, which supplies classification temperatures rather than alloy melting data. The liquidus is the temperature at which the alloy is fully molten, so time above liquidus should be measured from the board thermocouple crossing that value, not from oven setpoint.

theory.h: Alloy families set different thermal budgets
theory.p: SnPb profiles usually use a lower peak because the J-STD-020 classification temperature for SnPb eutectic is 220 C, while SAC305 profiles use a higher peak because the SAC305 classification temperatures are 260 C for small packages, 250 C for large packages and 245 C for very large packages. The practical target peak is set by paste wetting, component rating, and board stress, then checked against the classification limit.

theory.h: Ramp and soak control flux and gradients
theory.p: IPC-7530B gives typical guidance such as a ramp rate of 1-3 C/s and a soak that reduces thermal gradients. Heavy boards, large ground planes, and dense components need slower ramp or longer soak so that the coldest joint reaches liquidus without overheating the hottest joint. Verify the chosen ramp and soak against the paste and oven datasheets.

theory.h: Time above liquidus is a joint-quality window
theory.p: IPC-7530B gives typical guidance of 60-120 s above liquidus. This window allows wetting and intermetallic formation without excessive flux exhaustion or intermetallic growth. Heavy thermal mass may require longer time above liquidus, but the limit should be checked against paste datasheet and component moisture sensitivity.

theory.h: Peak temperature is a ceiling, not a target
theory.p: A SnAgCu peak of 245 C may be acceptable if the measured board temperature stays below the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size (260 C small, 250 C large, 245 C very large) and the paste datasheet supports it. The peak should be measured at the joint, not at the oven air, because board thermal mass and thermocouple placement can shift the apparent peak.

theory.h: Nitrogen changes oxidation, not the liquidus
theory.p: Nitrogen reflow reduces oxide formation on paste and pads, which can improve wetting and may allow a lower peak or shorter time above liquidus. It does not change the SnAgCu liquidus of 219 C (217 C is the solidus) or the SnPb liquidus of 183 C. Oxygen level, gas flow, and chamber uniformity must be verified because nitrogen can also change heat transfer and profile repeatability.

theory.h: Build the profile from measured board data
theory.p: For a given board thermal mass, attach thermocouples to representative joints, ground planes, and component leads. Record ramp rate, time above liquidus, and peak. Compare the measured values with IPC-7530B guidance and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 classification limits, then adjust zones until the coldest joint meets wetting requirements without exceeding the hottest joint limit.

calc.task: A board with measured thermal mass 90 J/K is reflowed with SnAgCu paste in air. The oven can deliver about 100 W to the board during ramp. The measured profile shows a ramp from 150 C to 219 C in 60 s, a time above 219 C of 75 s, and a peak of 245 C. Build the expected ramp from thermal mass and check ramp, time above liquidus, and peak against IPC-7530B guidance and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 limits.
calc.solution: 1. Use the SAC305 liquidus of 219 C from the paste datasheet as the reference for time above liquidus; 217 C is the solidus. 2. Estimate ramp rate from heat input and thermal mass: ramp rate = 100 W / 90 J/K = 1.1 C/s. 3. Estimate time from 150 C to 219 C: (219 - 150) / 1.1 = 63 s. This is close to the measured 60 s. 4. Check ramp against IPC-7530B typical guidance of 1-3 C/s: 1.1 C/s is within the guidance. 5. Check time above liquidus against IPC-7530B typical guidance of 60-120 s: measured 75 s is within the guidance. 6. Check peak against the J-STD-020 classification temperature for the package size (260 C small, 250 C large, 245 C very large): measured 245 C is below the limit for small and large packages and exactly at the limit for very large packages, so confirm the package size. 7. Confirm the 245 C peak is supported by the paste datasheet and component temperature ratings; if the board is run in nitrogen, re-run the profile because wetting and heat transfer may shift.

defect.symptom: Small solder balls appear around pads on a heavy ground-plane area after reflow, while the joints themselves look wetted.
defect.cause: The ramp was too fast or the soak was too short for the local thermal mass, causing flux and solvent to boil violently and eject paste material before the joint reached liquidus.
defect.action: Reduce the ramp rate toward IPC-7530B guidance, extend the soak, verify thermocouple placement on the heavy area, and re-run the profile while checking the paste datasheet for recommended ramp and soak limits.

title: Reflow defect atlas: tombstone, balling, beading, dewetting, voids, distortion

goals.text: Link a defect signature to a profile zone and propose a bounded change with verification.

blocks.alt: Six small joint views labelled with each reflow defect, shown beside a sound joint for comparison
blocks.caption: Reflow defect atlas: tombstone, balling, beading, dewetting, voids and distortion

theory.p: A reflow profile is read as a sequence of thermal zones: preheat, soak, reflow, and cooling. Tombstone and beading often point to preheat or soak imbalance, balling and dewetting often point to reflow wetting or surface condition, voids often point to trapped flux or paste rheology, and distortion often points to cooling restraint or uneven thermal mass. Link the observed signature to the zone where the defect is most likely to form before changing the profile.

Tombstone appears when a small chip component stands on end because a pad wets before the other. Beading appears as a rounded solder ball or bead at a pad edge when wetting is uneven or paste collapses. Both can be driven by pad thermal imbalance, paste collapse, or a ramp that makes liquidus arrival differ between pads. Verify pad copper balance, paste volume, and preheat ramp against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Balling is a discrete solder ball separate from the joint, often caused by paste collapse, excessive preheat, or contamination that prevents coalescence. Dewetting is a joint that initially wets but then pulls back, leaving a thin solder film or irregular edge. Dewetting often points to surface finish damage, oxide, or a soak that is too short for flux activity. Compare the defect location with pad finish, storage time, and soak behavior.

Voids are trapped gas or flux residue inside a joint, often visible by X-ray. They can increase when paste rheology, stencil aperture, or ramp rate traps volatiles before the joint closes. Distortion is board or component movement during reflow, often caused by uneven heating, fixture restraint, or cooling contraction. Void signatures need X-ray or cross-section verification; distortion needs dimensional measurement and fixture review.

A bounded change modifies a profile variable or a process variable, then verifies the result. For a tombstone signature, a bounded change might reduce ramp rate or extend soak to improve pad temperature balance. For a dewetting signature, a bounded change might adjust soak time or surface cleanliness. Avoid changing ramp, soak, peak, and cooling together unless the failure mode is clearly coupled.

Verification should include thermocouple traces on the suspect pad and a reference pad, visual inspection against the IPC visual acceptance standard, and X-ray or cross-section when voids are suspected. The change is accepted only when the defect signature is absent on a trial article and the profile remains within paste and equipment limits. Record the accepted change with the board, paste, stencil, and oven settings.

Practice-based values such as ramp rate, soak time, and pad thermal relief size should be treated as starting points and verified against your paste and equipment datasheet. The datasheet controls the allowable profile window, while the defect atlas guides which zone to adjust. When a change moves the profile outside the window, stop and re-evaluate paste, stencil, layout, or fixture before adding more profile changes.

calc.task: A small chip resistor tombstones on a board where the left pad is isolated and the right pad connects to a copper plane through a thermal relief. Estimate whether pad thermal imbalance is plausible, then propose a bounded profile change and verification.
calc.solution: Start by estimating effective pad area. Assume the isolated pad effective area is 0.30 mm^2 and the plane pad effective area is 0.60 mm^2. The area ratio is 0.60 / 0.30 = 2.0. Copper thickness 35 µm and laminate thickness 1.6 mm are typical starting values; verify against your stack-up. If the plane pad uses a 0.3 mm thermal relief, the plane pad may still have greater thermal mass than the isolated pad, so it can reach liquidus later and increase tombstone risk. Propose a bounded change: reduce ramp rate from 2.0 °C/s to 1.5 °C/s and extend soak by 10 s, not more than 20 s, if paste and oven limits allow. Verify with thermocouples on the suspect pad and a reference pad; confirm pad-to-pad temperature difference before liquidus is reduced. Inspect a trial article against the IPC visual acceptance standard and X-ray if voids are suspected. If tombstone persists, review layout copper balance or paste volume rather than continuing to extend soak.

defect.symptom: Small chip resistor stands on end after reflow, with one terminal soldered and the other lifted.
defect.cause: Pad thermal imbalance and wetting imbalance during reflow; the pad with lower thermal mass reaches liquidus earlier, solder wets that side earlier, and surface tension pulls the component upright.
defect.action: Reduce ramp rate and extend soak within paste and oven limits; add thermal relief or copper balance if layout change is allowed; verify with thermocouple and trial article inspection against the IPC visual acceptance standard.

title: Profile validation, documentation and change control

goals.text: Evaluate a measured profile and name which zone to change, in which direction, with the expected joint effect.
Link a defect signature to a profile zone and propose a bounded change with verification.

blocks.alt: A validated profile record with thermocouple locations and measured data, beside a change-control request routing the revision
blocks.caption: Profile validation, documentation and change control

theory.p: Profile validation checks whether the measured thermal history at the joint matches the paste, component, and board constraints. Use thermocouples on representative joints, not only oven air temperature. Compare the measured curve with the paste datasheet and component moisture sensitivity limits from the applicable IPC moisture sensitivity guidance.

A reflow profile is usually reviewed by zones: preheat, soak, reflow, and cooling. The preheat zone controls solvent evaporation and helps prevent thermal shock. The soak zone activates flux and equalizes temperature across the board. The reflow zone creates wetting and intermetallic formation. The cooling zone controls solidification and residual stress.

Validation should record the location of each thermocouple, the board orientation, the carrier or pallet, the oven setpoints, and the measured peak temperature. A profile is not valid if the thermocouple is loose, if the joint is not representative, or if the measurement is taken from a heavily loaded board without checking a lightly loaded board.

Thermocouple attachment affects the result. Use a high-temperature adhesive or solder point on the joint, and confirm the sensor is not lifted by conveyor vibration. Measure several joints across the board because thermal mass and airflow create gradients. If the oven has multiple zones, record the measured curve rather than relying only on setpoints.

When a defect signature points to a zone, choose the smallest change that can test the hypothesis. If wetting is poor, the reflow zone is the first candidate. If the board is cold at the joint, the preheat or soak zone may need more energy. If tombstoning appears, the preheat and soak zones may be too aggressive or the cooling may be uneven.

Bounded change control means changing only a single profile variable at a time, recording the old and new values, and verifying the result with measurement and inspection. For example, if the time above liquidus is short, increase the peak temperature or reduce the cooling rate slightly, then confirm that the joint still meets the acceptance criteria in the applicable IPC acceptance guidance.

Documentation should include the measured profile, the thermocouple map, the paste lot, the board stackup, the oven recipe, the change reason, the verification data, and the disposition. This makes the change auditable and reduces repeated trial and error. If the change affects moisture-sensitive components, check the applicable IPC moisture sensitivity guidance before releasing the recipe.

Change control should distinguish a recipe adjustment from a process qualification. A small bounded adjustment can be verified by profile measurement and joint inspection. A larger change, such as a new paste, a new board design, or a new oven, requires a formal qualification with statistical confidence and acceptance evidence.

calc.task: A measured lead-free paste profile shows ramp 1.6 °C/s, soak 150-190 °C for 90 s, time above liquidus 45 s, peak 242 °C, cooling 3.0 °C/s. The paste datasheet gives a solidus of 217 °C and a liquidus of 219 °C, recommended time above liquidus 60-90 s, and recommended peak 245-250 °C. Evaluate the profile and propose a bounded change.
calc.solution: The measured time above liquidus is 45 s, which is below the datasheet range 60-90 s. The measured peak is 242 °C, which is below the datasheet range 245-250 °C. The soak range 150-190 °C is within the typical window, so the defect signature of dull, grainy, non-wet joints points to the reflow zone rather than the soak zone. Propose a bounded change: increase the peak by 3-5 °C to 245-247 °C and reduce cooling from 3.0 °C/s to 2.5 °C/s to extend time above liquidus to 60-70 s. Verify against the paste and oven datasheet. Expected joint effect: improved wetting and more complete intermetallic formation, reducing cold solder joints. Risk: excessive peak can damage components or cause solder balling, and excessive slow cooling can enlarge grain size. Verification: remeasure the thermocouple profile, inspect joints against IPC acceptance guidance, check tombstoning and solder balling, and record the change in the recipe document.

defect.symptom: Dull, grainy joints with non-wet pads and insufficient fillet on a board that otherwise shows correct placement and paste volume.
defect.cause: Short time above liquidus and low peak temperature in the reflow zone, leaving incomplete wetting and weak intermetallic formation.
defect.action: Raise the peak temperature within the paste datasheet limit and extend time above liquidus by a bounded amount, then remeasure the profile and inspect joints against IPC acceptance guidance.

title: What each method can see: visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D, boundary scan

goals.text: Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.

theory.h: Visual inspection: visible top-side and through-hole features
theory.p: Visual inspection, with or without magnification, is a common initial check for defects that are exposed: missing or wrong components, polarity errors, tombstoned chip components, visible solder bridges on exposed pads, insufficient or excessive solder fillets on through-hole leads, mechanical damage, contamination, and flux residue. It is useful for gross assembly errors and cosmetic acceptability under IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies. It cannot reliably inspect joints hidden under packages, bottom terminations, BGA balls, QFN wettable flanks, stacked layers, internal voids, or through-hole barrel fill unless the joint is physically visible.

blocks.caption: Inspection layers: each catches a different defect family

blocks.alt: Five stacked inspection bands showing visual, AOI, 2D X-ray of a BGA with voids, laminar 3D slice and a boundary scan chain
blocks.caption: Inspection layers: what visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar 3D and boundary scan can each see

theory.h: AOI: optical screening of exposed assembly features
theory.p: Automated optical inspection uses cameras, lighting, and image analysis to inspect exposed top and bottom features. It can detect component presence, polarity, orientation, wrong part, missing parts, tombstoning, visible solder bridges, coplanarity issues, and some solder fillet or wettable flank features when lighting and 3D height mapping are adequate. AOI is fast for inline screening, but it can miss defects hidden under packages, occluded by tall components, inside BGA or QFN terminations, or inside through-hole barrels. Verify lighting, angle, and resolution against your equipment datasheet.

theory.h: 2D X-ray: projection imaging of hidden joints
theory.p: 2D X-ray produces a transmission projection and is used when the defect is hidden from optical methods. It can reveal BGA, QFN, PLCC, and CSP termination geometry, missing or collapsed balls, opens, shorts, misalignment, voids, and through-hole barrel fill. Because the image superimposes layers, void size, depth, and bridging location can be ambiguous, and thin wettable flanks may be difficult to judge when overlapped by traces or adjacent balls. Use 2D X-ray for screening hidden joints, and verify magnification and detector resolution against your equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Laminar/3D X-ray: tomographic imaging for depth and volume
theory.p: Laminar or 3D X-ray reconstructs slices or volumes, allowing depth discrimination that 2D projection cannot provide. It is useful when you need to locate a void, estimate void size, inspect stacked packages, separate overlapping BGA rows, judge QFN wettable flanks, or evaluate through-hole fill in dense boards. It can also support IPC-7095 Design and Assembly Process Implementation for BGAs guidance on hidden BGA features. The trade-offs are slower cycle time, higher cost, reconstruction artifacts, and sensitivity to calibration, so use it when 2D X-ray or AOI is insufficient.

theory.h: Boundary scan: electrical test of scan-capable interconnects
theory.p: Boundary scan, commonly JTAG, uses scan cells inside devices to observe and control package pins. It can detect opens and shorts on nets connected to scan-capable pins, making it useful for high-density BGA and QFN assemblies where optical inspection is limited. It does not inspect solder wetting, component value, non-scan nets, power and ground nets, analog nodes, memory arrays, or joints under non-scan devices. It requires design-for-test access, a working scan chain, and test vectors that exercise the nets of interest.

theory.h: Choosing the method from the defect and board feature
theory.p: Match the method to what must be seen. Use visual or AOI for exposed top-side defects, visible through-hole leads, polarity, missing parts, and visible bridges. Use bottom-side AOI when the joint is exposed on the underside. Use 2D X-ray for hidden BGA, QFN, PLCC, CSP, and through-hole barrel features. Use laminar/3D X-ray when void size, depth, stacking, or overlapping geometry must be resolved. Use boundary scan for opens and shorts on scan-capable nets, especially dense BGA or QFN interconnects, but combine it with physical inspection for non-scan nets and solder quality.

No single inspection method covers every defect. Optical methods depend on lighting, angle, component height, and surface reflectivity. X-ray methods depend on magnification, detector resolution, focus, sample orientation, and reconstruction settings. Boundary scan depends on scan chain integrity and test coverage. Acceptance should follow the customer-specified IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies class and relevant design guidance such as IPC-7351 Land Pattern Design Data Standard for Surface Mount and IPC-7525 Stencil Design Guidelines. For practice-based limits, use ranges from your equipment and paste datasheets rather than assuming a single value.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch BGA has 100 balls. 60 balls are connected to scan-capable signal nets, 20 are power or ground, and 20 are analog nets. The line suspects opens and shorts on signal nets and voiding under all balls. Choose the inspection methods and estimate boundary scan coverage.
calc.solution: First, classify the defects. Opens and shorts on scan-capable signal nets can be tested electrically by boundary scan. Voiding under all balls is a hidden physical defect and requires X-ray. Second, estimate boundary scan coverage. Scan-capable signal balls = 60. Total balls = 100. Coverage = 60/100 = 0.60. Third, interpret coverage. Boundary scan can test 0.60 of the balls for opens and shorts on scan nets, but it does not test the 20 power or ground balls, the 20 analog balls, or solder voiding under any ball. Fourth, choose physical inspection. Use 2D X-ray to screen hidden BGA balls and voids. Use laminar/3D X-ray if void size, depth, or overlapping rows must be measured. Fifth, combine methods. Use boundary scan for scan-net opens and shorts, 2D X-ray for hidden ball screening, and laminar/3D X-ray for ambiguous or acceptance-critical voids. Verify resolution and test coverage against your equipment datasheet and the customer-specified IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies class.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan fails on some scan-capable nets after reflow. AOI shows no visible BGA defect, and 2D X-ray shows collapsed or missing balls under the package.
defect.cause: Insufficient paste release or paste volume, stencil aperture area ratio outside the process window, paste slump, component coplanarity, or reflow profile that did not collapse the balls. Land pattern and stencil design may not match IPC-7351 Land Pattern Design Data Standard for Surface Mount and IPC-7525 Stencil Design Guidelines.
defect.action: Stop the line and quarantine the lot. Confirm the failure with boundary scan and 2D X-ray, then use laminar/3D X-ray to measure void size and ball collapse. Review stencil aperture area ratio, paste type, print pressure, squeegee speed, and reflow profile against IPC-7525 Stencil Design Guidelines and IPC-7095 Design and Assembly Process Implementation for BGAs. Verify ball coplanarity and land pattern, then re-run a qualification lot and accept results against the customer-specified IPC-A-610 Acceptability Requirements for Electronic Assemblies class.
