title: AOI program setup: windows, lighting, thresholds, the false-call/escape trade-off

goals.text: Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.
Compute escape rate, false-call rate and verification coverage from audit data and state their limits.

blocks.alt: An AOI camera view with component windows, lighting angles and a threshold slider, and a trade-off scale between false calls and escapes
blocks.caption: AOI program setup: windows, lighting, thresholds and the false-call / escape trade-off

theory.h: Match the inspection method to the defect and feature
theory.p: AOI is a screening tool for optically accessible features: component presence, polarity, tombstoning, skew, rotation, missing solder, visible solder fillet shape, and some coplanarity issues. It is weaker for hidden joints, voids, cracks under packages, and internal package defects. Choose 2D X-ray or laminar/3D X-ray when the defect is behind or under the component, such as BGA voiding, QFN wetting, package-under solder bridges, or internal lead separation. Choose boundary scan when the defect is an electrical open or short that can be exercised through boundary-scan logic, especially on dense BGA or fine-pitch devices, but remember it does not replace physical inspection for all mechanical or solder defects. Use visual inspection for unusual defects, program validation, and verification of AOI calls.

theory.h: Windows define what the AOI is allowed to see
theory.p: An inspection window is the region assigned to a component or feature, plus the expected model, fiducial alignment, and tolerance. Windows should account for placement tolerance, reflow shift, panel handling, warpage, and component substitution. If the window is too tight, the AOI may call a good board because the part shifted slightly; if it is too loose, it may inspect the wrong area or miss a defect near the edge. Build windows from the land pattern and component outline, then validate with golden boards and known defect samples. For panelized boards, confirm that fiducials, rails, and local alignment points are stable across the panel and across reflow.

theory.h: Lighting and optics set the signal-to-noise ratio
theory.p: Lighting angle, intensity, color, focus, and camera resolution determine whether a defect produces a measurable contrast. Shiny solder, matte components, gold finishes, black packages, and reflective pads can all confuse a single-light program. Multi-angle lighting, high dynamic range, and separate solder and component channels can improve discrimination, but they also increase program complexity. Resolution should be fine enough in micrometers to see the smallest defect feature that matters for the acceptability decision; verify against the equipment datasheet and a test coupon rather than assuming a camera specification is sufficient.

Thresholds are the numeric limits that turn measurements into pass or fail decisions: solder area, solder height, contrast, coplanarity, pin count, polarity, tombstone angle, skew, and rotation. They should be derived from the applicable acceptability standard for soldered assemblies, the land pattern data, component datasheets, and measured process variation. Default thresholds are a starting point, not a release condition. For each threshold, record the golden-board value, the process variation, the defect sample value, and the chosen limit. Where the AOI cannot measure the physical acceptability criterion directly, use a surrogate measurement and document its correlation to the acceptability condition.

theory.h: False calls and escapes are linked, not independent
theory.p: Tightening thresholds can reduce escapes but usually increases false calls; loosening thresholds can reduce false calls but usually increases escapes. The best setting is not the lowest false-call rate in isolation, but the point where verification capacity, defect severity, escape cost, and production throughput are balanced. A high false-call rate can hide real defects because operators become impatient and may dismiss calls without proper verification. A low false-call rate can hide escapes if the program is too permissive. Use defect severity and downstream impact to decide which trade-off is acceptable for each defect type. Practice-based false-call rates can range from low single-digit percentages to higher percentages per board depending on board mix and program maturity; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and process data.

theory.h: Audit data must be defined before it is used
theory.p: Escape rate, false-call rate, and verification coverage require clear definitions. A call is any AOI output requiring review. A true call is a verified defect. A false call is a verified non-defect. An escape is a defect that AOI did not call but was found later by audit, downstream test, or field return. Verification coverage is the fraction of AOI calls that were actually reviewed. If coverage is incomplete, escape and false-call estimates are uncertain. If the audit only samples certain boards, defect types, or shifts, the result applies only to that population.

Metrics are limited by sample size, timing, and detection capability. Escapes found after the audit window are not included unless the data are updated. Downstream inspection and test can miss defects, so measured escapes are a lower bound. False calls may be underreported if operators clear calls without logging. Different board mixes, component substitutions, and program revisions change the meaning of the same percentage. Report the denominator, the time window, the board mix, and the verification coverage with every rate.

calc.task: A line audits 10000 boards after AOI. AOI made 500 calls. Operators verified 450 calls and found 150 true defects and 300 false calls. The remaining 50 calls were not verified. A downstream audit found 20 escapes that AOI did not call. Compute verification coverage, false-call rate, and escape rate, and state the limits.
calc.solution: First, verification coverage = verified calls / total calls = 450 / 500 = 90 percent. Second, false-call rate among verified calls = false calls / verified calls = 300 / 450 = 66.7 percent. False calls per inspected board = 300 / 10000 = 3.0 percent. If the unverified calls are assumed to have the same false-call rate as verified calls, estimated false calls in the unverified calls = 50 * 300 / 450 = 33.3, total estimated false calls = 333.3, false-call rate among all calls = 333.3 / 500 = 66.7 percent, and estimated false calls per inspected board = 333.3 / 10000 = 3.3 percent. Third, escape rate using verified true calls only = escapes / (verified true calls + escapes) = 20 / (150 + 20) = 11.8 percent. If all 50 unverified calls were false, the escape rate remains 11.8 percent. If all 50 unverified calls were true, true calls = 200 and escape rate = 20 / (200 + 20) = 9.1 percent. If unverified calls are assumed to have the same true-call rate as verified calls, estimated true calls = 150 + 50 * 150 / 450 = 166.7, and estimated escape rate = 20 / (166.7 + 20) = 10.7 percent. Escapes per inspected board = 20 / 10000 = 0.2 percent. Limits: the 90 percent coverage means 50 calls are unverified, so the true false-call and escape rates are uncertain. The downstream audit may miss escapes, so the escape rate is a lower bound. The audit covers only 10000 boards and the sampled board mix, so the rates may not apply to other mixes or program revisions.

defect.symptom: AOI repeatedly calls missing solder fillet on small chip capacitors after reflow, but manual verification finds acceptable solder.
defect.cause: The inspection window was too tight for normal reflow shift, and the solder channel exposure was too high, so the fillet contrast fell below the threshold.
defect.action: Measure the actual placement and reflow shift in millimeters, widen the window to cover the verified variation, reduce or rebalance the solder lighting exposure, retrain the fillet threshold from golden and defect samples, then run a verification audit before releasing the program.

title: AOI metrics: escape rate, false calls, first-pass yield, verification workflow

goals.text: Compute escape rate, false-call rate and verification coverage from audit data and state their limits.

blocks.alt: An audit workflow diagram linking inspection result, verification call and disposition, with escape rate and false-call rate readouts
blocks.caption: AOI metrics: escape rate, false calls, first-pass yield and the verification workflow

theory.p: AOI metrics are process indicators built from audit data, not direct measurements of the true defect population. AOI is a screening step, so its reported rejects, passes, and escapes depend on program setup, optics, lighting, component library, panel design, paste, reflow, and operator verification. Metrics should be stratified by product, line, shift, program version, and defect type before being used for decisions. They are most useful when compared over time for the same product family and when paired with downstream test, rework, and field data. A metric that looks good at the AOI station may be incomplete if downstream steps mask defects or if verification is not audited. For this reason, escape rate, false-call rate, verification coverage, and first-pass yield should be reviewed as a set rather than as isolated station scores.

Escape rate is usually defects found after AOI divided by units inspected, panels inspected, or component opportunities inspected. The denominator must match the question: board-level escapes use boards, joint-level escapes use joints, and component-level escapes use components. Downstream sources include in-circuit test, functional test, manual visual audit, X-ray, rework, and field returns. Limits include detection capability of downstream steps, escapes below AOI resolution, intermittent defects, and time lag before field returns appear. A low escape rate can mean good detection, good downstream masking, or insufficient downstream detection. If the downstream audit is weak, the escape rate will understate the true problem. If the denominator is too broad, a small number of escapes can look insignificant even when a specific component or panel location is failing.

False-call rate is verified good rejects divided by verified AOI rejects. It requires a verification workflow that dispositions each reject as true defect, false call, marginal, or other category. If verification coverage is incomplete, the rate is an estimate from the verified subset and is only reliable when the verified rejects are representative of all rejects. Limits include operator bias, marginal acceptance, duplicate rejects, program changes, and differences between AOI images and physical inspection. False calls are not automatically waste; some may flag marginal conditions that later become escapes. A false call can also indicate that the AOI program is too sensitive for the current paste, stencil, or placement process. The disposition categories should be stable over time, because changing definitions can make the false-call rate move without any real process change.

First-pass yield is units completed without rework or repair divided by units started. In AOI context, distinguish AOI pass yield, which penalizes all AOI rejects including false calls, from line first-pass yield, which depends on final disposition after verification and downstream test. FPY can be misleading if rework loops, duplicate boards, batch holds, or late dispositions are not counted consistently. A high FPY with poor verification coverage may hide escapes, while a lower FPY with strong verification may reflect better detection of marginal defects. When FPY is used for improvement, it should be paired with escape rate and false-call rate so the team can see whether yield is improving because defects are prevented or because detection is being relaxed. Consistent definitions across shifts and products are essential.

A practical verification workflow starts with an AOI reject, then review of the image and physical board, then disposition against documented visual acceptance criteria. Verification coverage is verified rejects divided by total AOI rejects. Coverage should include random samples of passes as well as rejects, because pass audits estimate escapes that downstream may not catch. Coverage limits arise when only high-risk rejects are verified, when operators verify only obvious defects, or when the same AOI image is used without physical confirmation. Coverage should be reported with the false-call rate so the estimate can be interpreted. A verification workflow also needs disagreement audits, where another inspector reviews a sample of dispositions, and clear rules for marginal cases. Without these controls, coverage can be high in count but weak in quality.

Escape rate, false-call rate, and coverage are proportions, so small denominators produce unstable results. A few defects in a small audit can move the rate substantially, so control charts, confidence intervals, and Pareto analysis by defect type, component, package, panel location, shift, and program version are more useful than a single weekly number. Comparisons should be made between similar products and similar AOI programs. Practice-based thresholds should be set from historical capability, customer requirements, and equipment datasheets, then verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Thresholds should be reviewed when the product mix, AOI program, stencil, paste, or reflow profile changes. A target that is stable for one product family may be inappropriate for another because component density, package type, and panel design change the detection challenge.

False-call reduction usually starts with program tuning, lighting, fiducial quality, panel layout, component library accuracy, and threshold settings. Escape reduction may require better AOI coverage, added X-ray or functional test, and correction of paste, stencil, placement, or reflow variation. Verification coverage improves with training, clear acceptance criteria, disagreement audits, and sampling of passes. The metrics should drive containment and prevention actions, not just reporting. For THT, AOI may have limited visibility of pin joints, so escape metrics should be interpreted with X-ray, functional test, or manual audit data. Improvement actions should be tracked with before and after data, including the same denominators and verification rules, so the team can tell whether the change improved detection, reduced false calls, or simply shifted the problem to another station.

calc.task: A line inspected 12000 boards through AOI during a week. AOI reported 360 rejects. Quality verified 300 rejects and found 90 false calls. Downstream test and visual audit found 18 defects after AOI. Compute escape rate, false-call rate, and verification coverage, and state the limits of each result.
calc.solution: Escape rate calculation: downstream defects divided by inspected boards = 18 / 12000 = 0.15 percent. This uses a board-level denominator; it does not represent joint-level escape rate and depends on downstream detection. False-call rate calculation: false calls divided by verified rejects = 90 / 300 = 30 percent. This is based on verified rejects only; if unverified rejects differ from verified rejects, the estimate is biased. Verification coverage calculation: verified rejects divided by AOI rejects = 300 / 360 = 83.3 percent. Coverage below full verification means false-call rate is an estimate, not a census. Interpretation: report the three metrics together. A false-call rate of 30 percent with 83.3 percent coverage should be stratified by defect type, component, package, panel location, shift, and program version before setting targets.

defect.symptom: AOI false-call rate rises after a new panel design, while escape rate stays low.
defect.cause: Panel deformation or fiducial variation causes image misalignment, and program thresholds are too tight for the new placement variation.
defect.action: Verify panel and fiducial quality, retune the AOI program with golden boards, audit verified rejects, and monitor false-call rate and verification coverage.

title: X-ray interpretation: BGA ball size and voiding, bridging, through-hole fill

goals.text: Classify a defect image into a defect type and an accept / rework / reject disposition with the criterion named.
Choose the inspection method (visual, AOI, 2D X-ray, laminar/3D X-ray, boundary scan) for a stated defect and board feature.

blocks.alt: An X-ray view of a BGA package showing ball size variation, voids and a bridge, beside an X-ray view of through-hole fill
blocks.caption: X-ray interpretation: BGA ball size and voiding, bridging and through-hole fill

theory.h: What X-ray is used for in SMT/THT inspection
theory.p: X-ray inspection is used when the defect is hidden from optical methods: BGA ball collapse, voiding, bridging under a component, and through-hole fill behind a pad. AOI and visual inspection can verify component placement, polarity, tombstoning, and exposed solder fillets, but they cannot reliably see under a BGA body or inside a plated through-hole. For hidden solder joints, 2D X-ray is usually the first method; laminar or 3D X-ray is used when overlapping features, multiple layers, or true volumetric void measurement are required. Boundary scan is not an imaging method; it is an electrical test method for selected digital interconnects and may detect opens or shorts only if the design supports it.

theory.h: BGA ball size and collapse interpretation
theory.p: In a BGA X-ray image, each solder ball should appear as a discrete, roughly circular feature with consistent diameter and spacing across the array. Ball size is interpreted relative to the expected land pattern, paste volume, component specification, and reflow profile. A ball that is too small may indicate insufficient paste, paste bleed, poor stencil release, or excessive reflow loss. A ball that is too large may indicate excessive paste, paste bleed between adjacent lands, or insufficient paste separation. For BGA land and paste design, IPC-7095 provides guidance on land pattern and paste printing design; verify the specific land size, paste aperture, and volume against the component datasheet and your paste/equipment datasheet.

A void appears as a dark, low-density region inside a solder ball because X-rays pass more easily through gas than through solder. Small voids are common and may be acceptable depending on size, location, and product class. IPC-A-610 includes acceptability criteria for voids in solder balls; for many Class 3 applications, voids are commonly evaluated against a limit such as 25% of the ball area, but the exact class, revision, and customer requirement must be checked against IPC-A-610 and the applicable contract. Voids near the outer edge of a ball or voids that coalesce across multiple balls are more concerning than isolated central voids because they can reduce effective wetted area and increase thermal or mechanical risk.

theory.h: Bridging under BGA and fine-pitch components
theory.p: Bridging appears as a continuous high-density solder path connecting two or more balls that should be electrically isolated. In a BGA, this may be visible as a diagonal or horizontal line between adjacent balls, especially near the array edge or under the die shadow. Common causes include excessive paste volume, paste bleed, misalignment, collapsed balls, or reflow ramping that causes solder to flow laterally before wetting. IPC-7095 provides design guidance for BGA land patterns and paste apertures; verify paste aperture size, pitch, and stencil thickness against your paste and stencil datasheet. For fine-pitch QFN or QFP, AOI may detect exposed bridges, but BGA bridges usually require X-ray.

Through-hole X-ray is used to evaluate solder fill inside a plated through-hole, especially when the joint is hidden by a component body, shielding, or a second-side component. A good through-hole joint should show solder wetting the pad, hole wall, and lead, with fill height appropriate to the hole diameter and component class. IPC-A-610 includes criteria for through-hole solder fill and voids; for many Class 3 applications, voids are commonly evaluated against a limit such as 25% of the hole circumference, but the exact class, revision, and customer requirement must be checked against IPC-A-610 and the applicable contract. Verify hole diameter, lead diameter, and required fill height against the board and component datasheets.

Use visual inspection for exposed joints, polarity, missing components, tombstoning, and obvious solder defects. Use AOI for exposed SMT placement, solder fillet shape, tombstoning, and many exposed bridges. Use 2D X-ray for BGA voiding, BGA ball size, hidden bridging, and simple through-hole fill when overlapping layers do not obscure the feature. Use laminar or 3D X-ray when the board has stacked BGAs, dense routing, multiple layers, or when void volume and location in depth must be separated from overlapping features. Use boundary scan for selected digital interconnects when the board design supports it; it can detect some opens and shorts but does not replace X-ray for solder geometry.

Disposition should be based on a named criterion, not on appearance alone. Accept when the measured defect is within the applicable IPC-A-610 class and customer requirement. Rework when the defect is repairable and the board design, component type, and thermal budget allow repair without damaging adjacent features; for example, a localized BGA bridge may be reworked if the land pattern and component can survive the repair process. Reject when the defect violates the named criterion and cannot be reliably reworked, such as a void exceeding the allowed ball area, a bridge that cannot be removed without lifting pads, or a through-hole joint with insufficient fill that cannot be repaired to the required criterion. Always record the standard, class, measured value, and disposition.

calc.task: A BGA solder ball has a measured diameter of 0.45 mm. The X-ray image shows a void with an estimated diameter of 0.22 mm. Using a circular approximation, calculate the void area as a percentage of the ball area and classify the defect against a named criterion. Assume the applicable requirement is IPC-A-610 Class 3, voids in solder balls shall not exceed 25% of the ball area, and verify the exact class and revision against the contract.
calc.solution: 1. Ball diameter D = 0.45 mm. Ball radius r_ball = 0.45 / 2 = 0.225 mm. 2. Ball area A_ball = pi * r_ball^2 = pi * (0.225)^2 = pi * 0.050625 = 0.1590 mm^2. 3. Void diameter d = 0.22 mm. Void radius r_void = 0.22 / 2 = 0.11 mm. 4. Void area A_void = pi * r_void^2 = pi * (0.11)^2 = pi * 0.0121 = 0.0380 mm^2. 5. Void percentage = (A_void / A_ball) * 100 = (0.0380 / 0.1590) * 100 = 23.9%. 6. Compare with IPC-A-610 Class 3 criterion: 23.9% is less than 25%. 7. Defect type: void in BGA solder ball. Disposition: accept, provided the void location and any additional voids are also within the applicable IPC-A-610 class and customer requirement.

defect.symptom: 2D X-ray shows a continuous high-density solder path connecting two adjacent BGA balls near the array edge. The balls are otherwise similar in size, but the bridge is located where paste apertures are close together.
defect.cause: Excessive paste volume or paste bleed between adjacent apertures, possibly caused by stencil thickness, aperture design, paste rheology, or reflow profile. IPC-7095 provides BGA land and paste design guidance; verify paste aperture size, stencil thickness, and release behavior against the paste and stencil datasheet.
defect.action: Confirm the bridge with 2D X-ray and, if overlapping features make the extent unclear, use laminar or 3D X-ray. If the bridge is repairable without lifting pads or damaging adjacent balls, rework and re-inspect by X-ray. If the bridge cannot be removed reliably, reject the board. Correct the process by reducing paste volume, adjusting stencil design, improving paste alignment, or modifying the reflow profile, then verify with X-ray and electrical test.

title: Disposition language: defect, condition and class in workmanship terms

goals.text: State findings in workmanship-standard vocabulary so a second engineer reaches the same disposition.

blocks.alt: A decision ladder from observed condition, to defect classification, to acceptance class, with the standard term for each step
blocks.caption: Disposition language: defect, condition and class in workmanship terms

theory.p: In AOI, disposition language converts a visual or geometric call into a repeatable engineering statement. A second engineer should be able to read the finding and reach the same accept, reject, or rework decision without relying on the inspector's tone. The statement should identify the object, the observed condition, the applicable workmanship class, the evidence, and the verification status.

theory.h: Defect, condition, and class are different terms
theory.p: Workmanship vocabulary separates three ideas. A defect is a nonconformance to the applicable workmanship requirement. A condition is the observable state that may or may not be a defect depending on class and criteria, such as insufficient solder, lifted lead, tombstoning, or solder bridge. A class is the product or workmanship level, commonly IPC-A-610 Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3, which sets the acceptance threshold for the same condition.

theory.h: AOI output is evidence, not final disposition
theory.p: AOI can indicate a suspected condition based on height, area, shape, color, or position, but it may miss hidden defects and may produce false calls from shadows, reflections, or component tolerance. Use words such as indicated, suspected, or requires verification until the condition is confirmed by measurement, microscopy, X-ray, or manual inspection.

A useful finding sentence has a fixed order: location, object, condition, evidence, standard or class, and proposed action. For example: 'U7 pin 12: suspected insufficient solder fillet; AOI fillet height 0.18 mm; verify against IPC-A-610 Class 2 and paste deposit data.' This gives the second engineer the location, the measured evidence, the applicable class, and the next step.

theory.h: Class changes the meaning of a condition
theory.p: A condition that is acceptable for general electronics may be unacceptable for high-reliability assemblies. IPC-A-610 Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 describe increasing workmanship requirements; the same solder fillet, component tilt, or solder ball may be dispositioned differently. The class should be stated on the finding, not assumed from the product name.

theory.h: Disposition terms should match the process system
theory.p: Workmanship acceptance is usually accept or reject against the applicable standard. Manufacturing disposition may add rework, scrap, or use-as-is, but rework should restore the assembly to the original acceptance criteria. Rework and repair activities should follow IPC-7711/7721 or the customer-approved equivalent, and the finding should state whether rework is proposed or already performed.

theory.h: Handoff information for a second engineer
theory.p: For handoff, include enough information to reproduce the decision: panel or serial number, coordinate or reference designator, AOI program version, measurement value, uncertainty or confidence, applicable standard and class, and verification method. If a number is process-based rather than standard-based, label it as a process limit and cite the paste, stencil, or AOI datasheet; for example, AOI height uncertainty may be around 0.02 mm to 0.05 mm, but verify against the equipment datasheet.

calc.task: An AOI station reports 'suspected insufficient solder fillet' at Q1 pin 3. AOI measured fillet height = 0.18 mm. The internal process limit for this package is 0.20 mm minimum, and the AOI height measurement uncertainty is ±0.05 mm. The assembly is IPC-A-610 Class 2. Determine whether the finding should be dispositioned as reject, verify, or accept, and write the standardized finding.
calc.solution: 1) Record the evidence: AOI height = 0.18 mm. 2) Apply measurement uncertainty: lower bound = 0.18 mm - 0.05 mm = 0.13 mm; upper bound = 0.18 mm + 0.05 mm = 0.23 mm. 3) Compare with the internal process minimum of 0.20 mm. The upper bound exceeds the minimum, so the AOI call alone does not prove rejection. The lower bound is below the minimum, so acceptance cannot be concluded without verification. 4) Disposition: verify. Use manual inspection, microscopy, or a calibrated AOI re-run; if the confirmed fillet is below the applicable IPC-A-610 Class 2 criterion and the internal minimum, reject or rework per IPC-7711/7721; if confirmed at or above the criterion, accept. 5) Standardized finding: 'Q1 pin 3: suspected insufficient solder fillet; AOI height 0.18 mm ±0.05 mm; internal process minimum 0.20 mm; verify against IPC-A-610 Class 2 before disposition.'

defect.symptom: AOI repeatedly rejects a suspected solder bridge condition on QFP pins 14 and 15 at the same panel location after a stencil change.
defect.cause: Excessive paste deposit, paste release variation, or print misalignment can create bridge risk between fine-pitch leads; verify paste volume, alignment, and stencil condition against the paste and stencil datasheet.
defect.action: Quarantine the affected panel, verify the bridge with microscopy or X-ray if needed, adjust the printer or stencil process, rework confirmed bridges per IPC-7711/7721, then reinspect with AOI and record the disposition using the same workmanship vocabulary.

title: Classification drill: print, placement, reflow and THT images

goals.text: Classify a defect image into a defect type and an accept / rework / reject disposition with the criterion named.
State findings in workmanship-standard vocabulary so a second engineer reaches the same disposition.

blocks.alt: Four small board images in a row, one per process stage, each with a defect to classify
blocks.caption: Classification drill: print, placement, reflow and through-hole images

theory: In an AOI classification drill, the first task is to identify the process stage from image evidence before naming the defect. A print image shows paste deposits on bare board pads, usually matte and paste-like, with no component bodies or reflowed solder. A placement image shows components on paste, with leads or terminations contacting paste but not yet wetted. A reflow image shows solidified solder joints, often shiny or dull depending on process, and may show component damage or solder morphology. A THT image shows leads passing through plated holes and solder on the exit side, so the hole wall and lead-to-hole interface are primary evidence.

Classify the defect by the physical condition, not by the suspected machine cause. Use workmanship vocabulary such as insufficient solder, excess solder, bridging, solder ball, void, dewetting, lifted lead, tombstoning, misalignment, wrong polarity, missing component, insufficient hole fill, icicle, and cold solder. The same visual condition can arise from different causes, but the defect type and disposition should be based on what the image proves about the joint or deposit.

For print defects, compare the paste deposit to the stencil aperture and paste datasheet. Measure paste deposit height in micrometres against the stencil and paste datasheet, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Insufficient paste, bridging, smearing, misprint, and incomplete release are judged by whether the deposit can form an acceptable joint after reflow. If the image shows paste outside the intended aperture, classify the condition as bridging or smearing and note the pad or net location. If the deposit is thin, broken, or absent, classify it as insufficient paste or misprint. Disposition is usually rework of the print process and removal of the affected boards, unless paste contamination or damage makes the board unusable.

For placement defects, verify component presence, orientation, polarity, and termination contact. A missing component, wrong component, reversed polarity, rotated chip, or lifted termination is a placement or feeder issue until reflow evidence shows otherwise. If the component is on the correct pad but not seated, classify the visible condition as misalignment or lifted termination. If the component is on the wrong pad or has the wrong polarity, classify it as wrong component or wrong polarity. Disposition is rework when the component and board are undamaged; reject when the component is damaged, the pad is lifted, or the wrong part cannot be identified and replaced.

For reflow defects, judge the solder joint against the applicable workmanship standard, commonly IPC-A-610, and against the design intent. Tombstoning, solder balls, bridging, insufficient solder, excess solder, voiding, dewetting, and lifted leads are common image findings. A solder ball on the board surface may be reworkable if it can be removed without damaging the board; a bridge between adjacent pads is reworkable if the pads and traces are intact. If the image shows pad lifting, substrate damage, or a component crack, the disposition is reject because rework may not restore reliability.

For THT defects, inspect the exit side for hole fill, wetting, lead exposure, and solder shape. IPC-A-610 provides acceptability criteria for hole fill, wetting angle, excess solder, icicles, solder balls, and lifted leads, but the exact acceptance limits depend on product class and current revision, so cite the standard and revision in the finding. A dull, grainy, or non-wetted joint suggests insufficient heat, poor flux activity, or contamination. A long icicle or excess solder may be reworkable if the hole is not damaged and the joint can be reworked to an acceptable shape.

To make the disposition reproducible, record the finding as location, component or net, defect type, criterion, evidence, and disposition. Accept means the image meets the named criterion and no reliability concern is visible. Rework means the condition is repairable under IPC-7711/7721 or an approved repair procedure, and the board can be re-inspected. Reject means the board or component is damaged, the defect is not repairable, or the criterion cannot be met without unacceptable risk. This wording lets a second engineer reach the same disposition from the same image.

calc.task: Classify the following AOI image findings: a paste deposit outside the intended aperture; a chip component with one termination lifted before reflow; a reflowed joint with a bridge between adjacent pads; a THT joint with a dull, grainy surface and no wetting to the hole wall. For each finding, name the defect type and the accept, rework, or reject disposition with the criterion.
calc.solution: Identify the process stage from the image evidence. Name the defect using workmanship vocabulary. Cite the criterion that controls the disposition. Choose accept, rework, or reject based on repairability and damage. Record location, component or net, defect type, criterion, evidence, and disposition. For the paste deposit outside the intended aperture, classify it as bridging or smearing; rework the print process and remove the affected boards unless paste contamination or board damage makes the board unusable; cite the stencil aperture, paste datasheet, and IPC-A-610 joint acceptability after reflow. For the lifted termination before reflow, classify it as lifted termination or misalignment; rework placement if the component and pad are undamaged; reject if the pad is lifted or the component is damaged; cite IPC-A-610 placement and solder joint acceptability. For the reflowed bridge, classify it as bridging; rework if the pads and traces are intact; reject if pad lifting or substrate damage is visible; cite IPC-A-610 solder joint acceptability. For the THT dull non-wetted joint, classify it as cold solder or insufficient wetting; rework per IPC-7711/7721 if the hole wall and lead are sound; reject if hole wall damage or non-repairable contamination is present; cite IPC-A-610 THT solder joint acceptability.

defect.symptom: AOI flags a THT joint with a dull, grainy solder surface, poor wetting to the hole wall, and a lead that appears exposed at the exit side.
defect.cause: Insufficient preheat or dwell, low flux activity, oxidized leads, or hole wall contamination prevented proper wetting and hole fill.
defect.action: Quarantine the board, inspect adjacent joints, rework per IPC-7711/7721 if the hole wall and lead are sound, verify solderability and reflow profile against equipment datasheet, and update incoming inspection if contamination is confirmed.

title: What stays through-hole and why: connectors, mechanical load, power

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

theory.p: Through-hole technology remains useful when a joint must resist mechanical load, support a heavy connector, carry appreciable current, or survive repeated insertion and removal. A plated through-hole gives the lead a barrel to wet into, and the solder inside the hole can add retention and thermal path. The trade-off is process control: hole diameter, plating thickness, lead diameter, flux activity, preheat, and solder dwell all affect whether the hole fills and wets reliably.

blocks.alt: Through-hole solder joint cross-section with barrel fill and annular ring callouts, and a connector under mechanical load
blocks.caption: Through-hole joint cross-section: barrel fill, annular ring, and the mechanical load that keeps through-hole in the design

theory.h: Finished plated-hole diameter is the controlling dimension
theory.p: The drill size is not the final hole size. The finished plated-hole diameter is the diameter after copper plating and any final finish. For solder fill, the relevant gap is the finished hole diameter minus the lead diameter. A board supplier may control drill diameter, plated diameter, plating thickness, and hole wall coverage, but the assembly process must verify the finished hole diameter because it determines capillary gap and heat transfer.

Connector leads have nominal diameter and tolerance, and the board hole has its own tolerance. The worst-case clearance is found by combining the smallest hole with the largest lead, and the largest clearance by combining the largest hole with the smallest lead. For common small through-hole leads, a diametral clearance of roughly 0.10 mm to 0.30 mm is often workable for wave or selective solder, but the correct value depends on paste or flux, preheat, solder temperature, dwell, board orientation, and pad thermal mass. Verify against your paste, flux, and equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Clearance affects fill, not just fit
theory.p: If the gap is too small, flux and solder may not penetrate, trapped air may remain, and the joint may show incomplete fill or voiding. If the gap is too large, capillary action weakens, heat transfer to the hole may be less effective, and solder may not wet the full barrel. A radial clearance of roughly 0.05 mm to 0.15 mm is a practical starting range for many plated through-hole joints, but it should be confirmed by cross-section or X-ray for the actual board and component.

theory.h: Expected solder fill is a process result
theory.p: Expected solder fill can be estimated from geometry, but the actual fill height is a process result. The theoretical annular volume is the hole volume minus the lead volume over the hole depth. The actual fill may be lower because of oxide, insufficient flux activity, low board temperature, short dwell, poor hole wall wetting, or trapped air. Use a trial run and measure fill height, then use that measured fill fraction for prediction until the process is stable.

For connectors, the through-hole joint may be chosen for pull-out strength, shear resistance, and durability under cable strain. For power paths, the current may travel through the plated barrel and the solder joint, so hole plating quality, solder fill, and thermal relief design matter. Current rating should be checked against the connector specification and relevant IPC guidance for current carrying and thermal rise, rather than inferred from hole size alone.

Before releasing a through-hole design, verify finished hole diameter, lead diameter, hole depth, plating thickness, and pad geometry. Then run a solderability trial and inspect cross-sections or X-rays for fill height, wetting, voiding, and solder balling. Use IPC-A-610 acceptance for your product class as the pass/fail reference, but treat calculated fill as a prediction that must be confirmed by measurement.

Favors through-hole

calc.task: A through-hole connector lead has nominal diameter 0.80 mm with tolerance plus or minus 0.03 mm. The finished plated hole diameter is nominal 1.10 mm with tolerance plus or minus 0.05 mm. Hole depth is 1.60 mm. A trial wave solder process gives 75 percent hole fill. Calculate minimum and maximum diametral clearance, radial clearance, annular cross-sectional area, theoretical annular volume, expected solder fill height, and expected solder volume.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate lead limits. Minimum lead diameter = 0.80 mm - 0.03 mm = 0.77 mm. Maximum lead diameter = 0.80 mm + 0.03 mm = 0.83 mm. Step 2: Calculate finished hole limits. Minimum hole diameter = 1.10 mm - 0.05 mm = 1.05 mm. Maximum hole diameter = 1.10 mm + 0.05 mm = 1.15 mm. Step 3: Calculate diametral clearance. Minimum diametral clearance = minimum hole diameter - maximum lead diameter = 1.05 mm - 0.83 mm = 0.22 mm. Maximum diametral clearance = maximum hole diameter - minimum lead diameter = 1.15 mm - 0.77 mm = 0.38 mm. Nominal diametral clearance = 1.10 mm - 0.80 mm = 0.30 mm. Step 4: Calculate radial clearance. Minimum radial clearance = 0.22 mm / 2 = 0.11 mm. Maximum radial clearance = 0.38 mm / 2 = 0.19 mm. Nominal radial clearance = 0.30 mm / 2 = 0.15 mm. Step 5: Calculate annular cross-sectional area using hole area minus lead area. Minimum area uses minimum hole and maximum lead: area = 0.32 mm squared. Maximum area uses maximum hole and minimum lead: area = 0.57 mm squared. Nominal area uses nominal hole and nominal lead: area = 0.45 mm squared. Step 6: Calculate theoretical annular volume by multiplying area by hole depth. Minimum theoretical volume = 0.32 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.52 mm cubed. Maximum theoretical volume = 0.57 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.92 mm cubed. Nominal theoretical volume = 0.45 mm squared x 1.60 mm = 0.72 mm cubed. Step 7: Calculate expected fill height from the trial fill fraction. Expected fill height = 0.75 x 1.60 mm = 1.20 mm. Step 8: Calculate expected solder volume by applying the trial fill fraction to theoretical volume. Minimum expected volume = 0.75 x 0.52 mm cubed = 0.39 mm cubed. Maximum expected volume = 0.75 x 0.92 mm cubed = 0.69 mm cubed. Nominal expected volume = 0.75 x 0.72 mm cubed = 0.54 mm cubed. Step 9: Compare the measured fill height and wetting to IPC-A-610 acceptance for your product class, and verify the process against your paste, flux, and equipment datasheet.

defect.symptom: X-ray or cross-section shows connector through-hole joints with solder reaching only the lower half of the hole, while the upper barrel remains dry or lightly wetted.
defect.cause: The hole-to-lead clearance is too small for the selected flux and wave or selective solder parameters, or the board temperature at the hole is too low for the solder to flow and wet the full barrel. Pad thermal mass or a large ground plane can also draw heat away from the joint.
defect.action: Measure finished hole diameter and lead diameter, then calculate actual clearance. Increase preheat or board temperature within the flux and board limits, increase dwell time, verify flux activity and application, and check hole plating quality. If the geometry is the limiting factor, revise the finished hole diameter or lead diameter and re-run a solderability trial with cross-section or X-ray verification.

title: Hole and lead: diameters, tolerance stack-up, placement tolerance, percent fill

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

blocks.alt: A hole and lead cross-section with the diameter stack-up, the placement tolerance and a barrel fill percentage gauge
blocks.caption: Hole and lead: diameters, tolerance stack-up, placement tolerance and percent fill

theory.h: Plated-hole diameter is the assembly reference, not the drill diameter
theory.p: For a plated through-hole, the relevant hole size for lead insertion is the finished plated-hole diameter, not the bare drill diameter. The drill diameter is only one input to the stack-up; copper plating, hole wall roughness, and drill wear reduce the usable diameter. In practice, measure the finished plated-hole diameter on the assembly side and the component side, because barrel plating can make the hole slightly non-cylindrical. If the measured diameter is close to the lead diameter, insertion force, skew, and solder-fill risk increase. Verify the finished hole diameter against the PCB fabrication drawing and the board supplier's capability report.

theory.h: Lead diameter and tolerance stack-up determine insertion clearance
theory.p: The lead diameter must be treated as a range, not a single nominal value. Component leads may be round, rectangular, or formed, and the effective insertion dimension can be larger than the nominal wire diameter because of plating, burrs, or forming radius. The clearance is the difference between the finished plated-hole diameter and the maximum effective lead dimension. A small nominal clearance can disappear after tolerance stack-up. For production, calculate worst-case clearance using the minimum plated-hole diameter and the maximum lead dimension, then verify against the insertion equipment's alignment capability and the component datasheet.

theory.h: Placement tolerance consumes clearance before the lead enters the hole
theory.p: Placement tolerance is the positional error between the intended hole center and the actual lead center. It can come from feeder repeatability, vision calibration, tape-and-reel or tube handling, board warpage, and lead-forming variation. If the lead is displaced by more than the available radial clearance, it will bind on the hole wall or miss the hole. For manual insertion, operator alignment can reduce this error; for automated insertion, the placement tolerance must be included in the clearance calculation. Verify the placement tolerance against the insertion machine specification and the board panelization datum scheme.

theory.h: Clearance is not the same as solder-fill capability
theory.p: A joint can insert successfully but still have poor solder fill if the annular gap is too small or too large. Too little clearance can trap air, restrict flux flow, and prevent solder from wetting the full hole wall. Too much clearance can allow the lead to sit off-center, create a large void path, and reduce capillary control. The desired clearance is therefore a process window, not a single value. For wave soldering, the gap must support solder flow through the hole while maintaining enough capillary action to fill the joint. Verify the acceptable clearance range against the solder process, flux activity, preheat profile, and wave or selective-solder equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Expected solder fill depends on hole geometry, lead size, and process window
theory.p: Expected solder fill is usually expressed as the percentage of the hole depth filled with solder after the joint solidifies. It is influenced by hole aspect ratio, lead-to-hole clearance, surface finish, flux wetting, preheat temperature, solder temperature, dwell time, and whether the board is wave soldered, selective soldered, or hand soldered. A high aspect-ratio hole with tight clearance may fill less reliably than a shallow hole with moderate clearance. For production, use the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for the applicable product class and verify the actual fill with cross-sections or X-ray where required.

theory.h: Tolerance stack-up should be calculated before choosing the hole size
theory.p: A practical stack-up includes PCB finished-hole tolerance, lead diameter tolerance, lead-forming tolerance, placement tolerance, and any allowance for board warpage or panel distortion. The result should be compared with the minimum clearance needed for insertion and the minimum gap needed for solder fill. If the calculated clearance is marginal, adjust the hole size, tighten component lead tolerance, improve placement calibration, or change the insertion method. Do not rely on nominal values alone; use worst-case or statistical tolerance analysis depending on production volume and risk.

theory.h: Use measured data to close the loop between design and assembly
theory.p: The most reliable clearance and fill predictions come from measured data: plated-hole diameter distribution, lead diameter distribution, placement error distribution, and solder-fill results from pilot builds. If the design clearance is within the calculated range but fill is poor, investigate flux activity, preheat, wave height, conveyor speed, and hole wall condition. If insertion force is high, investigate drill wear, plating thickness, lead burrs, and placement repeatability. Record the measured values and compare them with the design assumptions so future hole and lead selections are based on actual process capability.

calc.task: A plated through-hole is specified with a nominal finished diameter of 1.00 mm and a PCB tolerance of ±0.05 mm. A component lead has a nominal diameter of 0.60 mm and a tolerance of ±0.03 mm. The insertion placement tolerance is ±0.08 mm. Calculate the minimum radial clearance, the worst-case insertion clearance, and the expected solder-fill range for a wave-soldered joint.
calc.solution: 1. Minimum finished plated-hole diameter = 1.00 mm - 0.05 mm = 0.95 mm. 2. Maximum lead diameter = 0.60 mm + 0.03 mm = 0.63 mm. 3. Nominal radial clearance before placement error = (1.00 mm - 0.60 mm) / 2 = 0.20 mm. 4. Worst-case radial clearance before placement error = (0.95 mm - 0.63 mm) / 2 = 0.16 mm. 5. Placement tolerance consumes radial clearance. If the lead center is displaced by 0.08 mm, the remaining radial clearance on the tight side = 0.16 mm - 0.08 mm = 0.08 mm. 6. Therefore, the worst-case insertion clearance is 0.08 mm radial, or 0.16 mm diametral, assuming the lead and hole remain circular and the lead does not bind. 7. For solder fill, use the nominal gap and the worst-case gap. Nominal gap = 1.00 mm - 0.60 mm = 0.40 mm. Worst-case gap = 0.95 mm - 0.63 mm = 0.32 mm. 8. A typical wave-soldered through-hole joint may show solder fill from about 75% to 100% of hole depth when the gap, flux, preheat, and wave parameters are within the process window. Verify the actual expected fill against the IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for the applicable product class and against pilot-build cross-sections. 9. If the measured fill is below the required acceptance level, investigate hole wall condition, flux activity, preheat temperature, solder temperature, dwell time, and placement repeatability before changing the hole or lead size.

defect.symptom: Leads insert with high force or partially miss the hole, and wave-soldered joints show incomplete fill, voiding, or solder that does not wet the full hole wall.
defect.cause: The finished plated-hole diameter is smaller than assumed, the lead diameter is at the upper tolerance limit, or placement error consumes the available clearance. The resulting gap is too small for reliable flux flow and solder capillary action.
defect.action: Measure the finished plated-hole diameter and lead diameter on the assembly line. Recalculate the worst-case clearance including placement tolerance. If clearance is marginal, adjust the PCB hole tolerance, tighten lead tolerance, improve placement calibration, or verify the wave-solder process window. Confirm the corrected process with insertion-force data and solder-fill cross-sections.

title: Insertion: seating, stand-off, polarity, clinch, insertion damage

goals.text: Choose board direction, clinch and masking for a layout to limit shadowing at the wave.
Identify insertion defects from a board image and name the process cause.

blocks.alt: An insertion machine head seating a through-hole lead, with stand-off and clinch callouts and a damaged-lead warning
blocks.caption: Insertion: seating, stand-off, polarity, clinch and insertion damage

theory.h: Wave shadowing is a layout and handling problem, not only a solder problem
theory.p: Shadowing occurs when a component, adjacent part, or fixture blocks molten solder from reaching a through-hole joint during wave soldering. The wave sees the board as a sequence of obstacles: tall parts, dense pin fields, large ground planes, and closely spaced components can create local dry zones. The practical goal is to choose board direction, clinch, and masking so that solder can flow into the hole and wet the annular ring without being deflected or trapped by nearby geometry.

theory.h: Board direction controls how solder approaches the joint
theory.p: Board direction should be selected so that the wave approaches the side of the component least likely to shield the joint. For a rectangular component, the long axis is often oriented parallel to the wave direction when the body would otherwise cast a shadow over its own leads. For a connector or tall part, the joint side should face the incoming wave where possible, or the board should be angled to reduce the shadow length. The exact angle is process-dependent; typical conveyor angles are small, often around 3 to 7 degrees, but verify against your wave solder equipment datasheet and trial boards.

theory.h: Clinch geometry affects both seating and solder access
theory.p: Clinching is used to hold components during insertion and transport, but it also changes the gap between the component body and the board. A tight clinch can improve seating and reduce stand-off, but it may also close the gap under the component and restrict solder flow. A loose clinch can improve access but may allow vibration-induced lift or misalignment. For many through-hole components, a controlled clinch that keeps the body stable while leaving a small solder-access gap is preferred; verify the clinch force and final stand-off against your insertion machine and component datasheet.

theory.h: Stand-off is a trade-off between seating, cleaning, and solder access
theory.p: Stand-off is the distance between the component body and the board surface. Too little stand-off can trap flux, prevent solder from reaching the joint, and make cleaning difficult. Too much stand-off can increase solder demand, expose leads to mechanical stress, and reduce board density. For many radial and axial components, a practical stand-off range is often around 0.5 to 1.5 mm, but this must be verified against the component body, pin length, flux activity, and wave profile. For components with molded bodies or heat-sensitive materials, use the manufacturer's recommended seating or stand-off limits.

theory.h: Masking can reduce shadowing by exposing only the needed solder area
theory.p: Masking is used to protect areas that should not be soldered, but it can also worsen shadowing if it blocks the wave path or traps flux. A good mask layout exposes the annular ring and lead while avoiding large mask walls directly in front of the joint. Mask edges should be placed so that solder can flow around the joint rather than being forced through a narrow channel. For dense layouts, partial masking or local mask openings may be better than a continuous mask band. Verify mask thickness, edge clearance, and solder resist compatibility with your wave process.

theory.h: Polarity and orientation errors are insertion defects, not solder defects
theory.p: Polarity errors occur when a polarized component is inserted in the wrong direction. Common examples include electrolytic capacitors, diodes, LEDs, connectors with keyed bodies, and ICs with pin 1 indicators. These defects are usually caused by feeder setup, tray orientation, vision system misalignment, manual insertion error, or a mismatch between the placement program and the physical component. A polarity error may pass visual inspection if the body marking is not checked, so the inspection method must include the correct marking orientation, not just the presence of the part.

theory.h: Insertion damage is often a mechanical or feeder problem
theory.p: Insertion damage includes bent leads, crushed component bodies, cracked ceramic parts, damaged pin plating, and torn board land patterns. These defects are commonly caused by misaligned feeders, excessive insertion force, worn insertion heads, incorrect pin straightening, or board support problems. The defect location often points to the cause: damage on one side of the board may indicate a feeder or head offset, while damage on a single component type may indicate a tray, tape, or feeder setup issue.

theory.h: Use a board image to separate process causes from cosmetic issues
theory.p: When reviewing a board image, first identify the component type, pin geometry, and board side. Then look for patterns: one component type affected suggests feeder or program error; one board location affected suggests head or support error; many similar joints affected suggests wave direction, clinch, or masking error. For shadowing, look for dry or insufficient solder on the side opposite the wave approach. For insertion damage, look for lead deformation, body cracks, or board damage near the insertion point. For polarity, compare the component marking with the board silkscreen and pin 1 indicator.

theory.h: Choose the control that matches the defect mechanism
theory.p: If the problem is shadowing, adjust board direction, clinch, stand-off, or mask layout before changing the wave temperature or speed. If the problem is insertion damage, correct the feeder, head alignment, pin straightening, or board support. If the problem is polarity, correct the feeder orientation, vision reference, program, or manual insertion aid. The goal is to remove the physical cause so the process can produce acceptable joints without relying on excessive solder or rework.

calc.task: A radial electrolytic capacitor has a body diameter of 10.0 mm and a body height of 12.0 mm. The board is moving through the wave at 1.2 m/min. The wave approach angle is 5 degrees relative to the board surface. Estimate the shadow length cast by the component body at the board surface, and decide whether a 0.8 mm stand-off is likely to help or worsen solder access if the adjacent component is 1.5 mm away from the capacitor body.
calc.solution: 1. The shadow length at the board surface can be approximated by the component height divided by the tangent of the wave approach angle: shadow length = height / tan(angle). 2. For a 12.0 mm height and 5 degree angle: tan(5 degrees) is approximately 0.0875. 3. Shadow length = 12.0 mm / 0.0875 = 137 mm. This is a simplified geometric estimate; actual solder flow, flux, and board support will change the result. 4. The 137 mm estimate shows that a low wave angle can create a long geometric shadow, so board direction and component orientation matter strongly. 5. The 0.8 mm stand-off is small compared with the 10.0 mm body diameter, so it may improve seating but can reduce solder access under the body. 6. The adjacent component is only 1.5 mm from the capacitor body, which is a tight gap for flux escape and solder flow. 7. A practical conclusion is that the 0.8 mm stand-off may worsen access in this tight layout unless the wave direction is changed, the clinch is loosened slightly, or the mask and component spacing are adjusted. 8. Verify the final stand-off, clinch force, and wave angle with trial boards and your wave solder equipment datasheet.

defect.symptom: A board image shows several electrolytic capacitors with one lead dry or insufficiently wetted on the side away from the wave, while the opposite lead is acceptable. The capacitor bodies are seated close to the board, and the adjacent component is less than 2 mm away.
defect.cause: The joint is being shadowed by the capacitor body and nearby component because the stand-off is too small for the wave approach direction. The tight clinch or seating condition reduces the gap needed for flux escape and solder flow, so the wave cannot reach the far lead reliably.
defect.action: Change the board direction or wave approach angle so the shadow falls away from the joint. Increase stand-off slightly within the component and process limits, or adjust the clinch to hold the part without closing the solder-access gap. If the layout is dense, revise the mask opening or component spacing to expose the annular ring and allow solder flow. Run a trial board and inspect the joint against IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria and your wave solder process specification.

title: Preparing the board for wave: carriers, pallets, masking, taping, orientation

goals.text: Choose board direction, clinch and masking for a layout to limit shadowing at the wave.

blocks.alt: A board loaded into a carrier with masked and taped areas and an orientation arrow, beside a pallet cross-section
blocks.caption: Preparing the board for wave: carriers, pallets, masking, taping and orientation

theory.p: In wave soldering, the board underside passes over a stationary solder wave. Tall components, connectors, heat sinks, shielding cans, and pallet supports can deflect the wave and leave pads downstream dry, underfilled, or poorly wetted. The preparation task is to identify shadow sources, locate critical pads, and choose board direction, lead clinch, and masking so that critical pads are not in the wake of a tall object. Use IPC acceptance criteria for electronic assemblies to judge wetting and flux residues.

For a single board or panel, rotate the layout so the long axis of tall rectangular components is perpendicular to the conveyor direction when possible. If critical pads cannot be moved, rotate the board by 90 degrees or use a small angle to move the wake away from critical pads. Verify the chosen direction with a trial board because wave turbulence, nozzle design, and flux activity change the shadow length.

Where leads are formed or clinched on the wave side, keep bends from lying across downstream pads. Prefer bends perpendicular to the wave direction or directed away from critical pads. Keep wave-side lead protrusion short and controlled, commonly 0.5-1.5 mm, and verify against your equipment and flux datasheet. Long or angled leads can act as small dams and increase shadowing.

Carriers and pallets should hold the board flat, prevent bowing, and allow flux and air to escape. Support pins and pallet edges should not block the wave path or cover pads. Maintain clearance under the board, often 1-2 mm, so the wave can contact the underside evenly. Verify flatness and support placement because a bowed board can create local shadowing even when orientation is correct.

Masking covers areas that should not receive solder and can reduce shadowing from large metal parts. Use high-temperature tape or liquid mask that survives preheat and wave contact. Cover connector bodies, heat sinks, test points, and surface-mount devices not intended for wave. Mask edges should be flat and sealed, and the mask should not trap flux or block drainage. Verify mask material against your flux and equipment datasheet.

Taping secures masks and protects edges. Use high-temperature adhesive tape with a release that does not lift during preheat. Seal tape edges so flux does not wick underneath. Avoid covering drainage holes or pallet vents. After a trial, inspect for lifted tape, flux entrapment, and residue on adjacent pads. Adjust tape width and overlap, commonly 6-12 mm, based on your line results.

Before production, run a trial board with the selected orientation, clinch, pallet, and mask. Inspect pads downstream of tall components for wetting, solder volume, and residue. If shadowing remains, change one variable at a time: rotate the board, change clinch direction, add masking, or adjust pallet support. Record the accepted combination so operators can reproduce it.

calc.task: A 120 mm by 80 mm board has a 12 mm tall connector near the center and critical pads 18 mm downstream of the connector. The line runs at 1.0 m/min with 4 s wave contact. Choose board direction, clinch, and masking to limit shadowing.
calc.solution: 1. Estimate shadow length. For a tall component aligned with the wave, use a practical range of 1.5-2.5 times component height. For 12 mm height, shadow length is 18-30 mm. 2. Compare with critical pad distance. The pads are 18 mm downstream, so they are at the near edge of the estimated shadow and may be at risk. 3. Rotate the board 90 degrees so the connector long axis is perpendicular to the wave. For a perpendicular connector, use a reduced practical range of 1.0-1.5 times height, giving 12-18 mm shadow length. 4. Because 18 mm is still borderline, add high-temperature masking over the connector body and extend the mask 5 mm upstream and downstream of the connector. 5. Set wave-side lead clinch perpendicular to the wave or away from the critical pads, with lead protrusion 0.5-1.5 mm. 6. Run a trial at 1.0 m/min and 4 s contact, then inspect downstream pads. If shadowing remains, increase mask extension by 5 mm or rotate the board a few degrees, and verify against your equipment and flux datasheet.

defect.symptom: Pads downstream of a connector are dry or underfilled, with solder balls near the mask edge.
defect.cause: The board ran with the connector long axis parallel to the wave, and the mask edge lifted, allowing flux to trap solder at the mask boundary.
defect.action: Rotate the board 90 degrees, replace the mask with high-temperature tape sealed at the edges, extend the mask 5 mm past the connector, and run a verification board before releasing the lot.

title: Calculation drill: clearance and expected fill for a real BOM subset

goals.text: Calculate plated-hole diameter versus lead diameter, clearance and expected solder fill for a through-hole joint.

blocks.alt: A calculation panel showing hole diameter, lead diameter, clearance and expected fill for a small set of through-hole parts
blocks.caption: Calculation drill: clearance and expected fill for a real bill-of-materials subset

theory.p: Through-hole joints depend on the interaction between the plated hole, the component lead, and the solder process. The finished hole diameter, the lead diameter, and the board thickness determine the annular space that solder must fill. A calculation drill helps the engineer see whether a BOM subset is likely to produce acceptable fill before the first build.

Plated-hole diameter is not the same as the drill diameter. Drill size, copper thickness, and plating thickness combine to set the finished hole diameter. Use the approved land-pattern library and the board fabrication drawing, and verify the finished hole size against the drill and plating capability. IPC-7351 provides land-pattern and hole-size guidance, but the final value needs to match the fabrication process.

Lead diameter is controlled by the component supplier and by handling. Measure the lead diameter at the seating plane and at the exit side if the lead is bent or deformed. A tight fit can block capillary flow, while a loose fit can allow solder to drain or form a weak joint. The engineer should record nominal and worst-case dimensions rather than relying on a single nominal value.

Clearance is usually evaluated as diametral clearance, the difference between hole diameter and lead diameter. Radial clearance is half of that value. Both matter: diametral clearance affects assembly and alignment, while radial clearance affects the capillary gap that draws solder through the hole. The process window is not only a design value; it needs to be compatible with the wave or selective solder equipment.

Solder fill is driven by capillary action, flux activity, preheat, and contact time. A clean, wettable hole and lead are required for the solder to climb and fill the annular space. Preheat too low can leave the hole cold and produce partial fill, while excessive preheat can oxidize the joint or dry out flux. Verify the preheat and wave settings against your paste and equipment datasheet.

Acceptance of hole fill is defined by the applicable IPC-A-610 class. IPC-A-610 sets a minimum vertical barrel fill of 75% for both Class 2 and Class 3, with Class 3 additionally requiring visible fillets on the primary and secondary sides. A documented exception allows about 50% fill, or 1.2 mm, for parts with fourteen or more leads whose barrels tie into internal thermal or conductor planes. Some customers specify 100% fill contractually, which is a customer requirement rather than an IPC-A-610 class limit. A process target should be set above the minimum for the required class, but the target is not a substitute for acceptance criteria.

For a calculation drill, use nominal dimensions first, then worst-case tight and loose cases. Calculate the annular volume and the expected fill volume. Compare the result with the required class and with the process capability. If the expected fill is close to the minimum, plan cross-section or X-ray verification before production.

calc.task: For a single axial resistor in the BOM subset, the lead diameter is 0.50 mm nominal and 0.55 mm maximum. The plated through-hole diameter is 0.90 mm nominal, 0.85 mm minimum, and 0.95 mm maximum. The board thickness is 1.60 mm. Calculate nominal diametral clearance, worst-case tight and loose diametral clearance, nominal annular volume, and expected solder fill at a 90% process target. Compare the expected fill with IPC-A-610 minimum hole fill for the applicable class.
calc.solution: Nominal radii: hole radius 0.45 mm, lead radius 0.25 mm. Nominal diametral clearance: 0.90 - 0.50 = 0.40 mm. Worst-case tight: hole minimum 0.85 mm, lead maximum 0.55 mm, diametral clearance 0.85 - 0.55 = 0.30 mm. Worst-case loose: hole maximum 0.95 mm, lead minimum 0.50 mm, diametral clearance 0.95 - 0.50 = 0.45 mm. Nominal hole volume: pi * 0.45 * 0.45 * 1.60 = 1.02 cubic millimetres. Nominal lead volume: pi * 0.25 * 0.25 * 1.60 = 0.31 cubic millimetres. Nominal annular volume: 1.02 - 0.31 = 0.70 cubic millimetres. Expected fill volume at 90% target: 90% of 0.70 = 0.63 cubic millimetres. The 90% target is above the IPC-A-610 minimum vertical barrel fill of 75% that applies to both Class 2 and Class 3; a customer requirement for 100% fill is contractual and is not an IPC-A-610 class limit. Verify the required class and process capability.

defect.symptom: X-ray or cross-section shows hole fill below the applicable IPC-A-610 minimum, with dull solder at the exit side and occasional open at the lead shoulder.
defect.cause: The hole-to-lead clearance is too tight for the wave or selective solder process, or preheat is too low, so capillary flow stalls before the hole fills. Verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, measure finished hole diameter and lead diameter, check drill and plating records, adjust preheat and contact time within equipment limits, and requalify with cross-section or X-ray.

title: Wave architecture: flux, preheat, wave types (single/dual, lambda, micro-wave)

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

theory.p: Wave soldering window is the interaction of flux application, preheat, wave contact, and cooling. For lead-free wave, the window is narrower because alloy wetting and intermetallic formation require adequate board temperature and short contact. Set the window by thermocouple profiling and cross-section, then verify against your paste and equipment datasheet.

blocks.alt: A wave soldering line side view with fluxer, preheat, a dual wave drawn as two overlapping fountains, and cooling
blocks.caption: Wave architecture: flux, preheat and the wave types — single, dual, lambda and micro-wave

theory.p: Preheat activates flux, drives off solvents, and raises board and component leads to a temperature where solder wets without thermal shock. Target top-side temperature before wave should be established by profiling; common practice uses a soak plateau, but the exact value depends on board mass, flux, and equipment. Use thermocouples on heavy ground planes and small pads, and follow IPC-7530 for profiling.

Contact time is set by wave length and conveyor speed. Too short gives insufficient fill and cold joints; too long causes excess solder, bridging, and thermal stress. Conveyor speed should be adjusted with wave height and pump condition, and verified with cross-sections and solder weight.

Wave height controls wetting pressure and contact. A too-high wave can flood through-holes and create icicles; a too-low wave can miss pads. Nozzle clogging and pump wear change effective contact time even if speed is unchanged.

Nitrogen reduces oxidation of solder and flux residue, improves wetting, lowers dross, and can reduce bridging. It does not replace proper preheat or flux selection. Oxygen level should be controlled and monitored, and the benefit is greatest on fine-pitch and high-density boards.

Flux solids, activation, and application density determine residue, wetting, and cleaning. Too little flux causes non-wetting and shading; too much causes residue, bridging, and cleaning burden. Flux density should be measured and trended, and residue should be evaluated by cross-section and ion chromatography or equivalent.

Cross-sections show whether the window is correct. Shading indicates oxidation or insufficient flux activity; excess solder indicates too much wave height, too long contact, or poor drainage; insufficient fill indicates low preheat, short contact, blocked holes, or poor wetting. Use IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria for evaluation.

calc.task: A board requires 4 s wave contact time. The wave contact length is 250 mm. Set conveyor speed. The board top surface must reach 105 °C before wave, starting from 25 °C, over 90 s. Calculate average preheat ramp rate.
calc.solution: First, convert wave length to meters: 250 mm = 0.250 m. Next, conveyor speed = wave length / contact time = 0.250 m / 4 s = 0.0625 m/s. Then convert to m/min: 0.0625 m/s * 60 s/min = 3.75 m/min. Next, preheat ramp = (105 °C - 25 °C) / 90 s = 80 °C / 90 s = 0.889 °C/s. Finally, convert to °C/min: 0.889 °C/s * 60 s/min = 53.3 °C/min. Verify the selected speed and ramp against your equipment, flux, and board thermal mass.

defect.symptom: Shading on through-hole barrels and pads after wave, with dull gray surface and poor wetting at hole entrance.
defect.cause: Flux activity too low, preheat too low, oxygen in wave zone high, or contaminated nozzle.
defect.action: Verify flux density and activation, profile board temperature, reduce oxygen, clean nozzle, and run cross-section.
