title: Flux selection and application: solids, activity, amount, pattern, verification

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

blocks.alt: A fluxer head spraying a pattern onto a board underside, with a solids readout, an activity class label and a verification coupon
blocks.caption: Flux selection and application: solids, activity, amount, pattern and verification

theory.p: Flux selection for wave and selective wave starts with board and termination condition: base metal, finish, oxidation, hole geometry, component mass, and acceptable residue. For THT, flux must reach hole walls and lead surfaces; for SMT selective wave, flux must wet pad and termination without excessive residue under components. IPC J-STD-004 provides flux classification by residue type and activity; use the datasheet to confirm compatibility with the finish and cleaning process.

Solids content controls residue, bridging, and post-solder cleanliness. Low-solids no-clean fluxes leave less visible residue but may need more precise preheat; higher-solids rosin or water-soluble fluxes can improve wetting on oxidized surfaces but increase residue and cleaning burden. Select solids from the flux datasheet and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet for spray viscosity and residue acceptability.

Activity must be high enough to remove oxides during preheat and wave contact, but low enough to avoid corrosion, solder balling, or residue that traps moisture. IPC J-STD-004 activity classes can guide selection: use low activity for clean, fresh finishes and higher activity for oxidized or high-thermal-mass joints, then verify by wetting and residue tests.

Apply enough flux to wet all solderable surfaces, but avoid pooling in holes, under components, or on non-solderable areas. For jetted or fogged flux, pattern uniformity matters more than peak thickness; verify coverage with flux indicator paper, residue inspection, or cross-section. Amount is usually controlled by nozzle pattern, pressure, board speed, and flux solids; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

Preheat activates flux, drives off solvent, and reduces thermal shock. Target board temperature should be high enough to activate flux before wave contact but below damage limits for board and components. Use thermocouples on heavy pads and component bodies, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and board material limits.

Wave height sets contact area and turbulence. Too low causes incomplete hole fill; too high causes bridging, solder balls, and erosion of pads. Fog height or selective wave height should be set relative to board thickness and hole pattern, then verified by cross-section and visual inspection.

Verification should include first-article wetting, hole fill, residue, cleanliness, and reliability checks. IPC J-STD-001 and IPC-A-610 provide acceptance criteria for soldered assemblies; use them with your internal limits for flux residue and cleaning.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm glass-epoxy board, 50 mm x 40 mm, has 100 through-hole pads with fresh finish. Select no-clean flux type, amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: First, board area = 50 mm x 40 mm = 20 cm2. Next, select no-clean organic flux with low-to-moderate activity per IPC J-STD-004 because the finish is fresh and residue must remain acceptable without cleaning. Then set flux amount as a deposition of flux solids: a starting range of 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 of board bottom area, which is 500-1500 µg/in² of solids and about 0.8-2.3 g/m². For 20 cm2 that is 1.6-4.6 mg of solids; take the mid value 0.15 mg/cm2, giving 3.0 mg of solids. With a 2.0% solids flux within a 1.5-2.5% starting range, the solution mass is 3.0 mg / 0.02 = 150 mg. If the fluxer output is 300 mg/min of solution, spray time = 150 mg / 300 mg/min = 0.5 min, about 30 s. State the basis before comparing numbers: figures quoted per unit of liquid, for example 0.5-1.0 g/ft², are several times larger than solids-based figures. Verify the solids deposition with a fluxometer in µg/in² or by weighing a witness card, and verify the range against your flux and equipment datasheet. Set preheat target to 100 C within a 90-110 C starting range, measured with thermocouples, to activate flux and reduce thermal shock; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and board limits. Set fog/wave height to 1.5 mm within a 1.2-1.8 mm starting range above the board underside for hole fill without top-side overflow; verify by cross-section and visual inspection. Finally, justify: low-to-moderate activity matches fresh finish, 0.15 mg/cm2 of flux solids and 2.0% solids balance wetting and residue, 100 C preheat supports activation, and 1.5 mm wave height supports hole fill while limiting bridging.

defect.symptom: Solder balls and partial hole fill on the underside after wave soldering.
defect.cause: Flux amount or solids too high for the preheat setting, causing flux to boil and eject solder; wave height may be too low for hole fill.
defect.action: Reduce flux amount or solids, increase preheat until board top reaches the verified activation range, and adjust wave height upward only after checking for bridging; verify with cross-section and residue inspection.

title: Preheat: board top vs bottom temperature, flux activation, thermal limits

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

blocks.alt: A board cross-section with top and bottom temperature probes, a preheat curve, and a flux activation temperature band
blocks.caption: Preheat: board top versus bottom temperature, flux activation and thermal limits

theory.p: In wave soldering, heat enters mainly through the bottom side, so the bottom surface can rise quickly while the top surface lags. The top surface temperature is the practical control point for flux activation and solvent evaporation. Place thermocouples on the bottom near the wave contact zone and on the top over a representative component or pad. For a typical 1.6 mm FR-4 board, a top-surface target of 90-130 °C just before the wave is a common starting point, but verify against the flux datasheet, board thickness, copper content, and component sensitivity.

Select flux by residue requirements, cleaning capability, and hole-fill needs. No-clean fluxes are often used when cleaning is not available and residue must remain, but they may leave visible residue and require tighter preheat control. Water-soluble fluxes are often chosen for through-hole hole fill and when aqueous cleaning is available, but they can be more corrosive if not cleaned. Rosin-based fluxes may be used for certain repair or legacy processes. Use the flux classification and residue requirements from IPC J-STD-004 and confirm compatibility with the board finish and cleaning process.

Flux amount should be enough to wet all bottom pads, lead tips, and hole walls, but not so high that it boils violently, lifts components, or creates fog. For spray application, the controlled quantity is a deposition of flux solids per unit of bottom area: a starting range of 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2, which is 500-1500 µg/in² of solids and about 0.8-2.3 g/m², with the lower end for thin boards and the higher end for heavy copper or through-hole holes. Figures quoted per unit of liquid, for example 0.5-1.0 g/ft², are several times larger and are not comparable. For foam application, adjust foam height and dwell so the flux reaches hole walls without dripping. Verify the amount by weighing a test board before and after fluxing, and compare with the flux supplier's recommended solids content and activity.

theory.h: Preheat level and top versus bottom temperature
theory.p: Preheat should raise the board enough to activate flux and evaporate solvents without causing thermal shock or premature flux degradation. A practical target is a top-surface temperature of 90-130 °C and a bottom-surface temperature of 100-140 °C immediately before wave contact, with a controlled ramp. Thin boards may need lower preheat to avoid overheating components, while thick boards or high copper planes may need higher preheat to bring the top surface up. Use a thermocouple profile consistent with IPC-7530 guidance and adjust until hole fill and wetting are stable.

Wave height should be high enough to wet bottom pads and lead tips, but low enough to avoid flooding the top side or creating excessive turbulence. For a 1.6 mm board, a starting wave height of 0.5-1.5 mm above the bottom surface is common; verify by visual inspection and by checking for solder balls, bridging, and top-side contamination. Flux fog is controlled by spray pressure, nozzle distance, flux viscosity, and preheat. A fine, even mist is preferred; dripping flux or visible fog on nearby surfaces indicates excessive application or poor atomization.

theory.h: Setting a process for a given board
theory.p: For a thin board with light copper and small through-hole leads, start with lower flux density, lower preheat, and lower wave height. For a thick board, heavy copper, or large through-hole leads, increase preheat first, then flux amount, then wave height only if wetting is insufficient. If the top side is too cool, increase preheat or reduce conveyor speed; if the bottom side is overheating, reduce wave height or wave temperature. Record the settings that produce acceptable hole fill without solder balls, bridging, or component damage.

Verify the process with thermocouple data, weight gain for flux, and solder joint inspection. Check hole fill, wetting angle, residue, solder balls, bridging, and component damage. Use IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria for the required product class, and document the flux type, flux density, preheat setpoints, wave height, conveyor speed, and wave temperature. If a change is made, re-run a profile and inspect a representative board before production.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 board, 100 mm x 150 mm, 28 µm copper, 0.6 mm pitch SMT on top, 0.8 mm diameter through-hole leads on bottom, no-clean flux, aqueous cleaning not available. Set flux type and amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: 1. Flux type: choose no-clean low-residue flux because cleaning is not available; verify flux activity and residue against IPC J-STD-004 and supplier datasheet. 2. Flux amount: bottom area = 100 mm x 150 mm = 15000 mm2 = 150 cm2. Set the target as a deposition of flux solids, 0.15 mg/cm2 within the 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 (500-1500 µg/in²) starting range for mixed SMT/THT with no-clean flux, giving 150 cm2 x 0.15 mg/cm2 = 22.5 mg of solids. Add 10-20% for through-hole hole walls if spray does not fully wet holes; target 25-27 mg of solids. At 2.0% solids that is 1250-1350 mg of flux solution. Verify by weighing a test board or witness card before and after fluxing and converting the result to µg/in² of solids with a fluxometer. 3. Preheat: set top-surface target 110 °C and bottom-surface target 120 °C before wave. Use a controlled ramp and verify with thermocouples. This activates no-clean flux and evaporates solvents while limiting thermal stress on 0.6 mm pitch SMT. 4. Fog: set spray pressure 0.15-0.25 MPa and nozzle distance 100-200 mm. For this board choose 0.18 MPa and 150 mm. Verify that the spray forms a fine mist, not drips, and that nearby surfaces are not coated with flux fog. 5. Wave height: for a 1.6 mm board, set wave height 1.0 mm above the bottom surface. This is within the 0.5-1.5 mm starting range and leaves 0.6 mm clearance to the top side. Adjust up only if hole fill is poor; adjust down if solder balls, bridging, or top-side contamination appear. 6. Justification: no-clean flux requires controlled preheat, so 110 °C top and 120 °C bottom are reasonable starting targets. A flux-solids density of 0.15 mg/cm2 is enough to wet pads and leads without excessive fog. A wave height of 1.0 mm should wet the bottom side without flooding the top. Verify all settings with thermocouple data, flux weight, and IPC-A-610 inspection.

defect.symptom: Solder balls and small bridges on bottom pads after wave, with flux residue on the top side.
defect.cause: Flux amount or fog is too high, preheat is too low causing violent flux boiling, and wave height is too high causing turbulence and splashing.
defect.action: Reduce flux density to the lower end, reduce spray pressure or adjust nozzle distance, increase preheat slightly, lower wave height, then re-profile and inspect a representative board.

title: Contact time and fog height: dwell calculation, wave height vs board clearance

goals.text: Calculate wave contact (dwell) time from conveyor speed and contact length and judge the result against the process window.
Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.

blocks.alt: A board passing through a wave with contact length and conveyor speed marked, a dwell calculation panel and a clearance dimension
blocks.caption: Contact time and fog height: dwell calculation, wave height versus board clearance

theory.h: Contact time and why it matters
theory.p: Contact time, or dwell, is the time the board underside remains in the wave. Calculate it as t = L / v, where L is effective contact length in mm and v is conveyor speed in mm/s. Dwell controls heat transfer, flux activation, hole fill, and solder penetration. Too little dwell can leave icicles, poor wetting, and incomplete hole fill. Too much dwell can overheat the board, burn off flux, damage components, and increase solder bridging.

Use the effective contact length, not only the nozzle length. The wetted zone can extend beyond the nozzle because of turbulence, wave height, board clearance, and capillary action in through-holes. Measure it with a witness board, thermal paper, or a short test run with a marked board. For dual-wave machines, record the contact length for each wave and the total board residence in the combined wave zone.

Dwell windows are machine-, flux-, and board-specific. Typical single-wave dwell may be around 4-10 s, and dual-wave total dwell may be around 6-15 s, but verify against your paste/equipment datasheet and trial results. Judge dwell by hole fill, wetting, residue, and thermal stress, not by time alone. A high-thermal-mass board may need longer dwell, while small components and thin boards may need shorter dwell.

Choose flux type from the board design and cleaning capability. No-clean low-solids flux is common for mixed SMT/THT boards when residue is acceptable. Water-soluble flux may be chosen for heavy oxidation or dense through-hole fill, but it requires cleaning. Flux amount is specified by the flux supplier, normally as a deposition of flux solids in micrograms per square inch (µg/in²) measured with a fluxometer; a typical recommended range is 500 to 1500 µg/in² of solids, which is about 0.8 to 2.3 g/m² (1 in² = 6.45 cm², 1 m² = 1550 in²). Always state the basis before comparing numbers: figures quoted per unit of liquid, for example 0.5 to 1.0 g/ft², are not comparable with solids-based figures and are several times larger. Take the range from the flux datasheet and verify it against your equipment datasheet. Too little flux causes poor wetting and dewetting; too much flux causes spatter, residue, and solder balls.

Preheat raises the board underside to a temperature that activates flux and removes solvent before wave contact. Measure temperature on the board underside near the wave entry, not only in the air. A common starting board-underside range is 90-130 °C, but verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Low preheat can leave solvent in the flux and cause solder balls or poor wetting. High preheat can burn flux, oxidize pads, and stress components.

Fog height, or wave crest height above the nozzle, sets how far the wave reaches toward the board. Board clearance is the gap between the wave crest and the board underside at entry. If the wave is too high or clearance is too small, the board may contact the wave too early, causing excessive dwell, bridging, and board damage. If the wave is too low or clearance is too large, the wave may not penetrate through-holes, causing icicles and non-fill. Set wave height and clearance together, and check board bow and support.

Set flux type and amount first, then preheat, then wave height and board clearance, then conveyor speed. Use a test coupon with representative through-holes, pads, and components. Adjust speed to bring dwell into the process window, then adjust wave height or clearance to improve hole fill without increasing dwell beyond the window. Inspect the coupon against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria and record the settings.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 board with 0.8 mm through-holes and small SMT components is run on a single-wave machine. Conveyor speed is 1.0 m/min. Effective contact length measured with a witness board is 180 mm. The paste/flux datasheet gives a dwell window of 6-12 s. Calculate dwell time, judge it against the window, and set flux type and amount, preheat level, and fog/wave height with board clearance for this board.
calc.solution: 1. Convert speed: 1.0 m/min = 1000 mm / 60 s = 16.7 mm/s. 2. Calculate dwell: t = L / v = 180 mm / 16.7 mm/s = 10.8 s. 3. Judge: 10.8 s is inside the 6-12 s window, but near the upper end. If hole fill is good and thermal stress is acceptable, keep the speed. If icicles or poor fill appear, first check wave height and clearance before increasing dwell. If overheating or flux burn-off appears, reduce dwell by increasing speed; for a target of 8 s, set v = 180 mm / 8 s = 22.5 mm/s = 1.35 m/min. 4. Flux setting: use no-clean low-solids flux for mixed SMT/THT if residue is acceptable. Set spray density from the flux datasheet range, for example 500-1500 µg/in² of flux solids (about 0.8-2.3 g/m²), measured with a fluxometer by the wet or dry method; adjust tank pressure and traversing speed, then verify coverage and residue against your flux and equipment datasheet. 5. Preheat setting: set board-underside temperature near wave entry to 105-120 °C to activate flux and remove solvent while limiting thermal shock; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. 6. Fog/wave height and clearance: set wave crest height to 10-12 mm above the nozzle and set board support so the board underside is 0-0.5 mm above the wave crest at entry, giving light contact without forcing the board into the wave. 7. Validate: run a coupon, inspect hole fill, wetting, residue, and component damage, then adjust speed, wave height, or clearance in small steps.

defect.symptom: Solder icicles and partial hole fill on 0.8 mm through-holes at board exit, with wetted pads but no bridging.
defect.cause: Dwell time is too short, or wave height is too low and board clearance is too large, so the wave does not penetrate the holes; flux coverage may also be low.
defect.action: Increase dwell by reducing conveyor speed or increasing effective contact length; raise wave height or reduce board clearance within machine limits; verify flux coverage and preheat; re-run a coupon and inspect against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria.

title: Shadowing and orientation: shading, pallets, board direction, lead geometry

goals.text: Predict shadowing from layout and orientation and change direction, masking or sequence to remove it.

blocks.alt: A wave with a component casting a solder shadow behind it, a pallet blocking the path, and an orientation arrow showing board direction
blocks.caption: Shadowing and orientation: shading, pallets, board direction and lead geometry

theory.h: What shadowing means in wave soldering
theory.p: Shadowing is a wetting or fill defect caused when a component, pallet, fixture, or adjacent part blocks the solder wave, flux, or preheat path from reaching a pad, lead, or joint. In wave soldering, the defect is not only optical obstruction; it also includes local cooling, flux depletion, turbulence, and poor drainage. Predict it by asking whether solder can reach the joint from the wave side and whether the joint can drain after contact.

theory.h: Layout and orientation as the first predictor
theory.p: Layout predicts shadowing when a tall or wide component sits upstream of a smaller joint in the wave direction. A connector, shield, transformer, or tall electrolytic capacitor can create a low-energy zone behind it. Draw the wave direction on the assembly drawing and mark the solder-side access path. If a downstream joint lies behind a body, pallet wall, or adjacent part, expect incomplete fill, voiding, or cold joints. Verify the result with a test coupon because wave turbulence can extend or shorten the affected zone.

Board direction changes the shadow length because the same component presents a different projected height to the wave. A long body parallel to the wave direction can shadow a row of joints, while rotating the panel or component 90 degrees can reduce the projected length. Conveyor direction, wave angle, and board angle should be checked together. If the line allows panel rotation, compare the shadowed side before and after rotation; if it does not, use pallet clearance or masking to compensate.

Pallets can cause shadowing when holes are too small, walls are too thick, or support rails cover pads. They can also cause shadowing by trapping flux, shielding preheat, or holding heat that changes drainage. A good pallet opens the solder side around each joint, leaves clearance around leads, and avoids covering adjacent pads. Masking tape, kapton, or pallet masking can remove shadowing by blocking solder from unwanted areas, but the mask edge must not bridge into the joint. Verify against your pallet material, adhesive, and wave equipment datasheet.

Lead geometry controls how much solder can enter the hole and wet the pad. Long leads, tight lead-to-hole clearance, bent leads, and large component bodies can reduce capillary action and drainage. Axial and radial parts behave differently: axial leads may be shadowed by the body if the body sits close to the board, while radial leads may be shadowed by adjacent leads or a pallet wall. Check lead diameter, hole diameter, pad size, and component seating height against your drill and plating data.

Sequence can be changed at the layout, pallet, or line level. Place shadow-prone joints where the wave has already stabilized, avoid placing them directly behind tall parts, and use a pallet that exposes the joint from the wave side. In some lines, a second wave, a different wave angle, or a selective wave can improve access. If the defect is caused by a downstream part blocking drainage, move the part, rotate the panel, or add a pallet opening. Confirm the change with cross-section or wetting inspection, not only visual appearance.

Use a simple line-of-sight model first: project the component height along the wave angle to estimate a shadow zone, then add a margin for turbulence and flux depletion. Treat the model as a screening tool, not a guarantee. For production, run a coupon with the suspected orientation, inspect the joint, and adjust direction, masking, or sequence. Verify against your paste, wave, and pallet datasheets because the same layout can behave differently on different conveyors and wave types.

calc.task: A wave line runs left to right. A 10 mm tall connector with a 25 mm long body is placed 2 mm upstream of a row of 1.0 mm through-hole pads. The wave contact angle is estimated at 20 degrees from vertical. Predict whether the downstream pads are shadowed, then propose one orientation change, one pallet change, and one sequence change.
calc.solution: 1. Draw the wave direction left to right and mark the connector body. 2. Estimate shadow length using a line-of-sight model: shadow length = height * tan(angle). For 10 mm and 20 degrees, shadow length = 10 mm * 0.364 = 3.6 mm. 3. Compare with the gap: downstream pads are 2 mm behind the connector, so 2 mm is less than 3.6 mm; predict shadowing. 4. Add a turbulence and flux-depletion margin of 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm; the affected zone may extend to 4.1 mm to 4.6 mm. 5. Orientation change: rotate the connector 90 degrees so the 2 mm wide end faces the wave; shadow length = 2 mm * tan(20 degrees) = 0.7 mm, which is less than the 2 mm gap; verify with a coupon. 6. Pallet change: open the pallet hole around the downstream pads and add 1.0 mm clearance around the connector body; ensure the pallet wall does not cover the pads. 7. Sequence change: move the shadowed row downstream of the connector by at least 5 mm, or place it after a stabilizing wave zone; if layout cannot move, use masking or a selective wave to expose the joint.

defect.symptom: Downstream through-hole pads show partial fill and voiding only on the side away from the wave, while upstream pads are acceptable.
defect.cause: A tall connector body and pallet wall shadow the wave, and the board direction places the pads in a low-energy zone with poor flux and solder access.
defect.action: Rotate the panel or component, open the pallet around the pads, and re-run a coupon; if the defect persists, adjust wave angle or use masking to expose the joint.

title: Wave defect atlas: bridging, balling, insufficient fill, bypass, lifted lead, blowholes

goals.text: Diagnose a wave defect from a solder-side image and name the parameter responsible.

blocks.alt: Six small solder-side views labelled with each wave defect, shown beside a sound joint
blocks.caption: Wave defect atlas: bridging, balling, insufficient fill, bypass, lifted lead and blowholes

theory.p: A wave defect atlas starts with the solder-side image because the defect shape records the last thermal and wetting events. Look at fill height, meniscus, wetting angle, solder volume, and whether the defect is isolated or repeats by component mass. Use the same field of view for comparison. Acceptance limits are defined in IPC-A-610; verify the applicable class and revision before judging a joint.

theory.h: Bridging: excess volume and poor drainage
theory.p: Bridging usually appears as solder between adjacent pads or leads after the wave. It is commonly caused by too much solder volume, poor drainage, low preheat, slow conveyor, or flux that leaves residue. For fine pitch, check wave height, solder temperature, and flux coverage. Typical wave height windows are equipment dependent; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Balling: poor wetting or premature solidification
theory.p: Balling appears as separate solder balls on pads, traces, or component bodies. It often indicates poor wetting or premature solidification: low preheat, oxidized leads, insufficient flux activity, or a solder temperature that is too low for the alloy. Balling can also come from excessive turbulence or poor drainage. Compare the ball location with the wave contact pattern and verify preheat and solder temperature against your paste/equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Insufficient fill: preheat and dwell control
theory.p: Insufficient fill is seen as a low solder column in a through-hole, often with a shiny meniscus at the bottom and little wetting on the lead. The responsible parameter is often preheat ramp or dwell: the hole top surface may not reach the temperature needed for capillary action. High hole aspect ratio, board thickness, and lead-to-hole clearance also matter. Typical preheat ramp rates are 1.0 to 3.0 °C/s and dwell times are 3 to 6 s, but verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.

Bypass is a joint that the wave did not wet, often showing a dry pad or lead with little solder. It can be caused by wave height too low, board warpage, poor flux coverage, conveyor speed too high, or a shielding effect from nearby components. Check the wave contact line and the board support. Verify wave height, conveyor speed, and flux spray pattern against your equipment datasheet.

Lifted lead appears as a lead that has separated from the pad or barrel after wave contact, sometimes with a small solder remnant. It is often a thermal-mechanical issue: high component mass, rapid heating, board expansion, or insufficient preheat can create differential movement. It can also be a handling or mounting issue. Verify preheat ramp, component mass, and board support against your process specification.

Blowholes appear as voids or craters in the solder joint, often near the hole wall or under the component. They are commonly caused by trapped moisture, solvent, or flux volatiles boiling during wave contact. A too-fast preheat ramp, low top-side temperature, high hole aspect ratio, or contaminated board can increase the risk. Verify preheat ramp, dwell, and board bake requirements against your paste/equipment datasheet and the applicable IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria.

theory.h: Diagnostic workflow from image to parameter
theory.p: For a solder-side image, classify the defect by shape: bridging, balling, low fill, dry joint, lifted lead, or void. Then map it to the most likely parameter: volume/drainage for bridging, wetting temperature for balling, preheat/dwell for insufficient fill, wave contact for bypass, thermal mass/support for lifted lead, and moisture/volatiles for blowholes. Confirm with a short DOE changing a single parameter at a time and record the image, profile, and paste/equipment datasheet limits.

calc.task: A solder-side image shows a through-hole with board thickness 1.6 mm, hole diameter 0.8 mm, lead diameter 0.5 mm, fill height 1.1 mm, preheat ramp 0.8 °C/s, dwell 2.5 s, and solder temperature 245 °C. Diagnose the defect and name the parameter most likely responsible.
calc.solution: Step 1: Classify the image. Low fill with a meniscus at the bottom is insufficient fill, not bridging or bypass. Step 2: Calculate hole aspect ratio: 1.6 mm / 0.8 mm = 2.0. A high aspect ratio increases the need for adequate preheat and dwell; verify the threshold for your board stackup and paste. Step 3: Calculate fill fraction: 1.1 mm / 1.6 mm = 0.6875, or 68.75%. Compare with the acceptance limit in IPC-A-610 for the applicable class; if the limit is higher, the joint fails. Step 4: Compare process values with typical windows: preheat ramp 0.8 °C/s is below the 1.0 to 3.0 °C/s range often used for through-hole fill, and dwell 2.5 s is below the 3 to 6 s range often used. Verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Step 5: Check solder temperature: 245 °C may be acceptable for some alloys but can be low for high thermal mass joints; verify against the paste/equipment datasheet. Step 6: Conclusion: the image and profile point to insufficient fill caused primarily by low preheat ramp and short dwell; adjust preheat ramp toward the verified range and dwell toward the verified range, then re-run with a single change at a time.

defect.symptom: Solder-side image shows low fill in through-holes with a shiny meniscus at the bottom, little wetting on the lead, and no bridging.
defect.cause: Preheat ramp is too low and dwell is too short for the hole aspect ratio, so the hole top surface does not reach the temperature needed for capillary action.
defect.action: Increase preheat ramp and dwell within the verified paste/equipment datasheet range, confirm top-side temperature at the hole, and re-run with a single parameter change.

title: Wave process control: bath contamination, tin consumption, records, first article

goals.text: Set flux type and amount, preheat level and fog/wave height for a given board and justify each setting.
Diagnose a wave defect from a solder-side image and name the parameter responsible.

blocks.alt: A solder pot with a contamination analysis readout and a tin consumption chart, beside a record sheet and a first-article board
blocks.caption: Wave process control: bath contamination, tin consumption, records and first article

theory.p: Wave process control sets the thermal and chemical conditions that allow solder to wet through-hole barrels and solder-side terminations without causing bridges, non-wetting, or spatter. The main controls are flux type and amount, preheat temperature, wave height or fog height, conveyor speed, and pot temperature. For a given board, justify each setting from board mass, copper content, component heat sinks, flux activation range, and the solder alloy liquidus.

Choose flux by the contamination level and residue requirements. Rosin mildly activated flux is common for general through-hole assemblies when residues can be cleaned or are acceptable. Water-soluble flux is used when oxide load is high or when cleaning is planned. No-clean fluxes are less common in wave because residue and spatter can be harder to manage; verify compatibility with the flux datasheet and cleaning process.

Flux amount is controlled as a deposition of flux solids per unit area of the bottom side. A practical starting range is 0.08 to 0.23 mg/cm2 of solids, which is 500-1500 µg/in² and about 0.8-2.3 g/m², then verify against the flux datasheet and spray pattern. Wet mass per unit area is several times larger because the flux is roughly 2% solids, so always state whether a figure is on a solids basis or a liquid basis before comparing it. Too little flux causes non-wetting and dull joints; too much flux can cause spatter, residue, and poor hole fill. Use a test coupon or board weight before and after fluxing to confirm coverage.

Preheat activates flux, removes volatiles, and reduces thermal shock. Measure the top surface or a representative thermal mass with a thermocouple. A practical entry range is 90 to 120 °C for many boards, but the flux activation temperature and board maximum temperature govern the final setting. If the board is too cold, flux boils violently and spatter appears; if it is too hot, flux can burn out before the wave.

Wave height controls how much solder contacts the board bottom. For a single wave, a crest height of 1 to 2 mm above the nozzle is a common starting point. For dual-wave machines, the first wave may be set near 1 to 2 mm and the second near 0.5 to 1 mm, with fog height often 2 to 5 mm above the nozzle. Verify against the equipment manual because nozzle geometry changes the relationship between crest height and board immersion.

Contact time is wave length divided by conveyor speed. A practical range is 2 to 4 s for many boards, adjusted for hole fill and component heat sinks. Pot temperature must be above the alloy liquidus. For Sn63/Pb37, 245 to 255 °C is a common range; for SAC305, 250 to 260 °C is common. Verify against the alloy datasheet and equipment capability, then record the actual pot temperature.

Wave bath condition changes wetting and defect rate. Copper, nickel, iron, and flux residues can enter the bath from boards, fixtures, and nozzles; monitor contamination against the solder supplier limits and change or filter the bath when wetting degrades. Tin consumption comes from dross, drag-out, evaporation, and replenishment losses; track solder added per board or per hour, dross handling, and pot level to keep the wave height stable.

Record flux type, lot, wet flux density, preheat temperature, wave height, fog height, conveyor speed, pot temperature, and any deviations. For first article, run the board, inspect the solder side against IPC-A-610 Class 2/3 acceptance, measure hole fill, and keep a solder-side image. If the first article fails, change one parameter at a time and record the result.

calc.task: A 1.6 mm FR-4 mixed assembly has 17 µm copper, 2 mm through-hole connectors, and small chip passives. The bottom area is 100 mm by 150 mm. Select flux type, flux amount, preheat level, wave height, fog height, and conveyor speed for a single-wave process, and justify each setting.
calc.solution: First, identify thermal behavior. The board is moderate mass with through-hole connectors that act as heat sinks, so preheat must be sufficient to bring the joint area to flux activation temperature without overheating the top side. Second, select flux. Use rosin mildly activated flux for general through-hole wetting, assuming residues are acceptable or cleaned; verify the flux activation range against the flux datasheet. Third, set flux amount. Target 0.20 mg/cm2 of flux solids on the bottom side, within the 0.08-0.23 mg/cm2 (500-1500 µg/in²) starting range. Bottom area is 100 mm x 150 mm = 15000 mm2 = 150 cm2. Required flux solids is 0.20 mg/cm2 x 150 cm2 = 30 mg per board; at 2.0% solids that is about 1500 mg of flux solution. Verify the solids deposition with a fluxometer or a weighed witness card. Fourth, set preheat. Target top surface temperature of 105 °C at wave entry, within the practical 90 to 120 °C range, then verify with a thermocouple on a test coupon. Fifth, set wave height. Use a single-wave crest height of 1.5 mm above the nozzle, within the 1 to 2 mm starting range, so the board bottom contacts the crest without excessive immersion. Sixth, set fog height. Use 3 mm fog height above the nozzle to pre-wet the underside before the main wave; verify against the machine manual. Seventh, set contact time. If the wave length is 80 mm and conveyor speed is 25 mm/s, contact time is 80 mm / 25 mm/s = 3.2 s, within the 2 to 4 s practical range. Eighth, set pot temperature. For SAC305, use 255 °C, above the SAC305 liquidus of 219 °C (217 °C is the solidus), and verify against the alloy and equipment datasheet. Ninth, justify. The flux amount supports wetting without excess residue, preheat activates flux and reduces spatter, wave height and contact time provide hole fill without excessive bridging, and pot temperature maintains solder fluidity.

defect.symptom: Solder-side image shows scattered small solder balls and spatter around through-hole connector leads, with some dull non-wetted pads nearby.
defect.cause: Preheat temperature was too low for the flux activation range, so flux volatiles boiled during wave contact and caused spatter; the same condition can reduce wetting and leave dull joints.
defect.action: Increase preheat so the top surface reaches 100 to 110 °C at wave entry, verify with a thermocouple, confirm flux activation range from the flux datasheet, and re-run first article. If spatter persists, reduce wave height or fog height slightly and check for board moisture or excessive flux volume.

title: Where selective beats wave: mixed assembly, heat-sensitive neighbours, throughput

goals.text: Choose nozzle and flux strategy for a joint group and defend the choice against the joint geometry.

theory.p: Selective soldering is used when a mixed assembly contains through-hole joints that cannot be processed by a full wave because nearby surface-mount components, plastic connectors, or heat-sensitive parts would be damaged by the thermal exposure. The process localises heat and flux to a joint group, so the engineer can protect neighbours while still producing a repeatable solder joint. The choice is not simply machine availability; it is a joint geometry decision. The joint group must be accessible from the bottom side, have enough clearance for the nozzle, and allow flux to reach the joint without being absorbed by adjacent paste deposits or trapped under components. IPC-A-610 acceptance classes should be agreed before the trial, because the same visual defect may be acceptable in one class and unacceptable in another. The engineer should also confirm that the selected process does not create new risks, such as flux migration, solder balls, or thermal damage to nearby joints.

blocks.caption: Selective soldering: a programmable micro-wave wets only targeted pads

blocks.alt: A mixed assembly with through-hole joints beside surface-mount parts, and a selective nozzle soldering one joint while the neighbours stay cool
blocks.caption: Where selective beats wave: mixed assembly, heat-sensitive neighbours and throughput

theory.p: A joint group is a set of joints that can be treated with a single nozzle path, one flux application, and one thermal profile. Common groups are isolated through-hole pins, connector rows, mixed through-hole and surface-mount pads, and repair or rework zones. Geometry controls the choice: pin diameter, hole plating, pad size, standoff height, component body height, and distance to the nearest heat-sensitive part determine whether a mini-wave, dip, or jet nozzle can reach the joint. A tall connector may require a taller nozzle or a different flux delivery method, while a low-standoff component may need a shallow wave to avoid flooding. Verify against the board layout and the nozzle datasheet before committing to a path. If the joint group includes mixed technology, confirm that the surface-mount joints are already reflowed or that the selective process will not disturb them.

Nozzle choice is a balance between wetting energy, thermal exposure, and reach. Mini-wave nozzles create a small solder wave and are often used for through-hole pins and mixed joints where the joint is exposed from below. Dip nozzles can provide a more uniform immersion for small groups but may increase heat exposure to nearby pads. Jet or spray-assisted nozzles can improve flux delivery and wetting on tight-pitch joints, but they require control of splash and solder mist. For a joint group with heat-sensitive neighbours, prefer the smallest nozzle that still produces complete wetting, and verify the nozzle height, wave height, and dwell time against the equipment datasheet. Typical practice values such as nozzle orifice size, wave height, and standoff should be recorded as a range until process capability is established. The nozzle must also be compatible with the solder alloy and flux chemistry.

Flux strategy must match the joint geometry and the contamination level. For clean boards with plated through-holes, a low-solids liquid flux applied by controlled spray or jet may be enough. For oxidised pins, high-thermal-mass connectors, or joints with limited access, a higher-activity flux or a pre-applied flux preform may improve wetting, but residues and corrosion risk must be evaluated. Flux volume should be enough to wet the joint and the hole wall, but not so much that it migrates to nearby surface-mount joints or causes solder balls. If the process uses aerosol or ultrasonic flux delivery, verify droplet size, spray pressure, and flux solids against the paste and flux datasheets, because the same nozzle can behave differently with different flux chemistries. Flux placement should be checked visually and by cross-section before production release.

Heat-sensitive neighbours are the main reason selective soldering is used, so the thermal budget must be controlled at the joint, not only at the nozzle. Preheat should raise the board and joint to a stable temperature before solder contact, reducing thermal shock and improving wetting without requiring a long dwell. The peak temperature and dwell time should be set from the component moisture sensitivity level and the solder alloy liquidus, with a margin agreed by the design and reliability teams. For components near the joint, measure the surface temperature at the component body or pin, not only the solder pot temperature. If the neighbour is a plastic connector, electrolytic capacitor, or small-signal device, verify its maximum temperature and time against the component datasheet and IPC J-STD-001 guidance for thermal exposure. Thermal profiling should include the worst-case joint and the nearest sensitive component.

Throughput is determined by the number of joint groups, the nozzle path length, the dwell time, the flux application time, and the time needed for preheat stabilisation. A single joint group may be processed quickly, but a mixed assembly often requires multiple passes, multiple nozzle changes, or multiple flux applications. The engineer should model cycle time as a sum of fixed and variable elements: flux application, preheat, solder dwell, cooling, and rework allowance. If throughput is too low, first reduce unnecessary path length or combine compatible joint groups, then adjust dwell and flux volume within the wetting window. Avoid shortening dwell below the point where hole filling and wetting are acceptable, unless a qualified alternate process is approved. IPC-A-610 acceptance should be used to confirm the joint, and IPC-7711/7721 should guide any rework.

theory.h: Decision method for nozzle and flux
theory.p: A defensible decision starts with the joint geometry. Draw the joint group, mark the nozzle access path, and identify the nearest heat-sensitive component. Then choose the nozzle that reaches the joint with the least thermal exposure, and choose the flux that provides wetting without migration. For a low-standoff joint near a plastic connector, a shallow mini-wave with low-solids flux may be preferred. For a high-thermal-mass connector with oxidised pins, a dip nozzle with higher-activity flux and longer preheat may be preferred. For tight-pitch mixed joints, a jet-assisted nozzle with controlled flux volume may reduce bridging. The choice must be defended by showing that the joint geometry, neighbour clearance, and thermal budget are compatible with the selected nozzle and flux. The defence should include trial data, not only vendor claims.

Verification should include cross-sections, hole filling, wetting angle, residue inspection, and thermal profiling at the joint and the neighbour. Record the nozzle type, nozzle height, wave height, dwell time, preheat temperature, peak temperature, flux type, flux volume, and spray parameters. Use a small trial matrix to find the process window, then confirm with production samples. For practice-based values, state them as ranges and verify against the paste, flux, and equipment datasheets. For acceptance, use the agreed IPC-A-610 class and the relevant IPC J-STD-001 requirements for materials and workmanship. If a joint fails, rework it according to IPC-7711/7721 and update the process window if the failure indicates a systematic nozzle or flux mismatch. Documentation should make the choice repeatable for another engineer.

calc.task: A mixed assembly has a 40-pin through-hole connector, a 0.65 mm pitch surface-mount QFP 8 mm away, and an electrolytic capacitor 12 mm away. The connector pins are 1.0 mm diameter and the board is 1.6 mm thick. Select a nozzle and flux strategy, then estimate cycle time and thermal margin.
calc.solution: Define the joint group as the 40 through-hole pins, because they share access, thermal mass, and flux requirements. Select a small mini-wave nozzle with an orifice of 1.5-2.5 mm, a wave height of 0.5-1.0 mm, and a standoff of 0.5-1.5 mm, because the joint is accessible from below and the nearby surface-mount QFP is 8 mm away. Select low-solids liquid flux delivered by controlled spray at 15-30 uL per joint group, because the pins are plated and the nearby joints do not require high-activity flux. Set preheat to 90-120 C board surface temperature, peak solder temperature to 245-255 C, and dwell to 2-4 s, then verify against the solder alloy liquidus and the component datasheet. Measure the capacitor body temperature during profiling; if the datasheet limit is 105 C and the measured value is 85-95 C, the margin is 10-20 C. Estimate cycle time as flux application 3 s, preheat 20 s, solder dwell 3 s, cooling 10 s, and nozzle path 15 s, giving 51 s per board. Defend the choice by showing that the mini-wave nozzle reaches the 1.0 mm pins without flooding the 0.65 mm pitch QFP, the flux volume is low enough to limit migration, and the thermal margin protects the capacitor. Confirm acceptance against IPC-A-610 and rework any defective joint according to IPC-7711/7721.

defect.symptom: After selective soldering, a through-hole connector shows intermittent opens and dull, grainy joints, while nearby surface-mount joints look acceptable.
defect.cause: The preheat was too low for the connector thermal mass, and the dwell was too short, so the hole wall and pin did not reach a stable wetting temperature; flux may have been insufficient or poorly distributed.
defect.action: Re-profile the joint group with a higher preheat and longer dwell, verify board surface temperature at the connector, confirm flux volume and nozzle standoff against the equipment datasheet, and rework affected joints according to IPC-7711/7721. Re-inspect against IPC-A-610.

title: Nozzle strategy: size and shape, flux-on-the-fly, dwell per joint, multi-pass

goals.text: Choose nozzle and flux strategy for a joint group and defend the choice against the joint geometry.
Build a selective program — path, order, dwell per joint, passes — for a given board.

blocks.alt: A set of interchangeable nozzles with a joint beside each, a flux-on-the-fly applicator, and a multi-pass sequence
blocks.caption: Nozzle strategy: size and shape, flux-on-the-fly, dwell per joint and multi-pass

theory.p: Nozzle strategy begins with joint geometry, not with a preferred nozzle. For through-hole leads, the nozzle opening must be large enough to let solder wet the lead and pad without dragging adjacent joints, yet small enough to keep the meniscus stable. For common lead diameters of 0.5 mm to 1.2 mm, a nozzle inside diameter of 0.8 mm to 2.0 mm is a practical starting range, but verify against your equipment and the adjacent pad spacing. For surface-mount pads, the nozzle footprint controls heat transfer and flux delivery, so the same joint can fail if the nozzle edge lands on an adjacent pad or misses the thermal mass.

Shape changes the thermal and wetting behavior. A conical nozzle concentrates heat on a small joint, which suits isolated through-hole pins and small surface-mount pads. A flat or annular nozzle spreads heat over a larger area, which helps large pads, ground planes, and multi-pin connectors where the joint must fill from the pad edge inward. A slot nozzle is useful for row connectors, shield cans, and long joints because it presents a narrow solder edge along the joint line. Choose the shape that matches the joint outline, then check clearance to nearby components and pads.

Flux-on-the-fly means flux is applied immediately before the solder wave or nozzle contact, so the flux is active when the joint reaches wetting temperature. The important variables are flux volume, pattern, viscosity, and solids content. A practical starting flux density is 0.05 mg/mm^2 to 0.25 mg/mm^2 on the joint area, or a joint volume of 0.5 uL to 3.0 uL for many selective soldering nozzles, but verify against your paste or flux datasheet and residue requirements. Too little flux gives poor wetting and pinholes; too much flux can cause residue, solder balls, or unstable meniscus behavior. Note the basis before comparing numbers: this figure is flux per unit of joint area for selective application, whereas the wave-soldering figures in Module 09 are flux solids per unit of board bottom area, so the two numbers must not be compared directly.

Dwell per joint is the time the joint is exposed to the solder wave or nozzle contact. It should be long enough to heat the joint, activate flux, and allow solder to flow, but short enough to avoid excessive intermetallic growth, component damage, or flux burn-off. For many through-hole joints, 0.5 s to 3.0 s is a reasonable starting range; for small surface-mount joints, 0.2 s to 1.5 s may be enough. Large thermal masses, such as connectors with ground tabs, may need longer dwell or a preheat pass. Use thermocouples on representative joints to verify the actual joint temperature rather than relying only on bath temperature.

Multi-pass programs separate functions that would otherwise compete in a single pass. A common sequence is a preheat pass, a flux pass, and a solder pass, or a wetting pass followed by a fill pass. For high thermal mass joints, a preheat pass of 100 C to 160 C can reduce thermal shock and shorten the solder dwell. Solder bath temperatures for common lead-free alloys are often around 250 C to 260 C, but verify against your alloy datasheet and equipment. Multi-pass can improve fill on large pads, but each pass adds cycle time and thermal exposure, so use the fewest passes that meet the joint.

Building a selective program means translating the joint list into path, order, dwell, and passes. Start by grouping joints by nozzle type and flux pattern, then order the path to keep the solder meniscus stable and avoid dragging solder across unsoldered joints. A practical order is to begin with low thermal mass joints to stabilize the process, then move to medium and high thermal mass joints, but verify with test coupons because board layout and component mass can reverse this. Keep the nozzle path away from tall components, avoid sharp direction changes over fresh joints, and use dwell tables so each joint group has its own time.

Defend the choice against the joint geometry by showing the physical reason for each parameter. State the lead diameter, pad area, component mass, access, and adjacent joint spacing. Then show that the nozzle size and shape cover the joint without bridging, that flux reaches the joint interface, that dwell heats the joint to the required wetting range, and that passes manage thermal mass. If a joint fails, change a single variable at a time: nozzle size, flux volume, dwell, or pass order, and record the result against your visual acceptance criteria.

calc.task: A board has 12 through-hole connector pins with 0.8 mm lead diameter and 1.6 mm pad diameter, 4 surface-mount power pads of 4 mm by 4 mm, and 1 ground pad of 8 mm by 8 mm. Choose nozzle size and shape, flux strategy, dwell per joint, and passes for a selective soldering program. Assume lead-free solder and verify against equipment datasheet.
calc.solution: Group the joints into 12 through-hole pins, 4 surface-mount power pads, and 1 ground pad. For the through-hole pins, choose a conical nozzle with inside diameter 1.2 mm to 1.6 mm, giving clearance around the 0.8 mm lead while avoiding adjacent 1.6 mm pads. For the 4 mm by 4 mm power pads, choose a flat or annular nozzle with footprint 4.5 mm to 6.0 mm to cover the pad edge and heat the copper. For the 8 mm by 8 mm ground pad, choose a slot or large annular nozzle with footprint 8.5 mm to 10.0 mm, or use a 2-pass strategy if the nozzle cannot cover the pad without adjacent risk. Use flux-on-the-fly with 0.10 mg/mm^2 to 0.20 mg/mm^2 on the joint area (a per-joint-area basis, not the flux-solids-per-board-area basis used for wave soldering in Module 09); for the ground pad, aim near 0.20 mg/mm^2 if residue allows. Set dwell: through-hole pins 1.2 s to 1.8 s; power pads 0.8 s to 1.5 s; ground pad 2.0 s to 3.0 s. Use 2 passes for the board: pass 1 preheat at 120 C to 140 C over high thermal mass joints, pass 2 solder at 255 C to 260 C. If the ground pad shows incomplete fill, add another pass with flux-only or lower dwell solder, then recheck.

defect.symptom: A 4 mm by 4 mm surface-mount power pad shows a dull, cratered fillet and lifted pad edge after selective soldering.
defect.cause: The nozzle footprint was too small, dwell was near 0.5 s, and flux density was near 0.05 mg/mm^2, so the pad did not reach wetting temperature and flux burned off before solder flowed.
defect.action: Increase nozzle footprint to 4.5 mm to 6.0 mm, raise flux density to 0.10 mg/mm^2 to 0.20 mg/mm^2, add a preheat pass at 120 C to 140 C, and increase dwell to 0.8 s to 1.5 s; verify with thermocouples and visual acceptance criteria.

title: Thermal budget of the neighbours: heat spread, monitoring, sensitive parts

goals.text: Estimate the heat exposure of neighbouring parts and specify the mitigation and the verification.

blocks.alt: A board cross-section showing heat spreading from a soldered joint into adjacent copper and components, with a temperature map
blocks.caption: Thermal budget of the neighbours: heat spread, monitoring and sensitive parts

theory.h: Thermal budget as a shared resource
theory.p: The thermal budget is not only the target joint profile; it is the cumulative heat that reaches nearby parts through conduction, convection, and radiation. In reflow, wave soldering, and hand soldering, the board, copper planes, leads, fixtures, and air all act as thermal paths. A neighbouring part can exceed its datasheet limit even when the target joint is within specification.

Conduction through copper planes and component leads usually dominates close to the heat source. Convection from oven air or wave solder flux vapour sets the background temperature. Radiation matters less at typical soldering temperatures but can contribute from hot fixtures or wave solder pots. The path with the lowest thermal resistance controls the peak temperature seen by the neighbour.

Large copper areas, thick board materials, high thermal conductivity substrates, dense component placement, and low standoff heights can carry heat farther. High paste volume, long time above liquidus, high peak temperature, and slow cooling extend the thermal exposure. Fixtures that contact the board can either sink heat or trap heat, depending on material and contact area.

Parts that often need attention include electrolytic capacitors, plastic connectors, LEDs, MEMS devices, sensors, adhesive-bonded components, and parts with moisture sensitivity. Their limits are usually defined by maximum body temperature, maximum time at temperature, moisture sensitivity, and mechanical deformation. Use the component datasheet and the assembly process specification to set the allowable thermal budget.

For early layout, estimate neighbour exposure by combining the measured or expected temperature of the heat source with an attenuation factor based on distance, copper connectivity, and local thermal mass. For production, replace estimates with thermocouple profiling at the worst-case location. Treat the estimate as a screening tool; the profile is the evidence.

Mitigation can be applied at layout, process, or fixture level. Layout changes include increasing spacing, adding thermal relief, reducing copper connectivity, and placing sensitive parts away from heat sources. Process changes include lowering peak temperature, shortening time above liquidus, using selective soldering, reducing paste volume, and adjusting conveyor speed. Fixtures and shields can reduce radiant or convective heat, while heat sinks can pull heat away from sensitive parts.

Verification should include a thermal profile with thermocouples attached to the target joint and the most exposed neighbour, functional testing after thermal exposure, and inspection for deformation, discoloration, or solder defects. Record the profile, the thermocouple locations, and the acceptance criteria. If the neighbour is near its limit, repeat the profile after any change to paste, oven setup, fixture, or component supplier.

calc.task: A wave-soldering line has a solder pot temperature of 250 °C (typical 245-260 °C; verify against equipment datasheet). The board top surface near the wave is 100 °C (typical 80-120 °C; verify against profile). An electrolytic capacitor is 8 mm from the wave contact and has a maximum body temperature of 105 °C. Estimate the capacitor body temperature using an attenuation length of 4 mm (typical 3-6 mm; verify against board and fixture trials).
calc.solution: Step A: Calculate the temperature difference between the pot and the board top: 250 °C - 100 °C = 150 °C. Step B: Apply exponential attenuation: rise = 150 °C × exp(-8 mm / 4 mm). Step C: Evaluate: exp(-2) ≈ 0.14, so rise ≈ 21 °C. Step D: Estimated body temperature = 100 °C + 21 °C = 121 °C. Step E: Compare with 105 °C; the estimate exceeds the limit. Mitigation: move the capacitor away from the wave contact, add a thermal shield, or use selective soldering. Verification: attach a thermocouple to the capacitor body, run a wave-soldering profile, and confirm the peak body temperature remains below 105 °C and the part passes functional test.

defect.symptom: After wave soldering, an electrolytic capacitor near the wave contact shows bulging, electrolyte leakage, or reduced capacitance.
defect.cause: Heat spread from the wave contact raised the capacitor body above its datasheet limit because the part was too close to the heat source and the profile was not verified at the capacitor.
defect.action: Stop the line, attach a thermocouple to the capacitor body, rerun the wave-soldering profile, increase spacing or add a thermal shield or selective soldering, then verify the peak body temperature and functional performance.
