title: Cleaning methods: aqueous, semi-aqueous, solvent, ultrasonic; material compatibility

goals.text: Select a cleaning method and chemistry for a stated residue and assembly type, including MSL/ESD constraints.

blocks.alt: A cleaning line with a wash chamber, rinse, ultrasonic tank and dryer, with a material compatibility matrix beside it
blocks.caption: Cleaning methods: aqueous, semi-aqueous, solvent and ultrasonic, with material compatibility

theory.p: Cleaning in SMT/THT assemblies is used to remove flux residues, particulates, ionic contaminants, and process aids before conformal coating, inspection, test, or final assembly. The method should be selected from the residue type, assembly construction, component sensitivity, and downstream process requirements. Rosin-based residues, no-clean residues, water-soluble residues, solder paste residues, and mixed contamination behave differently, so the cleaning chemistry and mechanical action must be matched to the residue rather than selected only by convenience. For coating applications, cleaning is especially important because residues can cause coating adhesion failure, localized corrosion, or electrical leakage after the coating is applied.

theory.h: Aqueous cleaning and its practical limits
theory.p: Aqueous cleaning uses water-based chemistry, often with surfactants, saponifiers, or alkaline additives, and may include spray, immersion, ultrasonic, or agitation. It is commonly effective for water-soluble flux residues, ionic contamination, and some no-clean residues when the residue is sufficiently accessible and the chemistry is compatible. Typical process temperatures are often in the range of 40 to 70 degrees Celsius, but the exact temperature, concentration, contact time, and rinse quality should be verified against the paste, flux, and equipment datasheet. Aqueous cleaning requires controlled deionized water quality, drying, and attention to trapped moisture under components, in through-holes, and inside connectors. For assemblies with MSL constraints, aqueous cleaning may require re-baking or controlled dry storage after cleaning if moisture absorption limits are exceeded.

theory.h: Semi-aqueous cleaning and residue removal balance
theory.p: Semi-aqueous cleaning usually combines a solvent or solvent-like chemistry with water or water-based rinsing, often using alcohols, glycol ethers, or modified alcohols. It can be useful when residues are partially soluble in water but also contain organic or rosin-like components that require stronger organic chemistry. Semi-aqueous processes may reduce drying time compared with fully aqueous processes, but they still require control of rinse water quality, drying, and chemical compatibility. For mixed SMT/THT assemblies, semi-aqueous cleaning can be a practical compromise when water-soluble residues are present but full aqueous cleaning risks moisture retention or component damage. Process parameters such as concentration, temperature, spray pressure, and dwell time should be validated on representative assemblies.

Solvent cleaning uses organic solvents or solvent blends to dissolve flux residues, oils, adhesives, and some coating residues. It can be effective for localized cleaning, rework, and residues that are poorly removed by water-based chemistry. However, solvent selection must consider flammability, toxicity, regulatory restrictions, material compatibility, and drying behavior. Solvents may attack plastics, labels, markings, conformal coatings, adhesives, and some elastomers, so compatibility testing is required before production use. For ESD-sensitive assemblies, solvent cleaning should be performed in a controlled ESD area using ESD-safe containers, dispensing tools, and grounding practices. Solvent cleaning is often more suitable for targeted cleaning than for large-area production cleaning unless the process is engineered for throughput and safety.

Ultrasonic cleaning uses high-frequency acoustic energy in a liquid bath to generate cavitation, which helps remove contamination from complex geometries, blind holes, through-holes, and under-component spaces. It can be effective for particulates, flux residues, and contamination trapped in areas that spray cleaning cannot reach. Ultrasonic action can also damage delicate components, thin wires, fragile terminations, unsecured parts, and some optical or MEMS devices, so power density, frequency, bath chemistry, and exposure time must be controlled. Typical ultrasonic frequencies are often selected in the range of 25 to 40 kHz for general cleaning, with higher frequencies used for more delicate work, but the final setting should be verified against the equipment and component datasheets. For MSL-sensitive assemblies, ultrasonic cleaning in aqueous baths may increase moisture uptake and should be followed by controlled drying or baking when required.

Material compatibility must be evaluated for the printed circuit board laminate, solder mask, silkscreen, component bodies, terminations, labels, connectors, seals, adhesives, conformal coatings, and any protective films. Cleaning chemistry can cause swelling, crazing, discoloration, marking removal, adhesion loss, or corrosion, especially when temperature, concentration, or dwell time are increased. Through-hole assemblies and mixed SMT/THT assemblies require attention to trapped liquid, cleaning agent residue, and drying in barrel holes and under component leads. For assemblies that will be conformal coated, cleaning must remove residues without leaving surfactant films, salt residues, or solvent residues that interfere with coating wetting. Compatibility testing should include visual inspection, electrical test, coating adhesion test, and, where relevant, ion chromatography or surface insulation resistance evaluation.

Moisture sensitivity level constraints are governed by the applicable MSL classification and floor-life rules, commonly referenced through IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033. Cleaning can expose moisture-sensitive devices to water, heat, and extended handling time, which may consume floor life or require re-baking before reflow. For MSL 3 or higher devices, cleaning should be planned so that total exposure time, drying time, and storage conditions remain within the allowed limits. If cleaning is performed after component placement but before reflow, the assembly may need to be dried according to the MSL requirements before soldering. If cleaning is performed after reflow, the concern shifts to moisture trapped in packages, underfills, or crevices, and drying should be verified against the component and assembly requirements.

Cleaning processes can introduce ESD risk through fluid flow, spraying, wiping, handling, and movement of insulating materials. Assemblies containing ESD-sensitive components should be handled in an EPA or ESD-controlled area consistent with ANSI/ESD S20.20, using grounded work surfaces, wrist straps where appropriate, ESD-safe containers, and controlled handling. Solvent wiping, compressed air, and dry cloth wiping can generate charge if non-ESD materials are used, so ESD-safe materials and controlled humidity should be considered. For coating-stage cleaning, the assembly may already be sensitive to contamination and ESD simultaneously, so cleaning stations should be designed to avoid both particulate generation and charge accumulation. Operator training and process qualification should include ESD handling, not only cleaning effectiveness.

theory.h: Method selection logic for process engineers
theory.p: A practical selection sequence is to identify the residue, define the assembly type, list material and MSL/ESD constraints, then select the least aggressive cleaning method that meets cleanliness requirements. Water-soluble residues often favor aqueous cleaning, rosin or no-clean residues may favor semi-aqueous or solvent cleaning, and trapped particulates may favor ultrasonic or immersion assistance. For conformal coating, the cleaning process must be validated by post-clean inspection and coating adhesion testing, not only by visual cleanliness. For MSL-sensitive assemblies, the cleaning route must include drying and floor-life control. For ESD-sensitive assemblies, the cleaning route must include controlled handling and ESD-safe materials. The final process should be documented with chemistry, concentration, temperature, dwell time, mechanical action, rinse, drying, inspection criteria, and rework limits.

calc.task: Select a cleaning method for a mixed SMT/THT assembly with water-soluble flux residue, trapped particulates in through-holes, MSL 3 components, and a downstream conformal coating requirement. Estimate whether a 60 minute aqueous cleaning and drying cycle can be completed within a 4 hour floor-life window, and define the minimum verification checks before coating.
calc.solution: Step 1: Identify residue and constraints. The residue is water-soluble flux with particulates, the assembly is mixed SMT/THT, components are MSL 3, and the assembly must be clean before conformal coating. Step 2: Select candidate method. Aqueous cleaning is suitable for water-soluble flux, and ultrasonic or agitation assistance may help remove particulates from through-holes. Step 3: Estimate cycle time. Assume cleaning 10 minutes, rinse 5 minutes, drying 45 minutes, and handling 10 minutes, giving a total of 70 minutes. Step 4: Compare with floor-life window. The available window is 4 hours, or 240 minutes. Remaining floor life after cleaning is 240 minus 70, which equals 170 minutes. Step 5: Check MSL handling. MSL 3 floor-life rules are governed by IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, so the actual floor life must be taken from the component specification and the current exposure record. If the assembly has already used more than 170 minutes of floor life, re-baking or a shortened cleaning route is required. Step 6: Define verification before coating. Perform visual inspection for residue and trapped liquid, check drying completion, verify cleanliness with a suitable method such as ion chromatography or surface insulation resistance testing, and perform coating adhesion testing on a representative coupon or sacrificial assembly. Step 7: Define ESD controls. Handle the assembly in an ESD-controlled area consistent with ANSI/ESD S20.20, using grounded surfaces and ESD-safe containers during cleaning, drying, and coating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating, localized coating lifting and white discoloration appear near through-hole connectors and under large SMT components, with occasional low surface insulation resistance readings.
defect.cause: Cleaning removed visible flux but left trapped aqueous rinse residue or surfactant film in through-holes and under components. The assembly was dried insufficiently before coating, and the cleaning process was not validated for trapped-liquid removal or coating adhesion.
defect.action: Stop coating release. Re-clean affected assemblies using a validated semi-aqueous or aqueous process with extended rinse and drying, then verify dryness and cleanliness before re-coating. Add through-hole drainage orientation, increased drying time, and post-clean surface insulation resistance or ion contamination checks. Update the cleaning process to include trapped-liquid inspection and coating adhesion qualification.

title: Cleanliness verification: ROSE, ion chromatography, particle count, visual

goals.text: Interpret cleanliness test results and decide pass or rework, stating the criterion.

blocks.alt: A ROSE tester extracting a board, an ion chromatography trace, a particle count readout and a magnified visual check
blocks.caption: Cleanliness verification: ROSE, ion chromatography, particle count and visual

theory.h: Cleanliness verification at the coating and ESD stage
theory.p: Cleanliness verification answers whether residues left by soldering, cleaning, handling, or coating processes can compromise adhesion, surface insulation resistance, corrosion, or ESD protection. At the coating and ESD stage, the board may be inspected before conformal coating, after cleaning, and after coating if the coating is expected to protect an ESD path. The result is not a measurement alone; it is a comparison against a defined acceptance criterion. A pass means the measured contamination is below the limit for the tested area and the visual condition is acceptable. A fail means the area is reworked, retested, or dispositioned by engineering. The criterion should be written before testing and should state the test method, the sampled area, the reporting units, and the action when a result is marginal. For ESD applications, cleanliness can affect surface resistivity and coating continuity, so the pass decision should consider chemical residue and physical defects. The engineer should also know whether the test is destructive, because destructive tests may limit retest options on expensive assemblies.

Cleanliness results are meaningful only when the sampled area, extraction method, blank correction, and reporting units are known. ROSE and ion chromatography usually report contamination normalized to area, such as micrograms of sodium chloride equivalent per square centimeter or micrograms of a specific ion per square centimeter. The tested area should match the area represented by the result. If a small high-risk area is tested, the result applies to that area, not the whole board. Blank correction removes contamination contributed by the solvent, container, and handling. For rework decisions, record the test method, area, instrument, date, operator, and any visible defects. Also record whether the sample was destructive, whether the area was masked, and whether the result was averaged over multiple sites. Averaging can hide a local residue pocket, so high-risk areas should be tested separately when the process history shows a risk. The report should include the cleaning chemistry, rinse water quality, and drying method because these variables can change the interpretation of a marginal result.

ROSE measures ionic contamination by extracting residues into a solvent and measuring conductivity or resistivity. It is fast and useful for process control, but it does not identify the ion, does not measure nonionic residues, and can be affected by weakly ionic or volatile residues. A ROSE result should be compared with the limit in the customer specification or internal process specification. If the result is above the limit, the tested area fails. If it is below the limit, the area may pass for ionic contamination, but visual inspection and ion-specific testing may still be required when the assembly is high reliability, uses fine pitch, or will be coated. ROSE is most useful when the cleaning process is stable and the same solvent, temperature, and extraction time are used. If the result changes without a process change, check the blank, the extraction solvent, the cell calibration, and the sampling area before blaming the board. ROSE can also be misleading when residues are trapped under components or under a coating, because the extraction solvent may not reach the residue.

Ion chromatography separates and quantifies individual ions, such as chloride, sulfate, nitrate, acetate, and formate. It is used when ROSE fails, when a specific flux chemistry is suspected, or when corrosion risk must be understood. Interpretation requires individual ion limits and, when specified, a total ionic limit. A total result can pass while an individual ion fails, or vice versa, depending on the limit structure. The laboratory should report detection limits; values below detection are not zero. For rework, the failed ion and the process that introduced it guide the cleaning method. Chloride often points to solder paste, water, or handling contamination, while organic ions may point to flux residues. Ion chromatography is slower than ROSE, so it is often used for qualification, failure analysis, and periodic verification rather than every board. When ion chromatography is used after coating, the test may require destructive extraction, so the sampling plan should protect critical areas and preserve enough evidence for failure analysis.

Particle count verifies that particulate contamination is controlled before coating or in the ESD-controlled area. Airborne particle counts are commonly compared with cleanroom classes from the ISO cleanroom particle count standard. Surface particle counts are often obtained by wiping, flushing, or using a particle counter on a defined area. The criterion should state the particle size threshold, the area or volume sampled, and the maximum count. A particle count result alone does not prove chemical cleanliness; it only shows that particles above the selected size are within the allowed range. For coating, particles can cause pinholes, poor adhesion, or localized corrosion if they retain moisture. For ESD surfaces, particles can interfere with coating continuity or create local high resistance. Sampling location matters because a cleanroom may pass while a board surface fails if handling or packaging introduces particles. The particle count method should also state whether the count is from a liquid extract, a wipe, or a direct surface measurement, because those methods are not directly comparable.

Visual inspection detects residues, flux staining, corrosion, handling marks, coating defects, and particles that are large enough to see. It is commonly performed under controlled lighting and magnification, using the IPC visual acceptability standard or a customer-approved visual standard. Visual pass means no unacceptable residue or defect is present in the inspected area. Visual inspection cannot detect all ionic contamination, so it should be combined with chemical tests when the risk is high. If a defect is visible, the area fails even if chemical tests pass, unless engineering provides a documented deviation. For coating and ESD work, visual inspection should include areas under connectors, near stencil apertures, and along board edges where cleaning solutions may not reach. Photographs and annotated drawings help when the result is marginal or when the same board is retested after rework. Visual inspection should also confirm that the ESD coating is continuous where required and that no masking material, tape residue, or handling damage remains.

The pass decision uses the most restrictive applicable criterion: customer specification, internal specification, or standard method guidance. A common logic is: visual pass, ROSE pass, ion chromatography pass, and particle count pass. If any test fails, the area is reworked using a validated cleaning process, then retested on the same area or a representative area. If the result is marginal, repeat the test and check sampling technique, blank, and instrument calibration before accepting. For coating and ESD applications, consider whether residue could be trapped under coating or could alter surface resistivity; if so, require ion-specific confirmation before coating. The disposition should state whether the board is accepted, reworked, scrapped, or released under a deviation. The retest result should be compared with the original criterion, not with a relaxed limit chosen after the failure. The final record should link the cleanliness result to the lot, the cleaning recipe, the coating lot, and the ESD control status so that future failures can be traced.

theory.h: Where the acceptance numbers come from
theory.p: A cleanliness criterion is never invented at the test bench: it is taken from the customer specification, the product reliability plan, or a published reference. The most widely used reference value is 1.56 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter, reported per IPC-TM-650 method 2.3.25 (ROSE) and historically applied to assembled boards through IPC J-STD-001 and to bare boards through IPC-6012. Many high-reliability customers tighten it: about 1.0 microgram per square centimeter for high-impedance analog and telecom hardware, about 0.75 for aerospace and military, and about 0.5 for medical assemblies, with ion chromatography per IPC-TM-650 method 2.3.28 used to confirm the specific ions. Two cautions matter in practice. First, ROSE reports a conductivity equivalent rather than a named ion, so two boards with the same ROSE value can carry very different corrosion risk; that is why the ion-specific test exists. Second, the current revision of J-STD-001 has moved away from a single fixed limit towards objective evidence: the assembly must be demonstrably clean enough for its intended life and environment, and the limit is then set and justified for that specific process and product rather than copied from a table. The practical rule for an engineer is to quote the method, the unit, the sampled area and the source of every limit used, and to expect an internal specification to be tighter than the published reference rather than looser.

calc.task: A cleaned board area is tested before conformal coating. The internal cleanliness specification is: ROSE <= 0.25 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter; individual ion <= 0.10 microgram per square centimeter; particles >= 5 micrometer <= 100 per square centimeter; visual inspection shows no visible residue. The ROSE extract measured 0.34 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter, and the blank was 0.03 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. Ion chromatography reported chloride 0.12 microgram per square centimeter and sulfate 0.06 microgram per square centimeter. A surface particle sample over 10 square centimeters counted 1400 particles at or above 5 micrometers. Visual inspection found no visible residue. Decide pass or rework and state the criterion.
calc.solution: Correct ROSE for blank: 0.34 - 0.03 = 0.31 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. Compare ROSE to limit 0.25 microgram NaCl equivalent per square centimeter. 0.31 is above 0.25, so ROSE fails. Compare individual ions to limit 0.10 microgram per square centimeter. Chloride 0.12 is above 0.10, so ion chromatography fails. Sulfate 0.06 is below 0.10, so sulfate alone passes. Normalize particle count: 1400 particles divided by 10 square centimeters = 140 particles per square centimeter. Compare particle count to limit 100 particles per square centimeter. 140 is above 100, so particle count fails. Visual inspection passes because no visible residue was found. Overall decision is rework because the most restrictive criterion is not met: ROSE, ion chromatography, and particle count all exceed their limits. Rework with validated cleaning, then retest the same area and adjacent high-risk areas before coating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating, localized corrosion and intermittent ESD path failures appear near a connector.
defect.cause: Residual ionic flux from wave solder was not removed; ROSE sampling averaged a large area and missed a local residue pocket, while particles trapped under coating increased moisture retention.
defect.action: Quarantine the lot, remove coating if possible, re-clean with validated ultrasonic or flush process, retest the connector area with ion chromatography and local ROSE, verify particle control, then recoat and retest.

title: Coating types and selection: acrylic, urethane, silicone, parylene, UV cure

goals.text: Choose a coating and masking strategy and check its compatibility with cleaning, rework and the assembly.

blocks.alt: Five coating chemistries shown as cross-section layers with a moisture barrier and removability rating for each
blocks.caption: Coating types and selection: acrylic, polyurethane, silicone, parylene and UV cure

theory.h: Purpose of conformal coating in SMT/THT assemblies
theory.p: Conformal coating is applied after assembly to reduce moisture ingress, ionic contamination, dust, fungal growth, and some mechanical abrasion. In SMT/THT process engineering, the coating decision is not only about the coating chemistry; it also affects cleaning, masking, inspection, rework, test access, thermal behavior, and reliability under thermal cycling. The selection should be driven by the service environment, board density, component sensitivity, cleaning requirements, and the rework strategy. For example, a high-density SMT board with bottom-terminated components may need a low-viscosity coating and careful masking, while a THT power board may tolerate a thicker silicone or urethane coating but still require connector and test-point protection.

theory.h: Acrylic coatings: easy rework but limited chemical resistance
theory.p: Acrylic coatings are commonly used when rework and repair access are important. They are relatively easy to remove mechanically or with compatible solvents, and they can be applied by brushing, spraying, dipping, or selective coating. Typical dry-film thickness is often in the range of 25 to 75 micrometers, but the target should be verified against the coating datasheet and the IPC-CC-830 qualification for the specific product. Acrylics can offer good dielectric performance and reasonable moisture protection, but they may have lower resistance to solvents, fuels, and some aggressive chemicals than urethane or silicone systems. They are often selected for consumer electronics, industrial controls, and assemblies where field repair is expected. A practical concern is solvent attack on nearby plastics, labels, or conformal-coated areas during cleaning or rework.

theory.h: Urethane coatings: balanced protection with more careful rework
theory.p: Urethane coatings generally provide better chemical and abrasion resistance than many acrylic systems and can be used in industrial, automotive, and outdoor electronics. They are available in moisture-cure, heat-cure, and UV-cure variants. Typical dry-film thickness may be around 25 to 100 micrometers depending on the product and application method, but the process window should be verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 test data. Urethanes can form a tougher film than acrylics, which improves protection but makes rework more difficult. Mechanical removal, localized solvent softening, or thermal removal may be required, and the method must be qualified so that pads, solder joints, and nearby components are not damaged. Moisture-cure urethanes can release carbon dioxide during cure, so thick films or restricted areas may need staged application to avoid foaming or trapped volatiles.

theory.h: Silicone coatings: high temperature and moisture resistance
theory.p: Silicone coatings are often chosen for high-temperature environments, high humidity, and applications where flexibility is important. They can remain flexible over a wide temperature range and may tolerate thermal cycling better than some rigid coatings. Typical dry-film thickness is often around 25 to 100 micrometers, but the exact range should be verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification. Silicone coatings can be removed mechanically or with selected solvents, but removal can smear or leave residues that interfere with soldering. A major process issue is silicone contamination near connectors, switches, relays, or gold-plated contacts, because silicone migration can cause contact resistance problems. Therefore, masking and boundary control are critical when silicone is used near electromechanical interfaces.

theory.h: Parylene coatings: thin, pinhole-free, and low stress
theory.p: Parylene is a vapor-deposited coating that forms a very thin, uniform, pinhole-free film. Typical thicknesses are often in the range of 1 to 25 micrometers, with many applications using 5 to 15 micrometers, but the required thickness should be verified against the coating specification and IPC-CC-830 or equivalent qualification data. Because the coating is applied as a vapor, it can cover complex geometries and high-aspect-ratio features without the bridging or pooling that can occur with liquid coatings. Parylene is useful for high-density SMT assemblies, medical electronics, and applications where minimal added thickness is required. However, it is difficult to remove selectively, so masking must be planned before coating. Parylene also requires vacuum deposition equipment and controlled process conditions, which can affect throughput and cost.

theory.h: UV-cure coatings: fast processing with shadowing limitations
theory.p: UV-cure coatings are used when fast handling and short cycle times are needed. They can be applied by spray, jet, or selective coating and cured by ultraviolet light. Typical dry-film thickness may be around 25 to 75 micrometers, but the process should be verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification. The main limitation is line-of-sight exposure: areas under components, under connectors, inside deep cavities, or behind tall parts may not receive enough UV energy to cure fully. This can leave tacky or uncured material that attracts contamination and causes adhesion problems. UV-cure systems may be combined with moisture-cure or heat-cure chemistry to address shadowed areas. Energy dose, wavelength, lamp type, and exposure time must be controlled and verified, and the coating should be checked for full cure in shadowed regions before final inspection.

theory.h: Masking strategy and compatibility with cleaning, rework, and assembly
theory.p: Masking is used to protect connectors, test points, switches, heatsink interfaces, optical sensors, antennas, and areas that must remain uncoated. Common masking methods include tape, caps, plugs, liquid mask, and selective coating. The mask must survive the coating process, cleaning, and any rework temperature exposure without lifting, bleeding, or leaving residue. For cleaning, the mask material and adhesive must be compatible with the cleaning solvent or aqueous chemistry; some adhesives can bleed under solvent exposure. For rework, the coating must be removable without damaging adjacent components or leaving residues that prevent solder wetting. IPC-7711/7721 provides guidance for rework and repair, and the selected coating removal method should be qualified against the board finish, component package, and solder alloy. For assembly, coating thickness and viscosity must be checked against component standoffs, connector mating heights, and thermal interface requirements.

A practical selection method starts with the environmental requirement: humidity, temperature, chemicals, dust, vibration, and expected service life. Next, define the board constraints: component height, bottom-terminated packages, test points, connectors, thermal interfaces, and rework frequency. Then match coating chemistry to those constraints. Acrylic is often selected when easy rework is needed. Urethane is often selected when chemical and abrasion resistance are higher priorities. Silicone is often selected for high temperature and flexibility. Parylene is often selected for thin, uniform coverage on dense assemblies. UV cure is often selected for fast throughput when line-of-sight cure is achievable. Finally, verify the selected coating against IPC-CC-830 qualification data, IPC-A-610 inspection requirements, IPC-7711/7721 rework guidance, and the assembly cleaning process. The final choice should be documented with coating type, target thickness, application method, cure method, masking method, inspection criteria, and rework method.

calc.task: Select a coating and masking strategy for a dense SMT/THT control board that must operate in a humid industrial environment, be reworkable at the board level, and must not contaminate a nearby gold-plated edge connector. Estimate coating coverage volume and check whether the selected coating thickness is compatible with a 0.50 mm connector mating clearance.
calc.solution:
Step 1: Define requirements. The board needs moisture protection, rework access, and connector protection. A urethane coating is selected for balanced moisture and chemical resistance, with acrylic selected as a backup if rework becomes difficult. Silicone is rejected near the gold-plated edge connector because silicone migration can increase contact resistance. Parylene is considered but rejected for this example because local rework is required and parylene removal is difficult. UV cure is considered but rejected as the primary coating because the board has tall connectors and shadowed areas.

Step 2: Select target thickness. The coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification data are checked. A target dry-film thickness of 50 micrometers is selected, with an acceptable process range of 25 to 75 micrometers. This range is verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-A-610 inspection requirements for coating coverage and thickness.

Step 3: Estimate board area. The coated area is estimated as 120 mm by 80 mm, or 9600 mm². The area is converted to square meters: 9600 mm² = 0.0096 m².

Step 4: Estimate coating volume. Volume = area × thickness. For 50 micrometers: 50 µm = 0.000050 m. Volume = 0.0096 m² × 0.000050 m = 0.00000048 m³. Convert to milliliters: 0.00000048 m³ = 0.48 mL. This is the theoretical dry-film volume only; actual dispensed volume will be higher because of overspray, masking, and process losses.

Step 5: Estimate wet volume. If the coating has 40 percent solids by volume, wet volume = dry volume / solids fraction = 0.48 mL / 0.40 = 1.20 mL. The 40 percent solids value is a practice-based example and must be verified against the coating datasheet.

Step 6: Check connector clearance. The gold-plated edge connector has a mating clearance of 0.50 mm. The coating is masked from the connector contact area. If the coating edge is allowed to approach the connector, the coating thickness must not create a step that interferes with mating. A 50 micrometer coating is 0.050 mm, which is 10 percent of the 0.50 mm clearance. This is acceptable only if the coating edge is outside the mating interface and the mask prevents coating creep. The mask boundary is set 1.0 mm from the connector contact area to allow for process variation. The 1.0 mm margin is a process example and should be verified against the coating viscosity, application method, and IPC-A-610 inspection criteria.

Step 7: Check rework compatibility. The urethane coating is tested on a sacrificial board using the planned rework method. Removal is checked against IPC-7711/7721 guidance for damage to pads, solder joints, and adjacent components. If the urethane cannot be removed without damaging nearby components, the process is changed to a localized acrylic coating or a masked urethane coating with a defined rework window.

Step 8: Final selection. The selected strategy is urethane coating at 50 micrometers nominal, masked from the gold-plated edge connector with a 1.0 mm boundary margin, applied by selective coating, and qualified for rework according to IPC-7711/7721. The process is accepted only after coating thickness, adhesion, cure, masking boundary, and rework damage checks pass.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and thermal cycling, a board fails ICT at a connector test point. Visual inspection shows a thin, clear coating film bridging between adjacent test pads, and the coating appears glossy and tacky under a shadowed connector.
defect.cause: The coating was applied too thickly near the test-point array, and the UV-cure step did not fully cure the shadowed area under the connector. The uncured or partially cured material remained tacky, attracted contamination, and allowed capillary flow into the pad gap. Masking was not sufficient to keep the coating away from the test-point spacing.
defect.action: Stop the lot and quarantine affected boards. Remove the coating from the affected area using a qualified rework method that does not damage the pads or adjacent components, following IPC-7711/7721 guidance. Re-clean the area and verify solderability and insulation resistance. Correct the process by reducing coating viscosity or application pressure, adding a mask or cap over the test-point array, and verifying UV energy dose in shadowed areas. Add a post-cure inspection step for shadowed regions and requalify the coating process against IPC-CC-830 and IPC-A-610 requirements.

title: Application and masking: spray, dip, selective, thickness, cure, repairability

goals.text: Choose a coating and masking strategy and check its compatibility with cleaning, rework and the assembly.

blocks.alt: A coating line with a selective spray head, a masked connector, a thickness measurement and a cure oven
blocks.caption: Application and masking: spray, dip, selective, thickness, cure and repairability

theory.h: Selecting a conformal coating for SMT/THT assemblies
theory.p: Conformal coating selection starts with the service environment and the assembly’s thermal, chemical, and electrical requirements. Acrylic coatings are easy to remove and repair, urethane coatings offer good abrasion and chemical resistance, silicone coatings tolerate high temperature and humidity, epoxy coatings provide strong mechanical protection but are difficult to remove, and parylene coatings give thin, uniform coverage but require vacuum deposition and careful masking. For mixed SMT/THT boards, verify that the coating does not attack flux residues, potting compounds, connectors, or test points. Use IPC-CC-830 as the qualification framework for electrical insulation, thermal shock, humidity, and chemical resistance, and confirm the selected material against the paste, solder mask, laminate, and component datasheets.

theory.h: Spray coating: coverage, viscosity, and process control
theory.p: Spray coating is common for low to medium volume production and for assemblies with complex topography. Typical spray viscosity is adjusted to the equipment range, often around 10 to 100 mPa·s for air-assisted systems, but the exact value must be verified against the coating supplier’s process window and the spray equipment manual. Atomization pressure, nozzle size, travel speed, and distance control film thickness and overspray. For SMT/THT assemblies, avoid high pressure directly over small components, exposed vias, connectors, and test pads. Measure wet film thickness with a wet film comb or gauge, then confirm dry film thickness after cure; target values are commonly 25 to 130 µm depending on the coating class and IPC-CC-830 qualification, but the final range should match the qualified coating system.

theory.h: Dip coating: uniformity and drainage control
theory.p: Dip coating can produce good coverage on through-hole assemblies and boards with open component spacing. The board is immersed and withdrawn at a controlled rate, commonly 100 to 300 mm/min, with dwell time adjusted to allow drainage and prevent bridging. Viscosity, temperature, and withdrawal speed determine wet film thickness; a typical process may aim for 50 to 150 µm dry film thickness, but this must be verified against the coating datasheet and IPC-CC-830 qualification. Dip coating can trap solvent under large components or under bottom-terminated packages, so preheat, dwell, and ventilation should be controlled to reduce voids and solvent entrapment.

theory.h: Selective coating for mixed SMT/THT assemblies
theory.p: Selective coating is used when only part of the assembly requires protection, such as high-voltage areas, exposed copper, or moisture-sensitive regions, while connectors, test points, heatsinks, and mechanical interfaces must remain uncoated. The process uses programmed dispensing or jetting to place coating only on defined areas. Key controls are nozzle path, coating volume, cure schedule, and edge definition. For SMT/THT boards, selective coating reduces masking labor and improves repair access, but it requires good CAD or Gerber data and verification of component height, pin spacing, and connector sealing. Check that the coating does not creep into connector contacts or under component terminations where IPC-A-610 class requirements for cleanliness and solder joint visibility apply.

theory.h: Masking strategy and compatibility with cleaning
theory.p: Masking protects areas that must remain uncoated, such as connectors, test pads, heatsink interfaces, potting areas, and repair zones. Common masks include high-temperature tape, silicone caps, liquid photoimageable masks, and removable wax or polymer masks. Mask selection depends on coating solvent, cure temperature, dwell time, and cleaning chemistry. For example, solvent-based coatings may attack some tapes, while high-temperature cure may lift adhesive or leave residue. Verify mask compatibility by running a coupon through the full coating, cure, and cleaning sequence. If cleaning is required after coating, confirm that the cleaning solvent does not swell, soften, or craze the coating; IPC-CC-830 includes chemical resistance testing, but production cleaning should still be validated on the actual assembly.

Dry film thickness affects insulation, mechanical protection, thermal behavior, and repairability. Too thin a coating may not meet IPC-CC-830 qualification or IPC-A-610 acceptability for the intended class; too thick a coating can trap solvent, crack during thermal cycling, or interfere with connectors and test probes. Use wet film measurement before cure and dry film measurement after cure, with thickness checked on flat areas, edges, and near components. Cure must be verified by the coating supplier’s method, such as solvent rub, hardness, adhesion, or FTIR conversion where applicable. For heat-sensitive SMT/THT assemblies, cure temperature and ramp rate should be checked against component and laminate limits, commonly keeping peak temperature below the laminate glass transition limit and within the qualified coating cure window.

Repairability depends on coating removal method, access to solder joints, and thermal exposure during rework. Acrylic coatings are generally easier to remove with solvent or mechanical action, while urethane, silicone, and epoxy coatings may require stronger solvents, abrasion, or thermal assistance. Parylene may require plasma or specialized removal. For rework and repair, follow IPC-7711 and IPC-7721 guidance for acceptable rework and repair methods, including preheat, temperature control, and post-rework inspection. Masking should leave enough uncoated area for probe access, soldering, and inspection without requiring excessive coating removal. If the assembly is expected to undergo field repair, specify a coating system and masking layout that allow localized removal and recoating without damaging adjacent components or solder joints.

theory.h: Compatibility with cleaning, assembly, and inspection
theory.p: A coating strategy must be compatible with the full assembly flow: soldering, cleaning, inspection, functional test, and repair. Residual flux, ionic contamination, moisture, or dust under coating can cause corrosion, insulation failure, or adhesion loss. Cleaning before coating should be validated against the laminate, solder mask, and component materials, and the board should be dry before coating. After coating, inspection should check for pinholes, bridging, voids, peeling, contamination, and coverage of exposed copper, using IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria for the applicable class. For connectors and test points, verify that masking or selective coating does not leave residue that increases contact resistance or prevents probe contact.

calc.task: A mixed SMT/THT board is coated by spray with a target dry film thickness of 75 µm. The coating has a volume solids content of 45% by volume. The wet film thickness measured on a coupon is 165 µm. Determine whether the wet film thickness is reasonable for the target dry film thickness, and calculate the expected dry film thickness from the measured wet film thickness.
calc.solution: Step 1: Use the relationship between wet film thickness, dry film thickness, and volume solids: DFT = WFT × volume solids fraction. Step 2: Convert volume solids to a fraction: 45% = 0.45. Step 3: Calculate expected dry film thickness: DFT = 165 µm × 0.45 = 74.25 µm. Step 4: Compare with target: 74.25 µm is within a practical tolerance of the 75 µm target, assuming the process tolerance allows approximately ±10 µm or the tolerance specified by the coating supplier. Step 5: Verify the result on the actual assembly after cure, because solvent evaporation, drainage, and surface roughness can change the final thickness. If the qualified IPC-CC-830 coating system or IPC-A-610 inspection class requires a different thickness range, adjust the spray parameters and re-measure.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and cure, a connector area shows white residue and intermittent contact resistance. The coating appears to have crept under the connector housing and left a soft film on the contacts.
defect.cause: The masking or selective coating boundary was too close to the connector, the coating viscosity was too low, or the spray/dispense volume was too high, allowing capillary creep into the connector. The cleaning solvent used after coating may also have softened the coating and redistributed it onto the contacts.
defect.action: Stop the affected lot and inspect other boards for coating creep. Remove the assembly from the line and clean or replace affected connectors according to IPC-7711 and IPC-7721 rework and repair guidance. Requalify the masking layout or selective coating path with a larger keep-out margin, reduce dispense volume or spray pressure, and verify coating creep on a connector test coupon. If cleaning is required, confirm solvent compatibility with the coating and connector materials before returning to production.

title: Contamination and coating defect cases: residue, white residue, corrosion, fish-eye, dewetting

goals.text: Interpret cleanliness test results and decide pass or rework, stating the criterion.
Choose a coating and masking strategy and check its compatibility with cleaning, rework and the assembly.

blocks.alt: Five magnified coated-surface defects shown side by side, each labelled, beside a sound coated surface
blocks.caption: Contamination and coating defect cases: residue, white residue, corrosion, fish-eye and dewetting

theory.h: Cleanliness testing is a decision tool, not a single pass/fail number
theory.p: Cleanliness results should be interpreted against the defect risk of the assembly, not only against a generic limit. For coated electronics, the relevant question is whether residue, ionic contamination, particulate, flux, or masking material can cause corrosion, insulation failure, solderability loss, conformal coating defects, or ESD-sensitive handling problems. A result that is acceptable for a low-density through-hole board may be unacceptable for fine-pitch SMT, bottom-terminated components, or high-impedance analog circuits. The pass/rework criterion should therefore combine the applicable acceptance standard, the cleanliness test method, the product class, and the downstream coating process.

theory.h: Common cleanliness tests and what they actually measure
theory.p: Visual inspection under magnification detects visible residue, flux, solder balls, masking bleed, and particulate. Solvent extraction conductivity or ion chromatography estimates ionic contamination, often reported as sodium chloride equivalent or as individual ions such as chloride, sulfate, nitrate, and bromide. Surface insulation resistance or surface resistance measures electrical leakage and can reveal contamination that is not visible. Cleanliness patch tests, such as ROSE-type methods, give a rapid ionic contamination estimate but may miss nonionic residue, rosin, polymers, or masking residues. For coating work, combine at least two methods when the risk is high: visual plus ionic, or visual plus surface insulation resistance.

A practical criterion should state the test method, the area sampled, the acceptance limit, the inspection magnification, and the action if the limit is exceeded. For example, a board may pass if no visible residue is present under the magnification required by IPC-A-610 for the applicable product class, and if ionic contamination is below the limit agreed for the assembly and coating system. If the result is marginal, rework is often preferred over retest when the residue type is known to interfere with coating adhesion or wetting. If the result is clean but the coating shows fish-eye or dewetting, the cleanliness result alone is not sufficient; the coating process, substrate energy, and masking residue must be investigated.

theory.h: Residue types and their coating consequences
theory.p: Flux residue can remain under components, in thermal relief pads, or under bottom-terminated packages. Rosin-based residues may be difficult to remove with aqueous cleaning and can cause poor wetting or coating adhesion. No-clean flux residues may be electrically acceptable in some designs but can still create coating defects if the coating solvent reactivates or lifts the residue. Masking tape adhesive, silicone release agents, and cured masking material can leave low-surface-energy films that cause fish-eye or dewetting. Particulate from solder paste, cutting, grinding, or handling can create local coating thinning, pinholes, or shorting risk after coating.

theory.h: White residue, corrosion, and moisture-related failures
theory.p: White residue often appears after cleaning, drying, or humidity exposure and may be a salt, flux reaction product, mineral deposit, or corrosion product. If the residue is conductive or hygroscopic, it can lower insulation resistance and promote corrosion under the coating. Corrosion may begin as discoloration, green or white deposits, lifted metallization, or intermittent electrical faults. A coating can hide the early stage of corrosion, so pre-coating cleanliness and drying are important. If white residue is found after coating, determine whether it formed before coating, migrated through the coating, or formed at an exposed area during rework or assembly.

Fish-eye appears as small circular areas where coating fails to wet the substrate. Dewetting appears as coating pulling back from an area, leaving thin or uncovered regions. These defects are commonly caused by low-surface-energy contamination such as silicone, mold release, adhesive residue, skin oils, or certain masking materials. They can also occur when the substrate surface energy is too low for the coating, or when the coating viscosity, solvent balance, or drying schedule is unsuitable. The first corrective action is usually to identify the contaminant source and remove it, then verify surface energy or adhesion before recoating.

Choose the coating type based on the required protection: acrylic coatings are easy to remove and rework, urethane coatings offer good chemical and moisture resistance, silicone coatings tolerate thermal cycling and humidity, epoxy coatings provide hard chemical resistance but are difficult to rework, and parylene coatings offer pinhole-free coverage but require vacuum deposition and special masking. Masking strategy should protect connectors, test points, heatsink interfaces, optical surfaces, and mounting areas. Masking must survive cleaning, coating cure, and assembly without bleeding, lifting, or leaving adhesive residue. Verify compatibility with the paste, cleaning chemistry, coating solvent, cure temperature, and mechanical assembly loads.

theory.h: Cleaning, rework, and assembly compatibility checks
theory.p: Before releasing a coating and masking plan, check that cleaning does not attack the mask, that the mask does not leave residue after removal, and that the coating does not swell or soften during rework solvent exposure. For rework, confirm that the coating can be locally removed without lifting adjacent coating or damaging component bodies. For assembly, confirm that coated surfaces do not interfere with press-fit connectors, screw threads, thermal pads, snap fits, or grounding contacts. If a coated area must remain conductive, use masking or a selected coating removal method and verify contact resistance after assembly.

theory.h: ESD considerations in coating and masking
theory.p: Conformal coatings can change surface resistance and may affect ESD-sensitive handling. Some coatings are insulating and can allow charge accumulation on the surface unless the assembly is handled with appropriate ESD controls. Masking materials and tapes may also generate charge during removal. For ESD-sensitive assemblies, verify surface resistance of the coated area and the handling path, and use ESD-safe masking and removal procedures. If the design requires dissipative behavior, confirm that the coating system and masking strategy do not create isolated insulating islands near sensitive pins or traces.

calc.task: A fine-pitch SMT board is cleaned, inspected, and tested before conformal coating. Visual inspection at 10x finds no visible residue. A solvent extraction cleanliness test reports 18 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. The agreed acceptance limit for this product class and coating system is 15 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. The board also shows two small fish-eye defects on a nearby test board coated with the same lot. Decide whether the board passes or requires rework, state the criterion, and calculate the percentage exceedance of the cleanliness limit.
calc.solution: 1. State the pass/rework criterion: the board passes only if visual inspection at the required magnification shows no visible residue and the ionic cleanliness result is at or below the agreed limit of 15 micrograms per square centimeter sodium chloride equivalent. 2. Compare the measured cleanliness result with the limit: measured value is 18 micrograms per square centimeter, limit is 15 micrograms per square centimeter. 3. Calculate exceedance: 18 minus 15 equals 3 micrograms per square centimeter. 4. Calculate percentage exceedance: 3 divided by 15 equals 0.20, which is 20 percent above the limit. 5. Decision: the board fails the cleanliness criterion and requires rework or additional cleaning, followed by retest. 6. Additional action: because fish-eye defects appeared on a test board from the same coating lot, do not recoat immediately. Investigate low-surface-energy contamination, masking residue, silicone sources, and coating lot compatibility before cleaning, retesting, and recoating.

defect.symptom: After conformal coating and cure, small circular uncovered areas appear around several QFN pads, and a white powdery residue is visible near a connector after humidity exposure.
defect.cause: The fish-eye areas are consistent with low-surface-energy contamination, likely masking adhesive residue or silicone transfer, preventing coating wetting. The white residue near the connector is consistent with ionic contamination or flux reaction product that was not fully removed before coating, then migrated or absorbed moisture through the coating edge.
defect.action: Stop coating release for the affected lot. Remove the coating locally or fully if needed, clean the board with a validated cleaning process, retest cleanliness using visual inspection and ionic or surface insulation resistance testing, and verify surface energy or coating adhesion on a test coupon. Replace or qualify the masking material if adhesive residue is found, control silicone sources in the area, and rework only after the cleanliness and coating wetting criteria are met.

title: Test levels and what each catches: ICT, flying probe, boundary scan, functional

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.

theory.h: Test level starts with defect modes and access
theory.p: A test strategy is a coverage decision, not a machine preference. The main defect modes are opens, shorts, wrong or missing components, wrong polarity, solder defects, damaged traces, and assembly errors that affect function. The chosen level should catch defects near their point of occurrence, provide repairable diagnostics, and fit production volume. Access, netlist quality, and component mix often decide whether a bed-of-nails fixture, probe access, scan chains, or functional stimulus is practical.

Test method comparison

Catches
Cost per board
Coverage
rows: Opens, shorts, wrong/rotated parts, some values

theory.h: In-circuit test catches structural electrical faults
theory.p: In-circuit test uses a bed-of-nails fixture to contact test points and measure electrical structure in ohm, farad, and volt. It can detect opens, shorts, incorrect passive values, missing components, and some polarity errors. It is strong for high-volume assemblies with good test-point access and stable netlists. It may miss faults hidden under devices or in nets without access, and it can be affected by guard circuits, power paths, and component tolerances. Fixture cost and cycle time should be checked against your equipment datasheet.

theory.h: Flying probe is flexible structural test
theory.p: Flying probe uses movable probes to contact pads, vias, or test points without a dedicated fixture. It is useful for prototypes, low-volume builds, and boards where fixture cost is hard to justify. It can find opens, shorts, and some component errors, but cycle time is longer and access is limited by probe reach, pad size, and obstruction. It is often paired with functional test when structural coverage is incomplete.

Boundary scan uses JTAG cells inside compliant devices to drive and observe pins while the board is powered. It can detect opens, shorts, and some solder defects between scan-capable devices, including fine-pitch and ball-grid-array connections that are hard to probe. It does not measure passive values, power delivery, or non-scan devices unless they are observable through scan logic. Coverage depends on device support, scan chain integrity, and whether the netlist includes the relevant pins.

theory.h: Functional test proves behavior under intended conditions
theory.p: Functional test applies inputs and checks outputs, timing in second, power in volt and ampere, communication behavior, and thermal behavior in degree Celsius. It catches assembly errors that prevent the board from working, including wrong firmware, connector faults, power problems, and some component mismatches. It can miss latent defects, marginal solder joints, and wrong values that do not change behavior under the test conditions. It is valuable as a final screen, but repair diagnosis can be harder when the fault is intermittent or outside the exercised path.

theory.h: Coverage tradeoffs between structural and functional levels
theory.p: Structural tests are usually better at locating a defect at the point of occurrence, while functional tests are better at proving system behavior. A structural test may pass a board that fails functionally because it does not exercise dynamic loading, timing, or analog performance. A functional test may pass a board with a latent defect because the fault is not excited. A practical strategy often combines structural coverage for manufacturing defects with functional coverage for operational requirements.

Choose a strategy by ranking defect risk, access, volume, and repair data. For high-volume dense assemblies with good test points, in-circuit test plus functional test is common. For low-volume or prototype builds, flying probe plus functional test avoids fixture cost. For dense digital assemblies with strong JTAG support, boundary scan plus functional test can cover hard-to-probe nets. For mixed-signal or power assemblies, structural test should include power-path checks, and functional test should include load and thermal conditions. Verify coverage against your paste, probe, and equipment datasheet before committing.

calc.task: A 1200-component assembly has 18% BGA, 40% boundary-scan coverage, 2000 units/month, and 30% of nets lack test points. Choose a test strategy and justify it.
calc.solution: First, map defect risk: BGA and fine-pitch solder defects are high, so structural coverage is needed. Second, compare access: 30% of nets lack test points, so in-circuit test alone leaves gaps. Third, use boundary scan for the 40% scan-covered digital nets, especially BGA connections. Fourth, use flying probe or in-circuit test for accessible passives and power nets, depending on volume. Fifth, add functional test to verify power in volt and ampere, timing in second, and thermal behavior in degree Celsius. Sixth, choose in-circuit test plus boundary scan plus functional for 2000 units/month if fixture cost is justified; choose flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional for lower volume. Verify coverage against your paste, probe, and equipment datasheet.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan reports an open on a BGA net, but functional test passes under nominal conditions.
defect.cause: A marginal solder joint or cracked BGA connection may remain conductive when the pin is not exercised under load, thermal stress, or vibration.
defect.action: Re-run boundary scan with known good boards, inspect with X-ray or cross-section if available, exercise the net under load and temperature, and rework or reject the board if the fault persists.
