title: In-circuit test: fixture, node access, test-point design, analog limits

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Specify design-for-test requirements as design requests with rationale.

blocks.alt: A bed-of-nails fixture with spring probes contacting test points, a node access diagram and an analog measurement panel
blocks.caption: In-circuit test: fixture, node access, test-point design and analog limits

theory.h: What in-circuit test measures and why fixture design matters
theory.p: In-circuit test uses spring probes to contact test points and measure analog electrical parameters such as resistance, capacitance, inductance, diode junctions, transistor junctions, open nets, and shorted nets. The fixture holds the board, aligns probes, applies controlled force, and isolates nodes from adjacent circuitry. A good fixture reduces false failures by controlling contact resistance, guarding, shielding, board support, and thermal drift. For dense assemblies, fixture complexity grows with net count, guarded analog nodes, fine-pitch access, and mixed power domains. Verify probe force and contact resistance against your probe and equipment datasheet; a common production target is contact resistance below 100 mΩ, but acceptance limits should be set from golden-board data and equipment repeatability.

theory.h: Comparing ICT, flying probe, boundary scan, and functional test
theory.p: ICT provides high throughput and strong component-level coverage when test points are available, but it requires a fixture and can be expensive for low-volume or frequently changing designs. Flying probe avoids a dedicated fixture and is useful for prototypes, small lots, and boards with limited test-point access, but it is slower and may have limited high-speed or guarded analog capability. Boundary scan tests interconnects and selected device pins through JTAG, making it valuable for BGA, QFN, and other packages where physical probe access is difficult, but it does not replace analog component testing. Functional test verifies board behavior under operating conditions and can catch system-level defects, but it often gives weaker diagnosis. A practical strategy often combines methods rather than relying on a single test.

theory.h: Choosing a test strategy for a given assembly
theory.p: Choose ICT when production volume justifies fixture cost, test-point access is adequate, and component-level analog coverage is needed. Choose flying probe when volume is low, design changes are frequent, or fixture cost cannot be justified. Add boundary scan when BGA, QFN, or fine-pitch devices create inaccessible nets and the devices support scan. Add functional test when analog performance, power sequencing, RF behavior, firmware interaction, or system timing cannot be verified by component-level tests. For a mixed analog-digital assembly, a common approach is ICT for passive and discrete component coverage, boundary scan for inaccessible digital interconnects, and functional test for performance acceptance. The selection should be documented with coverage targets, expected defect modes, and test time.

Fixture design must account for probe pitch, probe tip diameter, board support, alignment pins, hold-down method, thermal effects, and guard shielding. Spring probes need annular clearance around the test point so the tip can land cleanly without shorting to adjacent copper. Probe force should be sufficient to break through minor contamination but low enough to avoid pad damage; typical spring-probe force ranges are often around 0.5 N to 1.5 N, but verify against your probe datasheet. Single-sided access is simpler and cheaper, while double-sided fixtures increase cost and alignment complexity. For high-impedance nodes, guard rings and shielded probe paths reduce leakage and measurement error.

Design requests should ask for a test point on every net where practical, with clear naming and netlist correlation. For through-hole or large SMT test points, a diameter of 1.0 mm to 1.5 mm and spacing of 2.54 mm to 3.81 mm are common starting points, but verify against your probe pitch and paste process. For fine-pitch access, via test points may be used with a diameter of 0.3 mm to 0.6 mm and an annular ring of 0.15 mm to 0.3 mm, subject to probe tip size and drill capability. Test points should avoid component bodies, connector mating zones, high-current nets, and areas where probe force could damage nearby parts. Solder mask openings should be defined and consistent so probe contact is repeatable.

Analog test limits should be derived from component tolerance, fixture residual, leakage, temperature, solder effects, and measurement repeatability. Use four-wire measurement for low-resistance checks and guard high-impedance nodes to reduce leakage error. Diode junction tests often use small currents, for example 50 µA to 100 µA, and low voltages, for example 0.1 V to 0.5 V, to avoid forward biasing adjacent junctions or disturbing the circuit. Power-rail tests should use controlled voltage and current to avoid damaging devices. Set limits from golden-board data and equipment repeatability; a common starting guard band is around ±5% of nominal, but verify against your equipment datasheet and production variation. Temperature can affect junction and resistor measurements, so consider a controlled range such as 25 °C to 40 °C during limit development.

Design-for-test requests should be issued early, before layout freeze, and should include a netlist with test-point list, boundary-scan chain definition, analog net classification, power-domain map, test access points, keep-out zones, fiducials, and test-point naming rules. The rationale is to reduce fixture iterations, improve coverage, lower false failures, and make debug faster. Request that guarded analog nodes be identified so guard rings and test limits can be planned. Request that inaccessible nets be covered by boundary scan or functional test. Request that test points be placed on stable, low-risk copper and not on thermally sensitive or mechanically fragile areas. A DFT review should record coverage, expected test time, and residual risk.

Validate the fixture with golden boards before production release. Measure contact resistance, open and short coverage, analog limits, and repeatability across multiple boards and fixture cycles. Track failures by test point, net, component, and probe location. If failures cluster, check probe wear, board coplanarity, solder mask residue, fixture alignment, and guard integrity. Use boundary scan and functional test to isolate whether a failure is a fixture access problem, a solder joint problem, or a component problem. Keep golden-board data current because probe wear, board material variation, and solder paste changes can shift measured values over time.

calc.task: A multilayer assembly has 1,200 nets, several BGA packages, and annual volume 25,000. A design review finds that 82% of nets can be accessed with a single test point, 12% require paired test points for guarded analog nodes, and 6% are inaccessible. The planned test-point diameter is 1.2 mm, the probe tip diameter is 0.9 mm, and the required annular clearance is 0.15 mm. The available fixture has a 1,500 probe limit. Calculate accessible test points, total test points, minimum pad diameter, and choose a test strategy with reasons.
calc.solution: Step 1: Calculate single-point accessible nets. 1,200 nets × 82% = 984 nets. Step 2: Calculate guarded nets requiring paired test points. 1,200 nets × 12% = 144 nets. Step 3: Double the guarded net count to get test points for those nets. 144 nets × paired test points = 288 test points. Step 4: Calculate inaccessible nets. 1,200 nets × 6% = 72 nets. Step 5: Calculate total test points. 984 single-point test points + 288 paired test points = 1,272 test points. Step 6: Calculate minimum pad diameter. Minimum pad diameter = probe tip diameter + clearance + clearance = 0.9 mm + 0.15 mm + 0.15 mm = 1.2 mm. Step 7: Compare total test points with fixture limit. 1,500 probe limit - 1,272 test points = 228 probes of margin. Step 8: Choose strategy. Use ICT as the primary production test because annual volume 25,000 supports fixture cost, total test points fit within the 1,500 probe limit, and component-level analog coverage is needed. Add boundary scan for inaccessible nets and BGA interconnect coverage. Add functional test for analog performance, power sequencing, and system-level acceptance. Flying probe is not the primary strategy because volume is high enough to justify ICT, but it may be useful for early prototypes or fixture debug.

defect.symptom: ICT reports intermittent opens on guarded analog nets after extended production, with failures moving between adjacent test points and contact resistance rising above 100 mΩ.
defect.cause: Spring probe tip wear, solder mask residue, or fixture alignment drift reduces effective contact area. Guarded high-impedance nodes are sensitive to small increases in contact resistance and leakage, so the measurement shifts into the open or out-of-limit region.
defect.action: Stop production release, inspect and replace worn probes, clean the fixture and board test points, verify alignment with a golden board, and confirm contact resistance below the accepted limit. Re-run limit development with golden-board data, then review test-point placement and guard design for the next fixture revision.

title: Flying probe: when it wins, throughput ceiling, program effort

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.

blocks.alt: A flying-probe machine with movable probes contacting a board, beside a throughput-versus-volume chart and a program effort gauge
blocks.caption: Flying probe: when it wins, the throughput ceiling and program effort

theory.h: What flying probe is and when it wins
theory.p: Flying probe is a test method in which multiple movable probes contact test points sequentially or in parallel. It wins when fixture cost and lead time dominate, volume is low to medium, design changes are frequent, or component density makes a bed-of-nails fixture difficult. It is not a replacement for all ICT or functional test; it is a strategy choice based on coverage, throughput, program effort, and design maturity.

theory.h: Comparison with ICT, boundary scan, and functional test
theory.p: ICT uses a bed-of-nails fixture and can isolate components for shorts, opens, resistance, capacitance, inductance, diodes, and some powered tests. It usually gives high throughput and good analog coverage when test points are available, but fixture cost and test-point access can be limiting. Flying probe uses similar electrical principles without a dedicated fixture, so it is flexible, but probe movement sets a throughput ceiling. Boundary scan uses JTAG or similar scan chains to control and observe device pins, catching many interconnect defects and some device faults without physical test points, but coverage depends on scan design and does not replace all analog or non-scan component tests. Functional test applies power and stimuli to verify behavior, catching system-level defects, but it needs test vectors, fixtures, and can have lower throughput and less component-level isolation.

theory.h: When flying probe is the better strategy
theory.p: Choose flying probe when volume is low to medium, prototype or pilot lots are frequent, test points are sparse or access is difficult, and design iterations are expected. A practical check is to count accessible test points and estimate probe access: if a bed-of-nails fixture would require many pogo pins, complex fixturing, or would interfere with components, flying probe may win. Verify probe reach, probe force, and minimum pad size against the tester datasheet and IPC-7351 land-pattern guidance.

Throughput ceiling is set by mechanical motion more than electrical measurement. A rough model is: time per point equals average probe move time plus dwell plus measurement overhead, divided by the number of probes that can work in parallel, then adjusted for probe sequencing efficiency. Use your equipment datasheet for probe speed, acceleration, dwell, and collision avoidance. In practice, dense boards, small pitch, double-sided probing, calibration cycles, and many component tests reduce throughput. Typical flying-probe point rates can range from about 10 to 100 points/min, but verify against your tester, board size, and test program.

Program effort is not just writing a test sequence. It includes importing CAD, BOM, netlist, and test-point data; defining test limits from component tolerances and circuit simulation; creating probe access rules; checking for probe collisions; calibrating probes; and validating false-call rates. Flying probe programs can be faster to start than ICT fixtures because no bed-of-nails is built, but complex analog tests, powered tests, and tight limits can require similar engineering time. Boundary-scan program effort is lower when scan chains are complete and test points are accessible for the scan controller, but it may require JTAG design changes. Functional test effort is often highest because it needs stimulus, response, timing, and pass/fail criteria.

For a 50-piece prototype with 0.4 mm pitch components, limited test points, and no JTAG, flying probe can provide early coverage without fixture cost. For a stable 100,000-piece product with good test-point access, ICT plus boundary scan often gives lower unit cost and higher throughput. For a mixed-technology assembly with BGAs and critical analog circuits, use boundary scan for interconnect coverage, ICT or flying probe for component-level checks, and functional test for final system verification. The reason to choose each method should be tied to defect coverage, throughput, program effort, and design maturity.

Risks to manage include probe marks, contamination, false calls, probe wear, and damage to small pads or components. Probe marks should be evaluated against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria and your product quality requirements. Keep probe pads clean, verify probe force and dwell, and use calibration standards. If flying probe throughput is insufficient, consider adding test points, increasing probe count, reducing test coverage, moving to ICT for high-volume lots, or using boundary scan to reduce physical test points.

calc.task: Estimate the flying-probe throughput ceiling for a prototype assembly with 1,200 test points, 4 probes, average probe move 250 mm, probe speed 100 mm/s, dwell 0.20 s, measurement overhead 0.10 s, parallel efficiency 0.65, board handling 15 s, and availability 85%. Assume each point requires one probe move and one dwell.
calc.solution: 1. Move time per point = 250 mm / 100 mm/s = 2.5 s. 2. Electrical time per point = dwell + overhead = 0.20 s + 0.10 s = 0.30 s. 3. Serial time per point = 2.5 s + 0.30 s = 2.8 s. 4. Ideal parallel time per point = 2.8 s / 4 probes = 0.70 s/point. 5. Effective time per point = 0.70 s / 0.65 = 1.077 s/point. 6. Test time = 1,200 points * 1.077 s/point = 1,292 s = 21.5 min. 7. Cycle time = 1,292 s + 15 s = 1,307 s = 21.8 min. 8. Theoretical boards/h = 3,600 s/h / 1,307 s/board = 2.75 boards/h. 9. Availability-adjusted boards/h = 2.75 * 0.85 = 2.34 boards/h. 10. Points/min = 1,200 points / (1,292 s / 60 s/min) = 55.7 points/min. This is an upper-bound estimate; real throughput will be lower if probe collisions, calibration, component access, or test sequencing reduce parallel efficiency.

defect.symptom: Flying probe reports intermittent opens on fine-pitch test pads, and the same board passes after reflow cleaning and retest.
defect.cause: Flux residue, probe contamination, or oxide on small test pads increases contact resistance; probe dwell or force may be too low for the pad finish and probe tip condition.
defect.action: Clean the board and probe tips, verify probe force and dwell against the tester datasheet, inspect pad finish and probe marks against IPC-A-610 acceptability criteria, and re-run the program with a contact-resistance check or calibration standard before releasing the lot.

title: Boundary scan / JTAG: BGA access, structure, what it cannot find

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Specify design-for-test requirements as design requests with rationale.

blocks.alt: A scan chain of devices connected through BGA packages, with the test access port at one end and a shaded region it cannot reach
blocks.caption: Boundary scan and JTAG: BGA access, structure, and what it cannot find

theory.h: Why boundary scan matters for BGA assemblies
theory.p: Boundary scan is useful on BGA assemblies because the package hides solder joints and escape routing, so a tester may not be able to probe every net directly. IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG) defines a serial test access port and boundary-scan cells that allow a tester to drive or observe device pins through a small number of control lines. For a 0.5 mm pitch BGA, the practical value is not replacing all test methods, but providing electrical access to digital nets that would otherwise require dense test-point placement. Verify pitch, pad geometry, and probe access against your paste, stencil, and equipment datasheet.

A scan-capable device contains a TAP controller, an instruction register, and data registers. Boundary-scan cells sit between the internal core and the package pins. In EXTEST, the tester shifts a pattern into the boundary-scan chain, updates the cells, then captures the pin states. TCK clocks the state machine, TMS controls state transitions, TDI shifts data in, TDO shifts data out, and TRST is optional. Chains can be daisy-chained across devices. Keep chain length and TCK frequency within the limits of the package, board, and tester; verify against IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG) and your tester datasheet.

Boundary scan can find digital interconnect defects between scan cells, including opens, shorts, stuck-at faults, and some bridging on nets where both ends are scan-capable. It can also read IDCODE to verify device presence and orientation, and use SAMPLE/PRELOAD to observe normal operation. It is useful for in-system test and for boards where probe access is limited. Coverage depends on BSDL accuracy, netlist accuracy, and whether pins are configured as scan cells rather than special functions. A boundary-scan report should state tested nets, untested nets, and assumptions.

Boundary scan cannot find defects that do not change a scan cell's logic state or that lie outside the scan chain. Non-scan passives, analog circuits, power distribution, clocks, reset, configuration pins, and high-speed interfaces may be invisible unless additional test structures are added. It does not measure solder joint quality, mechanical strength, contamination, thermal behavior, or parametric performance such as rise time, noise margin, or current draw. A short on a power net or a missing decoupling capacitor may pass boundary scan while failing functional test. Treat boundary scan as one layer of coverage, not a complete assembly test.

theory.h: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan, and functional test
theory.p: Compare methods by access, coverage, speed, and cost. ICT uses a bed-of-nails fixture and can test many passive and active pin-level faults quickly, but it needs test points and fixture design, and fine-pitch BGA escapes may still be inaccessible. Flying probe avoids a fixture and suits prototypes, but it is slower and still needs probe access. Boundary scan needs few access points and works well for BGA digital nets, but it requires scan-capable devices, BSDL files, and DFT. Functional test exercises the product as used and catches system, firmware, timing, and analog defects, but it may miss latent defects and needs vectors, fixtures, and debug support.

Choose a strategy from the assembly mix. For a high-volume BGA board with many scan-capable digital devices, use boundary scan for digital interconnect, functional test for system behavior, and ICT or flying probe for non-scan passives if test points exist. For a prototype with few boards, flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test often gives faster feedback than a full ICT fixture. For a mixed-signal board, boundary scan may cover only a minority of nets, so functional and analog test dominate. State the reason for each method: access, fault type, volume, and debug needs.

Specify DFT as design requests with rationale. Request boundary-scan support on all digital devices and provide BSDL files, IDCODE values, and a board netlist so the tester can build chains. Request a stable JTAG access header or test points, with TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO, and optional TRST routed according to IEEE Std 1149.1 (JTAG). Request test points for non-scan passives, power, ground, clocks, reset, and configuration pins. Request that scan chains be short enough for the chosen TCK frequency and that device configuration pins be controllable during test. Request isolation for open-drain, pull-up, level-shifter, and bus-contention cases, because these can mask shorts or opens.

Practical limits include chain length, TCK frequency, power state, and pin multiplexing. Some devices require power and configuration before scan access; others support limited unpowered or powered-down modes, so verify against the device datasheet. Long chains increase test time and can degrade signal integrity; short chains and balanced groups help. Keep JTAG traces away from high-speed clocks and sensitive analog nets, and verify signal quality with simulation or measurement. For production, require a coverage report that separates boundary-scan coverage, functional coverage, and untested nets, then decide whether added test points or a fixture are justified.

calc.task: A BGA assembly has 1200 nets. Boundary scan can access 720 digital nets. Flying probe can access 600 nets and takes 18 min per board. Functional test catches 480 system-level defects but misses 240 latent opens. The boundary-scan chain has 1000 cells and runs at 10 MHz. Each vector shifts 1000 bits. Choose a test strategy for 5000 boards and state reasons.
calc.solution: Step 1: Boundary-scan net coverage = 720 / 1200 = 0.60 = 60%. Step 2: Nets not covered by boundary scan = 1200 - 720 = 480 nets. Step 3: Shift time per vector = 1000 bits / 10 MHz = 100 µs. Step 4: For 1000 vectors, shift time = 1000 * 100 µs = 100 ms; allow overhead and use 0.2 s per board. Step 5: Flying-probe coverage = 600 / 1200 = 50%. Step 6: Flying-probe time for 5000 boards = 18 min * 5000 = 90000 min = 1500 h. Step 7: Functional test catches 480 system-level defects but misses 240 latent opens, so it should not be the only method. Step 8: For the first 50 boards, use flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test to debug access, chain integrity, and system behavior. Step 9: For the remaining 4950 boards, use boundary scan plus functional test as the production baseline. Step 10: Add ICT or flying probe only for non-scan passives if the 480-net coverage gap is unacceptable after reviewing fault risk, test-point availability, and fixture cost.

defect.symptom: Boundary scan passes all digital interconnect tests, but the board fails functional test with intermittent resets and missing clock activity.
defect.cause: The reset and clock nets are not covered by boundary scan, and a marginal solder joint or missing decoupling capacitor affects power integrity rather than scan-cell logic state.
defect.action: Add test points or functional vectors for reset, clock, and power rails; review the coverage report for untested nets; verify the BGA escape routing and decoupling layout; re-run boundary scan, functional test, and a targeted flying-probe check on the affected nets.

title: Coverage math: node vs defect coverage, escape risk, where inspection ends and test starts

goals.text: Estimate test coverage and name the defect classes left uncovered by the chosen strategy.

blocks.alt: Two overlapping coverage circles, one for nodes exercised and one for defect modes detected, with the uncovered region marked
blocks.caption: Coverage math: node versus defect coverage, escape risk, and where inspection ends and test starts

theory.h: Node coverage and defect coverage are different
theory.p: Node coverage counts electrical nodes or nets exercised by a test method. Defect coverage estimates the share of likely defect modes that the method can detect. A board can have high node coverage but low defect coverage if the test only checks connectivity at nominal conditions and misses marginal solder joints, parametric drift, or thermal opens.

Visual, AOI, and X-ray inspection look for physical evidence: missing or wrong component, polarity, tombstoning, solder bridging, insufficient solder, foreign material, and visible component damage. These methods are effective for defects with optical or radiographic signatures, but they do not prove electrical behavior under power, temperature, or signal loading.

theory.h: Test detects electrical and functional faults
theory.p: In-circuit test, boundary scan, and functional test apply electrical stimulus and measure response. They can find opens, shorts, wrong component values, incorrect orientation when it changes electrical behavior, power faults, and functional errors. They may miss defects that are physically present but electrically invisible, such as cosmetic solder issues or contamination that does not affect current.

theory.h: Coverage math needs a defect model
theory.p: To estimate coverage, list the expected defect classes and assign each a detection probability for each method. The probabilities should come from your own process capability data, test logs, or pilot builds. Use a range, not a point estimate, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet. Use SI units such as millimetre and micrometre for physical inspection limits, and ppm as a dimensionless rate for escape risk.

theory.h: Escape risk is coverage plus occurrence
theory.p: Escape risk combines detection coverage with defect occurrence. If a defect class occurs at a known rate and a method detects a fraction of it, the residual escape rate is the occurrence rate multiplied by the undetected fraction. This gives a ppm estimate for planning, not a guarantee; actual escapes depend on process drift, test program quality, and intermittent defects.

theory.h: Where inspection ends and test starts
theory.p: Inspection ends when the defect has no reliable physical signature or when the signature is too small, hidden, or variable to inspect consistently. Test starts when the question becomes whether the assembly behaves electrically or functionally. For hidden joints, X-ray or boundary scan may bridge the gap, but neither replaces a test that exercises the node under representative conditions.

theory.h: Choosing a strategy defines the uncovered classes
theory.p: A strategy based only on AOI leaves electrical opens under packages, shorts under components, wrong values within tolerance, and parametric faults uncovered. A strategy based only on ICT may leave cosmetic solder defects, intermittent joints, thermal opens, and functional timing errors uncovered. The chosen strategy should be documented with the defect classes it does not cover and the compensating controls used.

calc.task: A board has 1200 electrical nodes. ICT exercises 980 nodes. Functional test exercises 150 nodes, of which 30 overlap with ICT. A defect model gives occurrence rates: visible solder and placement defects 1500 ppm, electrical open and short defects 800 ppm, parametric and wrong-value defects 200 ppm. AOI detects 70 percent of visible defects, ICT detects 90 percent of electrical defects, and functional test detects 60 percent of parametric defects. Estimate node coverage, weighted defect coverage, and residual escape ppm. Name defect classes left uncovered.
calc.solution: Node coverage: union of ICT and functional nodes is 980 + 150 - 30 = 1100 nodes. Node coverage = 1100 / 1200 = 91.7 percent. Weighted defect coverage: visible contribution = 1500 * 0.70 = 1050 ppm detected; electrical contribution = 800 * 0.90 = 720 ppm detected; parametric contribution = 200 * 0.60 = 120 ppm detected. Total detected = 1050 + 720 + 120 = 1890 ppm. Total occurrence = 1500 + 800 + 200 = 2500 ppm. Weighted defect coverage = 1890 / 2500 = 75.6 percent. Residual escape = 2500 - 1890 = 610 ppm, or 2500 * 0.244 = 610 ppm. Defect classes left uncovered include under-component opens and shorts not exercised, intermittent solder joints, thermal opens, wrong values within tolerance, parametric drift, contamination, cosmetic solder defects, functional timing errors, and firmware errors.

defect.symptom: AOI passes a QFN assembly, but ICT finds an open on the exposed pad net after reflow.
defect.cause: solder paste volume under the QFN was low or the pad was not wetted, so the joint was electrically open but visually acceptable.
defect.action: check stencil aperture and paste release, verify paste height with SPI, review reflow profile, and add X-ray or boundary scan coverage for hidden pad nets; rework per IPC acceptability guidance.

title: Choosing a strategy for a product mix: volume, complexity, cost, rework loop

goals.text: Compare ICT, flying probe, boundary scan and functional test for a given assembly and choose a strategy with reasons.
Estimate test coverage and name the defect classes left uncovered by the chosen strategy.

blocks.alt: A decision matrix of product volume against assembly complexity, with a test strategy recommended in each quadrant and a rework loop
blocks.caption: Choosing a strategy for a product mix: volume, complexity, cost and the rework loop

theory.h: Product mix and test strategy drivers
theory.p: A product mix is a test-strategy problem because volume, complexity, cost, and rework loop interact. High volume favors methods with short cycle time and repeatable contact, because fixture cost can be spread over many units and line balance becomes important. High complexity favors methods that can reach dense interconnects, verify component presence and value, and isolate faults quickly. Cost pressure favors methods that reduce escapes, rework, and test time, not just capital equipment. A short rework loop favors structural tests that localize defects before functional testing, because functional failures can be slow to debug. The choice should be based on measured access, board density, component mix, and your equipment datasheet, not on a preferred technology.

In-circuit test uses a dedicated fixture with pogo pins to contact test points on the assembly. It is strong for opens, shorts, missing components, wrong component values, and some solder defects when the net is accessible and the test program is well designed. Coverage is not determined only by the number of test points; it also depends on double-sided access, fine-pitch access, component orientation, and whether power, analog, and high-speed nets are included. Fixture cost and maintenance can be significant, and fixture design may need revision after layout changes. Verify coverage against your fixture design, equipment datasheet, and the applicable IPC acceptance standard for solder defects.

Flying probe test replaces a dedicated fixture with movable probes that access test points under program control. It is attractive for prototypes, low volume, high mix, and debug because fixture cost is low and program changes are faster. It can provide broad net coverage when test points are accessible, but cycle time is usually longer than in-circuit test, and probe reach can limit dense or double-sided boards. It may also require more careful test-point placement and can be sensitive to probe wear, contamination, and alignment. Verify probe reach, cycle time, test-point density, and repeatability against your equipment datasheet before using it as the primary production test.

Boundary scan uses JTAG to control device pins and test interconnects without physical probes. It is valuable when access is limited, when test points are scarce, or when the board has dense interconnects that are difficult to probe. It can detect opens, shorts, and some device-level faults on scan-capable interconnects, and it can support programming and debug. Its coverage is limited to scan-capable devices and scan-capable interconnects. It may not test non-scan components, analog functions, power delivery, some mixed-signal behavior, or solder defects that do not affect scan paths. Verify scan coverage against your design, boundary-scan tool, and the actual device pinout.

Functional test applies power, signals, and loads to verify that the assembly behaves as intended. It can catch programming errors, gross functional failures, some marginal defects, and system-level interactions that structural tests may miss. However, it may not isolate the failed net or component, and its coverage depends on the test program, stimulus conditions, and measurement resolution. Functional test can be slow and may require specialized fixtures, software, and calibration. It is often used after structural tests to reduce rework loop time, because structural tests can localize many defects before functional debugging. Verify test program coverage against your requirements and equipment datasheet.

For high-volume, high-complexity assemblies, a combined strategy of in-circuit test, boundary scan, and functional test is often chosen because it balances coverage, cycle time, and rework loop time. In-circuit test provides fast structural coverage, boundary scan adds coverage where probe access is limited, and functional test closes gross functional defects. For low-volume or prototype assemblies, flying probe plus boundary scan plus functional test may be preferred to avoid fixture cost and support design changes. For simple high-volume assemblies, in-circuit test plus functional test may be sufficient. Choose based on volume, complexity, cost, access, component mix, and rework loop, and verify against your equipment datasheet.

Coverage should be stated for nets, components, and defect classes, not as a standalone figure. A strategy may cover most nets but still miss under-component solder defects, non-scan analog faults, thermal or mechanical defects, intermittent contacts, contamination, programming errors, and marginal parametric drift. Coverage also depends on test conditions, such as temperature, voltage, and timing, because a defect may appear only under stress. When choosing a strategy, name the defect classes left uncovered and decide whether additional methods such as X-ray, thermal cycling, burn-in, extended functional testing, or inspection are needed. Verify residual risk against your acceptance criteria and failure history.

The rework loop is the time from defect detection to corrected unit, and it affects both cost and quality. A strategy that localizes defects quickly reduces diagnosis time and prevents repeated functional debugging. Structural tests can isolate opens, shorts, missing parts, and wrong values, while functional tests may only indicate that a subsystem failed. Cost should include fixture cost, test time, maintenance, program development, escapes, rework, and scrap. A low-cost test method can become expensive if it produces high escape rates or long diagnosis times. Use your line data to compare cycle time, first-pass yield, and rework time, and verify against your equipment datasheet and paste process capability.

calc.task: A high-density assembly has 1400 nets, 30% BGA, 25% non-scan devices, and monthly volume 4000 units. Flying probe cycle time is 180 s, ICT cycle time is 25 s, boundary scan adds 8 s, and functional test adds 45 s. Estimate coverage and choose a strategy with reasons.
calc.solution: Define total nets as 1400. Estimate ICT net coverage. With accessible test points and double-sided probing, assume 85% of nets are testable; verify against fixture design. ICT coverage = 1400 x 85% = 1190 nets. Estimate boundary-scan coverage. Scan-capable share is 75%. Assume scan tests 80% of scan-capable interconnects; verify against boundary-scan tool. Scan coverage = 1400 x 75% x 80% = 840 nets. Combine coverage conservatively. Assume scan adds 7 percentage points beyond ICT because many scan nets overlap with ICT. Combined structural coverage = 85% + 7% = 92%. Add functional test. Assume functional test adds 3 percentage points for gross functional and programming defects. Estimated total coverage = 95%. Compare cycle time. ICT + boundary scan + functional = 25 s + 8 s + 45 s = 78 s per unit. Flying probe + boundary scan + functional = 180 s + 8 s + 45 s = 233 s per unit. At 4000 units/month, the ICT-based strategy is more practical for the rework loop because it reduces test time per unit and keeps fixture cost amortized. Choose ICT + boundary scan + functional. Reasons: high volume amortizes fixture cost, ICT gives fast structural coverage, boundary scan adds coverage where probe access is limited, functional test closes gross functional defects, and cycle time supports the rework loop. Name defect classes left uncovered: under-BGA opens/shorts not detected by structural or functional tests, non-scan analog faults, thermal or mechanical defects, intermittent contacts, contamination, marginal parametric drift, and programming errors not exercised by the functional program. Verify residual risk against your acceptance criteria and failure history.

defect.symptom: Intermittent open after reflow on a fine-pitch QFP, with the fault appearing only after thermal cycling or handling.
defect.cause: Insufficient solder paste volume, poor paste release, misalignment, or contaminated pad surface can create a marginal joint that tests good initially but opens under stress.
defect.action: Check stencil aperture, paste release, SPI data, alignment, and pad cleanliness; review reflow profile; add stress screening or targeted inspection if the defect class is not covered by the chosen test strategy.

title: Defect data before opinions: taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity

goals.text: Structure a defect problem with measured data (taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity) before analysis.

theory.h: Start with measured defect data, not with opinions
theory.p: A defect problem in SMT or THT assembly becomes manageable when it is described by measured data before analysis begins. The first task is not to decide whether the paste printer, placement machine, reflow oven, wave solder process, or operator is at fault. The first task is to define what was measured, where it was measured, what unit was used, and what acceptance rule was applied. A statement such as 'the oven is causing tombstoning' is an opinion until it is supported by stage-specific defect counts, component references, board identifiers, lot data, process parameters, and inspection results. A statement such as 'reflow-stage confirmed defects are the largest contributor in this week's data' is a measured observation, provided the defect taxonomy and inspection integrity are known. Process engineers should treat defect data as a measurement system. If the measurement system is weak, the analysis will produce confident but misleading conclusions.

blocks.alt: A Pareto chart of defects by process stage with a data-integrity check panel beside it
blocks.caption: Defect data before opinions: taxonomy, Pareto by stage and measurement integrity

theory.h: Build a defect taxonomy that supports stage-based analysis
theory.p: A useful defect taxonomy records the defect mode, the assembly stage, the inspection or test point, the product, the board or lot identifier, the line, the shift, the equipment, the recipe, and the disposition. Defect mode describes what was found, such as insufficient solder, excess solder, misalignment, tombstoning, bridging, voiding, lifted lead, solder ball, component damage, or contamination. Stage describes where the defect was detected or attributed, such as incoming inspection, paste printing, placement, reflow, post-reflow inspection, THT insertion, wave or selective solder, cleaning, conformal coating, ICT, functional test, or final assembly. The taxonomy should distinguish between a defect call and a confirmed defect. An AOI false call is not the same as a confirmed solder defect, and an ICT failure is not always a solder defect. Controlled vocabulary prevents the same physical problem from being recorded under several names, which would distort Pareto ranking.

theory.h: Use IPC acceptance and rework standards as the defect language
theory.p: For visual and workmanship decisions, IPC-A-610 provides acceptance criteria for electronic assemblies, and IPC-7711/7721 provides guidance for rework and repair. These standards are useful because they give a common language for defect classification and disposition. However, acceptance depends on product class, customer requirements, and the specific defect condition. Do not assume that every visible anomaly is a reject, and do not assume that every anomaly can be repaired without limits. Where the standard allows different acceptance levels or repair conditions, the factory must define which class or customer rule applies and record that rule in the defect database. If a defect is accepted, reworked, repaired, scrapped, or returned to upstream inspection, that disposition should be stored with the defect record. This prevents analysis from mixing confirmed defects, false calls, accepted conditions, and rework loops.

theory.h: Pareto by stage reveals where the process is losing yield
theory.p: Pareto analysis by stage answers a practical question: which stage contributes the largest share of confirmed defects, escapes, rework, scrap, or test failures? A final-test Pareto alone can hide upstream causes. For example, a functional failure may be caused by a reflow defect, a placement defect, a THT insertion problem, or a test setup issue. Stage-based Pareto should separate incoming material defects, paste print defects, placement defects, reflow defects, THT insertion defects, wave or selective solder defects, cleaning or coating defects, ICT failures, and functional test failures. The ranking should be based on confirmed defect counts or a weighted metric such as cost of poor quality, rework time, scrap value, or escape risk. Raw counts are useful, but they should be interpreted with production volume and stage detection capability. A stage with high detection may appear worse than a stage with poor detection, even if the underlying process is better.

theory.h: Measurement integrity determines whether the Pareto is trustworthy
theory.p: Measurement integrity asks whether the inspection or test system can detect the defect it is supposed to detect and whether it avoids false calls. For SMT, common measurement systems include SPI for paste volume and area, AOI for component and solder condition, X-ray inspection for hidden joints, ICT for electrical connectivity, functional test for operation, and manual visual inspection. For THT, measurement systems include insertion verification, wave or selective solder inspection, X-ray for through-hole joints, ICT, and functional test. Each system has detection capability, false-call behavior, repeatability, reproducibility, and calibration status. A defect database should record whether a defect was detected by AOI, X-ray, ICT, functional test, manual inspection, or repair confirmation. If a system has a high false-call rate, raw defect counts may overstate a stage. If a system has a high escape rate, raw defect counts may understate a stage. Before root-cause analysis, the engineer should verify that the measurement system is capable enough for the defect type being analyzed.

theory.h: Record process parameters in SI units and trace them to the defect
theory.p: Defect data becomes actionable when it is linked to process parameters in consistent SI units. Paste print data may include stencil thickness in mm, aperture dimensions in mm, paste volume in mm³, squeegee pressure in Pa or N depending on the printer interface, print speed in mm/s, and paste temperature in °C. Placement data may include nozzle force in N, placement speed in mm/s, component offset in mm, and feeder pickup accuracy in mm. Reflow data may include profile zone temperatures in °C, time above liquidus in s, peak temperature in °C, and conveyor speed in mm/s. Wave or selective solder data may include solder pot temperature in °C, conveyor speed in mm/s, flux application rate, and preheat temperature in °C. These values should be traceable to the board, lot, shift, and equipment recipe. Verify actual parameter ranges against your paste datasheet, stencil design, printer datasheet, oven profile, wave or selective solder machine datasheet, and IPC-7525, IPC-7526, IPC-7530, or IPC-7711/7721 guidance where applicable.

theory.h: Define the denominator before comparing stages
theory.p: A defect count without a denominator can mislead. The denominator may be boards produced, boards inspected, components placed, joints inspected, test cycles, or units shipped. A stage defect rate should state the denominator clearly. For example, defects per board, defects per thousand boards, defects per million joints, or failures per test cycle are different metrics. If one stage inspects every board and another stage samples only a subset, raw counts are not directly comparable. If rework loops cause the same board to be recorded multiple times, the database must distinguish initial detection, rework confirmation, and final disposition. If a board fails at ICT and then fails at functional test, the analysis should decide whether to count both events, count only the confirmed root defect, or count both with a relationship field. The important point is that the rule must be defined before the Pareto is generated. Otherwise, different engineers will produce different charts from the same data.

theory.h: Use the Pareto to select the next measurement, not to assign blame
theory.p: The output of stage-based Pareto should be a short list of stages and defect modes that justify further measurement. If reflow-stage confirmed defects dominate, the next step may be to stratify by component type, package size, board location, paste lot, stencil design, oven profile, or AOI program. If paste print defects dominate, the next step may be to review SPI data, stencil condition, squeegee settings, paste rheology, and print registration. If THT insertion defects dominate, the next step may be to review lead form, insertion force, seating verification, and wave or selective solder parameters. If ICT or functional test failures dominate, the next step may be to separate test escape, test setup error, firmware issue, and physical defect. The Pareto does not prove root cause. It identifies where measurement uncertainty is low enough and defect concentration is high enough to justify deeper analysis. The engineer should then verify the top stage with measurement integrity data before launching a corrective action.

calc.task: A mixed SMT/THT line produced 12,000 boards during a week. The MES defect table before measurement-integrity audit contained these stage defect calls: incoming 18, paste print 145, placement 92, reflow 270, THT insertion 34, wave solder 56, ICT 71, functional test 48. An AOI audit reviewed the 270 reflow calls and confirmed 210 defects, with 60 false calls. A detection audit used 50 seeded reflow defects and found that AOI detected 48 and missed 2. Calculate the raw stage defect rate per 1000 boards, the raw Pareto ranking, the corrected confirmed stage defect rate per 1000 boards, the corrected Pareto ranking, the AOI false-call rate, the AOI detection rate, and the seeded escape rate. State whether the reflow stage is still the top stage after correction and what data action is needed before root-cause analysis.
calc.solution: 1. Raw total defect calls = 18 + 145 + 92 + 270 + 34 + 56 + 71 + 48 = 734. 2. Raw stage defect rate per 1000 boards = stage count / 12,000 x 1000. Incoming = 18 / 12,000 x 1000 = 1.5. Paste print = 145 / 12,000 x 1000 = 12.1. Placement = 92 / 12,000 x 1000 = 7.7. Reflow = 270 / 12,000 x 1000 = 22.5. THT insertion = 34 / 12,000 x 1000 = 2.8. Wave solder = 56 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.7. ICT = 71 / 12,000 x 1000 = 5.9. Functional test = 48 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.0. 3. Raw Pareto ranking by count: reflow 270, paste print 145, placement 92, ICT 71, wave solder 56, functional test 48, THT insertion 34, incoming 18. 4. Raw percentage of total = stage count / 734 x 100. Reflow = 270 / 734 x 100 = 36.8%. Paste print = 145 / 734 x 100 = 19.8%. Placement = 92 / 734 x 100 = 12.5%. ICT = 71 / 734 x 100 = 9.7%. Wave solder = 56 / 734 x 100 = 7.6%. Functional test = 48 / 734 x 100 = 6.5%. THT insertion = 34 / 734 x 100 = 4.6%. Incoming = 18 / 734 x 100 = 2.5%. 5. Raw cumulative percentage: reflow 36.8%, paste print 56.6%, placement 69.1%, ICT 78.8%, wave solder 86.4%, functional test 92.9%, THT insertion 97.5%, incoming 100.0%. 6. Corrected confirmed total = 18 + 145 + 92 + 210 + 34 + 56 + 71 + 48 = 674. 7. Corrected stage defect rate per 1000 boards: incoming = 18 / 12,000 x 1000 = 1.5. Paste print = 145 / 12,000 x 1000 = 12.1. Placement = 92 / 12,000 x 1000 = 7.7. Reflow = 210 / 12,000 x 1000 = 17.5. THT insertion = 34 / 12,000 x 1000 = 2.8. Wave solder = 56 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.7. ICT = 71 / 12,000 x 1000 = 5.9. Functional test = 48 / 12,000 x 1000 = 4.0. 8. Corrected Pareto ranking by confirmed count: reflow 210, paste print 145, placement 92, ICT 71, wave solder 56, functional test 48, THT insertion 34, incoming 18. 9. Corrected percentage of total = stage count / 674 x 100. Reflow = 210 / 674 x 100 = 31.2%. Paste print = 145 / 674 x 100 = 21.5%. Placement = 92 / 674 x 100 = 13.6%. ICT = 71 / 674 x 100 = 10.5%. Wave solder = 56 / 674 x 100 = 8.3%. Functional test = 48 / 674 x 100 = 7.1%. THT insertion = 34 / 674 x 100 = 5.0%. Incoming = 18 / 674 x 100 = 2.7%. 10. Corrected cumulative percentage: reflow 31.2%, paste print 52.7%, placement 66.3%, ICT 76.8%, wave solder 85.1%, functional test 92.2%, THT insertion 97.2%, incoming 99.9% before rounding to full total. 11. AOI false-call rate = false calls / AOI calls x 100 = 60 / 270 x 100 = 22.2%. 12. AOI detection rate = detected seeded defects / seeded defects x 100 = 48 / 50 x 100 = 96.0%. 13. Seeded escape rate = missed seeded defects / seeded defects x 100 = 2 / 50 x 100 = 4.0%. 14. Optional estimate of true reflow defects, assuming the seeded detection rate applies to the confirmed population and false calls have been removed: estimated true reflow defects = confirmed reflow defects / detection rate = 210 / 0.96 = 218.8. 15. Conclusion: reflow remains the top stage after correction, but the gap between reflow and paste print narrows from 125 raw calls to 65 confirmed defects. The data action is to remove false calls from the Pareto, record confirmed versus called defects separately, verify AOI program settings and defect library, and stratify reflow defects by component, package, board location, paste lot, stencil design, and oven profile before root-cause analysis.

defect.symptom: AOI reports a high number of reflow-stage solder defects, especially insufficient solder and bridging, but repair confirmation shows that many boards pass IPC-A-610 acceptance or are repaired without a confirmed process defect. The reflow stage dominates the Pareto, and operators blame the oven while the paste printer and stencil condition are not being reviewed.
defect.cause: The defect database is counting AOI calls as confirmed defects without separating false calls, and the AOI program has not been audited against IPC-A-610 acceptance conditions or a seeded defect library. The measurement system is therefore inflating the reflow stage and hiding the true upstream contribution from paste print or stencil-related defects.
defect.action: Freeze the current Pareto, rebuild the defect table with separate fields for AOI call, confirmed defect, false call, escape, disposition, and IPC-A-610 acceptance decision. Run an AOI false-call and detection audit using known-good boards and seeded defects. Correct the Pareto using confirmed defects only. If the corrected reflow Pareto still dominates, stratify by component, package, board location, paste lot, stencil design, and oven profile. If the corrected paste print Pareto rises, review stencil condition, aperture design, paste rheology, squeegee settings, and SPI data against IPC-7525, IPC-7526, and IPC-7530 guidance and your equipment datasheets.

title: Cause analysis tools: 5-Why, fishbone, fault tree, change-point analysis

goals.text: Separate root cause, contributing causes and the detection escape in a structured cause analysis.

blocks.alt: Four small diagrams side by side: a five-why chain, a fishbone with six bones, a fault tree and a change-point chart
blocks.caption: Cause analysis tools: five-why, fishbone, fault tree and change-point analysis

theory.h: Separate the failure, the causes, and the escape
theory.p: Cause analysis in SMT/THT starts by separating three questions: what physical failure occurred, what process conditions made it likely, and why the defect was not detected. A root cause is the condition that, when corrected, prevents recurrence under the same operating assumptions. Contributing causes are conditions that raise probability or severity but may not be sufficient alone. A detection escape is a gap in inspection, test, or sampling that allowed the defect to move downstream. In practice, a joint defect may have one dominant root cause plus several contributing causes and one or more escapes.

The Why-chain (5-Why) is useful when the failure mode is narrow and the sequence is mostly linear. Ask why repeatedly until the answer points to a controllable process parameter, a design condition, or a management-system gap, then stop and verify with evidence. For example, tombstoning can be traced from uneven wetting to asymmetric paste deposit, then to stencil alignment or paste rheology, then to setup verification. Avoid stopping at operator error unless the method, training, or error-proofing system is also examined.

Fishbone diagrams are better when many cause families may interact. For SMT/THT, use categories such as machine, method, material, measurement, environment, and management. Populate them with testable hypotheses: reflow profile drift, paste viscosity or metal content, stencil aperture wear, placement nozzle force, feeder misalignment, wave solder conveyor speed, flux activity, humidity, and inspection coverage. The diagram organizes investigation; it does not prove cause. Each branch should be linked to a measurement, sample, or experiment.

theory.h: Fault tree for combined causes and escapes
theory.p: Fault tree analysis is useful when the top event can result from several independent or combined causes. Define the top event narrowly, such as an open solder joint or a tombstoned component, then decompose it with AND and OR gates. For example, an open joint may require both insufficient wetting and mechanical disturbance, while a tombstone may occur if either paste asymmetry or placement offset is severe. Fault trees make detection escapes explicit by adding an inspection branch: the defect escapes only if the defect exists and the inspection fails to detect it.

theory.h: Change-point analysis for suspected process changes
theory.p: Change-point analysis compares process behavior before and after a suspected change. Common SMT/THT changes include paste lot, stencil, reflow profile, placement nozzle, feeder setup, wave solder chain speed, flux lot, or AOI program revision. Use a simple before/after defect rate, a control chart, or a change-point statistic when data are available. Confirm that the suspected change occurred before the shift, that the affected product and process window match, and that the result is not explained by sampling variation. Verify process settings against equipment datasheets and paste or flux datasheets rather than assuming nominal values.

theory.h: Report the three cause categories separately
theory.p: Separate root cause, contributing causes, and detection escape in the final report. The root cause is the item for corrective action, such as an unqualified paste lot property or a stencil aperture outside the qualified range. Contributing causes may include marginal reflow profile, worn nozzle, or high placement speed; these may be reduced through risk controls even if not the primary cause. The detection escape is addressed by inspection or test coverage, such as AOI program limits, X-ray sampling, functional test coverage, or IPC-A-610 visual acceptability criteria. The contract class and IPC-A-610 requirements determine what is acceptable; verify against the applicable class.

theory.h: Close with verification and updated controls
theory.p: Close the analysis with verification. Containment protects the customer, corrective action removes the root cause, and effectiveness checks confirm that the defect rate, inspection escape rate, or process parameter has returned to an acceptable state. Update the control plan, FMEA, work instructions, and inspection program. Use SI units for temperatures, times, distances, and volumes in the report, and state uncertainty or sampling limits. Avoid absolute language; standards and contracts may allow exceptions, so record the applicable IPC-A-610 class, IPC/JEDEC J-STD-001 requirements, and any approved deviation.

calc.task: A line produces 1000 boards/day. Tombstone defect rate for small chip resistors was 0.2% over 10 days. After a paste lot change, the rate was 1.5% over 10 days. AOI detects 80% of tombstones. Functional test detects 5% of the tombstones missed by AOI. Estimate daily escaped defects before and after the change, and state how to classify root cause, contributing causes, and detection escape.
calc.solution: First, convert defect rates to defects per day. Before: 1000 boards/day x 0.2% = 2.0 defects/day. After: 1000 boards/day x 1.5% = 15.0 defects/day. Second, estimate defects missed by AOI. AOI detects 80%, so it misses 20%. Before: 2.0 x 0.20 = 0.4 missed/day. After: 15.0 x 0.20 = 3.0 missed/day. Third, estimate defects missed by functional test. Functional test detects 5% of AOI misses, so it misses 95%. Before: 0.4 x 0.95 = 0.38 escaped/day. After: 3.0 x 0.95 = 2.85 escaped/day. Fourth, interpret the change point. The escaped defect rate rises from 0.38/day to 2.85/day after the paste lot change, so the paste lot change is a strong candidate change point if the timing matches. Fifth, classify causes. A likely root cause is a paste lot property outside the qualified range, such as viscosity or metal content, verified against the paste datasheet. Contributing causes may include stencil alignment drift, nozzle wear, or marginal reflow profile. The detection escape is the AOI program and functional test coverage that failed to remove the remaining tombstones.

defect.symptom: Tombstoned chip resistors after reflow; some passed AOI and reached functional test or downstream assembly.
defect.cause: A paste lot with viscosity or metal content outside the qualified range, combined with stencil alignment drift, produced asymmetric paste deposits and uneven wetting. The AOI program limits did not flag small tombstones, and functional test coverage did not reliably detect them.
defect.action: Quarantine the suspect paste lot and verify viscosity and metal content against the paste datasheet. Requalify stencil alignment, reflow profile, and placement setup. Update the AOI program and add targeted X-ray or functional test coverage. Run an effectiveness check on subsequent lots and update the control plan and FMEA.

title: Containment and traceability: quarantine scope, lot trace, retroactive search

goals.text: Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.

blocks.alt: A containment boundary drawn around work in process, finished goods and shipped units, with a lot trace chain and a retroactive search arrow
blocks.caption: Containment and traceability: quarantine scope, lot trace and retroactive search

theory.h: Why containment and traceability are separate controls
theory.p: Containment protects the customer while the cause is unknown, and traceability tells you what to contain. In SMT/THT, a defect can be created by paste, component, stencil, placement, reflow, wave solder, insertion, cleaning, or test escape. A good containment record starts with the detection point and works backward to the last verified good point. It should identify the product, process step, equipment, operator, program, material lot, and time window. If records are incomplete, the scope should be widened until the uncertainty is bounded, then narrowed with evidence. The goal is not to quarantine the whole factory; it is to isolate the population that could plausibly contain the defect. A clear scope also reduces the cost of investigation, because the team can focus on the process window, material lots, and equipment settings that actually produced the suspect units. When the scope is vague, teams often inspect too much product, lose line capacity, and still miss the escape. When the scope is too narrow, the escape can continue downstream, and the company may need to notify the customer under the applicable requirement in ISO 9001 or IATF 16949.

Quarantine scope is a bounded suspect population. Use timestamps from MES, ERP, test logs, and line audits. A practical scope includes work in process, finished goods, shipped goods, returns, and any product made between the last verified good inspection and detection. Include adjacent shifts and changeovers if the process was not verified after the change. If a paste lot change, stencil change, feeder change, wave solder program change, or maintenance event occurred inside the window, include it in the retroactive search. Where records are weak, use a conservative boundary and document the assumption. The boundary should be justified by the process risk, not by convenience. For example, if a wave solder program was edited but the verification sample was not retained, the suspect window should include the period before and after the edit until the program is confirmed. If the defect is intermittent, include units from the same equipment and same shift, because the cause may be related to thermal drift, flux density, or feeder behavior. The quarantine record should state the quantity, location, disposition status, and who authorized release. It should also state whether the suspect population is physically segregated or electronically blocked, because electronic blocks can fail if a scanner or ERP transaction is missed.

Lot trace should connect the assembly to the materials and process parameters that affected it. For SMT, trace the component lot, solder paste lot, stencil, placement program, feeder setup, reflow profile, and oven zone settings. For THT, trace the component lot, insertion program, wave solder program, flux density, preheat temperature, conveyor speed, and solder pot temperature. Verify settings against your equipment datasheet and process recipe. Traceability is useful only if it can be retrieved quickly. Store records in a searchable system, and keep a manual fallback for audits or system outages. The trace should also include the inspection or test that verified the process, because a lot is not truly traceable if the verification record is missing. For mixed SMT/THT assemblies, trace the surface mount and through-hole operations, because a defect signature may point to the wrong process if the trace is incomplete. A good trace record can answer which material lot was used, which machine produced the unit, which program was active, and which operator or technician made the change. This information supports the retroactive search and helps the team avoid blaming an operator when the process allowed the error.

Retroactive search looks for other units that may share the same latent cause. Search forward from the suspect materials and backward from the defect signature. Include units made before and after the detection if the process was not verified, and include units from the same equipment, same operator, same program, or same material lot. If the search is too large to inspect fully, use a sampling plan that matches the risk and the customer expectation. ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 can be used when a sampling plan is needed, but the plan should be documented and approved. Record the search scope, sample size, inspection method, and disposition. The search should also cover adjacent product families if they share the same paste, stencil, feeder, wave solder program, or test fixture. A defect that appears on a header may also affect a connector or a power stage if the same thermal profile or flux density was used. When the search is complete, document the negative results as well as the positive results. Negative results show that the containment was effective and help the team close the investigation without leaving an open risk.

An 8D report is a structured problem-solving record. It should name the team, describe the problem with product, quantity, location, and detection point, and state interim containment. It should identify the root cause and the escape point, then define permanent corrective action, implementation dates, owners, and effectiveness checks. The report should also address prevention by updating the control plan, FMEA, work instructions, training, and audit checks. Keep the language factual. Avoid blaming operators when the process allowed the error. Use evidence such as photos, test data, process logs, and inspection results. The problem description should be specific enough that another engineer can understand the failure without visiting the line. It should state the defect mode, the affected process step, the detection method, and the quantity found. The containment section should state what was stopped, what was quarantined, what was inspected, and what was released. The corrective action section should separate the cause correction from the escape correction, because a process can be fixed while the inspection method still fails to detect the defect. The prevention section should show how the change is sustained through controls, not just through memory.

Each containment and corrective action needs a named owner and a due date. Containment actions are usually short-term and should be verified before suspect material is released. Corrective actions need a longer window for validation. Effectiveness should be measured with a metric tied to the defect, such as solder defect ppm, initial pass yield, rework rate, test escape rate, or audit findings. Set the target from historical baseline and customer requirements, and verify against your paste/equipment datasheet for process limits. If the metric does not improve, the corrective action is not complete. The owner should be accountable for evidence, not just for attending a meeting. The due date should reflect the time needed to validate the change, including material consumption, equipment qualification, and inspection method verification. For a process change, the effectiveness check may require several production runs under normal conditions. For a training change, the effectiveness check may require an audit of work instructions and operator performance. The metric should be simple enough to collect without delaying production, and it should be reviewed by the quality owner before closure.

Closure requires evidence that the suspect population is dispositioned, the cause is corrected, and the process is stable. Disposition options include rework, scrap, use-as-is, or customer concession, depending on contract and product requirements. Rework should follow IPC-7711/7721 and be documented. Soldering acceptance should be checked against IPC-A-610 and IPC/JEDEC J-STD-001 where applicable. Update the control plan and FMEA, train affected staff, and add an initial-article check or layered process audit for a defined period. Keep the 8D open until the effectiveness metric is met and the records are archived. The closure package should include the quarantine record, disposition record, root cause evidence, corrective action evidence, effectiveness data, and updated documents. If the customer requires a formal report, use the customer format while keeping the same evidence. If the issue is internal, the same package supports the next audit and reduces the chance of recurrence. Closure is not complete when the line is running; it is complete when the process control is updated and the evidence shows the defect is no longer escaping.

calc.task: A line produced 1200 boards/h. A solder bridge was detected at 14:20. The last verified good inspection was at 13:50. The line stopped at 14:25. A paste lot change occurred at 13:45. Calculate the suspect window, suspect board count, and quarantine quantity. Then draft the containment, corrective action, owners, dates, and effectiveness metric for an 8D.
calc.solution: Start by choosing the earliest credible suspect time. The paste lot change at 13:45 is earlier than the last verified good inspection at 13:50, so use 13:45 as the conservative start of the suspect window. The line stopped at 14:25, so the suspect window is 13:45 to 14:25. The window length is 40 min. Convert the production rate to boards per minute: 1200 boards/h divided by 60 min/h equals 20 boards/min. Multiply 20 boards/min by 40 min to get 800 boards. Quarantine the 800 boards plus any work in process, finished goods, and shipped units from the same window. Containment owner: SMT process engineer; due date: 24 h. Corrective action owner: process engineer; due date: 7 days. Corrective action: verify flux density, preheat temperature, conveyor speed, and solder pot temperature against your equipment datasheet; rework per IPC-7711/7721; add an initial-article check after changeover. Effectiveness metric: solder bridge ppm; baseline 500 ppm; target 100 ppm; measured over 30 days. Close when the target is met and the control plan, FMEA, and work instructions are updated.

defect.symptom: Solder bridges between adjacent THT leads on a fine-pitch header after wave solder, detected at ICT.
defect.cause: Flux application was too heavy and preheat was below the range recommended by the wave solder equipment datasheet, leaving flux residue that prevented solder coalescence.
defect.action: Quarantine product back to the last verified good inspection, rework per IPC-7711/7721, adjust flux density and preheat within the equipment datasheet range, and add an initial-article check after each changeover.

title: 8D discipline: D1–D8 content and where 8D reports fail

goals.text: Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.

blocks.alt: A row of eight labelled steps D1 to D8, with the common failure points marked in red
blocks.caption: Eight-discipline discipline: D1 to D8 content, and where eight-discipline reports fail

theory.p: An 8D report is a structured problem-solving record for internal escapes, customer complaints, or repeated process defects. In SMT/THT work, it should connect the complaint to traceable evidence: product, lot, line, process step, component, paste, stencil, feeder, reflow or wave/selective solder parameters, inspection program, and test data. The report is useful only if another engineer can follow the logic, repeat the verification, and see whether the action actually worked.

theory.h: D1 team and D2 problem description
theory.p: D1 should name a small working team with authority and knowledge: process engineering, production, quality, materials, equipment maintenance, design, and supplier support when materials or tooling are involved. D2 should describe the problem as observed, not as a conclusion. Include product, line, process step, defect mode, quantity, date, lot, measurement method, customer impact, and whether the defect is occurrence, detection, or both. For SMT/THT, also record component type, PCB side, paste lot, stencil, feeder, reflow profile, wave or selective solder setup, AOI or ICT program, shift, and operator if relevant.

Containment protects the customer while the root cause is still being investigated. Typical actions include quarantining suspect lots, sorting outgoing stock, adding inspection, holding shipments, notifying the customer, freezing process changes, and reworking only under a controlled method. Each containment action needs an owner, a date, and a verification method. Containment is not corrective action; it reduces risk but does not prove why the defect happened or why it escaped.

theory.h: D4 root cause: occurrence and detection
theory.p: A complete 8D separates the occurrence root cause from the detection escape. Occurrence may involve paste rheology, stencil aperture design, reflow ramp and soak, component coplanarity, feeder accuracy, placement pressure, wave solder dwell, selective solder nozzle condition, flux activity, preheat, cooling, or thermal mass. Detection may involve AOI program coverage, ICT test coverage, visual inspection limits, test escape, or sampling plan. Use data by line, shift, lot, component, board position, defect type, and process parameter to support the conclusion.

theory.h: D5 corrective action and D6 validation
theory.p: Corrective action should address the proven root cause, not only the visible symptom. Examples include changing stencil aperture geometry, updating the reflow profile within the paste and component datasheet window, replacing or repairing a feeder, adjusting wave or selective solder parameters, updating an AOI program, adding a poka-yoke, or changing a supplier control. Implementation needs owner and date. Validation should use short runs, SPC, AOI or ICT results, functional test, and reliability testing when the failure mode justifies it. Record before and after defect rate, sample size, and acceptance basis.

Prevention updates the management system so the same class of problem is less likely to recur. This may include PFMEA, control plan, work instructions, operator training, design rules, incoming inspection, supplier agreements, tooling maintenance, and horizontal deployment to similar products or lines. Closure should be supported by evidence: containment records, root cause data, validation results, updated documents, and an effectiveness metric. If a temporary action remains, state its expiry and the permanent action plan.

Common failures include presenting containment as correction, stating a root cause without data, ignoring the detection escape, missing owners or dates, using vague language, omitting traceability, and closing without an effectiveness metric. Another frequent failure is no horizontal deployment, so the same defect reappears on a similar product. A good 8D is auditable: it shows what was found, what was done, who did it, when it was due, and how effectiveness was measured.

calc.task: Write a complete 8D for an SMT line where a customer reports tombstoned chip resistors on a production lot. Include containment, corrective action, owners, dates, and an effectiveness metric.
calc.solution:
D1 Team: SMT process engineer as lead, production supervisor, quality engineer, materials engineer, AOI programmer, and supplier representative if paste or component data are needed.
D2 Problem: customer reported tombstoned chip resistors on product X, line Y, reflow process step, defect mode tombstoning, lot traceability recorded, quantity reported by customer, measurement method visual and AOI, date of complaint recorded. The problem is both occurrence and detection because the defect reached the customer.
D3 Containment: quarantine suspect lots, sort outgoing stock, add AOI and visual inspection, notify customer, freeze process changes, and hold shipments until containment is verified. Owner: quality engineer. Date: 2026-01-15. Verification: audit sorted lots and outgoing inspection records.
D4 Root cause: occurrence root cause identified from data as unbalanced wetting caused by stencil aperture imbalance and reflow ramp rate outside the preferred window for the paste and component. Detection root cause identified as AOI program did not reliably flag tombstone on small chip components.
D5 Corrective action: update stencil aperture design, adjust reflow profile within the paste and component datasheet window, update AOI program, and add feeder and placement verification to the setup checklist. Owner: SMT process engineer. Date: 2026-01-22.
D6 Validation: run validation lots, measure tombstone defect rate, and compare to the effectiveness metric. Effectiveness metric: tombstone defect rate in ppm over validation lots, target from customer specification or internal control limit. Owner: quality engineer. Date: 2026-02-05.
D7 Prevention: update PFMEA, control plan, work instructions, operator training, and horizontal deployment to similar products using the same component family or stencil design. Owner: process engineering manager. Date: 2026-02-12.
D8 Closure: close when containment is verified, corrective action is validated, documents are updated, and the effectiveness metric is met. Owner: quality manager. Date: 2026-02-19.

defect.symptom: AOI flags tombstoned chip resistors on one side of the PCB after reflow, and the defect rate rises on the night shift.
defect.cause: Stencil aperture for one pad is too large and the reflow ramp is too fast, causing unbalanced wetting; the AOI program did not detect tombstone on small components.
defect.action: Quarantine suspect lots, sort outgoing stock, reduce aperture imbalance, adjust reflow profile per paste and component datasheets, update AOI program, validate with short runs, and monitor defect rate in ppm.
