title: Corrective vs preventive action and effectiveness verification

goals.text: Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.
Feed the result back into PFMEA, control plan and the auditor checklist through change control.

blocks.alt: Two branches from a detected nonconformity, one to corrective action and one to preventive action, converging on an effectiveness verification gate
blocks.caption: Corrective versus preventive action, and effectiveness verification

theory.h: Corrective and preventive action in SMT/THT
theory.p: Corrective action responds to a detected nonconformity, such as a solder defect found by AOI, X-ray, functional test, or customer complaint. Preventive action addresses a credible potential failure before it occurs, such as a stencil aperture that is close to a paste-release limit or a wave solder pot temperature that is drifting toward a control limit. In an 8D, containment protects the customer before root cause elimination, corrective action removes the root cause, and preventive action changes the system so the same or similar failure mode is less likely to recur.

theory.h: 8D content that an auditor can trace
theory.p: A usable 8D records the problem statement, affected part numbers and lots, containment quantity and disposition, team roles, root cause, corrective action, implementation evidence, effectiveness metric, and closure decision. Owners should be named by role, such as SMT process engineer, line supervisor, quality engineer, and PFMEA owner. Dates should be actual dates from the CAPA or 8D record, not assumed dates, because the auditor checks whether containment was timely and whether verification occurred after implementation.

theory.h: Containment that is proportionate and verifiable
theory.p: Containment can include quarantine of suspect lots, full inspection, rework, a temporary parameter lock, or a hold on shipping. The containment method should match the risk: a safety-related solder joint defect may require full inspection and customer notification, while a cosmetic issue may require sampling and disposition by a documented plan. Verify containment effectiveness by checking the inspected population, the inspection method, and the escape rate during the containment period.

theory.h: Root cause: occurrence, detection, and systemic cause
theory.p: For SMT/THT defects, separate the cause that created the defect from the cause that allowed it to escape. Occurrence causes include paste volume, stencil aperture design, reflow profile, wave solder temperature, flux activity, component coplanarity, feeder calibration, and handling damage. Detection causes include AOI program coverage, X-ray sampling, test coverage, and operator judgment. Systemic causes include missing reaction plans, stale control plans, untrained operators, or change control gaps.

theory.h: Choosing a corrective action that survives production
theory.p: Select the action that addresses the verified root cause and can be sustained. Examples include changing a stencil aperture, adding a poka-yoke fixture, revising a reflow profile, replacing a worn feeder, changing a supplier lot, or adding a sensor check. A parameter adjustment can be valid when the root cause is a drift or misconfiguration, but it should be supported by data and by the equipment datasheet. Verify against your paste, stencil, solder, and equipment datasheet before setting limits.

Define the effectiveness metric before implementation. Common metrics are defect rate in ppm, initial pass yield, AOI escape rate, X-ray void percentage, wetting quality, or functional test failure rate. The verification should cover enough production time and sample size to detect recurrence, and the acceptance criterion should be agreed with quality and the customer when required. If the metric does not meet the criterion, reopen the 8D instead of closing it.

A practical closure record can show: containment date 2026-01-15, owner line supervisor; corrective action implementation date 2026-01-22, owner SMT process engineer; effectiveness verification date 2026-02-05, owner quality engineer; effectiveness metric defect rate in ppm with target 500 ppm; PFMEA and control plan update owner PFMEA owner. The dates, owners, and metric should be copied into the 8D from the CAPA or change control record.

theory.h: Feeding the result into PFMEA, control plan, and audit checklist
theory.p: When the 8D is closed, update the PFMEA with the failure mode, cause, current controls, occurrence, detection, and reaction plan. Update the control plan with the new parameter, inspection method, frequency, and reaction plan. Add or revise auditor checklist questions so the next audit verifies the new control. Use change control to approve the revision, train affected personnel, and record the effective date.

calc.task: A THT wave solder line had 180 defects in 12000 boards before corrective action. After corrective action, 24 defects occurred in 15000 boards. Calculate the before and after defect rate in ppm, the reduction, and whether the after rate meets a target of 500 ppm.
calc.solution: Before rate = 180 / 12000 = 0.015 = 15000 ppm. After rate = 24 / 15000 = 0.0016 = 1600 ppm. Reduction = (15000 - 1600) / 15000 = 0.8933 = 89.3 percent. The after rate is 1600 ppm, which is above the target of 500 ppm, so the corrective action is not yet effective by the agreed metric. Continue monitoring, increase sample size, or strengthen the corrective action before closing the 8D.

defect.symptom: THT wave solder joints on fine-pitch IC leads show insufficient wetting and dewetting after wave solder, with AOI flagging a higher reject rate on a panel side.
defect.cause: The wave solder pot temperature reading was lower than the verified actual temperature because the thermocouple had drifted, and the setpoint was adjusted without a documented change control record. The resulting thermal profile did not meet the wetting requirement for the lead finish and flux used.
defect.action: Quarantine suspect boards, recalibrate the thermocouple, verify the pot temperature against the equipment datasheet, restore the approved setpoint through change control, revalidate with wetting and X-ray checks, update the PFMEA and control plan, and add a daily thermocouple check to the auditor checklist.

title: Closing the loop: PFMEA, control plan, auditor checklist, change control

goals.text: Feed the result back into PFMEA, control plan and the auditor checklist through change control.

blocks.alt: A loop diagram linking corrective action to a process failure mode analysis update, a control plan revision, an auditor checklist and change control
blocks.caption: Closing the loop: PFMEA, control plan, auditor checklist and change control

theory.h: Closing the loop means changing the control system, not just fixing the defect
theory.p: In SMT and THT process engineering, a corrective action is not complete when the line returns to normal output. It is complete when the learning is written into the PFMEA, the control plan, the auditor checklist, and the change-control record. The PFMEA records the failure mode, cause, detection method, and risk priority. The control plan records the process parameter, specification, measurement method, sample size, reaction plan, and responsible role. The auditor checklist verifies that the control is present, current, and actually being followed. If these documents are not updated, the same defect can return after operator turnover, product change, equipment repair, or shift change.

theory.h: Use change control to prevent uncontrolled process drift
theory.p: Change control is the route by which a process change is proposed, reviewed, approved, implemented, verified, and closed. In electronics assembly, changes may include paste type, stencil aperture, reflow profile, wave solder temperature, flux density, conveyor speed, component substitution, feeder change, nozzle change, placement program revision, or inspection criteria. A change should be controlled when it can affect fit, form, function, reliability, solderability, or inspection acceptance. For example, a change in peak reflow temperature or dwell time above the liquidus can affect solder joint microstructure and should be reviewed against the paste and component datasheets and against IPC-7530 Guidelines for Convection Reflow Soldering where applicable.

theory.h: PFMEA should reflect the current process, not the original design intent
theory.p: The PFMEA is a living risk document. After a defect investigation, update the failure mode if a new cause is found, update the cause if the root cause is different from the original assumption, update the detection method if the current inspection cannot reliably find the defect, and update the severity, occurrence, or detection ratings only when justified by evidence. For example, if tombstoning is traced to asymmetric paste volume rather than placement offset, the PFMEA cause should be revised to include stencil design, paste release, and reflow ramp effects. The revised PFMEA should then drive a control plan action such as stencil inspection, paste volume measurement, or first-article verification.

theory.h: The control plan must contain measurable process controls
theory.p: A control plan should not say only 'operator checks quality.' It should state what is checked, how often, with what method, against what limit, and what happens if the result is out of specification. For SMT paste printing, controls may include stencil cleanliness, paste viscosity or rheology per paste datasheet, print alignment, paste height, paste volume, and post-print inspection. For reflow, controls may include profile zones, peak temperature, time above liquidus, oxygen level if nitrogen is used, and oven calibration. For THT wave soldering, controls may include flux specific gravity, preheat temperature, wave contact time, wave height, conveyor speed, and solder temperature. Use ranges from your paste, component, and equipment datasheets, and verify against your own process window before locking limits.

theory.h: The auditor checklist verifies that the control plan is being executed
theory.p: The auditor checklist should ask whether the control exists and whether it is being followed. It should include questions such as: Is the current revision of the control plan available at the station? Are the measured values recorded at the required frequency? Are out-of-limit results handled according to the reaction plan? Are calibration labels valid? Are rejected materials segregated? Are change-control records closed? Are operators trained on the current revision? The checklist should not duplicate the entire control plan. It should sample the most failure-prone controls and the controls that were recently changed or recently failed.

theory.h: Feed the result back through a documented change-control package
theory.p: A practical change-control package should include the problem statement, defect data, root cause, proposed change, affected documents, risk assessment, verification plan, implementation date, responsible owner, and closure evidence. For an SMT example, if a new paste lot causes insufficient solder on fine-pitch QFN pads, the package may include paste lot traceability, stencil design review, reflow profile comparison, X-ray or cross-section results, updated PFMEA, updated control plan, updated auditor checklist, operator briefing, and first-article approval. For a THT example, if a wave solder bridge is traced to excessive flux density, the package may include flux concentration measurement, preheat profile adjustment, wave contact time adjustment, updated PFMEA, updated control plan, and updated inspection checklist.

theory.h: Use acceptance criteria and rework rules to avoid creating new defects
theory.p: When updating inspection criteria, use the applicable acceptance standard and the customer or internal specification. IPC-A-610 Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies provides acceptance classes and visual criteria for solder joints, components, and cleanliness. IPC-7711/7721 Rework, Modification and Repair of Electronic Assemblies provides guidance for rework and repair methods. If a change affects rework, the control plan should state whether rework is allowed, what method is approved, how many rework cycles are allowed, and what inspection is required after rework. Do not allow rework to become a hidden process control. If rework frequency rises, the PFMEA occurrence rating and the control plan reaction plan should be reviewed.

theory.h: Close the loop with verification, not only with approval
theory.p: After the change is implemented, verify that the defect rate has decreased and that no new failure mode has been introduced. Verification may include first-article inspection, in-process data, final inspection data, field return data, reliability test data, or audit findings. If the change is temporary, the change-control record should state the expiry date or the condition for permanent adoption. If the change is permanent, the PFMEA, control plan, auditor checklist, work instructions, and training records should all be updated to the same revision. The loop is closed when the documents, the line, and the data agree.

calc.task: A 0402 SMT placement line shows a tombstoning rate of 180 ppm on a fine-pitch board. Investigation shows the peak reflow temperature was 232 °C and time above liquidus was 48 s, while the paste datasheet recommends a peak temperature range of 235 °C to 245 °C and time above liquidus of 40 s to 70 s. A change-control proposal raises the peak temperature to 240 °C and time above liquidus to 55 s. Calculate the change in peak temperature and time above liquidus, determine whether the proposed values are inside the paste datasheet range, and define the minimum verification sample needed to confirm that tombstoning is reduced to below 50 ppm with 95% confidence if the observed rate after the change is 0 defects in the sample.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate the peak temperature change: proposed peak temperature minus current peak temperature = 240 °C - 232 °C = 8 °C. 2. Calculate the time above liquidus change: proposed time above liquidus minus current time above liquidus = 55 s - 48 s = 7 s. 3. Check the proposed peak temperature against the paste datasheet range: 235 °C to 245 °C. The proposed 240 °C is inside the range. 4. Check the proposed time above liquidus against the paste datasheet range: 40 s to 70 s. The proposed 55 s is inside the range. 5. For a zero-defect verification sample, use the binomial rule for zero failures: the probability of observing zero defects if the true defect rate is p is (1 - p)^n. To demonstrate with 95% confidence that the true rate is below p = 50 ppm = 0.00005, solve (1 - 0.00005)^n <= 0.05. 6. Take natural logs: n >= ln(0.05) / ln(1 - 0.00005). 7. ln(0.05) = -2.9957. ln(1 - 0.00005) ≈ -0.000050001. 8. n >= -2.9957 / -0.000050001 ≈ 59,913. 9. Round up to a practical sample size: inspect at least 60,000 units with zero tombstoning defects to claim 95% confidence that the true tombstoning rate is below 50 ppm. 10. If 60,000 units are not practical, use a lower confidence level, a higher target ppm, or combine inspection with process data such as reflow profile logs, paste volume data, and placement accuracy data. 11. Update the PFMEA cause to include reflow profile deviation, update the control plan to require profile verification at the defined frequency, update the auditor checklist to verify profile logs and calibration, and close the change-control record only after the verification result is accepted.

defect.symptom: After a paste change, the line shows intermittent insufficient solder on 0.5 mm pitch QFN pads. Final inspection passes visually, but X-ray shows reduced heel fillet and small voiding on some joints. The defect rate rises from about 20 ppm to about 150 ppm over three shifts.
defect.cause: The new paste has a different viscosity and slump behavior, but the stencil aperture and reflow profile were not requalified. The control plan still uses the old paste print parameters and the auditor checklist does not require paste lot traceability or post-print paste height verification. The PFMEA did not include paste rheology change as a cause for insufficient solder on fine-pitch QFN pads.
defect.action: Open a change-control record for the paste substitution. Requalify the stencil aperture and reflow profile using the new paste datasheet and verify against IPC-7530 Guidelines for Convection Reflow Soldering where applicable. Add paste lot traceability, paste height or volume measurement, and QFN X-ray sampling to the control plan. Update the PFMEA to include paste rheology change as a cause of insufficient solder. Add a checklist item requiring the auditor to verify that the current paste lot, stencil revision, reflow profile, and X-ray results match the approved control plan. Run a verification lot and close the change only when the defect rate returns to the target range and the documents are updated.

title: 8D workshop: full case from symptom to closure

goals.text: Structure a defect problem with measured data (taxonomy, Pareto by stage, measurement integrity) before analysis.
Separate root cause, contributing causes and the detection escape in a structured cause analysis.
Write a complete 8D with containment, corrective action, owners, dates and an effectiveness metric.

blocks.alt: A case timeline from observed defect through containment, root cause, corrective action and closure, with the evidence recorded at each step
blocks.caption: Eight-discipline workshop: a full case from symptom to closure

theory.h: Define the symptom with measured data
theory.p: Start with the observed defect, not a suspected cause. Record product, lot, stage, time in seconds, operator, equipment, and measured attribute such as solder volume in cubic millimetres, component offset in millimetres, or hole fill. Use a taxonomy that separates symptom families, for example insufficient solder, excess solder, misalignment, voiding, and non-wet. The taxonomy should be stable enough to compare lots, but detailed enough to guide containment.

theory.h: Pareto by stage before root cause
theory.p: Sort defect counts by process stage, such as paste print, placement, reflow, wave, and inspection. Pareto by stage tells you where the largest measured loss is, not where the most obvious cause is. If a stage has few defects but high cost or high field risk, keep it visible. Use the stage Pareto to decide containment priority and where to collect additional data.

theory.h: Check measurement integrity before trusting the Pareto
theory.p: A Pareto is only as good as the measurement. Verify the inspection method, sample plan, and operator agreement. For dimensional checks, confirm the gauge resolution in millimetres is fine enough for the tolerance and that the measurement uncertainty is small compared with the process variation. For visual defects, use boundary samples and cross-check independent inspectors. If measurement disagreement is large, fix the measurement before analyzing the defect.

theory.h: Separate root cause, contributing causes, and detection escape
theory.p: The root cause is the process condition that, when removed, prevents recurrence under normal conditions. Contributing causes make the defect more likely or more severe, such as paste viscosity drift, feeder wear, thermal profile variation in degrees Celsius, or conveyor speed variation in millimetres per second. The detection escape is the reason the defect was not found before shipment, such as a missing AOI program, a low sensitivity setting, or a manual inspection gap. A complete 8D report must address each element, because eliminating only the root cause may leave the escape open.

theory.h: Containment must be measurable and time-bound
theory.p: Containment protects the customer while the cause is being confirmed. It can include quarantine, full inspection, rework, or a temporary process limit. State the containment owner, the start time, the review interval, and the exit condition. The exit condition should be based on measured evidence, such as a clean inspection window or a verified process capability, not on elapsed time alone.

theory.h: Corrective action should change the process, not only the product
theory.p: Corrective action should remove the root cause and close the detection escape. Examples include changing stencil design, updating feeder calibration, adding a profile check, or modifying an AOI program. Each action needs an owner, a due date, and a verification method. Verification should show that the action works under normal production conditions and that the defect does not return when the action is removed from the temporary containment.

theory.h: Write the closure with an effectiveness metric
theory.p: Closure is not complete until the effectiveness metric is defined and measured. A common metric is no escapes in a defined verification window, with the window chosen from production volume and risk. Record the baseline defect rate, the post-action defect rate, and the inspection method used. If the metric is not met, reopen the analysis rather than closing the report.

calc.task: A line records 100 defects in a production window: paste print 40, placement 30, reflow 20, wave 10. Calculate the stage Pareto and cumulative percentage. Before using the result, confirm that the inspection method has adequate resolution and repeatability for the measured attribute; verify against your paste/equipment datasheet.
calc.solution: Total is 100. Paste print share is 40 divided by 100, which is 40 percent, cumulative 40 percent. Placement share is 30 divided by 100, which is 30 percent, cumulative 70 percent. Reflow share is 20 divided by 100, which is 20 percent, cumulative 90 percent. Wave share is 10 divided by 100, which is 10 percent, cumulative 100 percent.

defect.symptom: Wave solder line shows insufficient hole fill on through-hole connectors, with exposed land visible at the bottom of the hole.
defect.cause: Root cause is a preheat temperature setpoint drift in degrees Celsius that reduced flux activation; contributing causes are board loading density and conveyor speed variation in millimetres per second; detection escape is that final visual inspection did not include a hole fill check aligned with IPC-A-610 acceptance criteria.
defect.action: Containment: quarantine suspect lots and perform full inspection with boundary samples; owner: wave solder process engineer; date: containment due at end of shift. Corrective action: restore preheat setpoint, add a logged preheat check, and update inspection to include hole fill criteria from IPC-A-610; owner: wave solder process engineer; date: corrective action due before next monthly review. Effectiveness metric: no escapes in the next 10 verification lots.

title: How designers read process feedback: language, format, what gets acted on

goals.text: Convert a process limitation into a specific, testable design rule change.
Write and defend an ECN/DCR request against typical design objections.

theory.p: Designers act on feedback that is written as a constraint, not a complaint. A useful process note names the affected component or layer, the observed failure mode, the measurable process variable, and the proposed design rule. For example, 'small chip passives tombstone on the right side of the panel when paste apertures are asymmetric' is actionable; 'the board is bad' is not. The request should be short enough to read quickly and specific enough that a designer can change a rule file, a land pattern, or a stencil without asking for clarification.

blocks.alt: A process note written as a constraint, with the affected component, the observed condition and the requested change highlighted
blocks.caption: How designers read process feedback: language, format and what gets acted on
Cp / Cpk interpretation — thresholds are industry convention — TBD-REVIEW
head: Index
Reading
Action

theory.h: Translate process language into design variables
theory.p: Use language that maps process observations to design variables. Instead of saying 'the solder is not wetting well', state the design variable that controls wetting: pad finish, copper area, paste aperture area, stencil thickness, reflow ramp, or component mass. For SMT, designers can change land pattern geometry, paste apertures, copper balance, and thermal relief. For THT, they can change hole size, pad annular ring, solder mask clearance, and component lead form. Keep the sentence in the form: 'Because process variable X is outside the capability range, the design rule should require Y.'

theory.h: Use the format designers can approve
theory.p: The format that gets acted on is usually an ECN or DCR with a clear decision point. Start with the problem statement, then evidence, affected part numbers, proposed change, test plan, cost, schedule, and risk. Include the exact layer or file to change: paste stencil layer, solder mask layer, copper layer, component library, or assembly drawing. If the change affects acceptance, land pattern, board fabrication, or BGA design, name the relevant IPC standard or internal specification that the change must satisfy, but do not rely on the standard alone to prove the process problem.

theory.h: Make the change bounded and testable
theory.p: Designers prioritize changes that reduce a measured risk, fit the existing board, and can be verified without a full requalification. A request that only says 'make the pads bigger' may be rejected because it can affect routing, impedance, assembly density, or solder mask bridges. A request that says 'increase the paste aperture area on the low-volume side by 8% to 12% and verify SPI paste volume within the process window' gives a bounded change and a test. The acceptance criteria should be written as pass/fail measurements, not opinions.

theory.h: Convert a limitation into a design rule
theory.p: To convert a process limitation into a design rule, identify the physical cause, express it as a design variable, and set a measurable limit. For tombstoning, common causes are unequal paste volume, unequal pad copper area, asymmetric thermal mass, and placement offset. A testable rule might be: for small chip passives, the paste apertures on both ends shall have areas within ±10% of each other, the copper pads shall be symmetric, and the placement center shall be within ±0.05 mm of the pad center. Verify the placement limit against the pick-and-place repeatability and the component datasheet.

theory.h: Apply the same logic to THT
theory.p: For THT wave solder, a common limitation is insufficient solder fill or solder balls caused by hole-to-lead clearance, pad size, and flux activity. A design rule can specify a clearance range, pad annular ring, and solder mask web between pads. Because hole plating, drill wear, and wave profile vary, use a range and verify against the board fab and assembly equipment. Ask the fab for the expected drilled hole tolerance and plated hole size, then set the component lead diameter so the clearance stays within the capability range for the chosen wave process.

When defending an ECN or DCR, expect objections: the board worked before, the change costs money, the supplier cannot support it, the test coverage is incomplete, or the change affects another product. Answer with data and a bounded plan. Show the defect rate before and after, the affected part numbers, the test sample, the fallback if the change fails, and the parts or files that will not change. If the change is too large, propose a pilot panel or product family before full release.

theory.h: Close with a rule and a proof
theory.p: A good process feedback note ends with what the designer must change and what the process team will prove. It should not ask the designer to solve the process problem. Example: 'Change the small chip passive paste apertures to symmetric rectangles with equal area; process will verify SPI paste volume, AOI tombstone rate, and reflow profile on 300 boards before release.' This gives the designer a rule change and gives the process team a testable commitment.

calc.task: A small chip passive tombstone issue appears on 18 boards out of 4000 boards. Convert this into a design rule change and an ECN/DCR request. Determine the current defect rate, a target rate, the sample size needed to show the target with 95% confidence if no tombstones are observed, and the paste aperture area balance needed to support the rule.
calc.solution: Current rate: 18 / 4000 = 0.0045 = 0.45%. Target: set a target of <=0.10% (1000 ppm) based on line capability and risk; verify against internal quality targets. Sample size: for a no-defect demonstration at 95% confidence, use the binomial upper bound. With confidence = 0.95 and target = 0.0010, n = ln(0.05) / ln(0.999) = 2995. Round up to 3000 boards. Design rule: for small chip passives, paste apertures on both ends shall have equal area within ±10%; for a nominal aperture area of 0.011 mm^2, the allowable range is 0.0099 mm^2 to 0.0121 mm^2. Process checks: SPI paste volume per pad within ±15% of nominal, placement center within ±0.05 mm of pad center, and reflow profile within paste and component limits. ECN/DCR: change the paste stencil layer for small chip passives to symmetric apertures, remove asymmetric copper or thermal relief on the affected pads, and add SPI verification. Defense: show the current 0.45% rate, the target 0.10% rate, the 3000-board no-defect test, the affected part numbers, the fallback to the previous stencil if the test fails, and the fact that the change does not alter the BOM or board outline.

defect.symptom: AOI flags tombstones on small chip passives on the right side of the panel after reflow, and SPI shows paste volume low on the left pads of the same components.
defect.cause: Asymmetric paste apertures or stencil aperture damage create unequal solder volume on the two ends of the component, and placement offset may increase the imbalance.
defect.action: Stop release of the affected stencil, quarantine suspect boards, rework or scrap as required, correct the stencil apertures to symmetric geometry, verify SPI paste volume within ±15% of nominal, and update the design rule to require aperture area balance within ±10%.

title: The evidence pack: measured data, images with scale, defect rate, cost of poor quality

goals.text: Build an evidence pack that quantifies the process impact of the current design.

blocks.alt: A compact evidence pack with a measurement table, a scaled image, a defect-rate chart and a cost-of-poor-quality figure
blocks.caption: The evidence pack: measured data, images with scale, defect rate and cost of poor quality

theory.p: An evidence pack is a compact set of records that shows what the current surface-mount technology or through-hole technology process is actually doing, not what the process was intended to do. For a working process engineer, the pack should let another engineer or manager answer three questions without visiting the line: what is being measured, what does the physical evidence show, and what is the financial consequence of the current defect level. The pack should be reproducible, dated, traceable to a product, line, shift, equipment set, and paste or component lot where relevant.

theory.h: Measured data that belongs in the pack
theory.p: Measured data should include process parameters and output quality data. Typical inputs are stencil thickness, aperture area, paste volume, reflow peak temperature, time above liquidus, placement accuracy, and oven profile repeatability. Typical outputs are solder joint quality, defect counts, first-pass yield, rework count, and scrap count. For each parameter, record the unit, measurement method, sample size, time window, and operator or station. If a value is taken from equipment, state whether it is a setpoint, a measured value, or a logged average.

Images are evidence only when they can be interpreted later. Each image should include a scale reference, such as a calibrated ruler, scale bar, or known component dimension, and should state magnification or field of view. The image file name or caption should identify the board, panel, station, defect type, date, and shift. For solder defects, include both a close-up and a wider view showing the component, adjacent pads, and nearby joints. For paste defects, include the stencil side, board side, and, if possible, a cross-section or 3D measurement.

Defect rate should be defined clearly. A common board-level metric is defects per million opportunities, but the opportunity count must be stated. For example, if counting solder joints, define whether the opportunity is one joint, one pad, one component, or one inspection point. For surface-mount technology, defect density is often more useful than a simple pass or fail percentage because it can be compared across board sizes and component counts. Record the denominator used, such as total joints inspected, total boards inspected, or total placement points.

A single shift can be misleading if the line is running a mixed product mix or if a changeover occurred. The evidence pack should state the sampling window, such as one shift, one day, one week, or one production order. For process comparison, use matched conditions: same product, same line, same paste lot family, same stencil, and similar board mix. If matched conditions are not possible, state the differences and treat the comparison as preliminary. For practice-based sampling, use enough parts to see the defect mode; verify against your inspection plan, equipment capability, and the defect rate you are trying to detect.

Cost of poor quality should include scrap, rework labor, inspection labor, line downtime, expedited freight, warranty or field failure exposure, and lost capacity. For a line-level estimate, start with direct costs: scrapped boards, rework time, additional inspection time, and machine time consumed by rework. For a product-level estimate, include downstream test failures, repair, and customer returns. Keep the calculation transparent by listing each cost driver, unit cost, quantity, and source. If a cost is estimated, label it as estimated and state the basis.

The pack should connect measured data, images, defect rate, and cost into one argument. For example, if the defect is insufficient solder, show the measured paste volume distribution, images of the affected joints, the defect rate by station or product, and the rework cost per affected board. The conclusion should state the process impact in operational terms: yield loss, throughput loss, rework burden, or risk of escape. Avoid broad claims unless the data covers enough time, products, and stations to support them.

A practical evidence pack can be a short report, spreadsheet, or slide set, but it must be traceable. Include a cover page with product name, line, date range, author, and revision. Attach raw data or give a file path where raw data is stored. Use consistent units, preferably SI units such as millimeters, micrometers, grams, seconds, and degrees Celsius. For images, embed captions in the report and keep original files with metadata. For calculations, show formulas and inputs so another engineer can reproduce the result.

calc.task: Build a simple cost-of-poor-quality estimate for a surface-mount line producing 12,000 boards per week. The line has a first-pass yield of 96.5 percent. Of the failed boards, 70 percent are reworked successfully, 20 percent are scrapped, and 10 percent are held for further analysis. Rework labor is 18 minutes per board at a loaded labor rate of 45 euros per hour. Scrap cost is 120 euros per board. Additional inspection and handling cost is 3.50 euros per failed board. Calculate weekly rework labor cost, scrap cost, inspection and handling cost, total cost of poor quality, and cost per good board.
calc.solution: 1. Calculate failed boards per week: 12,000 boards per week multiplied by 1 minus 0.965 equals 12,000 multiplied by 0.035 equals 420 failed boards per week. 2. Calculate reworked boards: 420 failed boards multiplied by 0.70 equals 294 reworked boards per week. 3. Calculate rework labor hours: 294 boards multiplied by 18 minutes per board equals 5,292 minutes. 5,292 minutes divided by 60 equals 88.2 hours per week. 4. Calculate rework labor cost: 88.2 hours multiplied by 45 euros per hour equals 3,969 euros per week. 5. Calculate scrapped boards: 420 failed boards multiplied by 0.20 equals 84 scrapped boards per week. 6. Calculate scrap cost: 84 boards multiplied by 120 euros per board equals 10,080 euros per week. 7. Calculate inspection and handling cost: 420 failed boards multiplied by 3.50 euros per board equals 1,470 euros per week. 8. Calculate total cost of poor quality: 3,969 euros plus 10,080 euros plus 1,470 euros equals 15,519 euros per week. 9. Calculate good boards per week: 12,000 boards minus 420 failed boards equals 11,580 good boards per week. 10. Calculate cost of poor quality per good board: 15,519 euros divided by 11,580 good boards equals 1.34 euros per good board. 11. Interpretation: the current process consumes 15,519 euros per week in direct rework, scrap, and handling, equivalent to 1.34 euros per good board. This figure should be checked against your actual labor rate, scrap value, inspection cost, and any downtime or expedite costs before using it in a business case.

defect.symptom: After reflow, several 0402 chip resistors show tombstoning on one side of the board, and the defect rate rises from a baseline of about 200 defects per million placements to about 1,800 defects per million placements on the affected panel location.
defect.cause: The evidence pack links the defect to uneven paste release and thermal imbalance. Images with scale show one pad has paste volume near the lower end of the process window while the adjacent pad is near the upper end. The stencil design for that panel location has slightly different aperture areas, and the reflow profile shows a faster ramp rate than the paste datasheet recommends for the board thermal mass.
defect.action: Reduce the defect rate by adjusting the stencil aperture area balance for the affected pads, verifying paste release with 3D solder paste inspection, and slowing the preheat ramp rate within the paste and component thermal limits. Re-run a short production window, collect images with scale, record defect rate by panel location, and update the evidence pack with before and after data.

title: Writing the change request: problem, impact, proposal, alternatives, risk, verification

goals.text: Write and defend an ECN/DCR request against typical design objections.

blocks.alt: A change request form with the six sections laid out, each with a short example entry
blocks.caption: Writing the change request: problem, impact, proposal, alternatives, risk and verification

theory.h: Frame the change request as an engineering contract
theory.p: An ECN or DCR should state what is wrong, what is being changed, and how acceptance will be proven. It should identify affected part numbers, drawings, BOM levels, routings, test programs, and documents. For SMT and THT work, include board revision, panelization, feeder or insertion head, stencil, wave or selective solder, and inspection method. The request should be readable by design, manufacturing, quality, and purchasing without requiring verbal explanation.

The problem statement should include defect mode, location, occurrence, detection method, and consequence. Use measurable terms such as solder voiding on QFN pads detected by X-ray, tombstoning at a specific feeder, or lead seating error at a connector row. State sample size, lot, date, equipment, and operator when relevant. Where acceptance criteria are needed, cite IPC-A-610 and verify the applicable class against the product qualification and customer drawing.

The impact section should cover electrical, mechanical, thermal, assembly, test, reliability, inventory, and qualification effects. For a land pattern change, cite IPC-7351 for footprint geometry and IPC-7095 for BGA if applicable. For THT, include lead forming, seating, wave solder dwell, clearance, and possible interference with adjacent components. State whether existing inventory can be consumed, reworked, or scrapped, and whether requalification is required.

The proposal should specify old and new values, drawing revision, BOM change, process parameter changes, and work instruction updates. For paste changes, state stencil thickness, aperture dimensions, paste type, and verify against the paste and printer datasheet. For THT, state lead finish, seating tolerance, and wave or selective solder profile limits. Include traceability, first article requirements, and the documents that will be updated.

Consider at least two alternatives, such as process adjustment, component substitution, layout change, or test change. Compare technical feasibility, cost, schedule, inventory, and risk. A rejected alternative should state why, for example process window too narrow, no qualified component, insufficient test coverage, or unacceptable rework burden. This section defends the request against design objections by showing that the selected option is not arbitrary.

Use a simple risk table with failure mode, severity, occurrence, detection, mitigation, and residual risk. For rework and repair limits, cite IPC-7711/7721. For soldering process qualification, cite IPC J-STD-001. State controls such as SPC, AOI, X-ray, ICT, functional test, and environmental stress screening. Avoid claiming zero risk; state the acceptable residual risk and who accepts it.

Verification should include sample plan, acceptance criteria, data format, and disposition. For dimensional changes, measure with calibrated tools. For solder joints, use cross-section or X-ray inspection against IPC-A-610 where required. For reliability, define thermal cycling or vibration if the change affects joint stress. Close the ECN or DCR only when data, updated documents, and inventory disposition are complete.

calc.task: A proposed ECN reduces a chip resistor stencil aperture from 0.50 mm by 0.50 mm to 0.45 mm by 0.45 mm, with stencil thickness 0.12 mm. Calculate the paste volume change and a simple verification sample using n = 1 / target defect rate, with target 0.5% per board.
calc.solution: Step 1: Old aperture area = 0.50 mm x 0.50 mm = 0.25 mm^2. Step 2: New aperture area = 0.45 mm x 0.45 mm = 0.2025 mm^2. Step 3: Old paste volume = 0.25 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.03 mm^3. Step 4: New paste volume = 0.2025 mm^2 x 0.12 mm = 0.0243 mm^3. Step 5: Volume change = (0.0243 - 0.03) / 0.03 = -0.19, or 19% reduction. Step 6: Target defect rate = 0.5% = 0.005 defects per board. Step 7: Simple screening sample n = 1 / 0.005 = 200 boards. Step 8: This is a screening sample, not a confidence statement; verify the final sample size against your quality plan and customer requirements.

defect.symptom: AOI flags missing or tombstoned small chip components on one feeder lane, while adjacent lanes pass.
defect.cause: Stencil aperture or paste release may be out of process, placement nozzle vacuum may be low, feeder timing may be misaligned, or the component may be sticking to the nozzle.
defect.action: Stop the lane, quarantine suspect boards, measure paste volume, check stencil thickness and aperture condition, verify printer and placement parameters against the equipment datasheet, clean or replace the nozzle and feeder, then run a first article and requalify before release.

title: DFM/DFT asks that work: pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials, panelization, hole/lead spec

goals.text: Convert a process limitation into a specific, testable design rule change.

blocks.alt: A board layout with pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials and panelization callouts, beside a hole-to-lead specification table
blocks.caption: Design-for-manufacture and test asks that work: pad geometry, paste relief, spacing, test points, fiducials, panelization and hole-to-lead specification

theory.h: From line limitation to testable rule
theory.p: A DFM/DFT ask is useful only when it becomes a measurable rule. Start with the process limitation, not the component name. If placement repeatability is poor, the rule may be a larger pad or a larger component-to-component keepout. If stencil print is unstable, the rule may be paste relief, a different aperture shape, or a stencil thickness change. If wave soldering produces insufficient fill, the rule may be a larger annular ring or a hole-to-lead clearance change. If ICT access is marginal, the rule may be a dedicated test point size and spacing. Each rule should state the dimension, tolerance, inspection method, and pass/fail condition so that a pilot run can prove it.

theory.h: Pad geometry controls the joint, not just the footprint
theory.p: Pad geometry controls paste volume, wetting, self-alignment, and the risk of bridging. For passive components, land length and width should support the intended solder fillet while leaving enough space for adjacent parts. For QFN, MLF, and other exposed-pad packages, the center pad needs paste relief because full-area paste can push the package up, trap flux, or create voids. Land pattern design can be framed with IPC-7351, while paste aperture changes should be checked against IPC-7525 and verified with your paste and printer datasheet. A practical approach is to start with a reduced center-pad aperture, then adjust by SPI and X-ray until the package sits flat and the peripheral joints are consistent.

theory.h: Paste relief is a process control, not a cosmetic change
theory.p: Paste relief is a stencil or aperture change used to control volume, bleed, and bridging. Common methods include reducing aperture area, splitting a large pad into sub-apertures, adding a step stencil, or changing wall geometry. For fine-pitch packages, a small reduction in aperture area can reduce paste collapse without starving the joint. For thermal pads, splitting the aperture into several smaller openings can improve release and reduce trapped flux. The exact reduction should be verified against paste rheology, stencil thickness, and SPI results. A useful pilot rule is to compare nominal paste volume, print height, and bridging rate before and after the change, then lock the accepted aperture dimensions in the assembly drawing.

theory.h: Spacing must satisfy assembly, inspection, and electrical needs
theory.p: Spacing rules must satisfy electrical clearance, assembly access, inspection, and thermal or wave-solder shielding. IPC-2221 and IPC-2222 provide generic and organic-board design frameworks, but the final spacing should also reflect your placement accuracy, feeder clearance, and inspection optics. For SMT, component-to-component spacing should allow the nozzle to approach without disturbing neighbors and should leave enough open area for SPI and AOI. For wave or selective solder, spacing and orientation can affect solder flow and shielding. A good rule is to define a minimum spacing for each component family and then validate it with a representative board, not only with a CAD check.

theory.h: Test points need dedicated geometry and access rules
theory.p: Test points are often the first DFT failure because they are added late. A test point should be a dedicated pad with controlled size, plating, and solder mask opening, not a random via or component lead. For ICT, probe access needs enough pad diameter and enough spacing to prevent probe interference. For functional test, the pad should survive repeated probing and should not be hidden under a component or inside a panel rail. A practical rule is to specify pad diameter, solder mask opening, minimum probe spacing, and a clear keepout zone, then verify with the actual fixture or bed-of-nails. If the fixture uses spring probes, the pad and plating should be checked for wear after the planned number of cycles.

Fiducials convert a placement program into a repeatable coordinate system. Global fiducials should be placed near the panel corners, and local fiducials should be close to fine-pitch or high-accuracy components. The fiducial should have high contrast, a clean circular or cross shape, and a clear zone free of copper, silkscreen, and nearby pads. The exact size and clear zone should be verified against the placement camera field of view and lighting. A rule that works well is to specify fiducial diameter, solder mask opening, minimum distance to the board edge, and minimum distance to the nearest copper feature, then confirm with a placement accuracy study.

Panelization affects handling, deformation, breakaway quality, and the location of fiducials and test points. The panel should fit the conveyor, placement, reflow, wave, and ICT equipment, and it should not force the board to flex during depaneling. Rails, V-scores, mouse bites, and routed breakaways each have trade-offs. Fiducials should be placed on the panel or on rails where the camera can see them, and test points should not be cut off by breakaway features. A practical rule is to define panel dimensions, rail width, breakaway type, fiducial locations, and a maximum bow or twist limit, then verify with a full panel run.

theory.h: Hole and lead specs decide THT solder quality
theory.p: Hole and lead specifications are often the difference between a good THT joint and a weak or bridged joint. Drill size, plating, annular ring, and hole-to-lead clearance determine wetting and fill. IPC-2221 and IPC-2222 provide design frameworks, but the final hole size should be checked against drill tolerance, plating thickness, and lead diameter variation. For wave or selective solder, the hole and annular ring should allow solder to flow and wet the lead without excessive bridging. A testable rule can specify minimum annular ring, hole diameter tolerance, maximum lead diameter, and a cross-section or X-ray acceptance criterion.

theory.h: Write the rule as a change request with proof
theory.p: The conversion from limitation to rule should be written as a change request with a measurable target. For example, if SPI shows paste collapse on a fine-pitch QFN, the rule might reduce thermal-pad aperture area, add sub-aperture gaps, and set an SPI height window. If wave soldering shows insufficient fill on a THT connector, the rule might increase annular ring or adjust hole size. If ICT probes miss test points, the rule might increase test-point diameter and spacing. The rule is complete only when it includes the drawing change, the inspection method, the sample size, and the pass/fail limit.

calc.task: A 0.4 mm pitch QFN has a 4.0 mm x 4.0 mm thermal pad. SPI shows paste height near 0.16 mm with a 0.12 mm stencil, and the line sees paste bleed between peripheral pads. Convert this limitation into a specific, testable design rule change for the thermal-pad paste aperture.
calc.solution: Pad area calculation: 4.0 mm x 4.0 mm = 16.0 mm2. Target aperture area: 60% of pad area, so 0.60 x 16.0 mm2 = 9.6 mm2. Aperture pattern: use 4 square sub-apertures with a 0.10 mm gap between adjacent sub-apertures. If each sub-aperture is 1.55 mm x 1.55 mm, total aperture area is 4 x 1.55 mm x 1.55 mm = 9.61 mm2, which is 60.1% of the pad area. Layout envelope check: 2 sub-apertures plus the gap span 2 x 1.55 mm + 0.10 mm = 3.20 mm, leaving 0.40 mm of outer margin on each side inside the 4.0 mm pad. Nominal paste volume: 9.61 mm2 x 0.12 mm = 1.153 mm3. Acceptance window: SPI paste height 0.10 mm to 0.13 mm, no bridging at 0.4 mm pitch, and package seating confirmed by X-ray or cross-section per IPC-A-610. Design rule to release: thermal-pad aperture area shall be 58% to 62% of pad area, implemented as 4 sub-apertures of 1.55 mm +/- 0.05 mm with 0.10 mm +/- 0.05 mm gaps, verified on a pilot panel by SPI and X-ray.

defect.symptom: After reflow, 0.4 mm pitch QFN packages show lifted corners and voided center pads, while SPI shows high paste height on the thermal pad.
defect.cause: Full-area thermal-pad aperture plus a 0.12 mm stencil produced excess paste volume; the package floated on paste and trapped flux.
defect.action: Reduce thermal-pad aperture to 58% to 62% area, split into 4 sub-apertures with 0.10 mm gaps, re-run SPI with height window 0.10 mm to 0.13 mm, and verify seating by X-ray per IPC-A-610.

title: Negotiation, version control and closure with post-change data

goals.text: Write and defend an ECN/DCR request against typical design objections.
Build an evidence pack that quantifies the process impact of the current design.

blocks.alt: A negotiation exchange between process and design, a version-controlled drawing revision block, and a post-change capability chart
blocks.caption: Negotiation, version control and closure with post-change data

theory.h: Frame the ECN/DCR as a controlled problem statement
theory.p: An ECN or DCR should start with a measurable problem, not a preference. State the affected assembly, part numbers, revision, production quantity, and the process step where the defect appears. Include the current controlled documents: drawing revision, IPC-7351 land pattern revision, stencil thickness, paste type, feeder map, AOI program, and IPC-7530 reflow profile. If the change is only a temporary containment, label it as such and define the expiry condition.

theory.h: Quantify the current design before asking for a change
theory.p: Use at least 30 consecutive production days or 1000 boards, whichever gives a stable sample, and verify the sample size against your MES capability. Report boards started, boards passed, rework events, scrap, test escapes, cycle time, and downtime. Separate common-cause variation from special-cause events. For defect classification, use the acceptability class required by contract under IPC-A-610, and record whether defects were detected by SPI, AOI, X-ray, ICT, or functional test.

theory.h: Anticipate design objections with evidence, not opinion
theory.p: Typical objections are that the change affects electrical performance, lacks test coverage, increases cost, delays schedule, or creates thermal or mechanical risk. Answer each with data: solder joint geometry from cross-section or X-ray, thermal profile margin from thermocouple data, mechanical clearance, and test coverage maps. If reliability is questioned, state the relevant qualification status and the residual risk if the change is not made. Use IPC-7711/7721 for rework and repair limits only when discussing repairability, not as a substitute for design change data.

The ECN/DCR should list every document that changes and every document that remains unchanged. Include gerber revision, BOM revision, stencil file revision, paste lot or type, feeder map, AOI program, reflow profile, and work instruction. Assign a unique change ID, effective date, and affected serial or lot range. Mark superseded revisions obsolete in the PLM or document control system, and prevent mixed revisions in the line by using changeover checklists and scanner verification where available.

theory.h: Build an evidence pack that a design engineer can audit
theory.p: The pack should contain the baseline data, defect Pareto, representative photos, SPI and AOI results, X-ray or cross-section images, reflow thermocouple traces, rework and scrap records, cost of poor quality, risk matrix, proposed change, verification plan, and rollback plan. Use SI units and state measurement uncertainty where it affects the decision. For paste and stencil values, cite the paste and equipment datasheet and verify against your own process window rather than relying on generic rules.

Present options: no change, interim containment, and full design change. For each option, state expected defect rate, rework time, scrap, schedule impact, and residual risk. If the design team resists a land pattern change, offer a process-only trial first, such as stencil aperture adjustment, paste type change, or placement pressure change, but record the limits of that trial. Avoid absolute claims; state conditions, sample size, and confidence limits.

theory.h: Close the change with post-change data
theory.p: After implementation, run a pilot and then a production confirmation. Compare SPI, AOI, X-ray, functional test, rework, scrap, cycle time, and downtime against the baseline. Close the ECN/DCR only when the acceptance criteria are met, the controlled documents are updated, and the line is using the new revision. If the post-change data do not meet the criteria, reopen the change, identify whether the cause is design, process, or measurement, and update the risk assessment.

calc.task: A 0402 resistor land pattern on a 1.6 mm board shows tombstoning and insufficient wetting. Baseline over 30 production days: 12000 boards, 2.4 percent boards with rework, average 1.8 defects per reworked board, rework 3.5 min per defect, operator cost 45 EUR/h, scrap 0.3 percent boards, board cost 180 EUR, line downtime 0.5 h/month. Proposed ECN changes land pattern to IPC-7351 nominal and reduces stencil aperture from 0.30 mm x 0.30 mm to 0.25 mm x 0.25 mm; verify against paste datasheet. Pilot predicts boards with rework 0.6 percent, defects per reworked board 1.2, scrap 0.1 percent, downtime 0.2 h/month. Calculate baseline cost of poor quality, projected cost, annual saving, and whether ECN is justified if one-time change cost 8000 EUR.
calc.solution: Step 1: baseline reworked boards = 12000 x 0.024 = 288 boards/month. Step 2: baseline defects = 288 x 1.8 = 518.4 defects/month. Step 3: baseline rework time = 518.4 x 3.5 = 1814.4 min/month = 30.24 h/month. Step 4: baseline rework labor cost = 30.24 x 45 = 1360.8 EUR/month. Step 5: baseline scrap boards = 12000 x 0.003 = 36 boards/month. Step 6: baseline scrap cost = 36 x 180 = 6480 EUR/month. Step 7: baseline downtime cost = 0.5 x 120 = 60 EUR/month, using 120 EUR/h line cost; verify against your line cost model. Step 8: baseline COPQ = 1360.8 + 6480 + 60 = 7900.8 EUR/month. Step 9: projected reworked boards = 12000 x 0.006 = 72 boards/month. Step 10: projected defects = 72 x 1.2 = 86.4 defects/month. Step 11: projected rework time = 86.4 x 3.5 = 302.4 min/month = 5.04 h/month. Step 12: projected rework labor cost = 5.04 x 45 = 226.8 EUR/month. Step 13: projected scrap boards = 12000 x 0.001 = 12 boards/month. Step 14: projected scrap cost = 12 x 180 = 2160 EUR/month. Step 15: projected downtime cost = 0.2 x 120 = 24 EUR/month. Step 16: projected COPQ = 226.8 + 2160 + 24 = 2410.8 EUR/month. Step 17: monthly saving = 7900.8 - 2410.8 = 5490 EUR/month. Step 18: annual saving = 5490 x 12 = 65880 EUR/year. Step 19: payback = 8000 / 5490 = 1.46 months. Step 20: ECN is justified if post-change data confirm the projected defect reduction and no new reliability or test escape risk is introduced.

defect.symptom: After the ECN, AOI reports increased insufficient solder on 0402 resistors during the first 200 boards, while tombstoning decreases.
defect.cause: The new stencil aperture was reduced too far for the paste release window, and the stencil-to-board gap or paste volume was not requalified after the land pattern change.
defect.action: Stop the changeover, retain the old stencil and paste lot for comparison, measure SPI deposit volume and height, requalify the aperture and stencil thickness against the paste datasheet, then run a controlled pilot with thermocouple profiling and X-ray before releasing production.
